How do we have collective accountability for all those children so that they are not falling through the cracks? To their credit, the Government are taking that on, and it needs to be taken on. Whether that means we are working in a partnership called a trust, or working in a partnership called something else, we really need to incentivise what we see in the main: people working together on behalf of those children and young people. The accountability system needs to make sure that none of those children are disappearing. That is what I am interested in, and we were always advocating for that in our schools.

Q87 Can I follow up on your point about schools that join trusts and then maybe regret it ? A ccepting that it is G overnment policy now , how do we make sure that every school is in the right trust? Do you think there is a need for a change in the rules about how schools make trust-based decisions? For example, in my constituency, we have a school that is still part of a trust based a very long way away and with no geographical locus at all. For a time th e school was desperate to join a locally based trust. Under the current rules, that can only happen if the school is effectively released by its current trust: it was not willing to do that, so it could not be resolved. I wonder whether you could see a case for the Government joining up their agenda on place with practical decision-making arrangements and rules on the membership of different trusts?

In terms of what our position should be as an organisation, we have debated this point a lot. It is really tricky. Just for context, we have an equal number of members on either side, those in trusts and those in maintained schools or single-academy trusts. In an ideal world, we should have exactly what you describe, but there is a real challenge at the moment in unpicking the empire building that happened five or 10 years ago. The reality is that a lot of trust growth in the past was based on competition . T o Geoff’s point, the accountability system in this country perpetuates competition rather than genuine collaboration, so sometimes trusts have taken on schools to increase their school count rather than necessarily because the school fits their local agenda. My answer is yes, but that is not the official NGA position at this point in time.

At some point—I do not know how we will get there—the sector needs to be mature enough for some trusts to say, “Yes, I can see that you would be much better in a trust with local positioning around where you are.” We know some trusts have done that and have even asked for schools to be released to those trusts, but they have met barriers, and that is a problem.

Q88 Ministers have made narrowing the disadvantage gap one of their central objectives, and we all know that there are multiple challenges to that. There is the problem of identifying disadvantage in the first place; there is the problem of targeting resources effectively; there is the issue of all the factors outside the home that have an impact on a child’s disadvantage within school. In your view, which of those is the bigger problem, and what are the measures that are needed in order to achieve those outcomes?

That is a very big question, and it is an issue that has bedevilled the education system across the UK, including England. For me, the issue is how we incentivise leaders to go into those most disadvantaged communities, and how we incentivise teachers and teaching assistants to go and work there. At the moment, as we were saying, it can seem to be in my interest for some young people to go to your school and not to mine. It is definitely in my interest not to go into certain communities. We have seen all kinds of attempts to try to incentivise that, partly through pay.

I come back to the accountability measures: too often—there are some very well-known examples—it feels that if you get a bad Ofsted report , you will pay the price for it. I used to run a trade union. We were supporting people at first hand when their governors had suddenly lost confidence in them because of an Ofsted report. This is not to point the finger of blame only at Ofsted, which would be over-simplistic, but how do we give leaders—who know that it is going to take time to improve the school—a sense of long-term commitment? Part of what we need is to have teachers who are going to stay with us on that journey. Again, there are examples around the country . P erhaps the White Paper talking about its coastal mission, its mission north-east and so on can shine a light on how we get great people to go to the communities that are most in need of great teachers and great leaders.

Disadvantage is a big question, but it is the right question to ask, and it is the right question to try to pinpoint. Geoff is right, there are schools in particular parts of the country—particularly those with high poverty rates, but also with other social issues—where the teaching work force is struggling. People do not see them as a place to go to. We have also seen the opposite, where schools are thriving in similarly challenging areas. There is a different feel to those schools. People feel they belong, the staff feel proud to be there and proud to work in those communities. Sometimes they are very close to those communities. When you hear teaching staff and , in particular , support staff, you can tell by their accents that they have often come through those communities with a keen sense that, “These are our children and our responsibility.”

It is important to identify disadvantage. That can seem difficult because people do not like to label or be labelled, but if I come from a privileged background , I will have an easier life than if I do not come from that privileged background. My need will therefore be greater and provision must be made for that need; that may mean schools getting extra funding. There is a lot of talk about the way that schools are funded; in the past, some funding decisions actually moved money away from inner-city schools to areas that also have disadvantage. I heard a lot in the previous session about rural schools, and it is true that poverty exists in all pockets of the country. Resources need to be there at the right time, and help needs to be there at the right time, and needs should be identified as early as possible.

I completely agree with both Ian and Geoff. I would add that one thing the White Paper is doing well is opening up a conversation that in lots of ways has not been accessible. The time has come, not just to look at how we fund disadvantage through the funding mechanism—as the White Paper is doing—but to look holistically at how we define disadvantage in its entirety. We have had quite a narrow focus. One of the NGA’s pieces of work is in broadening the definition of disadvantage: I will be sure to send that afterward. Without wanting to sound like a broken record, it really comes down to the accountability narrative. I do not like saying it, but we need to incentivise schools to take a risk and take a chance. That corresponds with the story Geoff shared, which was really powerful. We need to see more schools taking risks that they have not taken before on children and young people , and widening the definition of disadvantage would help.
Q89 I have a rapid-fire question to finish. Before Ministers take these proposals forward, what aspects of the White Paper do you think they most need to listen to the sector on?

What does it mean to be a community anchor, and are you therefore listening to the right people? It is vital to include governance at a local level, local volunteers and people living in those communities who know their area.

They need to know that they are not going to be penalised for doing the right thing: looking at aspects of belonging and relational practice. It is hard work for schools to change cultures; typically it takes three years. They need to know that within that period they are not going to be pilloried for not toeing a particular line, whether that is with a multi-academy trust or their perception of what Ofsted is looking for: often it is not what it is looking for. They need to feel that they are supported.
Q90 Are you saying that in the context of accountability measures?

Yes, but when they need help—echoing both Sam and Geoff—collaboration is key. Collaboration between schools, local authorities and trusts is really important, so that we are sharing both best practice and resource where that is available. Educational psychologists, for example, are really hard to come by in some counties, and there needs to be a pool of some sort. I know the White Paper has elements that could address this, which would be a really important step forward.

I would tell Ministers what Winston Churchill said, “Headteachers have more power than the British Prime Minister.” Headteachers forget that they have more power than the Prime Minister. If Ministers think place matters, and I am a headteacher in this place, I am going to do what I believe is right for the young people in our community. You have given us 104 additional responsibilities. We are going to choose the things that we think will make a difference, and that means there will be some things in the White Paper that we will not be doing because we are going to focus on game changers, particularly for those children from disadvantaged backgrounds. I speak from experience as a trustee of the Royal Shakespeare Company, which goes into the most disadvantaged communities on a long-term, 10 - year basis. I went up to Cumbria and watched seven and eight -year-old kids debating whether they preferred “Titus Andronicus” to “The Tempest.” It was extraordinary, and the sense of pride was extraordinary. We need to re-empower our leaders and our teachers. Yes, place matters, but we cannot do everything that you might try to mandate from the centre, so we will choose the things that will make the biggest difference . H old us accountable for that.

Thank you so much. If there were any topics that we did not get to cover today, or if you have any further thoughts, please write to us afterward. We would really welcome that. Thank you, all three of you, for taking the time to be with us this morning to consider these important issues. That brings our evidence session to a close.

sessions.iT: The work of the Home Office
sessions.w: Rt Hon Shabana Mahmood MP (Home Office)

segs.tx: Home Affairs Committee
Oral evidence: The work of the Home Office , HC 6 6 2
Tuesday 15 September 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 15 September 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Dame Karen Bradley (Chair); Lewis Atkinson; Mr Paul Kohler; Ben Maguire; Robbie Moore; Margaret Mullane; Dr Peter Prinsley; Joani Reid; Bell Ribeiro-Addy .
Questions 1 - 110
Witness
I: Rt Hon . Shabana Mahmood MP, Home Secretary .
Examination of witness
Witness: Shabana Mahmood.

We are delighted to welcome the Home Secretary for her second appearance in front of us . Home Secretary. I am going to tell you that you are going to have to be more frequent than this . We want to see you more frequently, but we are very pleased you are here today.

We have questions for you . W e know how incredibly broad the scope of what the Home Office covers is. We know we have a limited amount of time . W e are going to focus our questions on policing , violence against women and girls , and — I suspect quite a lot of our questions will be on this topic — migration, regular and irregular. J ust to warn you, those are the areas we are going to be asking you about.
We appreciate and know your deadlines, so I do not think we need you to introduce yourself , i f that is okay .
That is quite all right.
W e will move straight into questions . I will start with Lewis Atkinson.
Hello , Home Secretary . G ood afternoon and congratulations on your reappointment.
Thank you.
Q1 Clearly we have a new Prime Minister . What is your assessment of what that means for your previously stated intention to reform and reduce the number of police forces in England and Wales ?
That is a good point. I will start with what has not changed and what remains exactly the same , and then talk a bit about the changes since Andy Burnham became Prime Minister.

F irst , the case for police reform remains unchanged . T he case has been made for some time now. We have a system that requires 43 different - sized police forces to be very good at providing a highly localised response to neighbourhood crime, antisocial behaviour and so on , and to perform national - level functions , responding to regional organi s ed crime, specialist investigations and so on. It is very difficult to do both those things to a sufficiently high standard such that you do not have a discrepancy in the standards of service either across those two functions or , indeed , across the country .

T he case for police reform remains as strong as it has ever been. That is why I very much believe we need to pivot to a new model of policing with local policing areas as the bedrock and foundation of the new policing model, coming down to local authority level ; a smaller number of regional strategic forces sitting above that , doing the specialist investigation work to a high standard ; and then the national police service on top providing system leadership and system - level efficiencies as well as taking over , ultimately , crime that is at national level or indeed has an international dimension.

What is different since the new Prime Minister came into post and the new A dministration were formed? Of course , he has personal experience of having oversight of policing in his role as Mayor of Greater Manchester . He has direct experience of the ability of m ayors in such authorities who have the convening power of wider public organi s ations within their mayoralty and can convene them particularly on issues relating to crime prevention and violence reduction .

G iven the new steer of the Government to be very focused on devolution by default and the paper from the C abinet , overseen by the Prime Minister , called “ Rewiring the State ” , which had lots to say about what levels of devolution will look like across the country, we have asked Lord Hogan-Howe , who is doing the independent review into what the new force structure should look like , to take into account the new Government’s position on devolution and to retest the evidence that he ha s collected as part of that review against the new stated intention and focus of the Government.

I am confident that that can be done . The Government’s paper recognises that we should go for alignment where possible. Sometimes there will be a case for not having direct one-to-one alignment, but the boundaries should remain aligned. It should be possible to incorporate the new focus of the Government into the work that Lord Hogan-Howe is doing for us. It has meant that that work will take a few more weeks than I anticipated, but I expect to have that report in the next few weeks and then I will be able to update Parliament.

Q2 You touched on it rightl y; I was going to ask you about Lord Hogan-Howe’s review. To that point around the alignment with “ R ewiring the S tate ” , you responded to me recently in the Chamber on the Cleveland police statement . U sing the north-east as an example, we have three relatively small forces. As you pointed out, that made the case for police reform. Is it likely that there will be a presumption against forces being any bigger than mayoral strategic authorities?

No. As “ Rewiring the State ” makes clear, where possible and where alignment works , not just for economic devolution or for the devolution of transport infrastructure decisions, which are and will be the primary focus of lots of the work of combined authorities , where it makes sense for operational reasons , there will be total alignment on mayoral boundar ies . I am sure that probably is not a million miles away from the work that Bernard Hogan-Howe and his panel have already been doing .

N ot all these authorities will be the same size. Tees Valley is a good example where the mayoral authority is relatively small, which makes sense from an economic devolution perspective but does not necessarily take into account the wider policing structures. If you were doing one-to-one alignment as the requirement going forward, that would mean that some current forces would become even smaller. Avon and Somerset would end up being shared between the Mayor of the West of England and an as-yet-unnamed new strategic authority. It would mean changes in Cheshire, where a part of that would go out into Merseyside. Humberside would lose around half of its force to Lincolnshire, and Thames Valley would shrink as well.

In the new structure, it is not the case that , even if you did one-to-one alignment , police forces would remain the same. In fact, some would go down in number, which again would have other operational implications. The new way of thinking about it is not hugely different from how we conceiv ed of the reform programme beforehand, which is to align one to one where it makes sense . That should be the way forward. W here mayors have oversight , we know that that works reasonably well. The new Prime Minister is a living example of that himself, but it will not work everywhere. Lots of parts of the country do not currently have a mayor and will not necessarily have a mayor either before the end of this Parliament and who knows when. It has to be a mixed approach.
Q3 Just quickly on Wales, would you consider devolving responsibility for policing to Wales as part of these reforms?

Again, Bernard is looking at the arrangements in Wales. I know that the full devolution question is contested within the Welsh political establishment between those who want full devolution of most elements of the criminal justice system and those who do not think that works for Wales . We do not need to get into those broader constitutional devolution questions, but we can recognise that Wales has a pretty unique public services landscape and we absolutely want to respect that. I am sure Bernard Hogan-Howe’s work is looking at that sensitively.

Certainly, once that review is in, I will want to continue engagement with the Welsh Government and Welsh colleagues here in Parliament to make sure that whatever structures we have make sense for Wales, given the broader public services landscape there.

Q4 I hear clearly that a bit more work is being done on the regionalisation of forces. T he Government’s intention remains to create a national police service . Could you just update us about the developing plans for that and its potential launch date?

Yes. Plans are well under way on the national police service . Much of the new underpinning for that police service , such as what powers the new commissioner will have, and the balance of power between the new commissioner of the national police service and the Home Secretary , will require a statutory underpinning. Work is under way on the planned police reform Bill.

A delivery authority that is jointly led between the Home Office and p olicing is looking at the whole area of police reform. Its biggest area of work is the setting up of the new national police service . There is a ministerial board as well as a programme board that looks at progress on the development of the policy and the legislation. That includes the National Crime Agency, counter - terror ism policing and other colleagues. They are working through what needs to be true on day one to get the national police service up and running and then , working backwards from that, thinking through issues on the workforce transferring over and all those operational questions.

Drafting of the Bill is also well under way , taking steers from the boards and m e . Once the Bill is presented to Parliament, we will be able to give a firmer deadline of when we expect that to get Royal Assent and where we hope to be by the end of the Parliament. It is the intention that most of the operational readiness of the NPS will be done by the end of this Parliament . I want to appoint a commissioner-designate as quickly as possible once we have the Bill introduced to Parliament so that we have a system leader , who will be charged with being the first ever commissioner of the national police service , up and running and able to shape the way in which the organi s ation develops.

If all goes to plan, most of the operational changes will be made by the end of the Parliament, with a view that , as soon as they mature early in the next Parliament, you transfer in the capabilities of the National Crime Agency and counter - terror ism policing . I gave a commitment that we would not do any of th e transfer of capabilities until it is ready for it . I am absolutely firm on that commitment. I do not want to go so quickly that we undermine the operational effectiveness of what are, in my view, exceptional agencies doing very good work.
Q5 H ow do you intend to fund police reform ? Would it be funded from existing Home Office budgets ? I f so, where would you find savings or move money from to fund it ?

Overall, the setting up of the national police service is £340 million or so, two thirds of which I have already committed through the current spending review allocation. We were funded to progress police reform in this spending review , so a large bulk of that money has gone towards the setting up of the national police service . About a third of that, I anticipate, will come from the next spending review . I am confident that those numbers are there and that this is a fully funded programme of work .

Q6 Lewis, before you move on— I know Peter wants to come in — I just want to clarify a point on police reform. L et us take the west midlands . W e are both west midlands MPs . A re you thinking that , because there is a mayor for the west midlands , you would expect the police force to be co - terminous with that? What happens to Staffordshire and West Mercia? Are you expecting them still to go in or not?

Having commissioned an independent review, it would not be right for me to set out expectations. I have asked Lord Hogan - Howe to consider what the new shape of strategic forces in the country should be. He is also looking at the local policing areas and what the relationship between the two should be. He is looking at whether they should be just on local authority boundaries or smaller than local authority boundaries in some cases. All that is the work of the review. It would be wrong for me to start giving my expectations .

I n general terms, is there a likelihood that some of the new model will reflect forces that are currently co-terminous with mayoral boundaries? Probably, yes. We will have to wait to see his full report, but it is probably not outside the realm of probability . L et me put it like that. I am not directing him and he has certainly not been given an indication that he has to make certain forces co-terminous because they are already up and running and have a mayoralty. He has been engaging with stakeholders . O f course , there is a lot of discussion about co ‑ terminosity, as you would expect.
Q7 On the national police service , would you be open to this C ommittee undertaking pre-appointment scrutiny of the appointment?

Yes. I am very happy to follow the established norms of how these things are done. As I say, I do want to move forward as quickly as is reasonable with a commissioner-designate because that will provide the system leadership that we need. I will update the C ommittee on the plans for when that will happen and the role of the C o mmittee in due course.

Q8 Home Secretary , I just wanted to quickly ask you about police and crime commissioners . W hat is your intention in this respect? For instance, in Norfolk , the police and crime commissioner resigned, and we had to have a by-election for a new police and crime commissioner , who is going to serve for an uncertain period. There has been a political change , and that police and crime commissioner is perhaps behaving in a way that is unexpected. I am wondering what your plan is in respect of police and crime commissioners going forward.
I would just observe that politicians often behave in ways that are unexpected. That is something that applies to all political parties, really.

We have already announced that we are going to be abolishing police and crime commissioners . They are up for re-election — the vast majority — in 2028. Those elections will not go ahead and we will transition to a new model.

Once the independent review come s back, we will be able to set out what we expect to be the governance arrangements. Where there is co-term inosity in the future model, the responsibilities for oversight and governance will sit with mayors. Where there is not co-term inosity, you move to a new crime and policing board . T hat might include multiple mayors and local authority leaders with a nominated deputy who leads on policing. There will be a strong governance and oversight framework that follows the abolition of police and crime commissioners .

As I have said before, it is not an indictment of any individual. It is just a model that was supposed to yield a new era of policing. It is not something that we believe has worked , and the levels of public engagement with this structure are just not there to justify it continuing. Given that we are looking at the new force structure and model overall, it is the right opportunity to move to a new governance framework as well.

Q9 F inally on police reform, when would you expect our constituents to notice a difference? Y ou have made the point previously, Home Secretary, that you cannot reform the funding formula for forces until the new force footprints have been confirmed. Are we expecting to see that sooner rather than later?

Once we have the review back , and the Government have responded to the findings of Lord Hogan -Howe’s review and said what our preferred model for all structures of policing is going forward, I will, as I said in the statement after the incident in Cleveland and the deaths of PC Blades and PC Clough, come back to the House with our plans on the funding formula because that will have to change to reflect the new model of policing. There is a long process for the review of a funding formula, but it starts with the new principles that should underpin the funding formula. We will come back to the House very quickly once we have settled policy on the new force structures.

O n broader change that people can see, this is a long programme of reform — deliberately so . It is learning the lessons from previous attempts to reform policing structures by not going too quickly and making sure that operational effectiveness is not compromised. As we move to the new national police service , I hope we will be able to realise more savings , because having one system leader, one way of doing things and one way of procurement is the right way forward , and those are all savings in the wider policing system , which again is to the benefit of our constituents.

As we then roll out the new local police areas , that is where you will get the biggest reset of relationships between local people and local policing . T he way that I envisage local police areas working is effectively the equivalent of a borough command , but this is your dedicated local policing , whose main focus is the everyday crime, antisocial behaviour and high street s issues that we see in communities all over the country . T hey will be absolutely laser - focused on that work in communities , which we know is the sort of thing that has decreas ing demand as you go up the chain.

Q10 Moving on to police leadership, there has been a report by Lord Blunkett and Lord Herbert about policing leadership . What is your assessment of the findings of that report ? W hat is your response to the recommendations made in it?

First, let me pay tribute to Lord Blunkett and Lord Herbert. They were commissioned by my predecessor. It is a very important piece of work . I really value and respect the effort that has gone into the production of the report as well as the findings of the report.

We did an initial statement in the House once it was published, which the Policing Minister took. We will respond later in the autumn with the Government’s full response to the 27 recommendations. We will come back on each of those specifically with a proper G overnment response and how we intend to take the work forward.

We welcome the broad thrust of the report, its central findings and the case for reform. There are some areas where we had already, through the White Paper and other policy decisions, made choices about going further, which aligns very well with some of the recommendations of the report, particularly on appointments, panels and being able to create a better pipeline for policing leaders and chief constable appointments. We had already said that we would move forward on the reform of the promotion system and making sure that there is much more consistency in that.
There are aspects of the report where work is already being taken forward, which we will press ahead with. There are other things that I will need to come back to the House on in the autumn.

Q11 I look forward to seeing that. Linking the culture of leadership to police forces , and to the wider question of morale and the recruitment and retention of police officers, what action are you taking to enable the police to increase morale among rank-and-file police officers ? What is your assessment of that ? You might also want to say something about how you hear the voice of normal police officers. It has been pointed out to some of us that the Police Federation has got quite a lot going on . W e wonder how Government hear the voice s of police officers and how the action that you take is informed by that.

O n broader morale, let me just say that the Government fund the College of Policing on its work for the National Police Wellbeing Service, which is incredibly important and has been operationalised after the deaths of PC Clough and PC Blades. That is good work. There is a new focus on what it takes to look after the wellbeing of police officers and to make sure that they go into the job with a good sense of how to look after their mental health and are supported to do so as they deal with very difficult incidents.
We have reformed the way in which we think about assaults on police officers, and there is legislative change as well to show the importance that we place on looking after our police staff.

M ore broadly, certainly in my old job as the Lord Chancellor, when we had the issues around the Chris Kaba shooting with firearms officers and big questions around anonymity , I was very struck then about how, after a particularly difficult incident like that, a police officer, as well as the family of the victim of a shooting, will go through many years of legal processes that can feel never-ending. I have heard directly from police officers about how that accountability system can take a decade off your life . E ven if you are found wholly innocent , and you acted wholly appropriately and in line with your training, you have lost a decade of your life and things for you will never be the same.

Our end-to-end accountability review, which is a six-month programme I started in July, will report to me and the Lord Chancellor. It is specifically looking at the whole accountability system to make sure that it is fair, fast and delivers for people on both sides of that equation — police officers as well as victims and their families. We made some decisions about the presumption of anonymity in firearms cases. That was responding legitimately to the particular pressures on policing. Across the piece , we are doing lots of work that is designed to make sure that we offer a service that the public can have confidence in and that police officers can feel confident going about their daily roles.

In terms of hearing from police officers, like all of you, I am a constituency Member of Parliament so I engage with local neighbourhood teams in my own constituency. I know the local officers pretty well and I hear from them directly. W hen I am out and about and meeting people, I make a particular effort to do that, although I have to say people are not shy about telling me what they think is really going on either in their police force locally or nationally. Of course, like a small number of other Ministers, I am protected by police officers too . B elieve me , b etween them and my local cops in Birmingham, I feel like I get a pretty authentic view of what is really going on.

Q12 F inally on morale, I recognise that you have set out a lot of action there on a number of things . H ow will you know whether that is making a difference across the bulk of policing in the country? A n observation would be that there is no unified national policing staff survey and that it is optional for forces to opt in to some of the surveys that exist. Is that good enough? If not, how will you measure the improvement that you have to make?
You are right . T here is a slight hampering of the data . I t is not possible to give a totally complete picture or to set a metric that you know is accurate and reflects the full national picture.

I n the future model, having a proper workforce strategy falls full square within the work of the new national police service . I would expect the new c ommissioner, once in place, to work with us in the Home Office to have a clear sense of what the workforce strategy should look like and to pay particular issue to the recruitment and retention of officers as well as promotion opportunities. We want to progress the licen c e to practi s e as well . That professionalisation work is all part of making sure that you have a workforce that work s to high standards, feels respected and appreciated , and has opportunities to progress.

Until we transition to that model, I have to work with the best of what I have available to me. On that basis, we are not targeting any one headline metric in particular. I just continue to take view s from system leaders and rank-and-file officers wherever I can to make sure that the current system at least can provide things such as the wellbeing service and answers on accountability before we transition to a new model where we can do this more systematically.

Q13 It is good to see you, Home Secretary. There have been various failures of leadership — in Northamptonshire , in Staffordshire and , as this Committee and you know too well, in the west midlands recently. There is a damning comparison in the Blunkett report from Sir Mark Rowley. He makes the point that a c olonel , 15 years after leaving Sandhurst , has had 72 weeks of training and leadership. A chief superintendent of comparable experience will have had two or three weeks. How can we expect leadership from our police if we do not invest in their leadership?

I agree. It was a Labour Home Secretary just before me who commissioned this work in the first place because we recognise that there is an issue around having the police leadership that we want more consistently all over the country. At the moment we do fund some bits of work, but the point of the review was to look more coherently across the whole system and think about everything from pipeline to performance , to promotion and on to discipline as well.

I recognise the case that they have made. The Government recognise d that they needed to do more on police leadership . W hen I set out the Government’s full response later this year, we will be able to say which of those recommendations we will be taking forward.
Q14 Are you able to give any commitment to invest more in leadership training for our police?
I am not going to give any new commitments today.
You will not give any commitments at all .
I am going to save that for a statement to the House later this year, but I am sure you and I, Mr Kohler, will have plenty to say to each other when I do.
We often do.
Yes, we often do.

Q15 Sir Mark Rowley’s deputy, Matt J ukes, wrote to every London MP last month . He t alked about the fact that the workforce was under sustained pressure and referenced the fact — this is all from his letter — that real-terms funding has reduced by a third since 2015 in the Met , that it has lost 3,300 staff in the last two years , and that it is about to lose another 1,000 staff because of more funding cuts. What do you think that does to morale in the Met , when the police are under such pressure and, according to the letter, the Met is now the smallest it has ever been per head of population?

T here is plenty that I agree with Matt J ukes on. I am not sure I necessarily agree with all his characterisation of the funding. Since we have been in g overnment, there has been a £2 billion uplift in police funding and a real-terms increase for every force in the country.

I recognise, as does every Government M inister overseeing any public service, that there are particular pressures, particularly given the inflation picture. It is why the work of the Government has been very clearly focused on bringing some of those pressures down, but I would just recognise that there has been a significant uplift in police funding since we have been in Government.
Q16 Not for the Met : t he Met is the smallest that it has ever been.

Every force has had an increase. Whether that money is able to cover all the inflation increase is a different question. In a difficult funding environment, it would be unfair to suggest that the Government ha ve not presided over a very significant increase in overall funding as well as delivering a real-terms increase for every force . T hat is true of the Met as well.

Q17 There are particular issues in London with NICC funding— Sir Mark Rowley constantly says it is badly underfunded . Y ou end up using neighbourhood police to police marches, etc . Is anything going to happen about the NICC funding?
I engage with all policing system leaders regularly, and I hear the cases that are made to me. We will have the next year’s settlement towards the end of this year.
Q18 You hear, but are you listening?

I hear and I listen. Can I always act ? D o I always agree that that is the one thing that should be prioritised over all others? I am a politician, as are you. Those are choices that have to be made. We are focused on making sure that forces can meet the pressures they have and on delivering an increase for every force, which is what we have done.

I recognise that it is a constrained environment , given the overall economic picture . I n that , we are making choices about protecting neighbourhood policing and the overall operational effectiveness of policing, but of course I hear about the pressures and I am sure I will do as we go into next year’s settlement as well . T hose will be choices to make, given whatever financial headroom we have.
Q19 Sir Mark Rowley and Matt J ukes have made the point that neighbourhood policing suffers in London because of the failure to properly fund the NICC commitment.

T he first year of neighbourhood policing growth was delivered by the specific grant for neighbourhood policing . T hat should not be skewing anything in any one direction. That was specifically for —
Q20 There is abstraction, though.

Again, w e are working with policing on dealing with abstraction issues , which I recognise is a problem, but money for neighbourhood policing was set aside to deliver neighbourhood policing . I n year one of the Government, it went beyond the number that was required. They were able to recruit more . T hat was specific money.

In y ear two , there is an ask of the policing system to redeploy from current resources in the manner that it see s fit . O n that , we have also responded to a request from policing leaders all over the country to remove the very distortive uplift programme, which was forcing choices that ultimately led to warrant ed officers behind desks . Y ou do not want to have a distortion in the way that the workforce is planned . W e removed that to give them much more flexibility over what their force looks like.

Q21 T hanks, Home Secretary, for coming in today. T he police leadership commission report by Lord Blunkett and Lord Herbert identified 78 misconduct investigations involving senior police officers since 2018, including eight current or former chief constables, two of whom are from my local force, Devon and Cornwall. Both those have been reinstated or retired at a cost of £500,000 to the taxpayer. J ust last week I got a freedom of information request , which said that by the end of August this year 17 officers in Devon and Cornwall were on full pay at a cost of £ 1.3 million a year, and one officer appears to have been suspended on full pay for more than four years . I t is estimated in that report that the national cost of suspended police officers on full pay is around £ 60 million a year.

We hear you loud and clear, Home Secretary, when you talk about this Government placing community policing at the heart of your strategy . I fully support that and I know my constituents do, but do you share my constituents’ frustration when they see £ 60 million spent on this and meanwhile a local police desk in my constituency , in a town called Launceston —it would probably cost £100,000 to get that reopened — is put completely on the back burner?

I understand . T he broader discipline programme has pressures of its own. Of course, not everyone who is suspended is ultimately removed from duty. People have the right to a fair system , proper due process rights and all the rest of it, but there are issues in this system . W hen I set out our full response to the leadership review later this year, let me assure you that we will be thinking very carefully about what this means for the wider system and police disciplinary procedures .

T he two things go hand in hand : a good disciplinary procedure and a good promotions picture. These things are all about investing in those in your workforce who are diligent and who do the right thing , and being able to remove officers who are not behaving as we would expect.

The details in the report about current cases and the things that we know of — I cannot comment on those specifics and I do not wish to prejudice any hearings — are always very worrying. T he public need to have absolute confidence that the person with whom they are dealing at the end of a phone or in their community , or the person to whom they are disclosing a serious incident , is a person they can trust who will deal with that diligently and professionally, as is the case for the vast majority of officers . W here it does not happen, the system needs to be faster . I t has to prove to the public that it can move quickly, not waste money, remove the so-called bad apples and really invest in everybody else who is doing the right thing.

Q22 At the recruitment stage, do you see that being an issue? C urrently , we have police and crime commissioners doing that recruitment . A s we move forward, how do you see that changing and hopefully improving at that early recruitment stage?

Moving to the senior appointments panel will help with the pipeline into policing, particularly for chief constable roles. If you think about — again, it was all done with good intentions — the idea of the PCC being in charge for their local area, in terms of recruitment that has meant you often get only one candidate for these jobs because locally it is known and understood who the deputy is or who the likely frontrunner is. That means you do not have the wider moving around the country that you tend to have with leadership positions in other types of service. In that respect, it has not worked.

T he person who is doing the oversight in the end has to be in charge of the appointment, but it is a wider system job to make sure that the pipeline for these chief constable roles is strong and you do not just get the locally preferred candidate , but y ou get a bit of competition. You are able to say to people who might be somewhere where there are lots of potential candidates around that they have a future somewhere else. T he senior appointments panel and that new process will help us to think carefully about the people who are in that pipeline for senior roles . W e can then take a system view of whether that pipeline is providing adequate opportunities for high-performing people across the system. We will be able to tell whether it is skewed in any particular direction as well .

The s e are things that we cannot do well at the moment because it is such a local is ed system. When it goes back to shades of the old model, if not quite the old model, that bit of the workforce strategy should come together better.
Just to warn you, Home Secretary, we have quite a lot more to get through .
Am I being too long?
No, you may want to consider the length of your answers. That is all I will say.

Q23 It is g reat to see you, Home Secretary. You said to Lewis that s ince the election neighbourhood policing has been the bedrock , as far as you are concerned , and I do not think there is a Member of Parliament who would disagree with that . A lthough you have pushed and promoted , quite rightly , neighbourhood policing roles, the overall workforce has shrunk. What you wanted to achieve has not been realised yet. Add to that the abstractions that my colleague Paul related to, and the fact that we are trying, quite rightly, to focus on serious crime, vape shops and high streets . That is very resource intens ive , and we need our police, really, to deal with that. Is it the case that what you set out to do was the right thing, but that , at the moment, with how the workforce is and police morale, it is not working?

N o, I do not think so. The Government had a manifesto commitment on neighbourhood policing, which we are cracking on with delivering. B y the end of this financial year, in March 2027, we hope to be at 4,750. T here is a lot more still to do to hit the 13,000 target . The trajectory of that is a decision for the future , but it is right that we have sought to invest in neighbourhood policing. We see it as the bedrock . W e know that visible policing — all the evidence shows this— is not just about public confidence in policing , but it has an impact on reducing crime and reducing demand in the wider system. It is the right thing to invest in.

On t he wider picture, I know that one of the critiques that people are making is that the focus on neighbourhood policing lead s to a loss of officers elsewhere. It is not quite such a simplistic picture . C ertainly , forces have not told me that the neighbourhood policing requirement is having a distortive effect as , say, the uplift programme did. It is something that I monitor very carefully . I am in regular contact with policing leaders to discuss what is happening in terms of workforce.

Q24 I have a quick follow-on from that . I t is what Paul alluded to. In my area, in the e ast BCU, neighbourhood polic e officers are often a bstr a cted . T hey might not necessarily share that with you because that is operational . I just wonder whether you think it is working.

O n the wider problem of abstraction , I would just recognise that there will be exceptional situations where you do need to move your officers out of their normal duties because you have a major incident and you need to surge resources somewhere. We should just accept that that is an operational need that occasionally presents itself. It should not be the norm . T he operating model should not be that you will just abstract officers every day from one set of duties to another.

We are working with policing to develop what you might call new national standards for how we think about abstraction, what is acceptable and what is not . That is also due for delivery by the end of this P arliament. I recognise the problem, and we are working with policing leaders to address it. W hat I would not recognise is the direct link between that and the discussion that we have just been having about neighbourhood policing.
Q25 F inally, how are the police going to have the flexibility to pay for technical staff, including civilians , and equipment to tackle modern forms of crime?

On modern forms of crime, I would recognise that by far and away the largest crime type is fraud, much of which is tech-enabled . T he last set of figures I saw suggested that something like 70% of fraud has an international dimension. That is why the Government have a specific fraud strategy , which is £ 250 million, including a new online centre , as well as all the work that we do with international partners to crack down on scam centres and the like , ultimately to see a decrease in fraud inciden ce here at home.

On the largest crime type, there is already a good strategy with a significant sum of money attached to it, which can make progress in terms of the investment needed and going after the tech companies — effectively the platforms on which this occurs — and scam centres more broadly.

O n wider technological developments, we have the new P oliceAI programme, which is about making the best use of AI and developing technology to either synthes is e data or analy s e evidence more quickly, so that the bit that only the police officer can do, which is to assess that evidence according to law, can be sped up. T here are different investments that are designed to make sure that we can keep up with the changing tech environment.

Again, in the future model of policing, this is exactly the sort of area where the new commissioner for the national police service can take a strong lead and provide the system leadership needed to make sure that every part of the country benefit s from positive developments in tech that improve productivity and investigation capacity , as well as looking at the broader trends on what new forms of crime are being tech-enabled.

Q26 Home Secretary, I am sure we will all agree that neighbourhood policing is the core of everything that goes on in our communities in challenging law and order issues. I just want to focus on the “clear, hold, build” strategy with neighbourhood policing, which would be widely recognised as being a success. This is about dealing with hotspot areas within communities where there is drug distribution and individuals in balaclav a s riding around on e-bikes and e-scooters .

O f course , this is something that happens in my own constituency of Keighley, where we previously did have a “clear, hold, build” strategy , b ut the challenge —this has been put to me locally — is that the funding has to be deemed to be cost - efficient by the Home Office , utilis ing existing resources, budgets and personnel already allocated to police forces and local authorities. Given that there is wide recognition that the “clear, hold, build” strategy works, why is there not dedicated funding specifically for it ?

First, let me say that “clear, hold, build” is a good operational response to particular patterns of local organ is ed crime and has been shown to be effective . I n fact , the Government ha ve just provided additional funding to Cleveland so that its “clear, hold, build” programme can be expanded to meet the current challenges that it is facing. I recognise the effectiveness of that type of work.

We are dealing with a broader system where there is a lot of demand . A s I say , we provided uplifts in funding and we will make new funding decisions for the coming year in December and January in the normal way. It is not possible to fund literally every type of programme that is effective . T here has to be a better balance between things that are business as usual and things that normal policing does without always requiring an additional stream of funding from the Home Office.

T he very fragmented system that we have has meant that you often get new operational capabilities only when the Home Office specifically funds a programme , but in the future you want policing to be able to make the best of its resources and to take a system - wide operational approach.

Q27 I t has been put to me at local level that there can be only one “clear, hold, build” strategy per local authority area . I n my area , Bradford has a “clear, hold, build” strategy live right now , but in Keighley we are being deprived of one simply because of that direction , which I think is inappropriate . I would encourage you to re-look at that strategy.
I would be happy for you to write to me . I can come back to you with a view on not just what is currently happening but what might happen in the future.

Q28 Of cours e, this is a partnership - led approach . A gain , I give a live example in my own constituency of dodgy shops and mini-marts . Again, this is not just in my constituency ; it is a common issue across the country where the system seems to fail . A gain , I will give you live example . O n Cavendish Street in my constituency seven of these dodgy shops were raided , quite rightly , by the police and counterfeit goods were taken away , but these shops are still live and active and , I dare say , have restocked their counterfeit illegal goods and are carrying out illegal operations. What seems to fail is that there is then not a combative approach by trading standards in its relationship with HMRC .

Home Secretary , what are you doing in relation to having that relationship with colleagues in MHCLG and HMRC to make sure that , when the police rightly do their actions , as I have experienced in Keighley , the system then does not fail by other services not coming in and dealing with the problem?

On this , there is a specific Home Office programme . J ust referring to my previous answer , the new high streets organi s ed crime work is building on a National Crime Agency programme that was shown to have a good effect . We have put some new money behind that.

Specifically, there are more office r s going after high street organ is ed crime . T hat is exactly your dodgy mini - marts or vape shops — the businesses that appear overnight and have blacked out windows and all sorts of nefarious activity happening behind the scenes . U sually , the local community has spotted and is well aware of that .

T he good thing about that new high streets organ is ed crime programme is that it is not just a policing response . T hrough that work , we are funding trading standards and HMRC , and taking along Immigration Enforcement as well . I have been on one of those raids , which involved all those different agencies . W e know that you need to have a full - spectrum response . S ometimes the evidence will be there on tax evasion or illicit tobacco, if it is not necessarily there in other areas . Y ou can have a quick and effective response when you have all those different agencies engaged . I t is a deliberate decision in that new work that we are funding to involve the other agencies.

It is fair to observe that trading standards overall across the country has had large numbers of cuts over previous A dministrations . T he price of that is being felt , but we are through this work at least funding some new work for trading standards and involv ing it in the high streets work that we are doing . I t will prove to be very effective. It is relatively new ly up and running, but it has got good engagement from other Government Departments. When we set it up, we were discussing with the Treasury on the HMRC side , MHCLG on the trading standards side , and of course I hold Immigration Enforcement . W e were all involved in designing it. As it has been effective over the coming year, we will be able to see what difference it is making and where future funding might then flow.

Separately, the new Prime Minister has had a lot to say about vape shops in particular and the new requirement for planning permission . C onstraining the environment in which these dodgy businesses operate is a key feature of the work that the Government are doing.

Q29 The Committee is looking at this as part of an inquiry that we are work ing on. Can I just ask two quick questions before we move on? You have talked about fraud being the largest crime type. The noble Lord Hanson is a great Minister, but I just wonder whether it is appropriate to have the biggest crime type being led from the House of Lords .

Lord Hanson is a very effective and exceptional Minister . I would not read anything into the fact that he sits for us in the Lords. All aspects of fraud policy and the strategy as it was being developed have been discussed directly between h im and me . H e is a very good Minister.
Q30 We can be confident that the answers that are given in the Commons reflect the up-to-date position .
Yes.

Q31 M y second question, before we move on, is around the independent r eview on public order and hate crime. We were expecting that before the summer. We have some very sensitive events coming up in the next few weeks. Are we going to see it before then?

I do not yet have a date that I can give to the Committee today. I can write to you with an indication of when we expect that to happen. That was delayed due to the change in Government and the access talks beginning . I t was not something that already had agreement and therefore could not proceed. I would hope to make progress on that very soon after c onference r ecess .

Q32 Home Secretary, how are you measuring success in reducing the impact of serious and organ is ed crime on local communities, including whether action against visible crime is leading to the disruption of the organ is ed criminal networks that sit behind them?

I have just been answering this question in relation to high street organ is ed crime at the local level . T hat is where you see the bulk of dodgy shops and the criminals who sit behind them moving into communities. The Government have a specific strategy and a funded work s tream on that. Of course, wider organ is ed crime sits within the usual structure of regional organ is ed crime units as well as work at the National Crime Agency.

In terms of effectiveness, that is business as usual, as it were, for those policing organ is ations. T he biggest change that our public have rightly noticed is the mov ement into the high street of organ is ed criminals, which is not a thing that used to happen before but is definitely a new feature of high streets today.

The Government are responding to that with our new strategy and our new work. I t is a three-year programme. At the end of year one, we will have a good sense of the increase in the number of premises that have been raided and the outcomes for HMRC , Immigration Enforcement and so on.

We also need to do some legislative change. As you might know, I have already announced that the period that you can get a closure order for will change. It will go to a year, which will give policing a much increased operational ability not just to close shops but to keep them closed. There might be more legislative change needed, which we will be looking at ahead of the third S ession of this P arliament.

Q33 How in particular will you be supporting smaller police forces? I am thinking particularly in rural areas such as mine in North Cornwall, which fac e lots of challenges from county lines gangs to rural theft. Y ou have mentioned already the high street issues that we are facing. Lots of these rural forces are already pushed to breaking point in trying to deliver the community policing that you have mentioned.

I am pleased that the Government have taken up the rural and wildlife crime strategy , but there is only something like £ 365,000 for the rural crime unit . S pread across our police forces , that is about £ 8,500 per police force, which is a bit of a drop in the ocean. I would be keen to hear what you think needs to be done to support smaller rural police forces.

E ach of the things that you have just mentioned —t here is a count y lines programme that is specifically funded by the Home Office as well ; t here is the high streets work that is also now specifically funded ; and you are rightly raising t he wider pressures — speak s to the need for police reform. At the moment, e ach time something new happen s the system does not have the flexibility at local, regional or national level to respond to that and to have a good policing response. T here is a lag between a new type of problem emerging and the Home Office being lobbied and work ing out what a new funding programme for that looks like, which is not a sensible way to do things. E ach small pot of money for each new type of activity becomes vulnerable when there is not enough money around and you cannot plan your resources effectively. That rather makes the case for police reform, if I might say so, first and foremost.

The re is one other thing that I would just observe . I take your point on the national rural crime unit , but , for a smallish operation, it has very good and effective co ‑ ordination capacity across different rural forces and a good understanding of what is needed in order to try to clamp down on the sorts of crime that you see only in rural areas, such as agricultural vehicle theft . I t came into being in 2023 and has been able to recover something like £30 million worth of goods. That is not a bad rate in terms of performance for the unit . I t is highly specialised and it does good work.

Can I just quickly ask a follow-up ? Y ou mentioned that you thought police reforms would really help in this area . I would quite like to know in particular what you think will improve as a result of those reforms . I am still hearing constituents who have had quad bikes or farm machinery nicked , and they are not even getting follow-up s from the police . T he police tell me that they are just too stretched to do that . I am quite keen to hear what those reforms will improve.

Q34 If I can come in on the back of that, I have exactly the same problem in my constituency. I met residents in Dovedale, right on the Derbyshire-Staffordshire border , this year. They have visitors galore —that is great ; w e love to have people come and visit us — but there is a lot of antisocial behaviour. There are a lot of barbecues being set , which is a worry for wildfires. There are a lot of people who are not observing the use of the lavatory facilities properly or parking properly. These residents expect police officers to come and patrol the streets and make sure this is not going to happen.

T hey are realistic. It is a very small place . T hey recognise that there are not going to be police there every moment of every day. If the police are being delivered out of Birmingham rather than out of Stafford, how is that going to make it better for them?

T he mistake is to think that the new regional force does exactly the work of the current regional force. That is not what is happening here. In t he new model, you are looking at local policing areas , at least at local authority level if not a bit smaller, being the effective equivalent of a borough command, as you see in London and elsewhere.

That is your new system-wide neighbourhood policing. These are exactly the officers who will be picking up all the local intelligence about changes in the environment . They will be picking up all the intel from local communities about what is happening on the high street. They will be doing the patrols. That is what good system-wide, consistent neighbourhood policing looks like. It will be embedded, including in statute , as the new local policing model. It will get right to the heart of the different needs in every local area, whether that is a rural area or a city centre in a city area such as mine.

That is the bedrock of the new policing model. On top of that, you then have strategic forces. You will have a smaller number of broader regional forces. I n the new model, this is where all your specialist capabilities sit. These are your specialists at rape or murder investigations ; t hese are the people who can surge public order resourcing into areas whe re it is needed.

At the moment , you have seen in Cleveland, for example, a relatively small force struggl ing to both do the day-to-day local policing and have the right number s to do public order policing when things got very tricky over the last couple of weeks. In the new model, that is a problem that you are trying to fix . A t strategic force level, you are able to have the flex that you need with all those specialist capabilities and your public order policing, so that the whole system is not just completely reliant on mutual aid between one small force and another. It wipes out many of those problems that policing is currently experiencing.

I would say this to you, Chair . Do not think that the new strategic forces in the new model will be doing exactly the same work as your current regional force is doing today . I t will be split between a local policing area, the equivalent of a borough command, and a strategic force above that that does the specialist work.
Q35 You are telling me that those residents will see a difference following police reform .

Absolutely, y our residents in the future will know what their local policing area is . T hey will have a direct relationship with the people who run their local policing area . T hat will be underpinned by statute.

Q36 Does that mean there will be more police officers , then? F orgive me, but there is no absence of specialism as far as rural crime goes. Among my local police officers, they are excellent on rural crime . I t is literally an issue of capacity. They cannot get out to Bodmin Moor or to more rural areas to investigate thefts, for example. U nder th e new national police service , will there be more officers dedicated to investigat ing these crimes?

In the new model, your local officers in your local policing area will be responsible for policing localities and focusing on everyday crime and anti social behaviour . In a patch such as yours, that will look and feel a lot more like rural crime. In a patch such as mine, it will look slightly different. These will be highly responsive to their local needs.

The strategic force on top is the standard of service and the consistency that you will expect wherever you are in the country. If you are a rape victim in your part of the world or in mine, you should get the same standard of service and it should not be dictated by the fact that one of us is in a very small force and one of us is in a much larger force that has that specialist capability. It will eliminate th e postcode lottery that you are getting in special is ed crime types.

In terms of the future funding and future size of workforce, those are questions to be determined as we decide what the new structure looks like and a s the reforms are carried out . T hey are being deliberately done over a longer period to make sure that they are embedded properly. I am sure that we will have discussions about what number s are needed at each part of the model once those decisions are a little more mature in the process.
Q37 We will have the existing local officers and then a new national force that sits above them. Is that right?
It is a three-tiered structure : local police areas, strategic forces and then the national police service .
Q38 Who will the local police report to?

T hese are questions to determine as the reforms are being developed . W e are still waiting on the review. Once that has published, I will be able to answer more of the detail about the interrelationship between all three tiers of the new structure. To be clear, the local police areas are just as important a part of these reforms as what the new strategic forces look like. Lord Hogan-Howe’s review will have things to say about what the local policing areas should look like as well.

Q39 I want to turn now to violence against women and girls, particularly around implementation. Do you have any specific update that you want to give the Committee? Also, could you explain to us the significance, particularly around implementation, of splitting the role of the Minister for Safeguarding and Violence against Women and Girls across two Departments ?

In terms of who does the work, the creation of the violence against women and girls strategy, as well as its implementation, is jointly led between the Home Office and the Ministry of Justice, which is where the two Ministers sit. There is a ministerial board that meets every month. In fact, it might be having its meeting either today or tomorrow . That is jointly chaired by Minister Kaur in our Department and then Minister Davies-Jones from the MoJ.

It is attended by up to about 18 different Government Departments, all of which have different elements of the strategy that they are responsible for delivering. They have taken on board the criticisms from the National Audit Office about how implementation and delivery are monitored, and whether that is effective. The new structure is being designed to make sure that it can reflect the learnings from the National Audit Office.

The creation of the strategy was a cross- government effort . The previous Prime Minister personally chaired the final meetings at which all aspects of the strategy were agreed. The Home Office and the Ministry of Justice effectively held the pen as that was being developed. Implementation is shared and joint . There is a board , and other Government Departments attend.
Q40 There is no specific, tangible implementation impact around this splitting of the Minister.

I do not think that the shared responsibility has an impact on the ability to deliver the commitments in the strategy. In fact, it helps, because the problem is that , if you look at something only through a Home Office lens, you are essentially looking at the point at which crime has been committed, or perpetrators and reducing re-offending, but the strategy is deliberately also trying to get further upstream of the problem and look at prevention and education programmes, some of which are really quite innovative and need to be tested in terms of what they can deliver in the future.

If it is something that is held only by essentially a criminal justice Department , you miss the broader requirement for the whole of Government , and indeed the whole of society , to have a response to what is a society-wide problem. It can help the implementation rather than hinder it. In the end, it comes from political impetus as well . All I can tell you is that that was very strong under the previous Prime Minister and is very strong under the new one as well.

Q41 There has been a commitment to speeding up the roll-out of the police rape and sexual offence teams by about 18 months. Do you believe that is a realistic objective? Do you think you will achieve it? What are you deprioritising to ensure that that is a success?

Yes, that can be achieved. We have been advised throughout by , and have been in communication with , the National Centre for Violence Against Women and Girls and Public Protection, which has been assisting in this work. Our current assessment is that something like half of forces already have a specialist team. In fact, the NCVPP is going to do a progress report on 1 October , so I will make sure the Committee is updated when we have additional numbers, which will show what the progress is. We are pretty confident, having discussed this with policing partners, that it is achievable and doable.

Does it require deprioritisation ? I do not believe it does. That is the wrong way to think about it, because in the end you are responding to caseload. You are trying to have a consistent way of approaching the caseload, and to have the same standard for how that caseload is managed and how those cases are dealt with. The NCVPP developed four different models for how this work might be done. It is up to forces to decide which of those they take forward and how they actually deliver. These forces have workload in the rape and sexual offences space. This is about making sure that the work of those cases , the development of those cases, the assessment of the evidence, the dealing with the victims and so on is done to a consistent standard.
Q42 So you would anticipate that the impact would be around case prioritisation within each force, as opposed to more wide ly .

It is about quality of investigation. You are trying to make sure that each force has a good way of handling what are really quite sensitive cases, and that you do not get the big discrepancies that you currently see across the system, where some forces are particularly good and have model ways of dealing with these particular types of cases, and others, which maybe do not see enough of this work, might have less well-developed structures for managing the caseload. As I say, the NCVPP has developed the four different approaches that could be taken, and they can choose which one is best for them. I am not here to tell polic e forces what is the right operational answer for them, but it is right to expect that they can handle these cases to a high quality and with consistency across the country.

Q43 On violence against women and girls online, you mentioned in the House that you believe that a new suite of policy responses was required. I know that a couple of the Baroness Bertin recommendations have been adopted. Have you given any more thought to what that will look like and what those policy responses will be? I understand that there is a pilot project around undercover policing online to tackle violence against women and girls. Can you give us more detail on that?

On t he undercover operatives , that is already a funded part of the violence against women and girls strategy from within the Home Office. That is one of our commitments under the strategy, and it is something that we are already delivering. We will assess progress a year in to see what the operational impact of that was, and then make decisions about what is then funded.

On the wider issue, you are referring to what I said in the Commons about the broader online space and the need to have a fresh look at what policy changes are needed, given the implementation of the Online Safety Act. There is a wide recognition across the political spectrum that we are going to have to take another look at what online safety looks like, especially in the age of AI, deepfakes and so on.

I know that it is work that the Secretary of State at DCMS is looking at. There has been a machinery of government change, but she now holds the pen on this. She gave the statement recently on device ‑ level controls and the Government’s broader approach to tech companies. We work very closely on this and we know it is a priority, so I would expect her to set out more in terms of the broader online safety environment , whether the tools we currently have are good enough and the extent to which they need to change.

As for our specific part of that, we have been working already on the policy, so on device ‑ level controls and the online officers. There is a bit of work that still needs to complete across Government , which is on Baroness Bertin ’s review, especially on the question of parity between offences committed online and then in the real world. That work continues; that is a cross- government bit with Home Office, DCMS and other partners across Government involved. I cannot give a sense today of when that will complete. It has been on the “being done but not finished” list for a while, so let me undertake to write to the Committee with when I expect us to be able to set out a new response on Baroness Bertin ’s porn review.

Q44 Thank you very much . We look forward to receiving that. Yesterday, the Attorney General set out the pressure that she is putting on the CPS to get to grips with the patterns around domestic abuse and stalking cases. I was wondering whether you were confident that police officers are capable of identifying these patterns before they get to the CPS.

There is a much broader societal understanding of different offences. There is a much stronger understanding across policing of not just different offences, but how to approach investigation and build the strongest possible case where the evidence is there. What the AG is specifically looking at is whether the CPS has a sufficiently robust attitude towards prosecuting such cases.

We know what the evidential challenges can be. We know how difficult some of those cases are to prosecute in trials. It is right that every bit of the criminal justice system considers whether it is forward-leaning, whether it is going where the evidence should be taking us in terms of prosecuting these cases and getting the best outcomes for victims , and making it clear that these are crimes that will face the full force of the law.

Of course, if there are issues in policing , we want to make sure that policing is as forward-leaning as possible. It is why the specialist teams are a policy innovation that it is important to roll out. There are questions across the CJS, which is what the AG was seeking to respond to.
Q45 You do not think at the moment that there are any specific problems that need to be addressed within police force s. You are confident that they are capable of identifying domestic abuse .

To separate that out, one reason why we have pushed specialist teams for rape and sexual offences is recognising the challenge of those cases , how difficult it is for victims to come forward, and what the evidential issues can be in getting a case successfully to prosecution and then to conviction. We know that every part of that journey can be fraught , which is why we have rolled out that policy on other offences that are in the violence against women and girls space, but are not covered by rape and sexual offence, so, exactly as you say, domestic abuse and stalking. Policing has a much more positive posture and is capable of identifying issues. Again, if there is evidence to the contrary, I would be happy to consider it . This is the sort of work that the NCVPP look s at very closely.

Q46 I just want to briefly turn to Scotland, if I may. We had fairly recent victim testimony of women and girls who have been trafficked across the border. In February, the Scottish Government announced that they were going to do their own statutory inquiry into organised child sex abuse. Given the victim testimony that we have all read and seen, have you had or are you aware of any conversations with the Scottish Government that ha ve looked to work together on this and to support each other in addressing the learning from the inquiries?

I know that the inquiry that we set up for England and Wales is engaging with the inquiry in Scotland. To the extent that there are independent inquiries, it would be wrong for Ministers to start trying to set the pace, as it were, on what the inquiries are looking at or what the lessons might be. The inquiries themselves, I believe, are in discussion. We would want to see learnings shared, with shared challenge. The fact that there is a border does not eliminate the horror of the crimes that have been committed. To the extent that there are independent inquiries, those are in touch and are discussing their emerging findings.
