On the specific policing response, even though you have devolution , there is always co-operation between law enforcement agencies. I do know that the team that is running Operation Beaconport , which is looking at historic cases here in England and Wales, is in touch with its operational policing partners in Scotland as well. At both operational level and inquiry level, that is work that is being led by the officials who are responsible.

Q47 There are some very high-profile organised cases. Are you going to bring all of that together into one place? Are we going to actually get to have some form of inquiry that looks at everything in the round so that we can get to the bottom of what happened to these poor victims?
Sorry, do you mean specifically on the grooming gangs inquiry?
Q48 No, I mean on the high - profile cases.
The wider UK picture.
Q49 Yes, the wider UK picture of the high-profile elite individuals.

I am happy to engage with you in writing, Chair. It is important that the inquiries that are currently under way can do their work, but I am sure once they are completing there will be broader lessons, both at the very high-profile end of the spectrum and then also, unfortunately, for those victims whose cases are not high profile, but the damage done to them is no less serious. Across the picture, I can undertake that we will make sure we have a proper response.
Q50 Victims all deserve to be treated equally , no matter who the perpetrator was.
They all deserve to be treated exactly the same.

Q51 Just sticking with the same theme, we now finally have the national grooming gangs inquiry, with a focus on Bradford and Keighley as part of one of those local areas. Can I just put a concern to you that has been reiterated to me many a time? The underlying issue of this is trust between those victims and survivors and the state, at all levels, which has failed them for far too long.

While it does not sit under your jurisdiction, the early prisoner release scheme has caused a massive issue with trust between those victims and survivors and the state. While the Prime Minister has said that those will not be released at 33%, we still have those perpetrators being released at 50% of serving their sentence.

I have a live scenario where many victims and survivors have contacted me. Fiona Goddard is one of them, where her perpetrator is being released early. My worry is that , with the independent inquiry now taking place, victims and survivors will potentially be reluctant to come forward, because they feel that there is not that trust that has been reestablished. My question to you, Home Secretary, is whether you are aware of this potential reluctance of victims and survivors to come forward to the independent inquiry .

Secondly, what are the Home Secretary and police forces doing to provide the protection that needs to be put in place for these victims and survivors to come forward to the inquiry? As it sits at the moment, I do not think that that is there. Fiona Goddard, who I have referenced, has had to move home. We are still in the process of trying to get her into a safe accommodation for fear. Are you aware of these challenges and what are you doing about it?

In respect of what happened to Ms Goddard, my understanding is that she was wrongly sent a letter about the circumstances of release of one of the criminals who offended against her, and that was not a case of an early release, but let me make sure. You have written about this, so let me make sure that you get a proper response. I do not want to misspeak on the record for what is obviously a very difficult and very sensitive case, but my understanding is that it is not a case of early release.

There has been a problem over at the Ministry of Justice where a series of letters have been sent out incorrectly, causing a huge amount of fear among victims. I know that the new Lord Chancellor is very focused on making sure that the MoJ is able to apologise where the wrong letters have been sent and then give very clear information to victim survivors about what is going to happen in their cases.

More broadly, of course, you will know that the Prime Minister has announced a series of exclusions. What you are talking about is not the progression model, which is about releases at a third of sentence with a third spent on tag, but the more serious offences where people normally serve two thirds of their sentence in prison. The Prime Minister has announced some exclusions to the policy that was going to drop that from two thirds to 50%.

Q52 Can I just ask, though, on protecting those victims and survivors? There is a real concern at the moment of not wishing to come forward to give evidence to the independent inquiry for their own fear. Can I just ask again: what is the Home Office doing to provide that reassurance to victims and survivors so that they can come forward and give evidence?

I understand that trust is a key issue here. It is one of the reasons why , once appointed, I moved very quickly on having the national inquiry and get ting that set up — to try to win the trust of victim survivors back. I know that is a process and it will take time. Let me just say here and now that I do want victims to feel like they can come forward. Now that you have raised this with me, I will engage with the Chair to see what more we can do to give confidence to victim survivors in coming forward. I will also undertake to work with colleagues in probation and elsewhere, such that the policing response is fully joined up with the other criminal justice agencies.

Q53 We need to move on. We have done two of our three topics, and we are now moving on to migration, both regular and irregular. Before we go into specific questions, I wonder, Home Secretary, whether you could perhaps give us your reflections, one year on, as to how you feel about migration, regular and irregular, knowing what you know now , perhaps what you did not know 12 months ago, what you have seen from the statistics, and what you have seen from the experiences you have had.

That is a very good question. My experiences are that it remains an issue of widespread public concern, and that the public are often ahead of where the political debate is. It has reaffirmed things that I had a sense of. As a constituency MP, I have always had a very large immigration caseload. I have a very diverse constituency representing every part of the immigration picture, whether that is on the legal, illegal or irregular — or anything in between — side of things. It has reaffirmed for me that public sentiment or public knowledge about things is usually ahead of where the political debate is.

My challenge is to make sure that the politics can respond to where the public is. It is a mistake to think that the spread of concern is only certain types of people in certain constituencies. Border security is a matter of concern, whether you are youngish in a seat such as mine —a city centre constituency — whether you are middle class, whether you are working class, and anything and everything in between. One thing that the political debate sometimes gets wrong is a sense that this is only of concern to people who are at one end of the political spectrum. That is wrong. In fact, all the public polling shows that that is wrong, but maybe that is not the prejudice that politicians sometimes bring to their discussion.

Q54 Home Secretary, I am thinking about some of the issues you just raised. Perhaps moving back slightly, these issues have sparked a lot of protests over the past few years. Lord Macdonald submitted a review to you on this in late May. I believe your office said in a formal response that it would be published shortly. I was just wondering when it will be published.

As I said in response earlier, the Macdonald review has been delayed only because of the change of Government. The access talks began in the week that we were due to publish. It will be published; we are just waiting for a new timeline. I will write to the Committee when I know what that is going to be.
Q55 More generally, can we expect any major changes to immigration policy under the new Prime Minister?

There are elements of migration policy that are to be settled ; for example, we have had a consultation running on settlement. We will be making policy decisions on that very soon. Of course, that will be shaped by the new Prime Minister, as it would have been under the previous Prime Minister. We have an immigration Bill in train, which will proceed. It has already had Second Reading . You are about to take oral evidence on the Bill soon, if you have not already. In any case, the Bill will continue to progress, as will other parts of the asylum policy statement and delivery. I have already had good conversations with the new Prime Minister about aspects of migration policy.

Q56 Next year, migrants who arrived in 2022 will start to qualify for settlement under the current system. You had previously told us that the earned settlement changes are targeted at migrants in these groups. Will these reforms be implemented by next year?

The earned settlement is not just for one group; it is a new model of settlement, which is about settlement being something that is earned through contribution and a new set of tests that lead to settlement. It is basically permanent residency in this country ; there is no meaningful difference in day-to-day life between somebody who has indefinite leave to remain and somebody who is a British citizen , so it is right to reassess the basis on which settlement is granted. At the moment, it is effectively an automatic process based on how long you have been here. It is for a broader range than simply new arrivals.

I am very aware that a large group of people who arrived in 2022, absent any change, would qualify in February 2027. We have to give certainty to the system. It remains the case that the rules that apply to you are the rules in force at the point of your application, not when you arrived in the country. That will continue to apply in the normal way. Later this year we will set out the new policy on settlement, taking into account all the consultation responses we have had, as well as any transitional arrangements we might decide to implement.
Q57 Is there an expectation about what time of year it will happen? That should be a guide for some people as to what their situation will be.

Again, I do not want to overspeak for the G overnment grid and decide my own timeline. We have always said that we would have a consultation. We had many more responses to that than we thought. The analysis of not just the responses but the modelling that underpins it has taken a little longer. Since then, we have had a change of Government. These are policy questions to be settled on transitional arrangements and so on, but that will happen later this year and in good time before you get the first round of people qualifying who arrived in 2022.

In terms of people being aware of what is going on, I would just say this is a highly informed cohort of people. There is a high degree of awareness. I know that people are anticipating changes, which, as I say, we will do later this year.
Q58 Just on that, how much notice do you expect them to receive? What steps will your Department be taking to make sure that people are aware of the changes as they come into place?

We make immigration rule changes twice a year every year, almost automatically. It has been settled case law, both at the Court of Appeal and in a House of Lords judgment, that the rules that apply to you when you make your application are the rules in place at the point of application. That is a long-settled principle.

As I say, this is a highly knowledgeable cohort. I know people have been following the debate very closely. That is also my experience as a constituency Member of Parliament. Before I came into office, leading up to summer recess in 2025, the Government set out their immigration White Paper, which signalled the change for indefinite leave to remain to move from five years to 10. It was in November that we set off the earned settlement consultation. That was once I had come into post. We have been doing that consultation, which closed in February.

I have said that we will announce changes in the not ‑ too ‑ distant future. People are aware of what is going on. We will publicise those changes and the rules that apply to people in the normal way. As I say, this is a highly knowledgeable cohort and they tend to know their rules very well.

Q59 It is just really for those who will see their pathway change, especially when there is not a cutoff date. There is a lot of anxiety that people may fall through the gaps and then there will be some problems. I just want to understand what the transitional protections would be.

The transitional protections are something that we specifically consulted on. There are a range of different options available for what transitional protections might look like. It is everything from passporting certain cohorts through—so no change, and they still qualify at five years—to different options for what you might do with other cohorts over a longer period. That is policy to be settled. I will obviously come to the House to inform the House of what that policy is once it is settled, and it will pass in the normal way. I am sure there will be lots of public debate, and the Home Office will make sure that those rules are clear.

Again, speaking more as a constituency MP now, if I think of the people I represent, there is a high degree of knowledge. People find out very quickly what rules will apply to them — let me put it that way. We will obviously do everything we are supposed to do to make that process as smooth as possible.
Q60 I want to ask some questions about the new family reunification policy. That was expected to cover all UK residents by the end of 2025. Can I ask why there has been a delay?

Again, t his was before I came into post , but the previous Home Secretary made a decision on suspending family reunion for refugees, on the basis that we were seeing much larger numbers than we had seen before, with a recognition that the rules that apply for family reunification for refugees are very privileged compared to others in the system, including British citizens who might want to bring a relative over from abroad , who have to meet an English language requirement and a minimum income threshold. I know that the income threshold is often very contested, including in my experience as a constituency MP, so there was a desire to try to bring the system to more coherence.

At the moment, there are something like 30 different routes for family migration and reunification. It is very complex. We want to take the opportunity to have a much more streamlined system where more of the same rules apply to everyone, regardless of whether you start ed off as a refugee and have been here with settled status, whether you are a British citizen who is applying, whether you are on a work visa, or whether you came on an asylum route. We want to rationalise that.

It is a very big piece of work. We have been very focused on trying to get the other changes to the asylum system and the Bill under way . I would expect to say more about policy in this area in the early part of next year.
Q61 There are about 30 routes overall, but nothing at the moment specifically for refugee family reunion.

Refugees can apply for members of their family to come over if they can meet the other tests in other parts of the family migration system. The specific family reunification route where there were no fees and a much more straightforward process with no language requirement or minimum income requirement is the one that has been suspended while we take a view of the broader policy and what rules should apply to everyone, regardless of whether you are a citizen or not.
Q62 Are you comfortable with the potential legal risks if there was no reunion route for a prolonged period?

The courts have previously upheld the principle on family migration and the need to look at people’s ability to support themselves. We are in line with jurisprudence in this area. We have not closed it permanently; we have suspended it while we think about how we rationalise policy so that you have a coherent system.

As I say, the worst-placed people in the system for family migration are British citizens, because of the specific hoops they have to jump through before they can sponsor a family member from overseas to join them in this country. There is a strong public fairness case for rationalising that system but, as I say, it is very complicated. There are over 30 different routes, and we just wanted to take the time to get that work right.
Q63 The concern is how long that is going to be, and what the issues will be. How long do you reckon the suspension will last?

I am not in a position to give you a timeline today. As I say, it is a big piece of work. Separately in the immigration Bill , we are also reforming the way in which article 8 will apply in future to cases , going further on the definition of family and what the family unit is, and creating some new presumptions that will underpin the way in which article 8 is applied to cases in the future.

There is a lot of work happening in this space . Because it is such a complicated area with all the different routes we have at the moment, it will just take us a little bit of time to make sure that , when we come forward with the proposals, they are right, they are fair to everyone, and they will stand the test of time.
Q64 I understand, but I suppose I will ask it in a slightly different way. How long would be legally problematic? What is the bar that you would set by which time you would definitely have something?

The Home Office is regularly in court having to explain reasonableness and so on. I think i t is perfectly reasonable for a Government to want to look at the system of family migration in the round, to not have a system of 30 different routes, and to not have such wide disparities between the rules that apply to refugees or to British citizens. That is perfectly fair. It is right to take the time that we need to in order to get that policy right. I would be very comfortable defending that position in court.

Q65 Your Department commissioned the Migration Advisory Committee to review the minimum income requirement. It suggested that thresholds between £21,000 and £28,000 would be reasonable, depending on how you calculate it. How did the Home Office come to the figure of £29,000 for the minimum income requirement? Do you plan to make any changes to it?

The £29,000 was something we inherited. Let me check that; I do not want to misspeak to the Committee. The MAC has since done its work, and its findings are part of the wider review on family migration policy, so it feeds into the work that we are doing. There is a question there about whether you have an income threshold, what it should be, how high it should be, and how it should be calculated in the future. We will fully tak e into account the MAC findings.
Q66 When do you plan to respond to them formally on that?
When we settle overall family migration policy.
Q67 Okay, so there is no date .

No. It would be irrational to go ahead and just speak to the income threshold bit, which at the moment applies only to British citizens, when in fact we are looking at the wider picture for family migration of all people who can apply, so British citizens or not, people with indefinite status, and people who have arrived as refugees. Because we are looking at the whole system of migration, the work of the MAC will feed into that as we assess where we want to land on the principle of income thresholds and then how they are applied. Sorry, they have just confirmed we inherited the £29,000 from the previous Government.

Q68 I want to ask you a question on child citizenship fees. In March, we recommended that child citizenship registration be charged at cost recovery, and that your Department run a campaign so that children know that the entitlement exists. We were expecting your response, which I do not believe we have had as yet. Children are still being charged over £1,000 to claim, while the administrative cost is just a fraction of that. The registration is actually a right in the British Nationality Act, so I was wondering whether you had any plans to change that.
Let me come back to you on the letter. Forgive me; I was not aware that we had something outstanding, so I will make sure that we do that.
Q69 It was a response to one of our reports.

Yes, sorry. I will make sure that that is in train when I get back to the Home Office today. It is important to remember that there are no fees attached to those who are unaccompanied asylum-seeking children, for example. For those who are looked-after children, effectively, there are no fees for them in any case.

On the other fees, the thing we take into account when we do fee waivers is wider affordability for families. Applications are made by parents, usually as part of a whole family regularising and seeking citizenship together. I would be happy to look at the recommendations of the Committee, but I am pretty comfortable with the principle of fees, and also the principle that fees are not just cost recovery for that specific element of the migration system, but are for the broader functioning of the migration and border system as well.

Q70 I suppose I ask because the cost is so high, and we have a situation where most people are being rejected when they apply for a fee waiver. You still have a lot of children—many have lived here since they were young, or were actually born here in some cases—who do not yet have British citizenship.

As I say, the right distinction is of those who are looked-after children, for whom the state is effectively the corporate parent. I do not think they should pay fees. That is the right thing to do. For all other children, that is part of a family grouping and it is right to level fees. It is right that those fees reflect the broader costs of the migration system. If we were to take that away, those costs would then fall on the wider taxpayer. It is a question of who bears the burden, but citizenship is a right. As I say, we take into account family circumstances when requests are made for fee waivers. Again, I will write to the Committee—I do not want to misspeak—but there were something like 15,000 fee waivers for the last year that we have data.

Q71 Just returning to earned settlement , you rightly said that there is a very informed cohort of migrants to this country. They are very informed, but they are also very anxious. One of the key principles in your consultation was about integration. I met a family last week—it could be one of a number of families in my constituency and many others—who do not feel that they can properly put down roots in the way that they want to, because ultimately in a few months’ time they do not know whether they are going to need to seek another job that has a visa, despite being at five years. It is then impairing their ability to integrate and to contribute to our city in the way that they wish to. Do you accept that that uncertainty is to some extent hampering the integration that I genuinely believe that you and the Government want to see?

I do not think so. Let me just separate out those points. Regardless of how they have come to be in this country, whether citizens, new arrivals or anything in between, reasonable people can understand that the Government have to be able to look at migration policy and to look at numbers. If numbers were more than anticipated, they have to be able to be fair, not just to those who have arrived, but also to those who are already here. It is a balance to be struck. Reasonable people can agree that it is perfectly right and proper that we have the freedom to do that.

Of course, people will have views on where policy should ultimately fall and how it should be implemented. I accept that there are a lot of people wondering what rules are going to apply to them. Of course there are; I hear that myself as well. People have views about what they want those rules to be. Some people will say—including from the cohort affected— we should delay access to benefits for longer or do things a different way. People have ideas. They have fed those ideas in. It is right that the Government have taken time to look at the consultation responses properly. We have engaged very widely on what the transitional arrangements look like and what the knock-on consequences of those arrangements will be.

I can assure people we are trying to do a proper piece of work, where we have the right arrangements that strike the right balance between our responsibilities to people who have come here to work, our recognition of the failures that we inherited as a Government, and also our need to do right by the people who are already here and who pay for the systems that we all rely on.

Q72 Finally and quickly, on the economic contribution of international students to the UK, do you think that international student numbers are still too high? If so, is your concern solely about asylum claims following student visas? We know the visa break has taken effect for some countries that have had particular suggestions of asylum abuse. Where are you in conversations with the Department for Education and universities about supporting the UK’s international education strategy?

My interest as Home Secretary is to make sure there is no abuse of the system for international students. What I am worried about is not the overall number . Legitimate students coming to this country are very welcome and make a big contribution. Our university sector is world leading and is something that the Government want to focus on, celebrate and prioritise. My issue is not with the numbers specifically; it is the number of people who then switch straight into the asylum system at the end of their student visa.

It is important that we uphold this principle that , when universities recruit students from abroad, they are effectively selling students access to a world-leading university and excellent education system, and the chance to improve their circumstances and gain excellent skills and qualifications. What they are not selling is immigration status. It is important that , where we can see abuse, we really do clamp down on it. I have taken action on visa brak e s. We will have more to say about abuse of the student route.

Going forward, I want to make sure that you can be confident that the system of international students is not also a backdoor for making an asylum claim in this country. That is the thing that we want to clamp down on, which has meant that we have higher expectations of universities as sponsors. We are taking other measures to clamp down on that abuse, but it is the abuse, because that goes to broader confidence for the public in the immigration system overall. If they can see that the numbers of people who go straight into the asylum system are high, the public would rightly be worried about that. They would think, “Hang on a minute; what is going on here?”
Q73 So if there i s no asylum abuse and as long as the numbers are fine—

It is a broader question for the Government and overall government policy, but I am not trying to artificially reduce the number of international students. I am trying to stop the abuse of the student route that goes straight into the asylum system. That is the thing I care about.

Q74 I have one final point on regular migration, because I am keen to move to irregular migration. We conducted a series of deliberative democracy workshops around the public’s attitude to regular migration, and work-related migration in particular. We published the outcomes last week and it was very clear from all three workshops that the public want prioritisation of training and opportunities for residents before migrants are brought in, so I just make the point.

We are about to launch an inquiry. The terms of reference will be published straight after this evidence session. We are very keen to support the Government and give you some recommendations that will help in terms of a whole-of- government approach that ensures that those that are resident here get priority for skills and training needed for work, rather than migrants being used just to fill holes without considering a native worker.

That is absolutely the approach that I can endorse and support. What you have seen in the care sector is a degradation in terms and conditions and a reliance on overseas labour, which is just designed to undercut what would be good terms and conditions for a broader workforce strategy. I definitely agree with that principle in the report and look forward to the Committee’s work in this area.

Q75 I have a question about how you are expecting the proposed work and study protection route to function in practice. Where people come here as refugee s , some of them will eventually move from court protection into work and study. What proportion of refugees do you expect that to apply to? For instance, if we have a shortage of care workers, would you expect the refugees to get into care work, or will they all go off to colleges? What will happen to them?

The first cohort to whom the new 13-month rule applies and whom we would expect to move into the work and study route falls in autumn 2028. Policy on the work and study route for people with protection status is being developed as we speak. It will look at exactly these practical questions of how people might move from one route into another, how to make sure that you do not penalise somebody who has moved into the work route and had a job, but then lost their job — or their employer went bust or whatever — so that you do not penalise people who are trying to do the right thing. All the technical elements of how the routes will work are being developed. Again, I would expect to be unveiling settled policy in this area over next year, in good time before the first cohort would be looking to move into a different route if available to them.

Q76 We just visited Denmark as a group . We were impressed by quite a lot of things that went on in Denmark, and I know you are too. One of the things is that the Department there is called the Ministry of Immigration and Integration. The second part of my question is what we are going to do to support integration of people who have become refugees or who have been granted refugee status, so that they can in fact contribute .

There are two things on that. First , all the work that is underpinning all the reforms in the migration space, whether asylum or earned settlement, is about setting the principles of fairness and contribution to be at the heart of both of these systems. I conceive of it all as one system, certainly because of the numbers of people from a work or student visa who then transfer into the asylum system. Any Home Secretary has to look at the whole system overall.

The reason those principles of fairness and contribution are so important is that they unlock, in my view, the generosity of the British public. If you have played by the right rules, you have done the thing we asked you to do and you have made a contribution—whether that is measured on income or other ways you can support yourself—that does unlock the inherent generous spirit of the British people in terms of welcoming people, wanting them to be part of our communities and seeing them as equal.

The bit that the Home Office can do here is about the rules of the game, to make sure that the public who are already here , who in the end have to welcome new people , are sufficiently confident in the system that we are running that they feel able to do that, because integration is a two-way street. It is for the community that is already here to be welcoming, and it is incumbent on the person who has come newly to this country to want to take steps to integrate themselves as well. It is a two-way street. Our job is to set the right rules and build public confidence so that individuals who are coming through our system are welcomed and people understand that this is a good , well-managed system.

The rest of the work on integration is an active process. It is not something you can passively just expect to happen. It speaks to local communities, resilience and so on. That is work that specifically MHCLG is taking forward. When the Government released their strategy on social cohesion, “ Protecting what Matters ” , we specifically committed to a broader integration strategy for migrants, which MHCLG is working on. I cannot tell you today when MHCLG will publish it, but I do know that the Home Office is fully engaged in that work, as are other Government Departments . There is a recognition that the Government need to do more in the integration space to smooth that journey, particularly given the hostility that we are seeing.
Q77 That was certainly what we saw in Denmark. They are very active about arranging for people to be integrated who have arrived. That was the take-home message I felt from our visit.

There are good lessons to learn from Denmark. As I say, I visited myself and have learned from some aspects of their system. Of course, other aspects of their system are not things we either could do or would want to do as a Government. They have thresholds for minorities who live in particular areas and then what they do to those areas. That is a matter for them; those are not policies we believe in or would ever seek to introduce here. We want policies on integration that speak to the sort of country we are, with very large diaspora communities that are well settled, have been here for many decades, and can then play a full part. As I say, it is an active process and it is something that MHCLG is drawing up.

Q78 Everyone would accept that channel crossings are decreasing. Do you think that is through what the Government have done, or do you think that it is more that the boats are generally in decline across Europe?

It is definitely a result of the policy environment changing, and particularly the law enforcement work. I have two things to say to that. First , while numbers of people into Europe are down this year by, I want to say, about 27%—I can write to the Committee with the exact number—there are a lot of people in Europe already. There is still high demand and no shortage of people wanting to get to the north of France to get on a boat. I do not think that it follows that just the European border situation hardening and fewer people arriving into Europe is causing the drop in numbers, because there is still plenty of demand.

We have seen welcome decreases. The numbers are 40% down this year compared to last year, which is very welcome progress. I am not complacent ; I want to build on that and go much further. It is impossible to say which one intervention is making the difference. It is a whole suite of interventions.

We are doing a lot of upstream work, not just in France, but with colleagues in Belgium and in Turkey, as well as further up the chain, in terms of disrupting the organised criminals who are behind the trade in people trafficking. We are seizing boats and equipment. There is a lot of disruption activity that happens long before you get to France with, again, much more intense work in France itself, so the whole of that picture is making a difference.
Q79 I agree with what you said earlier. Our public are very invested and very aware. Do you think that the decline in the numbers of arrivals will continue?

I hope so. It is a highly adaptive environment, and things change very quickly. As you can see already, you have had a displacement of activity by the gangs from beaches in the north of France. They are moving westerly. We have seen people try to have launches from Belgium as well. That change that we are seeing from the gangs is in response to the new environment from law enforcement, so we can expect them to keep trying to adapt. Unfortunately, these are highly adaptable, entrepreneurial people, so they will change, and we have to keep pace with any changes that they are making in their operating model in how we go after them with law enforcement.

As I say, it is a very welcome decrease that we have seen, and a very significant decrease particularly over the summer, but we are not complacent and we know that we need to go further. I am watching with an eagle eye what displacement activity is occurring and how the gangs are adapting in order to make sure, particularly with our partners in France, that we adapt just as quickly to their change in posture as we have to the previous operating model.

Q80 We have had quite a few presentations over the years to this Committee. Do you think that we have reached a point where there is a limit to what you can do with enforcement because it is so dangerous?

No, I do not think that we have reached a limit. We can and will continue to go further. Just last week, I was signing an agreement with my Belgian counterpart on law enforcement co-operation. He knows that our key priority there is organised immigration crime. We have already had good work with the Belgians, with a number of arrests made, people brought to justice, and a disruption of the trade there.

As the model of the gangs changes, we need to change alongside it, so I do not think that we are at a limit of what can be achieved with law enforcement alone. We have made excellent progress this year and can go further.
Q81 On the channel crossings from France, are you concerned about the change in tactics now to larger boats, which is a topic of conversation?

First , the move to larger boats is placing people in even more danger than they are in by getting on one of the regular-sized boats. I have seen these things. They are very flimsy and very dangerous. There have been incidents where one or two of them have nearly caught fire close to the French beaches, with a real, potential risk of significant loss of life. We know that people continue to die in the channel. It does not make news as it used to, but it happens and is a reality that we want to eliminate. We want people not to be putting themselves in danger in this way.

The change of tactics , so displacing further west in France, trying to get into Belgium and using different-sized boats , is all because there is real disruption happening. Boats and engines are being seized. The organised immigration criminals are being brought to justice in different parts of Europe. Other countries are taking a new posture. Germany has changed its law, having worked closely with us, so that it can go after these people more effectively, particularly where things are held in warehouses. As that is having an impact, of course, they are looking to change the way in which they do things as well but, just as we have gone after them in their current operating model, we will do that for any changes that they make as well.

Q82 We are paying France a lot of money to help us with the channel crossings. Would you say that we are getting good value for that? If you think that that is not happening, will you withdraw the funds, speak to the French, or change, disrupt and go a different way?

I signed a new agreement with the French for three years, for a total of £662 million. It is a three-year deal. It is a lot of money ; it is more than we were paying before. What the new deal does that the previous deal did not give us the flexibility to do is to pay for the things that we know are making a difference. We know the law enforcement tactics that make a difference on the ground and are now able to direct our funding towards that law enforcement response. That is the riot police being available ; it is the uplift in French law enforcement officers and boots on the ground. That is the thing that we paid more money for, and we know that that is effective and is part of the reason why the numbers are coming down.

Given history and all of that, there is lots of commentary about the relationship with the French, but these things are always a partnership . It is important that they see this as a shared challenge, not just a problem for the Brits —when the boats arrive, we have the problem ; they do not. They have put a lot of effort into delivering on the deal that we have agreed. They have recruited the additional law enforcement ; those boots are on the ground. They also changed their posture on maritime tactics and are now using them. That is a big thing for the French to have changed in their system, and it has helped. It has constrained the operating environment for the gangs.

I am very pleased with the co-operation that we have. I am pleased that the new agreement gives us flexibility, so we will pay for the things that work, and not fund things that are not making a difference to crossings. The combination of those two things puts us in the strongest possible position going forward.
Q83 You cannot tell us how the conversations went when you were speaking to the French, but you feel that you have enough levers and got what you needed to move this forward.

I am not going to get into discussions. I talk regularly to Minister Nuñez, my French counterpart. We would both say that we have robust discussions. He has views ; I have views , but they are exchanged respectfully. We are both happy with the deal that we have, and we are both very much in favour of the principle of flexible funding and funding the things that make a difference. The French system has recognised the fact that we want to show value for money, and we want to be able to say, “If we are paying more, we are paying for the things that work . ” We want to be able to show a difference in the number of crossings, and that is well understood in the French political system.

Q84 We did visit northern France just before Christmas last year, so we saw some of the stuff in action and welcomed the fact that the deal has been extended, but what we hear from law enforcement across the board is that the gangs that are behind this are largely Iraqi Kurdish gangs. Are the Government using their position and influence with that area to try to impact what is happening and to disrupt those gangs at source?

Without going into the sort of detail that might compromise operations, let me just say that, across the whole picture of the organised immigration crime network, from source countries all the way through to people who provide the equipment, where they are warehoused, and right down to what happens in the north of France, there is UK Government activity everywhere.

Q85 Home Secretary , I wanted to focus on this relationship with France on the so-called one-in, one-out deal. Just looking at the numbers, in the period between August 2025 and June 2026, 28,000 migrants arrived on small boats, yet only 1,087 went out of this country to France. We let more in—1,117—through the one-in, one-out deal. My question is simple. How much is this costing per person? Do you think that, as it is at the moment, this pilot is a success?

The number today is something over 1,400. I appreciate that you are looking at a different time period. As a first challenge, it is easy to take the numbers at a particular day and time, and to say, “We took more than they did , ” but, when you look at the trend, the numbers have tracked fairly evenly , so the numbers in and out are about the same. There is always a little discrepancy , depending on whether a flight has gone off on our side or on theirs, but the numbers have tracked.

The intention was one in, one out, and that is the way that the pilot has functioned. In any given week, they will look skewed in one direction or another, but that is not the trend and not what the treaty is about . The numbers are tracking as the same.

Second ly , this was always a pilot programme. It was designed to try to prove the concept that it is possible to have this kind of arrangement between us and the French, not just as an agreement politically, but to operationally deliver it and to overcome legal hurdles. There have been legal challenges all the way through, as I am sure you and other Committee members know. The aim was to prove the concept that such an agreement can work and that it is possible to provide a safe and legal route into the country from the north of France and, therefore, degrade the boats trade, as it were.

On the specific difference made by the pilot compared to everything else that we are doing in terms of law enforcement and the broader policy environment, it is not possible to separate out, “This one led to this decrease, and this led to the other . ”
Q86 Home Secretary, I asked how much it is per person, and whether you think it has been a success.
I will need to write to the Committee with the most recent figures. Per person, for the numbers that have been returned so far, it is about £56,000.
Q87 Has it been a success?

On its own terms, can you prove the concept that such a deal is viable and that you can get returns up and running? Yes. It has not been without its challenges. The numbers are still relatively small, and what has been more operationally difficult is to scale up very large numbers of removals every week into the French system. It is operationally difficult for them, as well as for us, and there are constraints on both sides on things such as detention capacity.

Q88 From my point of view, for constituents watching, 28,000 people is probably about the size of Ilkley, Addingham and Silsden in terms of population coming into this country on small boats over an 11-month period. With the in-outs varying on numbers, it is about the same based on what is coming in and out, so it does not look to me as if this is working as a deterrent. What is your assessment of this pilot scheme working as a deterrent?

Again, it is difficult to separate out any one of the actions that we are taking. Is it the case that people in the north of France are aware that there is another route that they might want to try to avail themselves of? Yes. Third-sector agencies such as UNHCR tell us that there are people who they know are not getting on boats because they think that there is a chance of being accepted through the one-in, one-out deal, so it is having some effect. As I say, it is not possible to separate out which one of the things is making the biggest difference. I have always said that you need a full-spectrum response to this problem, and that you have to go at everything as hard as possible in order to break the gangs’ business model.

Q89 Another measure that you announced in March this year, I believe, was a policy offering handouts of up to £40,000 to failed asylum seeker families who agreed to return home voluntarily. How many families have accepted that offer so far?

I do not have the exact number to hand today, but I can write to the Committee with it. They are relatively small numbers. It is a pilot that we have been running. It has not concluded yet, but it will soon.
Q90 When did that pilot start?
It started soon after I announced it in the asylum policy statement. I will have to get back to you with the exact date.

Q91 Could you write to the Committee with the exact numbers that have accepted that offer? Many people have been trying to get a firm answer from you, and the Home Office has stonewalled the response, but there is a narrative that asylum seekers are not accepting the family payout of £40,000 because it is more lucrative to stay in this country. I would like to understand: is that your assessment of this scheme so far.

I will make a full assessment when we have completed it and learned all the lessons. In the end, you are trying to affect human behaviour. We already have packages for voluntary removals. That is true in Denmark, which you guys visited not long ago, because it is a good way of persuading people who have no right to be here to move. It usually represents value for money because it is much cheaper for people to go through on a package such as that than a forced removal, which can be very expensive.

We were trialling that specifically on failed asylum-seeking families, but you are right. If you are a failed asylum-seeking family, what you are trading off is an offer of £40,000, which will help you resettle in your country of origin, versus access to free healthcare and education for your children. We are trying to assess what people respond to and behavioural changes.

It is right to have trialled something different to see whether we can break the logjam on the removals of failed asylum-seeking families. We are already consulting on new policy around the removals of families as well, because we know that there are large numbers. Policies of previous Governments, before the Labour Government came into power, changed the environment in terms of removals, which has led to more people choosing to stay.
Q92 What would be a measure of success for that policy that was announced in terms of numbers of families accepting it?

We are trying to assess whether people, if they are a family, respond to a more generous package. That is different from single individuals, but, with a family, do people respond? That is the thing that we will need to learn from in order to make decisions and policy choices in the future about what we do when we have families in supported accommodation who are from safe countries that they can return to. We will need to change policy to make sure that we are able to return people who have no right to be here.

Q93 Home Secretary, we have heard a bit of a mixed picture on the one-in, one-out deal with France. My understanding from that exchange is that you are still looking at and analysing it before any extension or expansion of that scheme is brought forward. Is that correct?

It has already been extended, because the pilot would have run out before the summer, into October. You will appreciate that I am not going to comment on discussions with the French or be drawn on where those discussions are heading or what the future there might be.

Q94 One thing that we found from talking to counterparts in Denmark was that they are part of the EU migration pact that has recently come into force. Is a broader returns deal with the European Union something that you or this Government might consider?

I get this quite a bit from other spokespeople in your party. It is a mistake to see the EU’s new pact as some sort of new silver bullet that , if we were in it, would somehow eliminate all the problems that we have. I would observe that, just on the one-in, one-out with France, more returns have happened than ever was the case under the Dublin arrangements, when we were still members of the EU.

I talk to my counterparts in Europe very regularly. They are very focused on trying to make that pact work for EU members, which is, itself, going to be a real challenge and places pressures on countries that people come to in order to access the rest of Europe, such as Italy and Greece. Getting the pact up and working is a work in progress for the European Union. We will always have discussions with colleagues everywhere on what we can do on a shared challenge, but it is a real mistake to think that that pact is the future and that, if we were in it, this problem would go away, because I promise you that it would not.
Q95 With respect, the one-in, one-out deal is considerably more expensive than the EU migration pact, so I would expect it to be more successful.
Yes, but £ 56,000 is still cheaper than, or just about the same as, supporting someone in a hotel for a year.
Q96 Which we are spending £2.2 billion a year on.
That is correct, and we should not be.

Q97 In terms of data sharing, this feels like a no-brainer to me, and I am not sure whether you agree, but, when a violent criminal comes into the European Union seeking asylum, we, as a country, are no longer able, following Brexit, to get that data under the Eurodac system. Is that something that you might support the UK co-operat ing with Europe on?

We definitely talk to European colleagues about data sharing, for law enforcement and immigration purposes. Again, it would be wrong for me to try to get ahead of discussions that may or may not be happening at the UK-EU summit, but, from a Home Office perspective, rest assured that data sharing is the first item on the agenda whenever I discuss these things with the European Commission and others.

Q98 That is good to hear. We have a large proportion of failed asylum seekers in the UK, who, for various reasons, cannot be returned to their home country. The figure is something like 5,000. Would you consider , as European counterparts such as Denmark and Germany are currently considering , having return hubs in a safe third country?

It is already G overnment policy to look carefully at arrangements with other countries for the purposes of returns. There is a lot of activity, both here and across Europe, on the whole concept of return hubs and trying to get agreements over the line. I will not say more than that today, but it is something that we are pursuing with interest.
Q99 Aside from return hubs, is there any other work under way to address this backlog of failed asylum seekers?

Where failed asylum seekers are capable of being removed, Immigration Enforcement will proceed with removal. Usually, the reason that you cannot remove is article 3 of the ECHR on the grounds of the safety of the country that you are seeking to remove people to. That is something that we just continue to work on, either to try to find somewhere else or to keep monitoring the situation in their home countries such that removal becomes a viable option.

Q100 SAMU Social Paris, which provides healthcare to the one-in, one-out returnees, has reported to the French Parliament on the harm that has been done to detainees in UK detention during transfer—things such as bruising, lacerations, handcuff injuries and skin lesions. There was even one man who arrived in such a state that he was sent straight to A&E. His injuries were consistent with restraint and abdominal pain from repeated blows. Home Secretary, are you aware of these instances, and what will your Department about the violent treatment of detainees in our care?

I do not recognise that picture. What you are describing would be a criminal offence in our country. It is not a picture that I recognise. It is not unusual for people who are being returned to seek to physically harm themselves. People will do quite a lot of damage in trying not to be put on a plane or be returned. Thank you for raising with me what you were describing. I was not aware of it and I will certainly challeng e whatever has been put to the French Parliament, but those are crimes.
Q101 I just want to focus on asylum decision making. What are you doing to address the poor quality of asylum decision making, which has been widely recognised, that is taking place at the moment?

There have been specific issues that we inherited from a 2023 decision-making model , which are being worked through. There have been a range of recommendations made by the ICIBI, all of which we are implementing in full to strengthen decision-making processes.

More broadly, though, decision making is in a stronger position than it has been. In particular, the grant rate has come down. Decisions are assured ; samples are taken and then measured against whether we think the decision was right. On the last round of figures, something like 93% of decisions were deemed correct at the initial decision point, which is not necessarily the same as the courts upholding those decisions.

As you will know, the circumstances between initial decision and a court appeal hearing are often significantly different, but the current assurance model for decision making suggests that around 93% are accurate and were the correct initial decision, based on the circumstances known to the official.

Q102 Mr Kohler: I was going to ask you about the Independent Immigration Appeals Authority, but I am told that we do not have time. All I would say to you is that Denmark was very surprised that we were moving from a judicial to an administrative system. I would ask you to look at what happened in Australia when they tried it and it failed.
It is a system of independent adjudication, to be clear, and perhaps Denmark does not have a 12 to 18-month lead time for hiring judges, as we do in this country.
Mr Kohler: As I say, there are doubts about whether it will work .
I am happy to answer questions, though.
Mr Kohler: I am not allowed to go any further.
You can ask questions. We have until 5 o’clock , so use your time wisely.

Q103 Mr Kohler: Turning to asylum accommodation, you inherited some terrible contracts . Private companies have made a vast amount of money out of the Home Office and taxpayers. The break clause is now exercisable. The contracts go until September 2029. In reality, is there any chance that the break clause will be exercised?

I do not think that the position on the break clause is much further on than when I was last at the Committee, when we had an exchange on the break clause. We have dealt with these two things before, but the break clause and getting out of hotels are not related. We can keep exiting hotels. Hotel accommodation was an addition to that contract , not the core contract.

I have been pushing the commercial arm of my Department to make sure that we are pushing as hard as we can on getting value for money from these current contracts that, as you rightly say, we inherited. The thing about exercising the break clause and getting out of the contracts is that I still need to have an asylum accommodation estate to move people to. The absence of that and other good, viable alternatives for doing this at scale and at speed is the real limiting factor on simply being able to rip up these contracts today. We do need to transition to a new model of asylum accommodation, but that is not something that the Government can do overnight. We also cannot have something like 90,000 people potentially homeless either.
Q104 Mr Kohler: You are tendering for the new contract post 2029. You also have a desire to bring in local authorities. How is that all dovetailing together?

Especially given the new Prime Minister’s focus on devolution, we are looking at how we work with local authorities. At the moment, for the dispersal of asylum seekers, there is what they call a full dispersal model, which tries to have an even spread around the country, but there is a recognition that, as closely as you might work with local authorities, no one place can have a veto. The Home Office still has obligations that it has to fulfil, and so , while we try to work as closely as we can with the local authorities, we cannot just agree that some places will have nobody and others will take all the strain. We are trying to go for as fair a spread as we can.

You are right that that is partly limited by how much we pay on the current contract. As we transition to a new model, there is a question around how you might have flexibility in what you pay. We want to work with local authorities. The problem with a fully devolved model, where local authorities either have, essentially, a statutory duty or take responsibility for fulfilling asylum accommodation need, is that you have to insure that system against some authorities not playing ball, not taking part and saying no—and we do have authorities that say no.

In fact, there are stresses and strains in Glasgow, for example, which have rightly had a lot of interest, and I am engaging with local Members of Parliament. That is because nowhere else in Scotland would take that complement, so Glasgow ended up taking all the pressure that should have been spread out more fairly across all of Scotland. There are authorities that do not play ball, and so , if you had a devolved model, you would still have to have an answer for what happens there.

You also need to be able to deal with surges in demand. Again, the reason why it works now is that the Home Office—believe me, I do not really want to be running such big accommodation estates—can surge capacity based on flows of people in to and out of the asylum system.

In security terms , we cannot lose track of who we have and where they are, so you would need a model that, with everyone doing things in their own way, still speaks to some sort of national structure such that you are not losing people into communities, and then you have lost track of them and they have disappeared.

There are quite a few structural challenges with having a fully devolved model, but we are leaning in to see what more we can do to work more effectively with local authorities as we move to a new contract in the future.
Q105 Mr Kohler: Do you envisage private companies still playing a role post September 2029?

It is a little too early to say. If I had to answer today one way or the other, I would say that they probably will. It is hard to see how we would have the amount of accommodation required without some element of private provision, but there are live discussions between us and MHCLG about how local authorities might be able to play a more innovative role in this space.

Q106 Mr Kohler: In Denmark, we saw that NGOs provided this function. They had a contract with a no-profit clause. If they did not spend the money on the asylum accommodation, they had to pay it back to the Government. The Red Cross running it made a huge difference to the whole tone of the debate. People in the local community were volunteering to help. Have we ever explored that approach?

We have not for what has been inherited or done so far. One thing that will definitely change under the Government is the model of asylum accommodation, with more use of medium-sized and large sites, as well as dispersed accommodation, so that all the pressure is not between hotels, which we intend to close, and dispersed accommodation. We want medium-sized and large sites to play a bigger role in asylum accommodation.

We are definitely looking at wh at different providers could be in this space. Again, without going into live conversations between us and other Government Departments, we are not looking to simply give the same contract to the same people.

Q107 Mr Kohler: Are you having active discussion with NGOs? The Red Cross has huge international experience on this. Are we talking to NGOs such as the Red Cross and bringing their experience into the British system?
Let me take that away from this discussion to see what specifically I could tell you about discussions with others that are not private providers.
Mr Kohler: I would say that it impressed the Committee how it changed the whole tone of what was happening. Am I allowed a bit more time?
We have three minutes.

Q108 Mr Kohler: Can I press you on Manston? Private Eye has made the point that MTC has just been awarded a long-term contract on the Manston return centre. MTC has a pretty chequered record , including with the London probation service, the New South Wales prison system and the Australian asylum system . Time and time again MTC has been found wanting. Are you confident that it will provide the service that we require?

I am happy to write to the Committee about the process that we have undergone and the standards that we hold ourselves to, but Manston is an important facility, and it is important that it is well run. I can assure you that my officials and I are very engaged on the overall effectiveness and performance of the immigration estate.
Q109 Mr Kohler: Is the history of MTC’s role in this type of contract relevant to the awarding process?

Let me write to you about the process that we had. Rather than engaging in Private Eye -related speculation, let me just write to you about the process that was followed and what was taken into account.
I have Joani Reid and Lewis Atkinson with quick follow-ups. Perhaps if you both give your follow-ups, and then you can respond, Home Secretary.

Home Secretary, you mentioned Glasgow. I accept that good progress has been made there, but the pressure is still acute. I do not need to go over the figures, but over 50% of asylum seekers in Scotland are in Glasgow, which has quite deprived communities. I know that a colleague has written to you. Can we pause? It really demands some sort of dispersal policy in Scotland. You mentioned it as an extreme example. Almost all of the pressure is on Glasgow, whereas the more affluent local authorities are taking zero . It really needs to be addressed.

Q110 As a continuation of that point, areas in the north-east such as Sunderland have had a significantly higher proportion of asylum seekers accommodated per head of population than elsewhere as a result of the contracts inherited from the previous Government. As numbers accommodated fall across the country, will you prioritise reducing numbers in local authorities such as mine that have had higher amounts?

I am very aware of the acute pressures in the areas that are above what their allocation should be. There are some areas that are very significantly above what their allocation should be on the full dispersal model.

On Glasgow specifically, as I said before, I very much recognise those challenges, partly borne out because other local authorities in Scotland have not stepped up to play their full part to enable a fairer distribution across the whole of Scotland. There has not been any procurement of new asylum accommodation in Glasgow since 2024.

Let me say to both of you that, as we go for a fairer spread, we have renegotiated the rates that we pay in some areas to bring in the ability to move out to slightly more affluent areas. As we do that, I am looking to reduce the pressure on places that are way above their allocation and to bring that down in a sustained way so that every area play s its full part.

As we move to more military sites, and then also more medium-sized sites, I want to, again, alleviate that pressure, and I will be targeting the areas that are above allocation to be first in line to see those reductions.
I am going to bring things to a close. Thank you, Home Secretary. We look forward to seeing you again before Christmas.
