Q362 In the previous panel, we spoke about the impact on the SRN, but the estimated additional 60,000 vehicle journeys a day will have some impact on local roads. Do you think that the draft NPS pays sufficient attention to those local roads?

Again, I don’t think so. It is all being looked at at too high a level at this moment in time. The theme that runs throughout the NPS is that more work should go into trying to justify what is actually required . We talked about the rail schemes before, but all the problems result on the local roads if you get the more strategic issues wrong. The rail is not secured. We talked about the public modal targets in the previous session. If you miss them, they hit the local roads and then it is too late. The roads around our local communities—around the airport—are some of the worst in London. There were problems on the M25 today. That causes carnage and block-ups all around Sipson and the little villages that we drove around.

Again, that comes back to what we were saying about T5. That is where the impacts fall on our communities. I do not think there are controls in the NPS to make sure that they will be avoided. To be clear, Chair, I think there should be some sort of managed growth. You should be unlocking growth when you have reached targets. You should not be missing targets and still being allowed to grow.
Q363 Is there anything in the NPS on monitoring and mitigating the impact on local roads, or anything that you specifically would like to see included?

This all comes back to Mark’s point about environment and managed growth. That has to go into the framework. The impacts on the local surface access network need to be monitored better. In particular, where charges are received from the airport, whether it is drop-off charges or some other form of car charging, they need to start being directed towards local solutions as opposed to just being put in someone’s back pocket.

Absolutely. Exactly as Ian says, you spend a lot of time thinking about the M25 and the M4 being a car park, but the reality of that is that people cannot pick their kids up from school in residential roads in Cranford, Bedfont or Poyle.

There is also the point about resilience. It will get more congested, with 60,000 additional vehicles—TfL calculated 55,000, but give or take 5,000 a day—being very significant. Assuming half of those are on the M25, that is a very significant increase in traffic on the M25, for example—13%, 14%, or 15%. Understanding what that means as BAU, but also when there are issues on the network, which there are almost daily, as Ian says, is really important . There is no obligation on either promoter to do that in the NPS, so the issue of resilience is really important .

There is also the issue of maintenance, which does not come up very often. We talked a lot about freight. Lorries have a hugely disproportionate impact on the asset integrity of roads. While many of those trips will be on SRN, many of them end or start on bits of Hillingdon’s, Hounslow’s or Surrey’s network. How we take the local authority burden of additional maintenance requirements from that is quite important.

The reason we would say that there is a case for surface access being a fifth test is that, yes, it has implications for air quality, carbon, economic prosperity, congestion and the rest of it, but it is also just about wellbeing. Being able to go about your business on a general day without being stuck in endless traffic is a significant part of enjoying life, right? That is the threat here if we do not get this right.

If I may add one final point, we are not just talking about the growth of Heathrow here. The mayor has a massive housing target and quite a lot of that has been put down on to Hillingdon. It is not just accommodating Heathrow expansion on our road network, but accommodating tens of thousands of extra houses over the next 10 years— 25,000 came out of the London plan for the London borough of Hillingdon to deliver. That is an incredible number of houses that we have to deliver on the same networks where Heathrow expansion is going to take place. It cannot all fit.
Q364 Are the public transport mode share targets in the draft NPS achievable and are they are ambitious enough?

As Anthony Smith of the Heathrow Area Transport Forum, of which HSPG is a member, said, anything is achievable if you put enough money at it. Is it ambitious enough? Well, 60,000 extra vehicles on the road a day does not feel like success to me.

Again, no. The thing that really irks is where those figures came from. It should be an evidence-based target because it might be that you can achieve that, but there is still massive carnage on the road. It should be an evidence-based target that informs whether we should have rail links as part of this scheme. At this moment in time, again, it seems a little bit of a contrived target, and again, what if they do not hit it? It might well be a challenging target for them to achieve, but what if they do not hit it?

The timings are so key, as Anthony was saying. The idea that you could get to 129,999,999 before you have to deliver a rail scheme, which is the suggestion within the surface access vision, is a difficult message to take for local authorities who are going to deal with that congestion.

Q365 There are road surface access improvements, but there are not rail surface access improvements. From the plans that you have seen, do you think there will be any improvements to the local infrastructure from the upgrades that are within the promoter’s plans?

The intention at the moment is for no net loss in capacity. We have not yet seen anything that requires additional capacity to future-proof growth in the area. That is not a requirement of the draft NPS either, so that is not great.

There will be new roads, which is great, but it comes back to, what are the maintenance arrangements for them? Construction is the biggest issue for us in the interim. How are you going to get everything on the network before you have even built some of that infrastructure?

The clear message that we have heard from our discussions with one of the applicants is that they are planning for interventions such as cycle lanes and potentially bus lanes. They have got a southern road tunnel which giveth and taketh in the sense that it might generate more traffic in some areas like Surrey and Hounslow, but it might also provide much better bus access into the central terminal area, which would have improvements.

How you bring all of that together and deliver it effectively is still unknown. They are also saying that they are probably not looking to fund those interventions that are off the network. How can you have a credible bus service to the airport if the bus lanes only start at Southern Perimeter Road? How can you get people there on bikes if there are no cycle lanes in Hounslow or Poyle or whatever?
Q366 We are now going to move on to noise pollution. Heathrow’s noise mitigation schemes have been the bane of my life as a councillor and as a MP.
And as a local resident.

Yes—I am not benefit i ng from any of the existing schemes. The draft HENPS points to the existing noise mitigation measures, including the residential insulation scheme and the one for schools and community buildings. It assumes that it will continue following the expansion. As the host authority, Ian, how effective have those measures been in practice?

Perversely, we are not actually impacted by noise that much at this moment in time because the airport sits neatly in the southern part of the borough and the take offs are to the east and the west of the borough.

However, we have been looking at a planning application for ending the Cranford agreement —the e asterly a lternation s. We have been getting into the weeds of those current proposals. Although the quieter neighbourhood scheme has been an improvement, there is still concern that its roll-out is not properly regulated. It is delivered by Heathrow Airport Ltd pretty much on its own terms, and it is not getting to the properties that should be prioritised.
It has been an improvement, but there is still a lot of work to do. The numbers that we are talking about if we go forward with the expansion exponentially increase.
Q367 Mark, maybe you are in the best position to answer both from Hounslow and the west side.

One of the primary reasons our councils came together was because they were end-of-runway authorities and would potentially be disproportionately impacted by noise. There is a lot of support for the mitigation schemes among the councils —there has been for many years —but there is also a recognition that they do not go nearly far or fast enough.

U nder the existing proposal — the quieter neighbourhood scheme — Heathrow have looked to put a lot more money into that, only to see the regulator effectively say, “N o , it ’s not necessary . The amount of money that you are spending at the moment is fine . ”

You went from a situation where Heathrow was looking to try and accelerate the provision of that mitigation so that all properties were insulated within about 20 years to a situation where, under the current spending that has been approved in the next regulatory period —if we assume d that carried on — it would take more than 100 years.

T he current scheme is welcome. They ha ve moved it from a situation where there was part funding to one where they are 100% funding and that has really helped with take - up. That is very much welcome, but it is nowhere near far enough.
L ooking at what the requirement is —
Q368 Just on the current one, I am seeing very slow progress . It looks good on paper, but we are not getting a sense of who i s going to get insulated and w hen ? Is that just my experience?

No, I think that is a fair comment. Basically, they started up this scheme with 100% funding. It has taken quite some time because, as Ian says, they are trying to do this to be a good neighbour; they are not obligated, in many cases, to do this. There needs to be some accountability, and there needs to be a pipeline of delivery. You need to get muscle memory about how you deliver this more quickly and more efficiently. They built all this up only to get knocked back, to the tune of a couple of hundred million pounds, from the CAA over that period. It is very significant. Now they are having to almost pick themselves back up again.

We cannot be in that situation during an expansion programme, when so many hundreds of thousands of households, possibly more, are going to be impacted. Much like surface access, this mitigation should be put in up front; it should be following new flights and new impacts. It is quite significant. We may get on to the discrepancy with what has been approved at Gatwick.
Q369 Do you want to focus on that? There is a discrepancy.

There is a discrepancy. In 2018, it was £3,000. We are six years on, and it is £3,000—I think there has been some inflation in between those two. It is unusual that we have not seen any indexation for it. Then you compare it with Gatwick, which is up at £6,500 for the same insulated property. There is a big gap there. Gatwick and Heathrow are in different circumstances, so there is a conversation about whether it should be exactly equivalent, but there should be some level of comparability between those two.

Some of our members would be concerned about the tension with affordability. We are very keen on pace and on coverage. Sometimes it might be better to have a little less money going into each property but getting more properties insulated. There is a discussion there, but the gap between Gatwick and Heathrow, and the fact that the money has not been indexed linked, is pretty concerning.
Q370 Have you had any feedback about the noise insulation schemes for schools and other community buildings?

We have not had as much feedback from members on that; I think there has been a feeling that Heathrow has tried to put quite a lot of effort into that over the years. Some of the concerns have been more about the maintenance of what has gone in, but the actual schemes are important.

It is also important to note that the whole issue of increasing the noise footprint will mean more cost for local authorities more generally when building any community facilities, because you will need more noise insulation. If you are trying to build council housing and respond to the housing crisis, all those units will cost more per unit because of the insulation. There are not just direct impacts on existing properties; unbuilt properties are going to be impacted.

Ian Thynne : In terms of the Gatwick-Heathrow comparison, the numbers are fairly contrived . Where does the £3,000 come from? That has not been assessed in the appraisal of sustainability that sits behind the draft NPS . There is no justification for that number; £3,000 does not really buy you too much, and it does not matter whether you are in a five-bedroom property or a one-bedroom flat—you still get £3,000.

There is also a real concern about the levels at which those kick in. Just as the consultation came out, there was the release of a new updated noise survey, which said that people are getting more annoyed at noise at a much lower level than they were previously, but the mitigation does not go down to anywhere near those levels. You can understand why: if you started to go down, the cost would go up exponentially, and then you are into the world of affordability again. It is not an evidence-based offer or an evidence-based test. Again, this leaves people exposed to noise harm.

Q371 Very briefly, Ian, the draft HENPS talks about a noise envelope, but no extra noise. What is the implication for residents of yours who will be significantly impacted by being underneath an approach path, when they are not at the moment ?

Ian Thynne : It says no extra noise from the 2024 baseline, but there will be new exposures. Within that noise contour, you could still get a lot of communities exposed to new levels of noise. In particular, flights going east on the new northern runway will take off to the north, over our areas of regeneration around Hayes, which have never experienced noise before. They will be exposed, and they will not be getting the noise mitigation that is required to protect their health.

Q372 This is probably not a very evidence-led question. Many of your residents presumably moved there knowing that there was a very large airport. Does it genuinely come as a surprise to them that it might be expanding? This has been talked about for a long, long time. Surely most people knew that this was a possibility when they got there, and put that into their thinking.

Ian Thynne : Some people lived there long before this came around . If we go back to the “no ifs, no buts, no third runway” from the former Prime Minister, it has not been delivered and people still live there, but some of those homes will be lost. Some people have hung around waiting to get compensation payments. Some people love the area, and why wouldn’t you? There is a tension within the communities as a consequence . When the people I was referring to in Hayes moved in, they had no intention that they would have flights taking off over them, because there were no expansion plans. Nothing has been approved; it has been talked about, but it has never been approved—there are no decisions. If that were the case, we would have no regeneration in Hayes until this is all sorted, and it has been going on for 20-odd years now.
Q373 I suppose the question I am asking is, is there surprise about this or is there just fear and anger?
Fear, anger—I do not think they are surprised it is coming around again.

Q374 Many people further east, underneath the approach path from central London, say, from 10 miles out to the areas in Hillingdon most affected, do not even know that they are under it, because no pathways have been published. Several hundred thousand people have no idea that they will have a significant—
Perhaps that goes back to your point about the lack of leaflet drops and the like.

Even if you were to go to the indicative flight paths, they are only indicative. At the point where this will get consented, there are all manner of changes to UK airspace and all the rest of it, and we will not really know who is impacted. They probably will not really know until the planes start flying over their heads. That is simply because these are two separate processes. The other thing, I think, other than fear and anger, is just fatigue. There is such a huge amount of fatigue, and it is sad when you see that in action.

The other more general point that this discussion raises is the differential impacts on subsets of the wider community of those affected by Heathrow. That comes through very strongly from the discussions we have with our member councils, that some suffer some of the impacts really acutely , as Ian has just set out, others experience them marginally and others do not have them at all. That will apply to a number of the issues we have discussed today. Coming back to the environmentally managed growth programme would allow you to pick up those differences in those different community experiences more acutely than you can in a generalised, high-level HENPS.

Q375 To clarify, I am guesting here from the Housing, Communities and Local Government Committee. It is my absolute pleasure to join you. We have talked about the impact on various communities. I want to home in on the impacts on local authorities specifically, given my role. How do the mechanisms that are set out in the draft NPS for addressing the impacts on local authorities compare, crucially, with those that have been used for other nationally significant infrastructure projects?

There has been quite a lot of planning reform and planning change over the past couple of years. The Planning and Infrastructure Act really compounded that, with the new guidance that has come through. Because the other NPSs are sector-specific and not project-specific, they are probably more general on local authority involvement and impact. I think it is fair to say that, because of the project-specific nature of this NPS, we do see more given on the type and requirements of information that should come out. Forgive me, I will not have the title right, but there is a new cost recovery system that is now in place for statutory stakeholders involved in the DCO process. It has been recognised over a large number of years that stakeholders such as local authorities and others, like the Environmental Agency, come under a fairly large workload in order to work with the promoters of these NSIPs. Once you submit as well, the timescales for going through an examination are quite tight, and quite a lot of work is required by all parties. There is this new basis in there, and the cost associated with attendance at meetings or the counter-evidence that may need to be produced will be impacted through that. Although it is not necessarily specified within the NPS, it is through some of the other national planning infrastructure guidance.

From our perspective, there is not enough attention on what is picked up by the local authorities in the area as a consequence of hosting the airport. That means public health, policing—all the public sector burdens that are placed on them by the millions of passengers coming through an airport all at once. It has impacts on our housing. You have the immigration issues—you know, it is a port authority, and I am not going to make any complaints about that, but that then falls on to the local authority to pick up.

What we have asked for during the process is a proper impact assessment for all the local authorities on what it actually takes . We are undertaking some of the work to put a fiscal cost on that at the moment . It is certainly fair to say that we do not recoup enough of the funds to enable us to undertake our statutory services. There is an extra burden of hosting an airport that is missed.

I totally agree with Ian. There is an absence of understanding of the cumulative impacts of those various demands and pressures. There are also the demands on the authorities in contributing to the process, both during the DCO process, which is part funded, but also post consent. In some of the activities that need to follow, requirements will be placed on the authorities as statutory bodies.

There are also impacts on their communities, as Ian has set out, that they will have to respond to. Noise, air quality and so on are all in there. I think the one that is perhaps overlooked the most is the housing issue: the pressure on housing of 20,000 workers coming into the area and of new people coming to work at the airport; the land pressure that the taking of the land for the airport creates; and, as Ian said already, the pressure to find the land to build the housing that is going to be needed, with the consequent impact that that will likely have on housing costs, because of the shortage and pressure created by demand. That all exacerbates the housing situation, which is, as we know, pretty intolerable .

Q376 I am going to take a guess from what you are saying that the answer to this question is no, but does the draft NPS address those impacts adequately, particularly the increased demand for schools, healthcare and housing, which we know the policy assessments have anticipated?
No.
No.
Q377 I could probably have guessed that one. Ian, moving on from that, what are your views on the decision to retain the compensation approach developed in 2018?
Compensation as in compulsory purchase?
Yes.

There are two fundamental issues with that. It is a massive loss to the borough—700-odd properties. That is a thousand people being put on to the open housing market, some of whom will have kids going to school in the area. That will have a pretty big impact on the housing market, which the local authority will probably have to manage—the airport is certainly not going to do that.

You then have the wider property offer zone. That is the land that is not within the land take for expansion. It is set out in the draft NPS as being offered to everyone below the M4, in effect, in the Heathrow villages. That is not actually correct. We know full well that Heathrow Airport Ltd has no intention of offering to buy all those thousands and thousands of properties. It will be subject to eligibility criteria. At this moment in time, we do not even know how many people will be left south of the M4. We do not know how many people will be entitled to this wider property offer—
Q378 So that is Longford, Harmondsworth and Sipson, basically?

Longford, no, because we know that that will be demolished, but Harmondsworth cuts in half, and then there i s Sipson and out towards Harlington as well. It is all in the zone. That makes it really difficult to plan for the future . In terms of school places, how many communities do you have to look after? How many kids are in those communities? How many recreation grounds do we have to look after? There will be a fundamental disruption to the way that the south of our borough works, and that is completely lost within the draft NPS; it is almost like we will have to pick up the pieces. We have asked for that, and we have had some discussions with the DFT, but there needs to be much more protection within the NPS to allow us to get to where we need to get to.

Q379 You talked earlier about the expectation on the local authority in terms of house building, generally speaking . Do you have any understanding of what replacement housing might be necessary as a result of Heathrow expansion and, if it is necessary, will it be on top of or a part of the expectations of house building in the borough? Or do you not know?
We know we don’t know.
Always a great start!

We know that there is going to be a big problem here. We know that there are going to be a load more workers. There is going to be a load more infrastructure that supports the airport that is not included within the development consent order process, such as extra hotels, and all that that brings. A lot of extra supply chains will hopefully come to the area, which means local benefit and local growth, and with that comes housing.

We are going to lose a lot of housing. The mayor has given us a massive housing target. Where all this goes, we just do not know. Th is comes back to some of the problems with planning. We have talked about biodiversity net gain. That might be in some of the areas where we would be looking for housing, for example. We just do not have the full picture.

We also do not know the phasing. At what point are they going to be demolished? At what point are hotels going to be demolished to make way? At what point are new hotels are going to come on to offset those ones? Again, getting into the weeds of it, there is a lot to plan and we just do not have that in front of us.

There is no requirement in the DCO for proper place shaping —well, w e spoke with them beforehand and there is a requirement for place shaping, but it needs to be reinforced. We were happy to see that addition. It was not in the previous version, so we worked really hard with the DFT to get it in. But it needs to go much further to enable us to get a masterplan out for what this might look like in the future—not what Heathrow wants now, but what we want to plan for in the future and what we have to plan for.

Q380 Mark and Michael , what role should local authorities, and the wider group of local authorities that you represent, be playing in shaping and determining compensation measures? D o you think it is reflected to any extent in the HE NPS ? Please do also come in on the issues that I have already raised and that Ian has responded to.

I think less so on the detail of the strict compensation measures. The work we have done, as a collection of authorities, with DFT colleagues—engaging with them over the last two years or so—has been to seek to strike a better balance between the impacts, the mitigations, the opportunities and the consequential benefits that might come to these local communities.

I agree with Ian that when we talk about growth from the perspective of local authorities, it is not necessarily growth at Heathrow airport or growth associated with the airport; it is the supply chains, the hotels and everything else that comes from the ancillary activities around the airport. Some of our members, particularly the chief executives and the elected leaders that we work with, are saying that they would really like to see some of that growth and benefit captured to devote and invest in the communities that have hitherto been disadvantaged or left behind, not just because of airport impacts, noise and air quality but because they have not had the infrastructure benefits. We have talked about surface access. They have not benefited from skills provision. They have not benefited from jobs or high-quality employment opportunities. We have seen this in the HENPS, in which there is a paragraph that says that promoters must come forward with plans for local, regional and national growth, and they must ensure that plans are in place, working in partnership with others to ensure that that growth is equitably distributed across the Heathrow subregional economic area.

We might be slightly bold in saying , “W e put that forward and it is now in the HENPS, ” but it took a lot of work to get it in there ; i t was not in the previous version in 2016. It is about ensuring that it gets delivered and carried through, and how we might look at opportunities and mechanisms. I do not think I am surprising Ian when I say that we are already working with others on how a business rates review programme might help to recoup some of the additional business rates.

I am not talking about taking anything away from Hillingdon, but we are looking at some of the additional business rates that might come from expansion. There is an opportunity to look at how that might be used differently from how it might currently be apportioned out, to create some of that benefit at a much more granular local level for those communities our authorities believe need it most. I suspect that Hillingdon has a similar set of communities who might benefit from that in a way that perhaps has not been reflected in the HENPS to date.
We would say that that might not necessarily be what the business rates are intended for.

There i s also a throwaway remark in one of the later paragraphs on community funding that that would come through the extra business rates from all the future hotels, and I got a little excited by that. I got a bit angry, because that is just not acceptable. There needs to be a much better funding package put up front to enable our communities to co-exist with a massive construction, as well as local authorities being able to give their services.

The compensation piece more generally is quite a confused chapter, because it talks about the compensation scheme for the property, it talks about the mitigation for the noise insulation, and then it talks about this £50 million-a-year compensation scheme, suggesting that it is above and beyond all these other things. Well, it was £50 million in 2018—we are in 2026, so that should be £70 million or £80 million, or whatever. It is not really clear how that is going to be used; there is no governance associated with it. More information is needed on all that. Then you have the business rate piece at the end, as well. I read that as it is being stacked; you read it differently, Ian. It is all a bit confused.

What we do know is that there needs to be a new compact between the airport and the local communities, so that success at the airport genuinely filters through to the communities, as opposed to what happens at the moment , which is just sort of inferred and tangential.

On the housing thing specifically, to Heathrow’s credit they are looking at worker accommodation in a way that they were not doing in 2018, so in that respect it is positive. But we think that there is a lot more we can do to that. I would draw your attention to some work that West London Business has done on employer-related accommodation, and the fact that the airport could help to bring on development schemes that may have struggled for viability or may not have moved through the planning pipeline as quickly as they could have by underwriting some of the demand for that housing. There is quite a lot of innovative thinking that could be done here that could make a net positive overall on this stuff.

Q381 Depending on which option is chosen, the scheme, if it goes ahead, will include some of the things you have already touched on, such as demolition and the need to replace schools, community facilities and community services. It is not just council-related; you also have the Colnbrook waste incinerator, the Harmondsworth immigration centre and a number of public services and public facilities that may be in different ownership. Should their replacement be funded out of this scheme? Is there any suggestion that some or all of them will be? Sorry, I have not mentioned council housing; I do not know whether any council housing is affected.
There is council housing affected. We would expect the council housing to be paid for under the same compulsory purchase arrangements as private property, so—
Q382 But will that fund the replacement housing at an appropriate cost?

Well, that is the next question. That is the next bit of work that we have to do. There is a tenant in there—what is our responsibility to that tenant, and does that require us to go on to the open market and buy properties? Is that sufficient? Because obviously it will not be in the south of the borough; it might be somewhere else. These are all the dilemmas and traumas that we are trying to grapple with at this moment in time. So is that funding package enough? I don’t know.

As for the other public buildings, we would expect them all to be paid for. We would also expect them to be safeguarded for future growth and capacity increases at the airport so that the public sector does not have to put its hand into its purse to improve them later down the line. I think that is a fair request. There are a lot of them, as well; there are a lot of impacts that we have to look at.
Q383 Anna, is there a precedent in planning policy for adopting a specific scheme as the basis to inform a national policy statement, and how do you think this has affected the draft NPS?
Is this with regard to the two airport proposals that are on the table right now?
Yes.

I am not personally aware of that going through. If you look at the other sector NPSs, there has not been a case like this. Going forward, however, if you are looking at needs of other infrastructure, it is somewhat predetermined by the locations of existing infrastructure. That is probably as far as I can answer that question.

We do not think that there is any precedent, and it is a huge concern for the councils. Dealing with one DCO is mind-numbingly terrifying; dealing with two at the same time is very significant. We think that there is a real risk , because at the moment the NPS is silent on how those two promoters should work together. There is not necessarily an obligation for there to be a common baseline or for them to have common forecasting, so you could end up at a development consent order examination , essentially arguing in two very different elements of the truth , and no one being clear on what the impacts or mitigations are. T here is a real requirement upon the NPS to set the rules of engagement in terms of competition between those two promoters . Otherwise, it is unworkable , and we just do not think it is there at the moment .

I would probably go a little further than that : I would say that it is absolute madness t o have two promoters on the scene at the same time. I think that, because of the way that the funding is given by the CAA , it is effectively getting one scheme for the price of two. A gain, that is ripe for challenge. The airlines are probably not going to want to see their money going down that route. I f two schemes are paid for , or allowed to be paid for , by the CAA , is that funding that is going to be taken off some of the other environmental improvements that the local authorities are seeking ?

W e talked about this on the trip : t he communities must somehow deal with two competing promoters and two competing DCOs . If someone i s trying to purchase their property and the aim is to get as many properties as possible purchased earlier in the process to enable the blight to be removed and people to make decision s, t hat is a resident potentially dealing with two separate law firms and two separate offers. It just starts to spiral from there , a nd that is before you have even got through to the examination, where you have two evidence bases , some probably different . I t is ri pe for legal challenge. It might speed things up now, but it is just kicking a massive can down the road , and it will be a massive problem when we get to the examination stage.
Q384 Do you think that there is a risk that the NPS could be predetermining some matters that would normally be examined at the DCO process ?

I would hope not , but if you have not predetermined some of the stuff between the two promoters, you are going to have fairly robust examination and two competing proposals being looked at equally. T hat is also fraught with danger . W e were talking about this before : the easiest thing to do would be for the planning inspector to approve both of them and give that to the Secretary of State to work out.

On the mechanism of it, you would see them as two separate applications that are also probably going through at separate timescales. I t is probably not a matter of planning policy, but in terms of the wellbeing of all people involved through a DC O process it will be incredibly challenging. How the Planning Inspectorate would have to manage that is a head - scratcher for me. W e want national policy statements to provide a clear foundation , but I think this one currently has ambiguity in it. T here are enough other areas we need to resolve ; t his might be one that we can get some agreement on to smooth what will be a challenging and complex process.

U ltimately, our residents just want certainty about what is happening next. T hey do not want to get through an examination process, and then have it all be taken to the courts with two developers having an argument in public. T hat cannot happen. There must be a way o f removing that risk , because it is going to be put on our communities , which have already had too much to bear.

Q385 Anna, how has the draft HENPS taken on board the legal challenges to the 2018 ANPS, and—this goes back to the debate about CNG I—could the strength of the economic welfare and strategic cases for expansion be tested through legal challenge?

I think that it has taken on a number of th e challenge areas , but this will be challenged in the courts going forward whether it has gone far enough or not, in the views of many. I think that it has gone quite a long way, but there i s still further it could go.

Q386 I s there anything else that you or any of the other panellists would like to bring to our attention that you have not already said , on how the draft HENPS will work as planning policy? We have covered quite a lot.

I think we have probably covered it ad nauseam. The thing to remember is that when we have normal planning development, it is set against a London plan as well as a local plan. A whole host of pass-or-fail tests sit within those policy documents. It comes back to that point that the draft HENPS seems to result in a yes, no matter what happens. That bit really is a concern for us. The last point is that if it does have to happen, our communities deserve better at the end of it than they got after the last time it was expanded.

The issue of affordability as a threat to achieving our obligations to safeguard our communities is a real challenge. The worst situation is that we put in blood, sweat and tears for the next couple of years trying to get the best possible—or least worst —scheme, only to be told, “Sorry, that is not affordable, so we are going to strip all this mitigation out.” That feels to me like a genuine risk in the current draft of the HENPS.
That is a case that the airlines have also raised with us.

It is. We are sympathetic to the airlines; we understand that they talk a lot about the cost of it and the fact that you undermine the very case for this by charging the £60, or whatever fees they were saying. At the same time, maybe this scheme is unacceptable—maybe that is the truth of it. At the very least, it must be mitigated in full. Who pays for that may be a different question.

To reflect a comment made on the previous panel, I think that the disjunction between the vision and intent and the detail on the deliverability and accountability is a real, critical factor with this. Some of the conditionality of the language—“may”, “seek to”, “try to” or “endeavour to”—makes it a very weak document in giving our local authorities some certainty and security around how this will play out in practice.
Anna, you said that it will be challenged and that there will be some kind of judicial review.
Well, it is likely.
Q387 I think you said “will”! Do you have a view on the grounds for that?

No, but I think it is fairly common that most DCO projects go through a judicial review process at the back end once a decision has been made. Whether the courts accept it or not, there are normally several lodged.

With the very nature of national infrastructure, you are creating an infrastructure asset regardless of its sector, and it has impacts on local people. Different promoters go about that in different ways, and that normally results in a challenge. The Thames Tideway tunnel, for example, is cheer-led as one of our national infrastructure gems—
Q388 So your view is that big stuff tends to be challenged; there is nothing specific in this proposal that concerns you.
Yes, my view is that big stuff gets challenged.
Q389 Does that add to the timeline?
Or has sufficient time been included? I know that they have factored in a legal challenge.

I am not a lawyer, and I can feel all my lawyer colleagues in NIPA staring at me from behind. There is obviously the JR reform process going on regarding judicial reviews on DCO projects, which is placing structural efficiencies in the process for national infrastructure projects. It would still add time to the process. Once a decision has been made by the Secretary of State in either direction, if there is a challenge, it will add time to the process. That goes to the certainty point that has been discussed here.

Thank you for your evidence and for the time you spent preparing for today. If there is anything that you did not get a chance to cover fully today and that you would like to expand on, please feel free to write to us.

sessions.iT: Scrutiny of the draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement
sessions.w: Heathrow Area Transport Forum; Transport for London; National Highways; Heathrow Southern Railway Ltd

segs.tx: Transport Committee
Oral evidence: Scrutiny of the draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement , HC 482
Tuesday 15 September 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 15 September 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Transport Committee members present: Ruth Cadbury (Chair); Steff Aquarone; Dr Scott Arthur; Jacob Collier; Daniel Francis; Alex Mayer.
Housing, Communities and Local Government Committee member present: Ashley Dalton.
Questions 280 – 3 37
Witnesses

I : Steven Costello, Director, Heathrow Southern Railway Ltd; Elliot Shaw, Chief Customer and Strategy Officer, National Highways; Anthony Smith, Chair, Heathrow Area Transport Forum; Alex Williams, Chief Customer and Strategy Officer, Transport for London .
Written evidence from witnesses:
– Heathrow Southern Railway Ltd
– Heathrow Area Transport Forum
– Transport for London
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Steven Costello, Elliot Shaw, Anthony Smith and Alex Williams.

Q280 Welcome to the fourth session of our scrutiny of the Government’s draft Heathrow expansion national policy statement. I welcome Ashley Dalton MP, who is joining us as a guest from the Housing, Communities and Local Government Committee . We will be hosting two panels this afternoon. During the first we will hear about surface transport to and from Heathrow airport, and our second panel will explore the impacts of expansion on the local area and the planning policy aspects of the national policy statement. C ould our first panel of witnesses please introduce themselves?
I am Steven Costello , director of Heathrow Southern Railway Ltd , the private company that is promoting a privately financed railway into Heathrow.
Good afternoon. I am Elliot Shaw, the c hief c ustomer and s trategy o fficer at National Highways.

I am Anthony Smith, the chair of the Heathrow Area Transport Forum, which is a statutory committee that brings together all the stakeholders, including National Highways and others, who are interested in how people and cargo get to and from the airport.
I am Alex Williams, the chief customer and strategy officer at Transport for London.

Q281 Transport for London was critical of the 2018 airports national policy statement—the last time the Government considered a third runway at Heathrow—saying that it failed to provide “a credible plan” for accommodating the additional surface trips caused by Heathrow expansion. Have the new draft HENPS and strategic vision now provided a credible plan? Heidi Alexander’s statement to the Commons said, in effect, that Heathrow expansion would have to prove that it could go ahead without turning the M25 and the M4 into a car park.

I was at the Select Committee in 2017 . I think you are probably quoting what I said, actually ; it is quite interesting to have it quoted back to you eight or nine years on. Unfortunately, I think we are in a worse position, in some ways—a weaker position—than we were in 2017. I think there are missed opportunities to address that and to strengthen the document.

We are weaker in the sense that in the previous version, there was a commitment or an aspiration from Heathrow to get no extra traffic. That is gone. The reality is that even if you met all the mode share targets—and I do not believe they will be met—you are still looking at 60,000 trips every day on the highway network in that vicinity. You will hear from Elliot on this, but we know that the M4 and the M25 are some of the most congested roads in the country, and adding that congestion to that part of west London will have a material impact on the economy, the environment and how the area functions generally. So ditching the no extra traffic aspiration is a step backwards, and not having anything on staff travel is a step backwards.

I think they have missed an opportunity on how you get more out of the existing infrastructure—the Piccadilly line, the Elizabeth line and HEx—because they could do a lot to help in this space. On western and southern rail access, there is a recognition that we should look at them, but the language is too weak. I think it refers to “necessary” and “may” in describing those schemes—we would use the words “essential” and “required”. So unfortunately we have taken a step backwards.

There are steps forwards, though. The Elizabeth line has come into operation and is a tremendous success. ULEZ has had an effect in dealing with the air quality issues. On the Elizabeth line, it is interesting and worth reflecting that when I was here eight years ago, looking at the mode share, the percentage of trips to the airport by public transport was 39.7%. Now, eight years on, we are at 42%. That is on the back of the Elizabeth line, effectively, and other changes—an £18 billion project gets you 2%. If you look at what we have to do with the mode share, we have to get another 13% on top of that, so the scale of the challenge is enormous, in the context of the growth of the airport as well. While the Elizabeth line is a benefit, it puts into context that that is the kind of investment you need to get genuine change in mode shift, really. I think a lot of what we said before still stands, but unfortunately in certain areas we are going backwards.
Thank you. I will give the others an opportunity to add to Alex’s comments.

We think the draft statement and the strategic vision for surface access that accompanied it has some really good ambition in it about making public transport the first and natural choice for people going to and from the airport, minimising the impact on the road network, prioritising environmental sustainability, and rail playing a central role. There is great ambition and great hope in there. Unfortunately, it is not quite clear how all that is going to be delivered and who it is going to be delivered by. I think that is what’s missing, essentially—the sense of delivery, the targets being stretching enough, who is going to be responsible for various bits and who is going to pay. There is lots more detail to come.

As Alex has said, it is worth reminding ourselves of the current challenge. Unfortunately, there’s two sets of data around about access—the Civil Aviation Authority’s and Heathrow’s own data. Looking at Heathrow’s own data, currently about one in two people get to the airport by a vehicle of some sort: about 28% are coming by taxi and private car, which includes the unfortunately named kiss and fly, and parking is about 22%. A lot of people are reaching Heathrow by vehicles, which of course has an impact on the local communities as well.

The public transport mode share is about 48.4%, on Heathrow’s figures, which is a big increase since 2015—in the last 10 years—so it is very much heading in the right direction. But it underlines the scale of the challenge that if you are going to go for 50% or 55% public transport, as the statement envisages, you need some pretty serious public transport interventions to make that happen. Of course, you are trying to attract people from the west and the south, which is not such a dense market. London is an easier market to serve—it is denser and a more tourism-orientated market. There is a huge challenge in there.
There is lots to praise in the Government’s documents, but an awful lot of detail is needed to make it a reality.

We have some thoughts similar to Anthony’s. When we look at the national policy statement, there is some really good ambition—we welcome the focus on surface transport, which is really good to see—but obviously the national policy statement itself sets out the criteria against which the promoter’s plans will be assessed. We will need to work with the promoters and see their plans in order to assess their deliverability. So that all needs to come. Our reflection is that it is early days at this point. There is lots of uncertainty and lots to work through, and we will need to do that as the plans come together.

As Alex said, the HENPS uses words like “may”, “could” and “ west and/or south ”. We are pleased that the strategic vision effectively describes our scheme—through-running services from Paddington and Heathrow down to Hampshire and Surrey, the Elizabeth line to Staines, and the Waterloo service—but of course that strategic vision has no statutory weight, and the HENPS is really almost silent on what is needed.

The vision also suggests that “upgrades to public transport can be made in an appropriately phased manner.” This is where it really differs from the 2018 NPS, which assumed that new runway capacity would effectively be full within two years of a new runway opening. Instead, this is a phased proposal—hence the triggers at 116 million and 130 million—but it is surely impossible to treat rail schemes in a phased manner. You cannot just switch on a rail scheme as and when capacity starts to hit this, to be honest, rather strange metric of terminal capacity. It is not passenger numbers but a notional metric around floor space.

The reality in our view is that there are complexities and timescales to consider, and the only way we should consider them in the NPS is by recognising that it needs a single, co-ordinated and integrated approach to both western and southern. These are not railways that are empty; the railways to the north and south of the airport are busy.

Also, there are not just the timescales to secure the infrastructure to consider. Even though we have spent 10 years developing a scheme that is credible and very widely supported and deliverable, we think we still need eight years to go out and build it and commission it.

The other reason why we think you need to take an integrated approach is affordability. Neither of the promoters’ cost estimates for expansion include surface access, and affordability is, as you heard from the airlines, a crucial issue.
To summarise, we think that it is important, if not essential, to move beyond recognition and ambition, and instead provide firm policy support for an integrated western and southern scheme.

Q282 On additional surface trips, and to pick up on what Anthony said, I noted that somebody’s evidence said that kiss and drop, and particularly private hire and quite a lot of taxis, can be four trips, whereas somebody driving and parking is two trips. Does anybody’s modelling understand that distinction? Is it significant, and if not, should it be?

It probably should be, yes. Understanding the demand management side of all this is very important, because to a degree the relative attractiveness of public transport is to do with the cost and convenience of the alternatives. Therefore, the cost of a taxi, the cost of parking and the cost of drop-off fees are very important. At some stage we need to understand from the promoters what they are suggesting in those areas, in order to understand what the drivers towards public transport are going to be.

For a lot of people taking a taxi is a very obvious choice. For disabled passengers, if you have luggage or if you are only making one trip a year, it is worth shelling out £50 or whatever to get to the airport. If you are really going to shift people and give them an incentive to use public transport, there has got to be quite a dramatic shift in understanding how all those capacities can be used better, and how the price signals to consumers can be more effective.

May I add a statistic ? You are quite right that it is important to recognise the disconnect between passengers, which in turn includes interlining passengers who never go out of the airport. Our modelling shows that currently—or, in 2025—with 84.5 million total passengers going through Heathrow and a declining number of interlining passengers putting more stress on the surface access network, it generated around 165,000 vehicle trips a day, excluding Heathrow staff.

Q283 The CAA stats have something like 27% of people travelling by tube, metro, subway or tram. Is that the last mile bit? Are they from London and have just used that, or might they have come by some other form of transport and then got on the tube? Do we know whether that distinction is being captured?
Is this the CAA surface access figures?
Yes.
We believe it should capture all public transport.
Yes, and they are saying it is now 42% by public transport.

Q284 Right. The public transport mode share targets remain very similar to those in the 2018 ANPS despite, as you have said, Heathrow making some progress towards those levels. Are the proposed targets in the HENPS achievable, and if so, are they sufficiently ambitious?

It is interesting that it is the same numbers as before. They are different timelines, but it is still the 50%, going up to 55%. It is interesting that last time, in 2017, we asked, “What is the evidence base behind that?” Effectively, I think it is what Heathrow thought could be achieved, rather than any evidence base from the DFT. This time we have asked the same question, “What is the evidence base for 50% and 55%?” Again, I think it is just a straight rollover from last time, rather than there being a good analytical base to say what is needed. The challenge we have is that even if they hit that level of 55%, you are still looking at substantial increases in highway trips on the network: 60,000 vehicle movements a day, if they meet those targets.

To go back to your core question about whether they are achievable, my concern, which I think is probably shared by colleagues from Southern Rail, is the lack of commitment or requirement for the additional connectivity in respect of western and southern rail. The lack of a funding strategy means that those schemes may not actually happen. If they do not happen, you have very little chance of achieving those mode shift targets.

The other important thing in the HENPS is that it does not recognise the importance of doing more with your existing assets, like the Piccadilly line, the Elizabeth line and the Heathrow Express. In London, for the first 20 years of our existence we achieved big changes in mode shift. We did not build any new infrastructure for that; we sweated the existing assets. What I find a bit disappointing in the HENPS as drafted is that it is silent on what more you can do on the existing assets. And you can do a lot. You could do the signalling on the Piccadilly line and that would substantially increase—
Eventually!

Well, the new fleets are coming. Four trains are in London being tested. They will come next year, but you do not get the maximum benefits unless you do the signalling there. You could more on the Elizabeth line. We have five more trains coming, and that will help in that regard, because you get four trains an hour to T5. But the converse is true on the Heathrow Express route, which has a reducing ridership and is taking up valuable paths that are not actually well used. There is a way of repurposing that to be more affordable and more attractive, and carry more public transport users.

To achieve that you have to do two things: capacity, which is sweating your existing assets, and connectivity, which is the new infrastructure that we have talked about before. As drafted, it is too weak on both of those issues.
That was really interesting, Alex, but we have a lot to get through and we need to keep responses succinct, please.
Anthony, do you want to add to that?

Any target is potentially achievable : if you invest enough in the thing and the alternatives are sufficiently unattractive , you will drive people towards using public transport, or attract them even better towards using public transport.

The piece of the jigsaw we are missing at the moment is: what are the rail schemes that are going to do the heavy lifting to deliver all these extra passengers to the airport? These are very significant numbers of extra passengers. Until the Government declare their hand , in a sense, about which rail schemes they are behind and are supporting, it is very difficult to see how the whole jigsaw fits together. Ultimately, the Government are going to have to say, “Yes, what’s being proposed fits in with the national rail network, and with the emergence of Great British Railways and its increased role in transport, rail access and planning.” We need to know what the Government are going to do. In theory, the answer is yes, but we need more detail.

Steven Costello : If I may say so, there is a simple solution. West and south need rail access. Heathrow says that, and we are very pleased that Heathrow supports our scheme. The HENPS actually describes our scheme. For us, it is a simple click over the ratchet for the NPS to support the western and southern rail schemes that we propose, which can be privately financed and brought forward before these, in effect, cliff-edge targets hit. Otherwise, you are expecting an airport operator to anticipate by eight to 10 years when it is going to hit these metrics—116 million and 130 million—and then hope that, at that time, there is rail network capacity, fleet and all of that available to implement. It would be much better to do it now and turn that ambition into reality.

From a highways perspective—other colleagues are better placed to talk about the deliverability of public transport schemes—we would expect, through the DCO process, the promoter to build confidence that there is a credible plan and then understand the knock-on impact for the highways.

There is an awful lot of uncertainty around the numbers at the moment. There is a wide variety of potential numbers around highways trips. That is going to depend on things like vehicle occupancy rates and passenger transfer rates—how many people are actually going out of the airport. We then need to understand the distribution of that: where it is impacting on the network, the timing and so on. There is a lot more work to do to understand the impact of that and what mitigations are necessary, and you would expect that to come through the DCO process .
Q285 Alex, what is stopping TfL doing the work on using existing capacity better? Why do you have to wait for the Government to point you in that direction?

We are doing some of that work. Piccadilly line trains are coming—four trains are being tested, and we have an order for the fleet to come in—and there are 10 trains coming on the Elizabeth line, which will increase the frequency to Heathrow. We are doing our bit, but you need to do more to deal with the huge increase in demand that you will get from Heathrow expansion. Signalling on the Piccadilly line is a key part of that, as is investigating what more you can do on the Elizabeth line. As I say, the Heathrow Express is an underused asset, and it is within the Government’s gift to make a decision on that. The biggest part of this is the Piccadilly line signalling, which does require money. That is the reality of it.
Q286 Is the draft HENPS clear about what will happen if public transport mode share targets are not met? Steven, you are shaking your head, so we will start with you.
It is in contrast with Gatwick’s DCO, where there is clear conditionality.
Does anyone have anything to add?
Same—it is not clear what will happen.

It is interesting that the Gatwick DCO was approved by the current Secretary of State; I find it a bit odd that that conditionality is missing from the HENPS. Further measures to ensure that it happens are really important.

Q287 Is a problem with our system that the DCO for a third runway will be just for what is within the perimeter, which the promoters will provide, and that the process does not allow for any other infrastructure outside the perimeter to be included in that DCO? It would have to be a separate DCO or another planning process. Is that correct?

I think so. What I would say, though, is that that adds weight to the importance of the HENPS getting it right. It is fine to have two separate consents. For example, with the Northern line extension to Battersea power station, we had a planning decision for the power station and a separate decision for the underground. They were connected by a Grampian condition that required it, but we had a very clear planning framework in which the two went together. This planning framework is not clear enough in my view.
Q288 Could it be?
That is why I think the language is important. Rather than saying that it “may include” these projects, it should say that they are required.

Q289 If it did say that, even though Heathrow Airport Ltd or Heathrow West Ltd do not operate and are not rail authorities, you could have a decision making that an absolute prerequisite for opening and running a third runway.

From a planning perspective, you have something called a Grampian condition. It basically says that it is not within the direct control of the applicant, but they cannot deliver the scheme until this other element has been delivered. I would use that principle, although I do not know how that would work with the DCO. That mechanism works from a planning perspective. You would not have got the Northern line extension without it, to be honest. It increases your leverage. You could increase your leverage over Heathrow by saying, “Actually, this is essential. You need to put your hand in your pocket.”

The HENPS does talk about the applicants—plural, perhaps—needing to bring forward a credible plan. In the interests of trying to present solutions rather than problems, our intention is to bring forward a transport and works Act application, in any case. When we started HSR, it was on the basis of a viable, deliverable and privately financeable scheme, with current two-runway capacity. It is certainly our intention to bring that forward next year, which is welcomed by Heathrow.
Q290 If it were conditioned, would it be conditioned within the DCO? Would there be in the HENPS some kind of expectation that was stronger than the current language?

Yes, but the other thing this leads to is the funding conversation. Part of the problem with the western and southern rail schemes is that the former Chancellor ruled out recourse to the public purse. Heathrow are saying they will make a contribution, and DFT is saying in here that it should make a contribution. There is a big gap there. From my perspective, it worries me that that gap will not be filled and the schemes will not happen. This uncertainty about funding leads us to believe that maybe those schemes will not happen.
Q291 Do you mean that the third runway could go ahead but the rail schemes not happen?

Because there is not funding certainty. To my mind, there is no route to fund those schemes at the moment. The HENPS should help you in that regard, in the way it did for the Northern line extension or the Barking Riverside extension.
Thank you. It is useful to get all of that on the record.
If I may, we do have a funding proposal.
Yes, I am aware that you have a funding proposal.

Q292 Dr Arthur : Alex, I will ask you a leading question, if that is okay, because it will save us a bit of time. About 80,000 people work at Heathrow airport. The 2018 plan had a mode share target just for the staff, with the staff travel plan coming in. The current plan—the HENPS—does not have a mode share target, does it? Is that good enough?
You want me to be brief, so I will say no. The other context is that the employee base is going to grow, isn’t it?
Q293 Many of them are low-paid staff, of course, in some posts—that is an important consideration.

This is the omission, really. Not having a workplace target is an omission in my view. Often in the planning process, you would refer to a travel plan for this, and that is not even referenced. The fact on staffing numbers is that there is not a target, but there is significant growth with expansion. I think that is an error and an omission. I do not understand why it is not there. We were suggesting combining the two so that there would be an overarching target for passengers and staff.
Q294 Getting that right makes it easier for them to recruit staff to work in those positions.
Yes.

Q295 Thinking more broadly, we have heard a lot about trains, particularly from Steven. Another part of the jigsaw is buses and, for Alex’s benefit, coaches. Is there enough in the current plan to think about how bus and coach services will connect to the site, thinking about the road network and the site itself?

For one, we have invested a lot in buses to the airport through the Superloop network, which is well received and well used. To be fair to Heathrow, I think they are looking at improvements to the bus services in the area, because I think they recognise the employment—
Q296 But is there enough in the plan for the expansion?

I think there could be more there. To be fair to them and DFT, I think there is a recognition that the bus has an important role to play, particularly if you think about this as a 24-hour operation. A lot of the buses start very early in the morning to deal with the shift patterns that they have. On coaches, it is also a really important catchment if you think about those coming from Oxford or Reading. In the absence of rail connectivity, coach has a big role to play. The coach facility at Heathrow is, I think, the largest in the UK after Victoria, so I think there is a recognition of the importance there. I probably need to have another look at whether you could do more there, but, to be fair to them, I think they recognise that that is an important mode that they need to protect to serve the airport going forward.

Q297 Overall, in terms of getting the modal shift just right, is it enough just to invest in bus and coach connections—as well as train connections—or should we be putting restrictions on the scale of parking in and around the site? Obviously, that is an important income source for the airport—about £200 million a year just now—but should we be constraining the site on parking? We do that with other applications, do we not?

We do. At the moment, we have 21,000 parking spaces in Heathrow, and we are looking to go to 36,000—some of the largest car parks in western Europe. They will be very near the road network. The concern is that the scale of increase in demand is counter to the modal shift targets. If you make it easier for people to park very near a terminal, with immediate access from the motorway network, and improve that convenience, how will you encourage them to get on the train?

There is also a contrast between all the highway assets. The car park and the M25 are all fully paid for. None of them the public transport products is committed in terms of funding, other than the stuff that we are doing on Picc line trains, so although I think public transport first is a nice statement, in reality the funding is principally there for the road infrastructure and getting there by car.
Q298 You are looking restless, Anthony, as we talk about car parks.

It always makes me nervous. I think it is a very good point about staff. Currently about half the staff at Heathrow do not work for Heathrow, so it has much more limited control over them. About one in two people come in by car. It is a tough nut to crack with the staff because, to a degree, it forms an attractive part of the proposition for employers. If you have come off shift at three in the morning, do you want to wait at a bus stop or get in your own warm car? But it generates an awful lot of traffic and needs thinking about.

The amount of car parking and the relative cost of it is crucial. As I said before, this whole debate needs to be thought about very carefully. Bus and coach are really important. Yes, they have a lot of lifting to do in and around the local communities. Coach has been relatively successful, I think, and Heathrow, to its credit, has invested quite a lot in the bus network around the airport as well, with good success. With sustained funding and good advertising, it is starting to build up some quite good traffic. That just needs to be massively sustained and grown, although sometimes people say, “The last thing I want outside my house at three in the morning is a bus idling”, so there is an interesting tension with the local communities there. Bus and coach have a lot to do in this.

Q299 Everyone wants to be near a bus stop, but they do not want it right outside their door. Do you support the idea of capping parking provision on site as well, but perhaps with a separate limit for staff?

I think it will naturally have a limit, but how that impacts the affordability of the overall schemes and the availability of funding for public transport is very interesting. There is a whole debate here about potentially hypothecating some of these income streams for public transport so that people know there is going to be quite a lot of car parking, but all the income for that will go towards clear public transport schemes. There is lots more debate there.

From our perspective, we need to understand all the trips that are on the road. I agree that it is about passengers, but it is also about staff. Freight, particularly during construction, will be important as well in terms of parking. I think that should be set out within the wider context of the transport plans. It is about how all that comes together. We would expect the promoter to pull all that together in their modelling.

Q300 On local buses, a local resident said that the free bus scheme for the airport’s immediate environment, which local residents benefited from, was paused during covid and is still not back up and running. Is that correct?
That is correct, yes.
Q301 Do we know why?
Funding, presumably.
Q302 But the airport funded that?
Yes. It would be very attractive to reintroduce it.
They have an income stream with the drop-off charge that could be used for this purpose.

I do not want you to think that we are obsessed with rail only. Our modelling looks at the whole picture. In its July 2025 submission to Government, Heathrow said that increasing public transport mode share targets is not possible through bus and coach alone. Local bus is very strong for staff. It can serve much more discrete local markets and get people closer to the workplace, but coaches just are going to be on the same overcapacity bits of the road network that everybody else is.

On terminal drop-off charge, what Alex says is right, and we are pleased that the vision supports hypothecation, as do TfL and HATF. It was always intended that the drop-off charge should be used to fund sustainable surface access. Alex spoke earlier about how you make mode share tick up with new heavy rail. It is interesting that history shows that increasing the terminal drop-off charge does not move the dial at all on mode share.
We were out visiting the local authority, and it said it thought originally that the drop-off charge was hypothecated but that it had not been connected through.
Let us move on to specifics of the rail schemes , although some of the questions may have already been answered.

Q303 Steven, you said that you cannot just switch on a rail scheme. The HENPS and the strategic vision talk about requiring a credible plan for any future rail enhancement. What do you think that would look like?

I think you know what we are going to say—it is our scheme. When we say that we have spent 10 years developing it, people sort of look a bit askance. It is because we started by looking all the way back to 1957 and Sir Alfred Bossom’s monorail and all the various schemes that many of you will be familiar with, most recently things such as Airtrack, the mayor’s scheme and SWELTRAC . We wanted to examine the reasons why they had failed. Heathrow is unique among huge airports in just being at the end of a branch line. We found that it was a mixture of local impacts, things such as level-crossing barrier downtime, cost, journey times not being competitive with road but also affordability.

The sweet spot that we have settled on is a scheme that is a very short piece of new railway that is almost all tunnelled so that there is very little surface access or community impact. It is relatively cost efficient and is an efficient piece of design. Although we do not specify the services that should operate over the infrastructure, because that is not in our gift, we have modelled three service patterns, and they attract both airport and non-airport users. Even on a two-runway business case, it has a very compelling financial business case, but also a very high benefit-cost ratio and even higher wider economic benefits.

We think that is the credible plan, and we are pleased that Heathrow support it. It is not as if we have plucked something out of the air; it is a scheme that has been engineered, costed, independently validated and tested. As well as bringing forward an application, the next step for us is that we are pleased to have support for what we call a “senior reference group that pulls together the various agencies and actors that control the various bits of the puzzle needed to bring this together.

Q304 On western rail access, we have had written evidence from Hillingdon that the land originally required for construction is no longer available under the third runway masterplan. Is western rail access actually deliverable if Heathrow expansion does go ahead?

When we started, although we are called Heathrow Southern Railway, we always took the view that you need an integrated approach to both western and southern access. You cannot abandon one corridor to be reliant on road. I think the scheme you are talking about was originally known as “WRATH” and then became “Western Rail Link to Heathrow”. That was abandoned in 2021. It was a scheme that simply linked terminal 5 to the Great Western main line, heading in a north-westerly direction. The problem with that was twofold. One, it was very expensive, and it only had any utility for airport passengers. Also, it assumed use of the Heathrow Express train paths —that the trains that come out of Paddington along the Great Western would go through Heathrow and then carry on up to Reading. That effectively precludes any southern scheme from serving Hampshire and Surrey , as we do. You end up with two shuttle services each side of Heathrow, which is a waste of that very valuable Great Western capacity, which TfL recognises.

We have developed an alternative scheme, which I will not go into detail on, but it is cheaper and delivers the same or greater benefits. It is useful to non-airport passengers, so it still provides that very important western access, but in an integrated way with the southern one.
Q305 Alex, what rail enhancements does TfL need to see?

As I said earlier, we believe that there is one on capacity improvements of existing assets, and another on connectivity. We very much believe that some form of those western and southern rail schemes is needed. The HENPS recognises that, although we think that that language should be strengthened.

One thing I would add to what Steve said is to look at the contrast with where we were in 2017. In 2017, NR and DFT had teams working on both those projects. We got close to a TWA application for western rail, and there were teams looking at private financing for southern rail.

Now you do not have clear accountability about who is leading on that. There i s no one in DFT working on it, as far as I know. NR has not responded to this consultation; it transitioned to GBR. There is an issue about who is picking up and running with those schemes . Steve and his team are advocates for them , but f rankly , it should be a public body that leads and runs with them. That ambiguity is not helpful when everyone here is saying those schemes are essential, and we have a funding challenge as well.

That is where we have stepped backwards from 2017: there is no clear leader or resource leader . T hose are complicated schemes, and you need a lot of work to get the evidence base for the consent to get them over the line. At the moment, no one is leading them.

I think your question is also very relevant because of the timing of all this . T he expansion statement and the targets should support and enable the expansion . That means the public transport alternatives need to be there relatively early, so that people start using them and embedding the habit early. I f you are trying to shift people out of cars in 20 years ’ time, when you have 130 million passengers , it is harder, harder, harder. T he point about the credible plan is really also to do with timing and getting the alternatives in place.
W e could write to the Committee afterwards to expand on Alex ’ s concern, because we are working with DFT, the Treasury, Network Rail and others.

Q306 Okay , t hank you. M y question is about th e matrix of potential future and existing rail and underground lines , and so on. A ll are coming in and out of the existing airport and terminals. That means those terminals —t erminal 5, terminal 4 and the c entral t erminal a rea — have to link to the new infrastructure. Does that present physical challenges? H as either promoter provided you with an adequate explanation of how passengers and staff will move between the existing airport and what is effectively a new airport to the north?

We are working closely with promoters. It is important on t erminal 5 to recognise that, in a great piece of foresight, there is the passive provision for two new platforms and the tunnels extend ing out. The CTA station is constrained, but our starting point was that Heathrow ’ s own network and the wider rail network are both constrained. We cannot just drop extra trains on.
Q307 All those links are currently underground, and you will have many more passengers moving through them.
We have not got into the detail of that . T o be fair to them , I think they would be up for that kind of conversation.
Q308 Is there a shortage of space for that increase in passengers?

Potentially, yes. T hat is something we have to look at. There is also a secondary debate about construction because this will not be a quick scheme ; it is going to be a long time . I f you think about how long T5 took —
Do you have a nything to add, Anthony?

Only that more detail is needed. Y ou are quite right that t he scale of this is immense, and a lot of it will be underground .
