Moving on to the aspect of community sentences, you mentioned already the feedback that you had from children about experiences of community sentences in terms of victims, but what about those who are receiving those sentences? What feedback have you had from them?

Community sentences can be really effective . Where youth offending teams are strong, the community sentences are really good . They are particularly strong where there is some mentoring involved and where there are some really clear and robust actions. Psychologically, it is good for young people when they have done something wrong, when they have offended, to make reparation, put things right and have a moment of reflection.

I have seen good community sentences. I am pleased about the rehabilitation orders going to first-time offenders. I think w e should do more of it. That is what I wanted to say. I have given you examples, haven’t it?

Q144 Yes. If you had the responsibility for improving community-based sentences and making them more effective for children, in terms of both the offenders and the victims, what changes would you make?

Sometimes courts are too chaotic. The experience is really chaotic . Children’s education and care arrangements are often missing. You get a community sentence, but they have not thought about that side of it. For victims, it is really effective communication. So o ften victims say to me, “If only someone had just written to me and told me.” Victims need to know what is happening , be kept in the loop , understand it and have a sense that this will have an impact and this is good. It is more about communication.

Rather than carrying it out in a perfunctory way, we need to listen to both the victims and the offenders, talking through their experience with them and making sure we are thinking about the evidence base. Again, I go back to those Southport rioters. When I went and spoke to all of them, the ones who got custodial sentences and otherwise, whatever they had been accused of doing, their experiences were all different. They had a unique take on it, and what worked for them was different.

For some of those Southport rioters, just going on that course and learning about the people who could have been sitting behind the window when they had thrown the bricks through them was enough to horrify them. I talked to boys who said, “I was horrified about the damage I could have done.” In that community sentence, they learnt about that. For some of them, it was getting a mentor, someone who would support them.

It is about listening to the young people, understanding their experience and getting it right, but not disrupting their care or their education situation as well, because you can mess up something that is going to be the thing that will really help get that child on the straight and narrow , such as a college course. It is really disheartening when you see that.
Q145 You mentioned that the courts are chaotic.
They can be.
Q146 Is that because the children are not being dealt with in the youth courts? Is that because they do not have legal representation? What is going on? Courts should not be chaotic.
I do not think the moment is chaotic.
Q147 You think it is not addressing their education. That is important.

Yes. There is a movement to think about whether we should have youth courts. I have seen youth courts in the States , for example, with superb, really well-trained judges in the youth courts who are so impressive. In LA, they were amazing in the way they talked to young people, took their views, and the decision making and the thoughtfulness of it.

Maybe it is more of a reflection of our entire system and the pressure on it at the moment . I have spoken to the P resident of the Family Division about this ; I have not talked to the criminal judges as much. There is something about being able to communicate and speak to young people , and understand what their lives might look like when it comes to some of the decisions that are made.
Q148 Is there a training issue for judges here?

We have incredibly well-trained judges. This is simply an observation. I have had pushback when I have spoken to judges about this , but I was very struck by how skilled the judges in LA were at working with youth and families. They were incredibly skilled. It made children in absolutely harrowing cases feel safe, protected and heard. That is what we want, is it not, for victims and for perpetrators?

Q149 Thank you. We have spoken about the target to reduce those who are remanded in custody. The Government have a target. The Government believe that the sentencing reforms and widening the use of community sentences will reduce the number of children in custody by about 20%. I have a couple of questions on that. First, is that a sufficiently ambitious target?
Were they talking about the overall number of children in custody by 20% or the remanded children by 20%?
Q150 No, this is the overall number.

Okay. We are obviously all aware that the number of children in custody has shrunk, and it is a success story. There are only about 450 or so children in the YOIs, and that is a success story. As to s hrinking that by another 20% , g iven that 50% of those probably are on remand, that leaves 30% still on remand in there. They could do better.

Come on. I would want to give them a bigger target than that. Of the remand population, 5% to 10% of the current population might need remanding into YOIs — nobody else. We have to do better. It costs a fortune. I would rather see local authorities setting up really good secure accommodation and offers. It would be much better.

Q151 Thank you. I have one more question. I do not know if anybody else has any other s . D o you have any other reflections on the broader work that you have done on the state of the secure youth estate? Y ou have given a lot of information today, which has been really helpful , but do you have any final reflections?

I am really pleased that Jake Richards, the J ustice Minister, asked my team and me a few months ago—and we have been working hard on it—to look at education in the YOIs and to make some suggestions about the way forward. That was with him knowing that I think we should close them. None the less , there are mainly boys there. It is all boys now, is it not? They need a decent education.

In terms of a silver bullet, or some ways forward, we have to do better than the current education offer. I have talked extensively to governors, to prison officers and to those delivering education. I have been taking in educators from AP and mainstream schools to look at it . There is a huge will to do better. The boys themselves talk to me about wanting to make sure they can pass their exams, their maths, their English, and have tutoring to get that done. Often, the YOI classroom does not work. Having a one-on-one tutor for that would help.

They talk about the desire for more vocational courses, which is really good for them. I have spoken so harshly about Feltham, but actually I have seen some of the best vocational work going on there such as horticulture and painting. There is just not enough, and the governor knows that. We should invest in this. They should be out there doing that every day. They want sport.

The Education Act tells us that every child is entitled to spiritual, moral, social and cultural education, and those children in the YOIs no less. They need to think about who they are as human beings and how they are going to function afterwards. We will shortly publish a way forward, and we would love to talk to this Committee about it. We are proud of the Minister for being bold enough to ask us to have a look at that.

Q152 Thank you for that. That sounds more optimistic in terms of YOIs really being significant and making a difference in children’s lives . A s well as the education to improve our YOIs like Feltham —i t is really positive to hear that —w here else do you think that really significant positive changes could take place , briefly?

Education is my big one. I also think things like community work and the boys working and engaging in the running of their YOIs is good . I sat with a little boy the other day in Feltham, and I said, “What do you want to be?” He said, “I want to be a chef.” I said, “I’ll find you a chef to talk to. We’ll get you some work experience when you get out.” Also, get him helping running the food.

There is something about recognising that the YOI needs to be home. If it is going to be home, we have to treat the young people in it so that they can help run it and be part of it. In the old days, although there was lots wrong 30 years ago in the system, the prison officers had the time to sit on the wing with the boys, play a game of draughts, mentor them and have an almost fatherly relationship, which is often something that is missing. That is important.

Think of the human. I want to read you one thing. When I was in Feltham, the boys were writing letters to their future selves. Most of them said, “My future self will have made my mum proud. I’ll have sorted myself out.” They are boys. Here, o ne boy said, “To my future self. Well done for changing your mindset, not for focusing on the easy, illegal money any more . I’m so proud you’re standing here today with all of your building qualifications and your bricklaying business, and the fact that you came from a broken home but managed to defy all the odds is something to be proud of.” That is what we need to be tapping into.

I did not see one letter “ T o my future self” from the boys at Feltham that was not hopeful, that was not grateful to their parents, that was not thinking about their education and trying to think about becoming better people. That is what we need. We need the YOIs, if they are going to exist, to turn into engine rooms to support this.
That is a lovely, positive note to end on, especially for our YOIs. Thank you.

Q153 It is really encouraging to hear. It is the experience of this Committee as well , when we have been into prisons and we have seen some of the educational and practical work that they do , that it is very good but there is not enough of it.

It is patchy, is it not? They have the space. It is t hinking about what the education model should be. Lots of these big firms build prisons. They can build some vocational spaces. We have to make it better if we are going to use them. We have to make it better.
I agree.
Q154 We will wait to receive the report that you will be doing. As a general comment, what do you think we should be doing more to improve the standard of education in YOIs?

I will go with something really practical . If you are sent to a YOI, you should have the best teachers in the country. The moment of greatest crisis is when we need the best teachers in there. They need to be the personal tutors who are doing the maths and English. I have met children in there who have serious special educational needs and who need basic literacy help. I have met absolute geniuses who should be doing their Open University physics course.

There should be that personal tutoring. We should draw on our brilliant education system. All the school trusts and schools that I talk to are putting their hands up. They are saying, “Let us do that.” We need to somehow unleash that.

Then it is vocational. The stress relief of learning to paint, painting the house, whatever the vocation al is, combined with the skill development so that when you go out there is a job to do and you do not have to go back to the easy money , is absolutely right . We also need skilled philosophers, theologians and personal development people talking to those boys and saying, “If you’ve killed someone, you ’ re going to think hard about what it is to exist and who you are.” We need to be answering that with both whatever religious tradition they come from and people who can help them work through that. It is not just trauma - informed and therapy ; i t is more than that. On the education side, there is a piece to do.
Th at brings us to the end of the questioning and the end of this session. Thank you very much for your evidence ; i t has been really helpful and informative.

sessions.iT: Broadcasting in Wales

segs.tx: Welsh Affairs Committee
Oral evidence: Broadcasting in Wales, HC 598
Wednesday 9 September 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 9 September 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Ruth Jones (Chair); Ann Davies; Simon Hoare; Gerald Jones; Llinos Medi; Andrew Ranger; Steve Witherden.
Questions 1- 5 0
Witnesses
I : Delyth Evans, Chair, S4C, and Geraint Evans, Chief Executive, S4C.
I I : Garmon Rhys, Interim Director of BBC Cymru Wales, and Rhys Evans, Head of Corporate Affairs, BBC Cymru Wales.
II I : Zoe Thomas, Head of News and Programmes, ITV Cymru Wales, and Magnus Brooke, Director of Strategy, Policy and Regulation, ITV.
Written evidence from witnesses:
– [Add names of witnesses and hyperlink to submissions]
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Delyth Evans and Geraint Evans.

Q1 Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to this oral evidence session of the Welsh Affairs Committee. My name is Ruth Jones. I am the Member of Parliament for Newport West and Islwyn and Chair of the Committee. Today the Committee is holding a one-off evidence session on broadcasting in Wales, and we have three short panels, with Welsh interpretation for those who require it among the Members, witnesses and those in the Public Gallery. Before I ask the witnesses to introduce themselves, do any Members have any interests to declare?
Members indicated dissent.
Will the witnesses introduce themselves—very briefly, please?
(Translation) Good afternoon, everybody.
(Continues in English) My name is Delyth Evans and I am the chair of S4C.
(Translation) Good afternoon.
(Continues in English) I am Geraint Evans and I am the chief executive of S4C.
Q2 Thank you very much and, as I say, thank you for appearing before us in person this afternoon; it is much appreciated.

Between the two of you, could you set out the state of play for S4C in the current media landscape? Obviously, we are here to talk about the charter, but could you give us a very broadbrush, but very brief, setting for it?

We are the only Welsh-medium public service broadcaster in the United Kingdom. We serve audiences across Wales and outside of Wales in all parts of the United Kingdom who wish to access our services. We have a linear channel, but we are increasingly moving towards digital platforms: we have a presence on YouTube, we are on iPlayer, we have our own player called Clic and we are on all the social media these days, as everybody has to be. We are increasing our younger viewers on those platforms, which is obviously a key audience to us, while maintaining our linear services, which are also very important for older audiences.
Q3 Thank you. Geraint, Delyth mentioned digital and online streaming. To what extent do global streaming services and other digital content pose a threat to S4C as a public service broadcaster?

Thank you, Ruth. I think there is a threat and an opportunity. Thanks for the opportunity to give evidence today, because we are at a critical time for the future of public service broadcasting in the UK and in Wales. A number of things have been passed, such as the Media Act. We are still waiting for the prominence code from Ofcom, which should be here in a year’s time or so. In the meantime, we are still having to compete for prominence on connected TVs. We have a new Green Paper from the Government, of course, which we will be happy to discuss. All these things are coming together at the same time as charter review, which will decide on the future funding of S4C. That is the key thing for us.

There are two key elements that really do feel important for S4C. One is prominence, so that we are able to compete on all platforms, on connected TVs, with other broadcasters, and the other is future funding. We were very pleased to see in the charter review that the Secretary of State is reinforcing once again that S4C needs sufficient funding. We were very grateful to hear that.

The question will be: what does “sufficient funding” mean, and for what purpose? For us, it has to be more than maintaining a linear TV channel. As Delyth mentioned, we have to serve numerous platforms—players as well as social media and YouTube—and that takes more money. In our submission on charter review, we very much made the case that S4C will need at the very least the same funding we have now, with inflationary increases, for a significant period to come, but we will need even more if we are going to be able to serve all audiences, including younger people, and to really tackle the competition that we face. The competition now is from the streamers, of course, and from YouTube, where people are increasingly spending their time—and people are not watching television as much any more.

All those things come together at a crucial point. I do not think I am exaggerating when I say that this is as crucial a time for S4C as when people campaigned for this channel, because without sufficient funding, the very future of S4C and Welsh language broadcasting is in jeopardy.
Thank you, Geraint. Let me bring in Steve Witherden.
Q4 Will you outline the reach of S4C in terms of viewers, and its economic impact in terms of commissioning content and supporting production companies in Wales?

Data is measured in lots of different ways now, Steve. We measure our linear TV reach, which can be, on an average week, around 300,000 people. The bulk of those are within Wales, but we reach audiences beyond Wales as well because of the Welsh-speaking diaspora across the UK, and also sometimes because our content, particularly maybe sports content, appeals beyond our borders. There is that reach in one sense.

Increasingly, we are also measuring the digital platforms. Following a recent development with BBC iPlayer—where we have gone into a new deal with iPlayer so S4C’s content is more prominent on the homepage, whereas previously it was in a walled garden where you had to go looking for it—we have seen the reach and the number of monthly active users on BBC iPlayer increase quite significantly from where it was last year. It is up from around 200,000 monthly users last year to 250,000 monthly users now. We are seeing that growth, but again, that underlines the need for investment in platforms and the importance of negotiating deals for prominence.

Q5 Fe wna i siarad yn Gymraeg os yw hynny’n iawn. Yn eich hymateb i’r Papur Gwyrdd, gwnaethoch chi ofyn am gyllido dros nifer o flynyddoedd er mwyn sicrhau ansawdd rhaglenni Cymraeg ac i gael rhaglenni o ansawdd. Ydych chi’n hapus gyda’r cyfle rydych chi wedi cael a’r mewnbwn rydych chi wedi gallu rhoi mewn i’r broses o ymgynghori sydd wedi bod yn rhan o’r Papur Gwyrdd?

(Translation) I am going to be speaking in Welsh, if that is okay. In your Green Paper response, you asked about multi-year funding so that the quality of Welsh-medium programmes could be assured, and for there to be high-quality programmes. Are you happy with the opportunity that you have had and the input that you have been able to have as part of the consultation process around that Green Paper?

Fi’n teimlo ein bod ni wedi cael cyfle i fynegi barn a chael gwrandawiad teg. Mae gyda ni berthynas agos gyda swyddogion yn yr Adran Ddiwylliant, felly mae’r trafodaethau yna’n mynd yn eu blaen. Gwnaethon ni anfon papur i mewn yn cynrychioli’n safbwynt ni’n gryf iawn ac yn esbonio’r angen am barhad cyllideb ar gyfer darlledu trwy’r Gymraeg. Ers i ni roi’r papur yna i mewn, mae yna lot o fynd a dod wedi bod, cwestiynau ychwanegol, a maen nhw eisiau eglurhad. Fi yn teimlo ein bod ni wedi cael cyfle teg i fynegi’n safbwynt a dadlau’n achos, ond mae penderfyniadau mawr yn dal i gael eu gwneud, a bydd rheiny’n andros o bwysig i ni.

(Translation) I feel that we have had the opportunity to express our views, and we feel that we have been listened to fairly. We have a close relationship with officials in the Culture Department, so those discussions are ongoing. We sent in a paper that clearly represented our standpoint that there was a need for continuity of funding for Welsh-medium broadcasting. Since we put that paper in, there has been a lot of to-ing and fro-ing, lots of additional questions, and they want clarification on certain things. I do feel that we have had a fair opportunity to express our standpoint and argue our case, but these major decisions remain to be made, and they will be very important to us.

Ac eto, rydyn ni’n ddiolchgar i chi am ein gwahodd ni fan hyn i roi tystiolaeth heddiw. Dyw S4C ddim wedi rhoi tystiolaeth seneddol penodol ar adolygiad y siarter tan y pwynt yma. Fel corff sy’n cael ei gyllido gan y broses yma—gan y ffi drwydded—a bydd ein hariannu yn y dyfodol yn cael ei benderfynu o ganlyniad i’r broses yma, rydyn ni yn credu ei bod hi’n bwysig bod llais S4C yn cael ei glywed fel ein bod yn gallu parhau i wasanaethu ein cynulleidfaoedd ni gyda chyllid digonol ar gyfer y dyfodol.

Ar rai o’r pethau rydyn ni wedi gofyn amdanyn nhw, dw i ddim eisiau manylu gormod ar beth dw i wedi dweud yn barod, ond rydyn ni angen mwy na beth rydyn ni’n ei gael ar hyn o bryd er mwyn gallu gwasanaethu cynulleidfaoedd yn effeithiol. Os ydyn ni’n credu mewn darlledu gwasanaeth cyhoeddus, os ydyn ni’n credu yn nyfodol yr iaith Gymraeg, os ydyn ni eisiau i bobl ifanc fwynhau cynnwys S4C, mae’n rhaid i S4C fod yn gallu gwasanaethu ar blatfformau maen nhw’n gwylio ac mae hynny’n gofyn am gyllideb tipyn mwy na chyllideb teledu llinol fel mae wedi bod yn y gorffennol.

Yr un pwynt arall hoffen i ei wneud o ran yr adolygiad siarter ac un pwynt sy’n bwysig i ni; yn ogystal â’r ffi drwydded sy’n ariannu S4C gyda tua £100 miliwn ar hyn o bryd y flwyddyn, rydyn ni hefyd yn cael cyflenwad o raglenni gan y BBC, sy’n cyfateb i tua £20 miliwn y flwyddyn. Un o’r pwyntiau dw i wedi ei wneud yn eithaf clir yn adolygiad y siarter yw ein bod ni’n awyddus nid yn unig i sicrhau bod ’na gynnydd chwyddiant i’n cyllideb ni, ond bod yna gynnydd chwyddiant yn cael ei warchod ar gyfer y cyflenwad rhaglenni yna hefyd, achos heb hynny, mae ’na berygl y gallai fod yn agored i gael ei dorri. Rydyn ni’n ymwybodol o’r heriau ariannol y mae’r BBC yn eu hwynebu ar hyn o bryd. Mae posibilrwydd y gallai hynny effeithio ar gyflenwad rhaglenni S4C. Beth ry’n ni’n gofyn i’r Ysgrifennydd Gwladol i’w wneud, felly, yw diogelu’r cyflenwad yna yn adolygiad y siarter fel bod y gwerth yna, yr £20 miliwn, yn cael ei warchod a’i gynyddu gyda chwyddiant.

(Translation) We are very grateful to you for in viting us here to give evidence today, because S4C has not given parliamentary evidence specifically on the charter review until this point. As an organisation that is funded by this process—by the licence fee—and as our future funding will be decided on the basis of this process, we feel that it is important for S4C’s voice to be heard so that we can continue to serve our audiences, given this big issue of sufficient funding for the future.

Q10 I want to ask about some possible changes to the BBC’s public purposes. If those changes are made, how can minority language broadcasting be recognised and strengthened in those changes?

Q11 The BBC’s fourth public purpose is to “r eflect, represent and serve the diverse communities of all of the United Kingdom's nations and regions ”. Does that complement or compete with S4C’s objectives?

It very much complements our objectives. We are both public service broadcasters and public service media organisations. Our role is to represent the communities across Wales, and the BBC across the whole of the United Kingdom. Our strapline is “ showing our world through the Welsh language ”—“ dangos ein byd drwy’r Gymraeg ”. That is about giving a voice to communities. Ofcom has done quite a lot of interesting research on what people value in public service broadcasting from both the BBC and S4C. It is about hearing their own lives and seeing their own experiences reflected back at them. In a world that is so dominated by the big American streaming platforms, having somewhere representing our communities and our cultures in both Welsh and English is absolutely critical to the future of how the UK operates and to us bringing people together. That is part of the role of the BBC and S4C.

And there has been talk of growth becoming another public purpose for the BBC, so that the BBC can be a catalyst for economic growth. We feel very much the same way. In some ways, we adopt the public purposes that the BBC has in what S4C does. What you will see from the funding that S4C gets from the licence fee is: the GVA that is delivered is around £1.70 for every £1 that we receive from licence fee funding; we support 2,500 jobs around Wales; and we support work and skills development in communities all over Wales. Of our spending, 57% of that is spent outside Cardiff, which is very important to us, because we want to support skills development and growth in the creative industries in north-east, north-west and west Wales, as well as in Cardiff. We would very much adopt that public purpose.

Q14 Welcome back to our second panel on broadcasting in Wales. Can I ask our witnesses to introduce themselves?
I am Garmon Rhys. I am the interim director of BBC Cymru Wales.

Q15 Brilliant, thank you very much. It is good to see you both again. We are looking at BBC Cymru Wales now. How well do you think BBC Cymru Wales is performing in the current media landscape?

BBC Wales plays a unique role in Welsh national life. We reach 88% of the audience every week, provide trusted news and information services, reflect Wales to itself and the rest of the UK, support Welsh culture, and help sustain democratic debate and understanding.

Our challenge is that we need to change the way we serve audiences in both languages. Consumption habits are changing, and we have been going through the process of changing the way we work and the way we deliver our services for many years, but that change is only accelerating. We want to ensure that we remain the most trusted, valued and relevant media organisation in Wales, so we need to do more to continue to grow our reach on our digital platforms, but also do more on third-party platforms. But the challenge is that we need to do that while our funding is under significant pressure. The fundamental challenge is that 94% of people in the UK consume the BBC every month, but only 80% of households pay the licence fee. My concern is that, without reform of the licence fee, we will be facing a position of managed decline.

I would start by saying how vital it is that we are having this debate today. This is a pivotal moment, not just for BBC Cymru Wales institutionally but for Wales as a nation. So much of Welsh culture, be that Anglophone culture or Welsh language culture, relies on what BBC Cymru Wales and—you heard from them just now—S4C do.

We are in the charter review process, and we are very much listening to what our audience is saying. We had a very big survey out last year that had 38,000 respondents. To go over it very briefly, 92% of Wales said that it was very important that the BBC continues to provide trusted information. Some 85% said that it is important that the BBC provides the best home-grown storytelling, and 74% said that it is important that the BBC uniquely brings the nation together. Alongside that, there is a clear desire for the BBC to have greater independence, and for its independence from any Government to be reinforced. Alongside what Garmon just said about financial pressures, those are the key things we are looking at in the charter review, having also listened to our audiences.

Q19 It is g reat to see you both again. Could you set out for us what the BBC Cymru Wales ask is for charter renewal ?

The first point that we would emphasise , which has been touched on , is reform of the licence fee. Th is is urgent. There is a choice here , and it is a whole-society choice. We can either s et the BBC on a continuing course of managed decline , or recogn ise that there needs to be urgent reform of the licence fee . The BBC currently faces a £500 million deficit, which in Wales translates to a bout £9 million in savings and the closure of at least 50 FT E roles in BBC Wales , but additionally and as importantly , a reduction in the number of independent TV , radio and digital companies that we commission from. So, reform of the licence fee is not an esoteric or abstract question ; it is an urgent and vital question if we collectively want not just to hang on to what we have, but to grow the presence of BBC Cymru Wales as a trusted voice with news, high - quality entertainment, drama, orchestra l music and so on in Wales.

The second point that I would emphasise is independenc e. I ndependence from Government is vital if our people are to have confidence and trust in the BBC. The final point is regulatory reform so that the BBC can, in a very fast - moving media landscape, adjust and , as we have just discuss ed in terms of understanding audiences , serve audiences appropriately across a range of platforms.
Q20 What specifically was the process that BBC Cymru Wales had? What was th e process whereby you could feed into the BBC response to the Government Green Paper on charter renewal?

It has been a very thorough process , including internally in the BBC . Garmon and I have been engaged over many months in th e charter review process and, as you would expect, making the case for , arguing for , not just BBC Wales institutionally but what the BBC does in Wales . E xternally , fora such as this are hugely important in making sure that collectively there is recognition of the needs and the voice of Wales. The final point is that engagement with DCMS is very good , very strong. For example, tomorrow I have a meeting with DCMS in which we will be looking specifically at the needs of Welsh language broadcasting , alongside other minority language requirements , on the BBC.
That is really good to hear. Thank you very much.

Q21 Are we not in danger of just accepting the year-on-year reduction in people paying the licence fee as a fait accompli? What, if any, representations or ideas has the BBC fed into Government about pausing and then reversing that trend?
T he BBC has stated very clearly the implications of not reforming the licence fee , but the decision on the revised funding mechanism is one for Government.
Q22 T he Committee will appreciate that , b ut has the BBC given to Government some suggestions as to how that could be done?

As you would expect, t hose talks with Government are ongoing. There is a process. The BBC is very much in listening mode around what the best means of securing sufficient funding to deliver our universal requirements are.

To your point, there are three key questions. First, there are the means. Does the future licence fee, or whatever you want to call it, allow the BBC to deliver its universal mission? Secondly, there is the mechanism. Thirdly, there is the question of the sum that would be levied on individuals to pay for the future requirements of the BBC.

We are between the Green Paper and the more definitive, harder White Paper, which is why this meeting is so helpful and important. Those conversations are ongoing. The BBC is still listening. As I am sure you will have seen, we have ruled out two specific proposals for raising money for the BBC. The first is subscription, which would fundamentally change the nature of the BBC, and definitely BBC Cymru Wales. The second potential solution is advertising. Again, that would not be a helpful idea. As we have seen with the sad news from Channel 4 today, advertising revenue across the whole of the UK is under a huge amount of pressure. The BBC entering that market would destabilise the precious PSB ecosystem we have even further.

As part of that whole discussion, there has been talk of a household levy as a potential option because that model is in operation in some European countries. Again, it is ultimately for the Government to decide, but modernising the scope of the funding model could also be a realistic way.

Q23 Obviously, it is up to the Government to decide, but is the answer to the question “yes”? Has the BBC put to Government some thoughts or suggestions on either an alternative funding model or how to make the current one work more effectively?

The prospect of effective status quo is an option. We need reform and the numbers bear that out. There are 3.7 million households in the UK that do not presently require a licence—the no licence needed households. Last year, 500 million fewer people paid the licence fee. No effective change is not an option. However, as you would expect, we are in an ongoing process with DCMS around what the best solution is for the BBC and for broadcasting in the wider sense.

Q24 Just in the interest of time, in response to Mr Ranger’s earlier question, you said that your proportion of the £500 million savings would be £9 million. You also mentioned an FTE headcount reduction of approximately 50, with a knock-on effect to the supply chain in and around the creative industries. What is that £9 million as a percentage of BBC Cymru’s annual budget?
It is just above 10%.
Q25 What about the 50 redundancies as a percentage of the workforce?
Just below 10%.
Q26 So , it is about a 10% reduction on both?
Yes. But as well as employing our own staff who deliver our content, we also commission from the independent sector.
Q27 While difficult, is that liveable with?

I think it is challenging because if you look at what we provide in Wales, all our services are unique, and whatever we step away from or do less of, there is not another party that will step in and fill that gap. Our concern is a scenario where we appear in front of the Committee annually to talk about further reductions. That is why the funding is critical.

To your liveability test or question, we need to bear in mind that across this charter licence fee period, BBC Wales is down by around £30 million in our buying or spending power, which equates to around 25% of our budget. For the last 16 years, there have been nine licence fee freezes, so the incremental pressure on BBC Cymru Wales has been ratcheted.
Yes, it has been compounded.
And the efficiency challenge increases, because, as we have delivered year-on-year efficiencies, we have to go more into changing content to deliver those savings.

Q28 My final question is that the BBC director general, slightly bizarrely, some might argue, recently declined to guarantee the future of BBC Scotland. I personally could not imagine a BBC without BBC Cymru Wales. I think we play an integral part.

Q29 I am sure your Scottish counterpart would say exactly the same if they were asked about the future of BBC Scotland. But as your own director general recently declined to guarantee, as I understand it, when asked a specific question about the future of BBC Scotland—
Can I add to what Garmon was saying there?
Q30 No. If you could answer the question, that might be quite helpful. Should we also regard BBC Cymru Wales as being at risk?
I do not regard BBC Cymru Wales as being at risk, no.
Q31 And have you had that assurance from the director general?
I have not had any conversations to suggest that there is any risk to BBC Cymru Wales.

Q32 The absence of a conversation does not necessarily mean that it is safeguarded. In the light of the failure to guarantee with regard to Scotland, has it not crossed your mind to ask the director general’s view on Wales?
I do not perceive a risk to the future of BBC Cymru Wales, so that is not a conversation I have had, for that reason.
Q33 As a result of this exchange, might it be?
Again, I think the contribution of BBC Cymru Wales to the delivery of BBC services in Wales is fundamental, and I cannot foresee that position being under threat.

Q34 But I make the point again: your Scottish counterpart would likely answer exactly the same question in exactly the same way. He or she would see the Scottish brand of the BBC as very important. You clearly see that with BBC Cymru Wales, and we all do, but in the light of the absence of a guarantee, has it not crossed your mind just to check in with a short email to the director general?

No, for the simple reason that there is no risk whatsoever to BBC Cymru Wales. The far bigger risk to BBC Wales is a process of continuous, continuing cuts such as the ones we have seen since 2017. As I said, we now need to save £9 million. In all likelihood, there will be additional savings up to 2028-29, not just for BBC Cymru Wales but for the rest of the BBC. Unless there is future licence fee reform, we are set on that inevitable path of managed, continuing decline. To answer your question very directly, BBC Cymru Wales is here to stay, but I am not so confident about the type of content that we presently produce and distribute so effectively, because we just do not have the money for it.
I hope your confidence is well founded.

Q35 Thank you, Simon. You have clearly identified the safety of BBC Cymru Wales. The Committee would want to make sure that the Welsh language, heritage and culture involved in the BBC, ITV and S4C is protected, and obviously we would stand behind you there. You talked about the managed decline. The £500 million cut is significant. Even I have noticed it in this place. When I first started, when we were interviewed, we would have a cameraman and a lighting person as well as the reporter-journalist, and now we are down to two if we are lucky.
Or a man and a phone.

Yes. Now it is sometimes just one person, as Simon says, with a phone. I am anxious because these are people’s jobs , and once they’re gone we do not get them back. So how are you managing this? Obviously, any cut is dangerous. How are you managing and working with it?

You as Members will have seen how we have driven efficiencies, as you have described. We need to continue to look for efficiencies and challenge ourselves in terms of whether we are operating as effectively and cleanly as possible. Particularly as technology continues to evolve, that will be a continuing area of scrutiny. In terms of looking at how we approach the challenge of reducing our spend by £9 million in the first instance, we have two principles. We aim to sustain output with the highest audience value and impact, and also meet audiences where they are and not do anything that prevents future routes to growth or impacts activities in areas where we already face challenges, such as reaching younger audiences.

We are looking at the potential of more than 50 FT E post closures. We engaged in the voluntary redundancy expression of interest process with staff across the summer. We are working through our savings plan in parallel and are currently concluding that process. We will talk to staff and the sector about our plans relatively soon.
Thank you. Llinos Medi is next.

Q38 Welcome to our final panel. It is good to see you both before us. Will you briefly introduce yourselves?
Thank you. I am Zoe Thomas and I am the head of news and programmes at ITV Cymru Wales.
I am Magnus Brooke and I am group director of strategy, policy and regulation for ITV.

Q39 We have heard from S4C and BBC Cymru Wales. Where does ITV Cymru Wales sit in the Welsh broadcasting landscape? You are competing with both of those, and they have very distinct remits and purposes. How do you fit into that?
We probably have a two-part answer to that: the ITV Cymru Wales bit and then the wider ITV land as well.

For ITV Cymru Wales specifically, we are the only commercial PSB in Wales. We are the only other provider of national and regional news, in contrast to the BBC, which provides for both BBC and S4C. On a practical level, we employ 100 staff, as well as the 300 who are employed by ITV Studios and Boom. We provide that plurality: a different voice and a vital difference to our other PSB partners.

What is quite often forgotten, because we are the smaller partner in the PSB stakes in Wales, is that as well as the four hours of news every week, we also provide 78 hours of English-language programming every week. We are a national broadcaster in that sense, but we are also a provider of content to the other broadcasters, whether that be through the long-standing arrangements we have with S4C to make programmes like “Y Byd yn ei Le” and “Y Byd ar Bedwar”, or whether it is the network unit, which increasingly makes content for both the BBC in Wales and ITV. In Wales, specifically, we have a two-part role. We are a smaller partner, perhaps, but we are a really fundamental part of that cornerstone of the creative economy. Then, obviously, ITV has a wider role as well.

At a network level, as ITV, what we are trying to do as a public service broadcaster is reflect the whole of the UK to itself. We are the biggest commercial public service broadcaster, and we have a nationwide role in reflecting the UK. Of course, part of the UK is Wales, so a really important thing for us is to make sure that we are showing Wales to the whole UK and we are showing the rest of the UK to Wales. That is our role as a distinctive UK player.

One of the things that we have made a very active effort on over the last three or four years is building more network production coming out of Wales. We have a very good relationship with Creative Wales that we have fostered over the last two or three years. We took a lot of commissioners down to Wales a couple of years ago and opened ourselves up to all the production community in Wales to foster those connections, rather than expecting people to come to London. We are going to repeat that in January of next year because it was very successful, and we now have a really good relationship with Creative Wales.

I am pleased to say that, as we speak, we are filming a couple of network dramas in Wales. There is something called “Code Zero”, which is a thriller that will be on next year. An even bigger thing for us is “Majesty”, which is a really big period drama about a young Elizabeth I in the court of Henry VIII. It has some big-name Welsh talent in the lead on it, which we have not announced yet. Both of those are done in partnership with Creative Wales as well.

That is how we see it, and after the BBC we are probably the biggest commercial investor in production across the UK, both in relation to all the various genres of programmes and to network news—national and international news—which is clearly a UK-wide dimension. We have an ITN correspondent in Wales who reports on Wales for the network news and so on.
Q40 That is very interesting, considering the link between the Tudors and Wales. That is the little link there, so we will see how that develops—it will be lovely.
Yes.
Ann is available. I think that was her bid!
Q41 I am Elizabeth I—wrong colour hair, but never mind!

Going back to business, the licence fee obviously does not affect you, but will the settlement have any effect on the work that you do, how much money you have or how ITV Cymru sits within the PSB in Wales? Does the charter review affect you in that way at all?

Yes, it does. Zoe deals with the specific bits in Wales, but it really does affect us. The point is that it is an ecology. There are three sources of funding for the UK broadcasting ecology: there is the licence fee, advertising and subscription. It does matter to us; the BBC is substantially and proportionately funded from public resources, so it would make a big difference to us, for example, if the BBC was funded through subscription or even advertising. That would have a serious impact on the commercial broadcasting sector and would take money out of the overall ecology.

ITV is both a PSB, through our channels business and ITVX, and a programme maker. We make a lot of programmes for the BBC across the UK, and we make some of their biggest titles through ITV Studios and various labels in ITV Studios. It matters to us as a creative business that the BBC is well-funded and has sufficient resources—and, of course, that it is efficient as well, which is also important. One of the pressures we feel is the extraordinary competition that we face from the SVODs, YouTube and more traditional competitors. We have had to get incredibly efficient and make enormous efficiency cuts to maximise the amount of value we put on screen. But we recognise the pressure that the BBC has been under from the declining licence fee, and we want a sustainable and proportionately funded BBC form public resources.

From a Welsh point of view, there is all of that, but on a very national level, in terms of Wales, that competition is a good thing—having a strong, healthy competition drives up standards for us both. It means that there are opportunities for the people working in Wales to move between two or three really strong broadcasters. I already mentioned the programmes that BBC Wales are commissioning from us now, and obviously a weakened BBC might mean that that form of income stream disappears for us. It is incredibly important that the BBC has a strong and sustainable economic future.

Q42 We have a huge creative industry in Wales—it is just so important. What does the charter renewal need to do to achieve the maximum growth or output and safeguard the culture and language in Wales?

The most important thing it needs to do is establish a more sustainable funding model for the BBC from public resources. As you have heard, most people in Britain are consuming from the BBC, but an increasing number are not paying for it—for a variety reasons; some of that is evasion and some is that they are legitimately not using the BBC services. It benefits the UK to have a universally available and universally funded BBC. That is our perspective as ITV.

We do not have so much of a perspective on exactly what the mechanics should be. I think that is ultimately a political question about how you want the BBC to be funded and what the mechanics are. Do you extend the obligation to pay the licence fee, for example, to people who are consuming other sorts of services? That is one option, and of the few remaining options left on the table, it seems to be one of the leading options. We do not have a significant view about that. We do have the view that there should be fair competition, and therefore we would be very concerned if you had an extended mechanic that did not cover all the relevant competitors, so you would want to make sure that, if you were going to put an obligation on people to pay the licence fee because they use ITVX or More4, that it also covered Netflix, Amazon and particularly YouTube.

The growth of YouTube has been extraordinary, in both viewing and advertising. In the last two or three years they have pretty much doubled their consumption in the UK, across all demographics—not just young people—and it is long-form, high-quality, highly produced content. There are some extraordinary stats. More than half of YouTube consumption in the UK now is on the big television set. That is such a rapid change from a world where people were looking at cats on skateboards on their phone. That is not YouTube any more. They say themselves that they are television. That is a grandiose statement, but they are on the way to being that, if they are not there already. To make sure that there is a playing field for everybody else, we would be concerned that you didn’t exclude certain people if you were going to say, “You have to pay the licence fee if you are consuming one service or another.” That would be our main observation about potential mechanics.

Q43 We know that advertising has a huge effect on ITV, as well as on Channel 4. What is your perspective on the possibility of the BBC opening up to other platforms and starting to engage with them more fully? I know they have dipped into YouTube—they are dipping into the BBC iPlayer system—but what do you think about their developing other systems or partnerships that would give them a platform for their programmes on other platforms, such as Prime?

If the question is whether the BBC ought to go to where audiences are, in terms of how audiences choose to consume content, absolutely they should. It takes you back to the conversation we were just having about the universal availability and funding of the BBC. Clearly, if more than half of YouTube consumption is on the television, then the BBC needs to be there. Indeed, the BBC recognises that now, I think. Four or five years ago it had a sort of “fortress iPlayer” strategy. Given the way the market has moved, I think they have recognised that that is not enough, because it is not necessarily the case that everybody is going to come to you; you are going to need to go to where they want to be as well. The BBC has recognised that and started embracing YouTube, in particular, but I suspect there are other platforms that it is going to need to embrace as well.

The great advantage the BBC have, which is much more difficult for us, is that they do not need to be paid to do that. They do not need to make advertising revenue. They do not have a problem of the amount of money they have to give away to YouTube, which is a major problem for us, because they are not a commercial player. They can put their content wherever the audience is and not have to worry about whether they are going to get paid for it. In fact, the opposite is true: the more they spread their content around, the more likely it is that people are going to accept that the licence fee is providing something for them, because the BBC is providing that content wherever they want to consume it.
Q44 But they have to pay to go on to YouTube, I would imagine. YouTube are not going to open the door without being paid for it, are they?

I don’t think the BBC have to pay YouTube. It is an open platform. I can go and load a video up on YouTube and it will not cost me anything. You would need to ask the BBC, but I do not think the BBC is paying YouTube. The BBC is not getting any advertising revenue from YouTube and should not be taking any advertising. There should not be adverts on BBC content on YouTube because it is being paid for by the licence fee. That is really important, because that is about licence fee payers seeing that they can get BBC content for free without having to watch adverts.
Do you want to follow up, Ann?
No, that is fine. I will check my facts.

Q45 It is nice to see you both again. I want to develop the line of discussion we were just having about changing audience habits and the streaming platforms, which obviously affect you as a broadcaster that relies on advertising, or is funded through advertising. Can you describe what the effect has been?

The effect has been profound. If you look at the competition for viewing and the competition for advertising, we face a competitor set now that is unrecognisable from 10 years ago. Our biggest competitors now are still Channel 4, Sky and so on , but above all, the SVODs. Even five years ago, who would have thought that some of our biggest competitors would be subscription VOD services such as Netflix, Disney and HBO, all of which are now hybrid pay-and-free advertising finance businesses. Suddenly, you have got a whole new competitor set with a mass audience competing both for viewing and for advertising.

Again, YouTube is a formidable competitor which is integrated into the whole Google ecosystem. Its data is astonishing because anybody who uses any Google product is effectively feeding the machine and that includes YouTube. It is a formidable advertising competitor, and its reach is now greater than ITV. It is greater on some measures than the BBC and it is growing very fast. It is a mass-reach platform with an incredibly data-rich advertising offer, and which is amortising its costs across the whole world. We are investing in advertising technology in ITVX for one market, for one UK country, which is a medium-sized country. All our competitors are now amortising their costs more or less across the whole world.

That is a really tough place to be and if you look at our revenues, we have lost about £500 million of total advertising revenue in real terms since 2021. Our margins have halved. We have had to invest a huge amount in ITVX and in advertising technology. It is really tough. To be honest, it is one of the reasons why, as the strategy director, one of the things we did two or three years ago was ask: if we take a five-or-more-year view, where are we going to be and where do we need to be? The conclusion was that we had to have a partner in this market. That was the main reason why we approached Comcast and proposed that we did a deal with Sky to combine our broadcasting and streaming businesses to try and create an entity with sufficient scale and heft in the UK and that was capable of sustaining our PSB obligations with a really strong economic base to do that. That is why we have done that deal.

If I can just add, on a practical delivery level, as people on the ground trying to deliver the best content that we can all the time, that perpetual squeeze means that it becomes harder to do that. What has happened simultaneously is that there are more platforms to do that on. You are trying to tell stories in different ways on different platforms, and those platforms just increase in number while your need to be on those different platforms does not decrease—one does not go away just because another starts. You have a perpetually growing arena of places that you need to put your content, and you need to position that content slightly differently but with the same resource. On a practical level, that is the effect of all of that.

Q46 Is the change that you are losing the volume of advertising that is coming to you because there is so much other choice that the people who want to advertise can go to? Or is it the value that advertisers feel that it has and that they want to pay less to advertise on your channels because they have got other places to go to as well? Or is it a mixture of both?

It is largely choice. There are just so many other places that they can go. Those places are very attractive mass-reach products. The USP of TV used to be mass reach and there was nowhere else to go. The truth is you can get mass reach from a number of other players now and there are lots of other places to go. Even more than that, they will give you an even richer data offer than we can necessarily, given the limited amounts of data that we have. We have some data, but we do not have vast amounts. In fact, a lot of the data we have to buy in, whereas they have it innately within their ecosystem. It is quite a battle.

One thing I would say, and this is the only glass-half-full point I think I would make on this, is that it does force you to be more efficient. We are very efficient now. We have taken a lot of cost out. To the conversation we had earlier about three people going to an interview, we do have one person going to an interview now, and—as Zoe knows better than anyone—we have made the budgets for things such as regional news go further, because the truth is that we are now providing a digital news service alongside all of the linear broadcast TV that we traditionally did. If we were still sending three people to each story, we would not be doing that.

Q47 That is quite interesting. Thinking of Sky, Now TV and Channel 4 more than ITV specifically, I have noticed that when watching a film, you now get quite a long gap where it says that the programme will continue shortly—I am guessing it is to do with the scheduling. That used to be filled with adverts. I suppose my question, really, is whether there are not enough people wanting to advertise , because you cannot fill those gaps.

It is a good point. If you think about the number of hours of television now, you could probably watch every single drama ever released somewhere on television in Britain, and probably every single film, more or less. That is extraordinary. If you set off and said, “I’m going to watch every single piece of content currently available on a video service in the UK,” you would be dead, I think, before you finished.

Yes, there is a huge amount more supply, and yes, advertising has increased. It has expanded. The market has increased. TV’s share of that, by the way, has not increased; it has gone down. Yes, there is more demand—there is more advertising around now—but the supply of opportunities to advertise has also massively increased.

Q48 As an older person who likes to go back to “Inspector Morse”, “Lewis” and all those sorts of things—they are obviously not Welsh, but I am sure they would be if they could be—looking at the data side of things, could you just expand, for a non-techy person, on what you mean by data, how you are harvesting and all that sort of thing?

The truth is that we don’t harvest all that much data from ITVX. We want the sign-up process to be as smooth as possible, so I think we get your e-mail address, your name and probably your address, to enable us to supply the right regional news and versions and so on. We are not collecting huge amounts of first-party data. We do then, for advertising purposes, sometimes match data that we buy in from Experian or whatever to try to match those data sources up. But the truth is that if you’re on YouTube, you are in the whole ecosystem of Google; they know your entire search history, your Google Map history, when you were interested in buying a new car, if there is a life event coming up or whatever it is, and they can use that data on YouTube to target their advertising. That is formidable competition if you are ITV, because we do not harvest that level of data.

One of the reasons why the Sky transaction is important is that, in the US, Comcast does have some quite sophisticated advertising technology. We are having to invest in that technology ourselves in the UK, for one country. What we really need is some more sophisticated advertising technology, the cost of which is amortised across a number of markets, particularly the US, because it is the biggest market. One of the attractions of this from our and Sky’s point of view is that that technology can be deployed in the UK, which saves us money, bluntly. We have a product called Planet V, which we have invested tens of millions of pounds in. It is an automated programmatic advertising platform. Agencies can buy directly from us, without necessarily even having to go through the sales team, but to do that in one country was a massive undertaking, with buying the intellectual property, the know-how and all the rest of it. Our competitors are all amortising that cost across the whole world—and spending billions, by the way; we are not spending billions on that at all.

That was just a microcosmic example of why something like Sky makes a difference, but there is also content. Sky loves content. It has a lot of sport, a lot of other UK content, and there is more that can be done in terms of enhancing our channel. I am due to speak to them about their specific plans, but it ultimately helps Wales: there is an ecosystem on ITV where you increase the number of people who watch the channel, and that will increase the number of people who then engage with what Zoe and the team are doing in Wales.
Q49 You talk about economies of scale and things for the big companies, but obviously, we are talking about Wales. I suppose the question is, what is your unique selling point?
In Wales specifically?
In Wales.

I think it goes back to what I said earlier. In being the only commercial broadcaster, we are that alternative voice; we do reach different audiences. Traditionally, we reach slightly socioeconomically lower audiences. We provide that different voice to people. In the election, I think you could see that the BBC, S4C and us were doing very similar things, but doing them in different ways and to different audiences.

T he importance of that plurality, of those voices continuing, and of us being able to do that and being a significant player in that market should not be undervalued. We do different things : t he purpose of the BBC is to do those things that perhaps commercial broadcasters cannot afford to do, but I think that we provide a n important alternative voice, both in Wales and across the rest of the UK.

Q50 Thank you very much. As I said with the other witnesses, we are coming to the end of our session , so i s there anything else that you feel we should know but we have not brought out in the questioning today? I will start with Magnus and then go on to Zoe for the final word .

The only thing that I would say — just to reiterate what I have said already — is that the health of commercial PSB across the UK has a direct impact on what we can do in Wales. Wales is part of that overall ecology. B luntly , t here is a cross-subsidy between the money that we can make as a network service and the amount of money that we can put into Wales.

T he single most important thing for us is getting the Sky deal away. Sky ha s committed to delivering all our PSB obligations for the entire length of the current licence. T hat it is really important. If you look at what has happened with STV in Scotland, for example, we are really clear that we would not want to go there . That is an example of how you have to have a sustainable economic model in order to deliver a national service of scale in Wales or Scotland.

O bviously, as Magnus said, we are part of that ecosystem, so all of that is crucial for us. But, on a more national or local level, it is just about doing what we already do, which is amplifying our content and celebrating it to both your constituents and other parliamentarians, to make sure that people realise the value of what ITV Wales and the other PSBs bring to cultural life and the creative economy in Wale s .

Thank you very much. That brings this session to a n end . Zoe Thomas and Magnus Brooke , I want to thank both of you for attending today. I also need to pay special thanks to our interpreter, Nerys, who is in the box over there and has been very patient. Thank you very much to you all. I will now bring the session to a close.
