We hope that the session will allow us to discuss the findings of your research so that we can make informed recommendations about future policy, legislation , and funding and support for our communities living near these former industrial sites.
B efore I begin, can I ask M embers to declare any interest s relevant to today’s session ?

My wife and I are both featured in the documentary. My wife is a community councillor in the area where one of the chemical plants we are going to be speaking about was. She used to work there and had her blood tested as part of the documentary. We live about 100 metres away from the site in question.
Thank you, Steve. Let me start with Mr Sheen. Can you tell us how your interest in the topic was piqued and how your subsequent involvement with the documentary came about?

Thank you very much for inviting us to come today. It started very randomly, really, for me. I was living in Los Angeles at the time. I was contacted by a teacher in the Rhondda Cynon Taf area. Before I replied to this lady, who was doing a school project, I thought I would look up what Rhondda Cynon Taf actually means, so I went on to Wikipedia.

On the Wikipedia site, I saw one little entry that said, “Environmental controversy: Brofiscin quarry has been named as the most toxic place in Britain”—and that was it. I thought it seemed very strange that there was nothing more about it. I looked into it, and by the end of that day I was terrified and fascinated by what I had found out.

To cut a long story short, I came across the story of a man called Douglas Gowan, who had spent his life on this, it seemed. First of all, in the mid-‘60s, when he was a younger man working for the National Union of Farmers, there had been a call from a farmer in the Gros-faen area near Llantrisant, who had seen strange things happening to his livestock—aborted foetuses, malformed foetuses, dead crayfish and such in the streams—and wanted someone to come and investigate. Douglas Gowan went out to investigate. He tells a very powerful and emotional story about finding a lamb that was deformed and dying, with no genitalia.

He then discovered that there was a quarry nearby—Brofiscin quarry. It was a disused quarry that was being used for dumping from the Monsanto factory in Newport—the dumping of what turned out to be canisters of something called PCBs, polychlorinated biphenyls.

Douglas spent many years after that testing and finding out what PCBs were and slowly piecing together a story that seemed to indicate that the dumping of these PCBs in Brofiscin quarry was leading to it leaching out and affecting the local farmers’ livestock, and contaminating what was happening there. Douglas then took that story on, because he believed there should be accountability and responsibility taken, and that led to a huge saga just around that Brofiscin quarry site.

Anyway, on that day when I was reading up about this and finding out a bit more about Monsanto as a company, both historically and in the years ahead, I was struck by two things. First, there seemed to be a terrible injustice, potentially, and not only a historical failure on many levels to protect people, but a very present danger and possibly a danger in the future. Douglas talked about how this was not just an idea in the past, but an issue for us now and for our children and our children’s children. I was very struck by that. I was equally struck by how little information there seemed to be that you could find out about this. There was essentially one big report in The Ecologist magazine and very little else.

That led me, ultimately, to trying to find out if this man, Douglas Gowan, was still alive, and he was. He lived in Norfolk. I asked if I could come and see him and get his story and he said, “Yes, please come and see me, but come quickly, because I think I’ll be dead soon.” I went with a friend who had a camera. I recorded him for two days and got about seven or eight hours of footage of him telling his entire story. Within about six months, he was indeed dead, and he believed that it was because of the effect of PCBs on his system. The story that he told was an absolutely extraordinary one. Me, Lucy and Dan have tried to sift through that story for a long time, and some of the most extraordinary and unbelievable things in it are the most true things. That formed the basis of my interest in this.

I then did something called the Raymond Williams lecture in 2017, and I mentioned it. I am not an investigative journalist—I did not know how to take this on. I was interested in it as a drama as well as a piece of investigative journalism, but in terms of following that on, I could not do it, so I mentioned it in the lecture, hoping that someone would pick up on it. It took a while, but eventually, years later, I had a call saying that Lucy and Dan were interested in telling Douglas Gowan’s story as part of a wider story about not only PCBs, but what are known as forever chemicals. We talked about it, got together and ended up making the podcast series “Buried” and, ultimately, the documentary series.
Thank you for setting the scene.

Q2 Thank you all for coming today. We are mindful that we want to avoid any undue public alarm on the topic, but can you tell us—I am directing this at Lucy Taylor and Dan Ashby—about your findings related to PCBs at former industrial sites?

It is interesting that you talk about undue alarm, because that is exactly where we began as well. I remember the three of us having a conversation when we first started the podcast, which came before the documentary, and saying, “We have to be sure that everything we say is watertight here, because it is going to scare people, and we don’t want to scare people if it’s actually not a risk to them.” As we have gone further through this journey, we have shifted on that and felt that what we are finding out is quite scary. The public emphasis is towards thinking, “It can’t be that bad, because they wouldn’t allow that to happen,” when actually some of what is happening is quite worrying.

For example, we did soil sampling for the TV series in 14 different sites, and 13 of them showed above average or high levels of these chemicals in the soil. One of those was so dangerous that, if you touched it, it would be dangerous to health; the scientist we were with told us that if a dog ran through a puddle, the dog could die because of the levels of chemicals in the soil. Beyond that, we have done blood testing and found those same chemicals in the blood of people who lived in the surrounding areas. In some cases, they were at high or above average levels, and some of those people have experienced rare cancers. It is worrying, and this is just the beginning.

One thing that is worth emphasising is that we did indicative testing. We are a small team—we are not the Environment Agency or NRW. We tested only a handful of sites, and we found some truly alarming results. In my mind, it raises the question, “What would we have found if we tested hundreds of sites?” We just chose specific locations. As Lucy said, one of the places was so high, it was off the scientists’ charts. In almost all the locations across Wales, the scientists came back and said they warrant further investigation. They might not have been as high as the 2,000 or 12,000 times over of the highest result, but because they were more than 100 times over in places across Wales, and they were sometimes going into streams or on land close to people, the Royal Society of Chemistry scientists said, “Look, this does warrant further investigation.”

Q3 You have touched on it already, but obviously there are some limitations to the research you have done because of the sheer scale of this. You have quite clearly said that there needs to be more testing, and we need to find out a lot more about this across the whole country—across the whole UK, probably. You have said that the research in the documentary is indicative, but do you think that there are more limitations to it?

With forever chemicals, and indeed chemical testing—you are probably familiar with this from looking at lead—there are two stages. There is testing, where you can find out specific concentrations in soils, and then there is a risk assessment, where you look at whether those concentrations are getting into people; scientists talk about a pathway and a receptor. We do not have the budget or the expertise to do the full risk assessment, but the chemical hits we got in some places were big red flags, in places where there is either no testing happening or very little. From our journalistic perspective, it certainly warrants more investigation. We cannot categorically say the risk without doing a full risk assessment, though.

It is also worth saying that the person who did that testing for us was Dr Dave Megson, who is from Manchester Metropolitan University, with the Royal Society of Chemistry. He is one of the world experts on this. For the TV documentary, we were also supported by the Open University, which went back and scrutinised what he did for compliance reasons to make sure that what we put out to the public was fair. Although it is indicative, it is indicative because of the budget we had and the fact that we are not an environmental regulator that can survey the whole area, not because we are a TV crew. It is still quite robust testing; it is just limited in scope.

It is probably useful to say that the testing up until what we did with the documentary has been done by councils. It is difficult to see how that testing could be trusted by the communities as being appropriate, extensive and rigorous enough when, if the result of that testing went one way, it could lead to the potential bankrupting of those councils. People are being asked to trust testing that has an understandable but quite strong agenda behind it, and that is part of the point. However limited the testing we did was and whatever restrictions there might have been on it, I would suggest that there were even greater restrictions on any other testing done before this.
That is a fair and interesting point, and we will come on to it later.

Q4 In the course of your research, have you identified anything that tells you that the companies or individuals doing the dumping in the first place did it with the knowledge that it was potentially harmful and injurious to public health? Or did they not know because of the time it was done, and did they just think they were storing a by-product of whatever they were doing in an appropriate place? Do you have a view on that from anything you have unearthed or discovered?

I immediately think about the case that happened in Anniston, Alabama on behalf of the community there. We spoke to one of the lawyers who took on that case, and he showed us internal memos from Monsanto dating certainly as far back as the ‘50s and potentially back to the ‘30s that indicated that there was an awareness in Monsanto of the effect on the community. We also found internal memos from the time it go to the point when they had to shut down production of PCBs in the plant in Anniston that said, “We cannot afford to lose one dollar of business.” It was at that point, as we discovered in that moment in the documentary when Dan told me, that they turned their sights on Newport in south Wales, knowing—I would say full well—what damage had been done to the community in Anniston, and they just moved production to Newport.

Of course, there is a history across south Wales of heavy industry and chronic illness. If one wanted to be cynical about it, you could say that there was the possibility of masking any potential damage to the community because of what already existed there, as well as a desperate desire for employment and jobs to come in and take the place of the industry that had gone, and communities that perhaps do not get listened to as much. We are not talking about Oxfordshire , where there was a case recently.
The big waste crime site in Kidlington.
Yes.
I am mindful of time, so I will move on to Ben Lake.

Q5 You mentioned the testing of particular sites. I want to scrutinise how much we understand about the total number of sites that may be contaminated in Wales. In the documentary, you referenced NRW figures that state that some 15,000 sites may have been contaminated. How confident are we that the figure of 15,000 is accurate and reliable? I ask because in another strand on lead contamination there is a question about how much we understand about the extent of contamination. Do you have an idea how the regulator came to that figure? What sources of information is it relying on to state that there are 15,000 sites?

There are different numbers quoted for contaminated land. Friends of the Earth did its own look at council records and said that there are potentially 45,000 contaminated land sites. Interestingly, it said that something like 80 had been declared contaminated, but that many councils do not keep public registers or even have full inspection teams.

The NRW figure is much lower. I think we can say with some confidence that there are thousands of contaminated, risky sites across Wales—I would say probably more than 10,000. The question is, how contaminated are they and what contaminants are we talking about? From what we have seen from Douglas’s evidence, internal Monsanto memos and years of our own testing, our worry is that there are many sites with high levels of PCBs.

Remember that, as Michael alluded to, PCBs are much scarier than lead in some senses because PCBs in tiny amounts can affect you for the rest of your life. Not only that, but you pass them on to your children, so they contaminate from generation to generation. They are the godfather of forever chemicals. For us, the risk is higher and the thresholds are lower. The NRW will also be looking at those. One of the scary things is that there are fewer rules around PCB testing than, say, some water testing, so in many cases they do not need to test for PCBs.

Q6 How much record-keeping was there for the sites that we fear have been contaminated by illegal dumping so that we can know what was potentially dumped? The numbers are big—10,000, 15,000, 40,000 sites. I imagine one of the first things we need to do is try to categorise them according to potential risk. In order to do that effectively, we would need some information about what has actually been deposited. From your investigations, how much information is there to guide that sort of undertaking?

Each site is different. Douglas did really well at finding the right memos and documents in the councils. NRW also knows what is in many of the sites. For some sites, to be honest, nobody knows. The authorities will come out and say, “We just don’t know.” There are organisations like Watershed, which has tested all around the UK and published a map. That is a great start, because it is pulling in public data from everywhere so that localities will say, “My goodness, we’ve got this on our doorstep.” But there are many thousands of so-called orphan sites where nobody knows what is in them.

In the documentary we have people talking about looking out their window at night as children to see trucks dumping stuff in the darkness of night and coming out the next day and finding a jelly-like substance on the road, and kids playing with it. I don’t know if that is being recorded by anyone, but it doesn’t look like it.

One final thing on the testing that I do not know if we emphasised is that we are talking about mostly former landfill sites, or in some cases former industrial sites, but we did not test the sites themselves; we tested the public land around them. Everywhere we tested and got higher levels was public—footpaths, public woodland, public sports fields, roads. You would expect higher levels in the sites themselves, but we are talking about the public land, so we are talking about chemicals leaching out of those sites.

Exactly. Because a lot of these places are fenced off now, which, of course, does not stop contamination getting out, we cannot actually get into the place to be able to do the testing that we would like to do, so we have had to rely on a lot of anecdotal stuff. But when you hear someone like Michael in the documentary, who is up in the Wrexham area, and who played in the lagoon as a child, saying that he got cancer, and it was such a rare form of cancer that his surgeon said to him, “You getting that cancer is like you’ve won the lottery, in a negative way,” and then his best friend, who also played in the lagoon, gets exactly the same rare form of cancer, and the surgeon says, “That’s like winning the lottery every day for six months,” that anecdotal evidence starts to make you think that we need to get inside these places and test this stuff.

On that lagoon, I was speaking to a really well-placed contact who works with the regulators, and he said that when he watched the documentary he almost thought he was drunk on Rattler, as he put it. He is an expert. That lagoon is a shame on Britain, and it is a scandal really that it is there. With Kidlington, there was an action plan, and it was cleared up; that the lagoon has stood there for 20 years is outrageous. I think Wrexham council would acknowledge that, and acknowledge their frustration that they do not have the money to clean it up. Probably NRW would as well. That should not be there today.
I am conscious of time, and I know we have a lot more questions to go, so I will ask for brief questions and brief answers.

Q7 Following on from the question about Natural Resources Wales, Lucy and Dan, how on earth can we make a balanced assessment of the genuine concerns posed by PCBs if we have no idea which sites are contaminated and which are not?

There are obvious low-hanging fruits here—many people would say that the lagoon is an obvious thing that needs to be cleared up. Look at what the authorities and councils are saying. If you look at the internal paperwork, when Wrexham council assessed that lagoon, the first choice was to clean it up, but it would cost £40 million. The second option was, if you do not have the money, put a fence around it and just monitor it—but that is only if you do not have the money; if health and the environment came first, you would clear it up. So look at the low-hanging sites that even the authorities agree on.

Where there is contention and where people are not sure, there should be more funding. Whether that is a national fund I will leave to the policymakers, but there should be rigorous funding for more testing, so that remediation is an option, not a burden. Remember, until 2014, this country had a national remediation fund. At the moment, we are the laggards in the world: America is digging and cleaning up these sites, and PCB levels in fish and oceans are falling much faster in America. We have some of the worst seas around Britain for PCB contamination and we do not have a national fund any more. If we do not have that, the question is: who is paying for it?

Q8 As a follow-up, given that we are talking about councils and NRW, councils report that some of the sites have been investigated but did not meet the legal definition of contaminated land. We are told about the thresholds—“It doesn’t meet this threshold.” With that in mind, do you think that the legislation needs to be updated to address that?

I would question—and I think it is a sensible question—that if the judgment around thresholds and what is safe for communities comes from councils that , if they judge it not to be safe for communities , cannot afford to pay for the remediation, it is very difficult to take that at face value. In any conversation around any of this, we have to start by saying that the people responsible for doing this in the first place seem to have got away with it. They seem to be protected, buffered and inured to any responsibility. Everything we are talking about, and will presumably go on to talk about, is in the absence of the original perpetrators of this action getting away with it.

Q9 My question leads on nicely from that. From the research, what response do we need from the Government to make sites with contamination or PCBs safe? When answering that question, could we think about the point that was just made and about who, in your opinion, should pay for identifying and remediating the sites?

I have come to believe more and more, the longer we have worked on this, that the burden has to be taken off the councils. At the moment, it feels like there is a sort of stand-off. You have councils that are terrified of making a judgment one way, regardless of what the data, evidence or information might be, and in fact are probably very nervous about really looking into it too far because if they were to find out that they were financially responsible for this, that would be the end of that council. We have to go beyond that; we have to take it off the councils. The testing has to be done completely independently, and there has to be a fund beyond the council at a national level—I would say even possibly at a multinational level, but certainly at a national level—that means that councils are not just sitting there, terrified of looking into this too much. That would be my take on it.

The British policy differs from the American one in that we have tried to outsource remediation and decontaminating to companies, really. In Britain, the advice is to try to get developers to come in and sort it out for us. In some cases, they do a good job—they test beforehand and they remediate—but in many cases, there is no incentive; the developer does not want to clear up that mess, so the land just stays there. In other countries, if the land is contaminated and it is a risk, the Government move in and pay for it.

In terms of “polluter pays”, to be honest, Britain has a woeful record on that when you compare it with other countries. We are not taking up many of these cases and going back to, as Michael says, the people who did this—many of whom have budgets set aside to pay for this sort of thing. We need to look at why “polluter pays” is not working. Why are we “polluter profits”, not “polluter pays”, and how does that change? If you look at the figures, we have taken up so few cases over the past 20 years.

Q10 I will take my questions slightly out of order, if I may, to get them both in at the same time. Mr Ashby, picking up on the point you were just making about how America does it, we all know that there is a huge difference in its capitalist model, if you will, and in the federalist Government and the state Government, so it is often very difficult to compare America with the UK. Could you point us to a European country that has also had a long industrial past that has done remediation well, which we should be looking at as an example? These are not unique problems to Wales or the broader UK, are they?

One of the ironies here is that we do not have the companies to do some of this remediation stuff, because we do not remediate. The Dutch are particularly good at some of the remediation, as well as the Germans. In terms of forever chemicals more generally, you are seeing the EU go much further than Britain in legislating to stop the pollution getting there in the first place. The prevention is more what I know about; I do not know about specific models of remediation in Europe. In America, one big consideration is that they have class action lawsuits, which are really effective for enforcing change and which we do not have.

One of the added complications is that, when we talk about the original perpetrators of this, they have managed to transform their companies, so it is incredibly complicated to find out who is now ultimately responsible for this—who actually owns everything. Just trying to find that out is complicated enough, and that tells its own story.

Q11 I suppose, Mr Sheen, that this is a question to you. You and your colleagues have highlighted that private companies have caused the problem, and that there is now a legitimate expectation that the taxpayer, whether the local taxpayer or the national taxpayer, somehow picks up the tab for that, which demonstrably does not seem to be particularly fair. I wonder, taking your point about councils and their exposure—their financial vulnerabilities and so on—has anybody, post the broadcast, picked up the phone to you, whether from the Welsh Government, the Wales Office here or whoever it may be, to say, “Come in; we want to have a chat. There are some strategies that we are evolving, and we would like to pick your brains about it,” or has it just met a stony silence from officialdom in its broadest sense?

To me personally, no . I got in touch with the First Minister before the documentary went out, and invited him and whoever he would like to bring forward to watch the documentary before it went out publicly. This is not about trying to point blame at anyone. I thought it was a very good opportunity for an incoming First Minister to be able to get on board with this—to look for solutions.

I have always said that everything that we are doing with this is not about just shouting about it; it is about looking for a practical way forward—a practical solution. So I invited the First Minister to have an opportunity to look at it and talk to us about it. Unfortunately, that offer was not taken up. Subsequently, I have not personally been contacted by anyone that you have mentioned. Has anyone got in touch with you, Dan?

No. We had right of repl ies from DEFRA, but they were mostly towards our concerns. Obviously, we got replies from anyone we made allegations against. This issue has been met with either indifference or an attitude of not knowing what to do or not wanting to engage from pretty much across the political spectrum.

That is surprising because I don’t think that chemical contamination and toxins in our communities is a politically divisive issue. It is not something like climate change where you are seeing divisions in parties. It is stunning to me. We have had so much response from the public and so many people have said that the angriest moment for them was reading the end slates—the responses. That is what made everyone’s blood boil.

When you say that there is an expectation for the taxpayer to take this up, I would disagree. No; my expectation is that the people who are responsible for this originally should pay for it. The problem is that there appears to be a lack of appetite to take it to them from the people in power—yourselves. Not you personally, but the reason we have come here is because, as I said earlier, we are having to talk about second best options because the people who are actually responsible for it do not seem to be held accountable.

Q12 I take your point entirely on that, but have any of you done any research? It is not an area of my expertise. I am still trying to work out what my area of expertise is. But are there any residual liabilities that the perpetrators have through public liability insurance that they may have carried, etc, that may provide an avenue for exploration for funding? As you say, these companies have transformed over the years. They are different parent companies. They change the name. They change the purpose of the business, etc, for motivations that we will not necessarily go into. But they will have always had some form of insurance, so the question is whether there is any historic legacy insurance that could be tapped into as a way of, either in whole or in part, meeting remediation costs. Has anybody come to you with that as a thought or an avenue to be explored?

Yes. The liabilities are there. As Michael says, they are incredibly complicated, and you would need someone like a specialist law firm to go through the liability contracts. They are not always there because they sort of disappear over time. We had one case where a council bought the site for £1 and stupidly took all the liabilities. But in many cases, they exist.

Q13 One of the documentary’s biggest impacts on me was actually the impact on people who live in those areas and in those communities. Mr Sheen, can you describe the impact that contaminated land has had on the people that you met in those communities?

There is huge fear, because so little is known. We talk about the two Jans, as we call them. They feel like they have been pushing back against their local council. They do not feel that they can trust the information they have been getting from them about the contaminated land. You saw the meeting that we had where local people were talking about the effect on their pets—their dogs. I was hugely affected by Michael, who I alluded to earlier. He had played in the lagoon when he was a child, as had his best friend, and both of them then got the same very rare form of cancer. He talked about his son saying to him, “Have I got it as well?” I still—I will never forget that.

Y ou see the effect on people . T hey are just terrified about what might have happened to them historically . There was Paul and Wendy; Paul and his father handled this stuff on their land, and Paul’s father died of cancer. Paul does not know what will happen to him. The levels in his blood were through the roof, and on that land. You can just see the fear in people’s eyes, because of what is not known. That is why I think we have to push for testing. The best outcome would be that testing is done and we find out: “No, it’s going to be okay. There’s a way to deal with this.” But unless that testing is done, people are going to have to live with this fear.

That was the gamble, I suppose, that we have taken with the documentary and all the work that we have done. The last thing that we want to do is terrify people and scare people, and then not be able to follow through with anything that allays those fears. I think the testing has to be done. For me, with everyone we met who talked about how it affected their lives and how they are worried that it will affect the lives of their children and their children’s children, that is what will stay with me forever.
It was very powerful for me as well.

Q14 You have talked a lot about the effect of PCBs on human health. How can we raise awareness among the public? To be honest, “Buried” has certainly done that; we are talking about it, hence your being here today, and we need to move forward. But what can we do to move forward and raise awareness within these communities and within the agricultural community as well, because at one time sheep dip was a PCB? We have lived with this within the agricultural community as well, to be honest. How can we raise awareness, on top of what you have already done?

I think you are seeing the first stirrings of a genuine public campaign forming. I went to Wrexham afterwards and nearly 200 people turned up. It was a hair-raising moment, where people stood up and broke down in tears, and told stories. They were people we had never heard from before, and we have had an enormous response from the public. We have had people email from inside the authorities, and emails from people who worked in Monsanto. There is more to this story and certainly our ambition, as storytellers, is to keep telling it, in order to bring about change; that is the main thing.

The problem always is that many hands that make light work. We are only part of the journey. If there is not a political reaction, and if there is just silence, it is all for nothing, because you can see with the Post Office and many other examples that you need the storytellers, you need the communities, and you need the politicians all to be in favour of change, and also outraged by what they are seeing.

One of the difficult things about this story is that so many people have come up to us and said, “What can I do?” or “My brother had cancer, what can I—?” But actually, as individuals, there is very little that people can do. They do not know that these chemicals are there; they are invisible, they are odourless, they cannot see them. People cannot just quit smoking to reduce their risk of these chemicals, because they are there on public land, and they are in our food, and they are in our seas. So, I do not think that it is something where individuals can step up, other than by campaigning and trying to bring the issue to people in power like yourselves. This needs authorities to take it on and protect people; it is not something that individuals can do for themselves.

Our conversation now, and literally when we leave here we will continue the conversation, is about what we can do to keep this momentum going. People have clearly engaged with this and are alarmed by it. As Lucy said, people are saying, “What can we do about it? What can we do about it?” Well, from our point of view, we need to keep moving forward with this story and keep telling the story. But from the public point of view, the most important thing would be that, once these fears are raised, they see that something is being done about it and that they are being heard.

Like I say, I do not think it is a coincidence that all the places—the main places—where this dumping has been done, not just in Wales but across the world, tend to be in communities that do not have much of a voice and do not necessarily expect to be heard. We need to show that their voices are heard. That was what was so powerful about bringing people together from all over Wales to the Senedd, because those people did not even know that the others existed; they thought they were in isolation working on this stuff and now suddenly they are coming together. That makes a difference.

The fact that we have come here today and you have very graciously listened to us—if people know that that is happening and then something is done about it as well, it is taken forward. We are not going to get to the end in one go; this is a long road. As Dan says, it is going to take many different strands to make this work. But if people see that something is being taken seriously and moving forward, I think that will do a huge amount, rather than thinking, “Well, we can’t do anything about this, can we? It’s just another one of those things.”

Q15 This has been touched on already in relation to cancers. This is very personal to me. I refer back to my declaration of interests: three generations of my wife’s family worked in the Monsanto plant featured in part two of the documentary. Why do you think that so little research has been done into the correlation between PCBs and cancer clusters in the UK?

It comes back to something that Simon alluded to earlier. To begin with, people did not know. When PCBs were first being produced, they were this sort of miracle thing. They made things safer for us. They are in electronic goods. They are a coolant. They are in paint and all kinds of things. It took so much work by people like Douglas Gowan to start to highlight that there is actually a problem with this stuff.

Moving forward from that, it is difficult to get the people who are actually responsible for this to admit it—they still don’t—and to get any evidence showing they were aware that it was harmful. That is hard enough as it is. To get them to take responsibility and do something about it is incredibly difficult. Given that, you are then asking the taxpayer and councils to step in when the perpetrators are not prepared to do it themselves. That is a hard place for those people to be.

L ike I keep saying, while they are in charge of the testing, it is very hard to take the results of that testing at face value. That is why we have to call for an independent body to be in charge of testing.
Q16 Thank you, Michael. Dan, do you want to come in?

When we think about illness, there are different levels. First, there are people who are directly affected by interacting with those places, such as Michael Phillips . There will be hundreds of those people whose cancers will have been caused by playing in the tip. So many people have emailed in. They are obviously at risk. There will be people who worked in the factories who will be really at risk. For me, it is unacceptable that those people have cancers, but cluster surveys will not necessarily pick up those people because they are not massive clusters; we will be finding localised people. They might be in the tens or the hundreds—we don’t know. They might be in the thousands across Wales.

Then there is the bigger concern of communities who live nearby. I want to reassure people that living within a mile of a dump does not mean you will get ill—that is not the case. But there will be cases where people are getting ill, and it is not always cancer. We do not survey for all the other illnesses. There is asthma and there are deformities and things, which are not really surveyed. My fear is that we are not surveying properly for all the illnesses. Even on cancer, the problem is that with PCBs, there is a lag in time, so it will turn up many decades after the pollution happened. I want to reassure communities that they do not need to suddenly panic, but at the same time, I do not think we are scrutinising enough.

I am conscious of time. Could the witnesses spare us an extra five or 10 minutes? I am conscious that we will move on to testing shortly, and we are looking for the way forward. Today we are looking for solutions, so if you could stay, that would be really helpful.
Yes, of course.

Q17 This question is more for Lucy Taylor and Dan Ashby, but feel free to chip in. During the research, did you come across any of the UK Government’s guidance on how we manage human exposure to PCBs, and what did that look like?

We have an approach in Britain where we try to limit—let me go backwards a bit, because this might shock any members of the public listening. Think about these sites as the poison tap, if you like, and the communities we worry about are trying to stop the tap and splashing around. The poison is obviously flowing towards all of us, because over the last 50 years, PCBs have gone into the streams, into our fish and into our food chain, and we are all eating them. We have all had our blood tested and we all have 80 PCBs in our blood. You all have PCBs in your blood and there is no safe level, so you are being harmed in some way—hopefully in a small way. Hopefully it is taking days off your retirement rather than years, but we do not know.

To answer your question, the UK manages it by setting a kind of toxicity diet. There are officials out there who are trying to make sure that you eat enough PCBs that it does not hurt you too much. Your toxic quota, if you like, is really contested among scientists. To give you an example, the EU sets a much lower threshold than Britain. The EU worries that our thresholds are too high and are creating hormone defects and all sorts of things. British scientists say, “No, we think we have the right amount.” The challenge with that approach, though, is that it has to make some really big assumptions. It makes assumptions about how much meat and fish we are eating. We went out and tested supermarket fish and we found that if you ate two portions of fish a week and other foods, you would be well over your PCB quota—you would be being poisoned. One fish we tested was so high that it was illegal to sell. Officials should go in and take it off the shelves.

Our worry is that these chemicals have built up more than we think in all of us. Again, we are not all going to collapse suddenly and get cancer and die, but we are worried that more of us are getting ill from PCBs and other toxins. The worry is that cancer rates in under-50s are spiking in the UK, and some scientists believe that the cause is in the environment. It is a worry. PCBs are part of a worry about what is getting into all of us. Does that answer your question?
Q18 Kind of. I wanted to know about the UK Government policies on that exposure and mitigating it. Did you come across anything?

On the land side, the only other thing to say is that we have thresholds—we have soil guideline values. For commercial use, allotments and residential, the Environment Agency says, “Here is the maximum allowed,” and if you hit that number, it says that you should do a risk assessment. The difference with America is that it is a lot stricter. There is a strong limit and if it hits that limit, they send in diggers and remediate much quicker. Ours is more complicated. We go through this complicated risk assessment procedure.

Q19 We will move on to testing. I congratulate you on what you have achieved in raising awareness and the way that you have done it with these communities. Thank you for being with us today to raise awareness. We have to be careful, because we have to find the answer. I think the answer starts with the testing, because if we are going to find who is accountable and will pay for it, we are losing time. The testing has to happen, and that is where the remediation comes from. There are examples of where it has worked. You mentioned the USA, but we also have examples in the UK of where it has worked. Can we focus on the testing now? We need to recognise who is accountable. Which body is it? You have said that it needs to be done independently, but funding that must come from somewhere. I believe that it is the UK Government’s responsibility, because of the legacy of these sites. I believe that the UK Government should find a legal way of getting that money back. Where do you believe that that ownership starts? Do you think that we have the capacity and the capability, given the scale of the sites in Wales and across the UK, to deliver that testing in a timely manner?
What do you two think? It’s the big question.

No. I don’t think the NRW has the capacity to do this, and I don’t think the Welsh Government have the budget or certainly the will to do this. A lot more funding would be needed, for sure. I have spoken to many people in the NRW, I have seen documents over the years, and you can see that the NRW is really stretched. We are facing an environmental crisis. It is facing all sorts of pollutants. Contamination is going up. No, we are not meeting this challenge with enough resources. I think that is a fact. In terms of who pays for it, I probably would not want to answer that. That is more political, but from a factual basis, there are certainly not the resources. Would you agree?

We were talking about this earlier. There is a precedent for the companies that are the original perpetrators of this getting involved with payments. It becomes very complicated when it comes down to taking responsibility and that kind of stuff. What did they call it? Good-will payments or something?
Yes—voluntary payments.

Voluntary payments. So it is not impossible. I know it is going to be very difficult for us, the two Jans, Rev. Paul, or whoever, to get the top level of where this all started from to do that, but it is not impossible to get it done, historically speaking. We have to always hold on to it. Every time I talk about anything to do with this now, I force myself to say that the people who are responsible for this are somehow buffered from paying for it or taking responsibility. Everything we are talking about, around councils, taxpayers and all this stuff, is all secondary to what ideally should happen. That always has to be the first thing, because otherwise we just write it off and let them get away with it. That has to be said, so whenever there is anything to do with “W ho pays for this ?” , that always has to be the first thing that we look at.

Next to that, the testing itself , which was done for us by Dave Megson, was independent, obviously, because it was done by scientists and they were not working on behalf of anyone. What is the body that becomes the umbrella organisation and takes responsibility for making sure that the testing is done, and who pays for that ? As Dan alluded to, there was a fund pre-2014 ; w e are not necessarily asking for something that has never happened before , so that is maybe a starting point.

It is also worth saying that it falls between the cracks quite a bit, because NRW is obviously responsible for the environment, as is the EA, and c ouncils are primarily involved in land and some human health, but then you have the public health agencies . W e have seen it fall between all of that , s o that is a problem.

The one thing I do know is that, if individual councils are worried that they are going to be held financially responsible themselves , nothing is going to happen —n othing will change — because it can ’ t.

It goes back to Steve’s question about legislation : t his testing could happen. On the whole, it is the local authorities’ responsibility, although in many cases they are not legally required to test for PCBs, and there is n’t anybody policing and checking that they are doing that .

In terms of declaring contaminated land, the guidance is for any other solutions to be found first. Essentially, declaring it contaminated is a last resort. That might work in cases where developers are coming in and the responsibility can be passed on to them , b ut for most of these very contaminated sites in rural areas of Wales, there might not be developers coming forward to do it , s o what is the back - up option?

There is a sort of gap in who is policing th is and overseeing whether testing is actually done. In a number of cases, when we looked into these sites and asked the councils , “Well, when did you last test?” , there had been no testing for many, many years. We would hope and assume that there would be a regular programme, but in many cases there is not .

One important point in all this is that the UK Government are obviously dealing with risk all over the place —t here are so many different pollutants. It is a bit like during covid, when they had to make a calculation —“What’s an acceptable number of people to allow to die before you shut down the economy ?”, and all those debates t hey were having . T hey are doing that all the time with pollutants , o f course ; they cannot stop every single pollutant.

I think the questions that “Buried” really raises are: “H ave we set an acceptable risk level here? ” “ Is Wales bearing a disproportionate brunt of the harms? ” And it’s not just Wales; there are places in England , too. “ Have we got the risk assessment right? ” Our early evidence suggests that we have got it wrong and that what ’ s happening is n’ t fair.

Q20 D id you find any evidence that th at change in 2014 changed the attitude of those responsible? Did the attitude change? Is there any evidence that you have seen since th at decision to stop the funding in 2014?

I think it is fair to say that there has been much less remediation . The other big thing was that there was statutory guidance issued in 2012 on how to interpret the original legislation. The original legislation was really radical ; i t was kind of amazing stuff in terms of environmental foresight, saying, “If there is a significant possibility of significant harm to people, rivers or the environment, it should be cleaned up.” But guidance was issued in 2012 that really qualified that and said, “Well, the first port of call is to get developers in . D o n’ t always declare it contaminated land. Do n’ t trigger ‘ polluter pays ’ legal action. ” “ Go for the more pragmatic approach,” I think it would say. I think that guidance has really changed the picture in the UK.

Remember, it wasn't until two years later after the fund went that I came across this story, and I could find very little about it even then. I t shows the difficulty that there is in getting involved in this stuff in the first place —a nd that was two years after the fund had gone.

Q21 We recently wrote to Stephen Kinnock , the Secretary of State, to ask for a four-nation approach on this and th at testing happen s to communities across the UK near to post-industrial sites where people are now living. Do you agree that that is the way forward : a UK -wide, f our -n ations approach?

A bsolutely. T he bigger the umbrella , the better. O n the one hand , that spreads resources, which is good. The danger is that the bigger the umbrella becomes, the more chance there is of it dissipating somehow. I definitely think that a f our -n ations response is right— and possibly even beyond the four nations. I know that there are some complications around that.
Yes, r emediation and testing is phenomenally expensive. I think that pooling resources is probably a must to deal with this.

Q22 F ollowing from that , as a Committee, what is the best way that we can support the communities , specifically for us in Wales , when we go through the testing ? W hat can we do as a Committee to ensure a way forward with this?

I think that political parties and the Government are not taking this seriously enough. The Committee can be a voice for how serious this issue is . W e are seeing MPs such as Steve, who live in the community, who are utterly outraged by this, but we are not really seeing anybody assessing this risk seriously. That change within political parties is one thing. T he problem is the anonymity of the environment . If w e never see the child who has died from cancer , because they are never a headline, then we all feel better about it. However, statistics show that those children and families are out there. I f you can change the attitudes of the part ies, then that is the first thing . I t is weird for us as environmental reporters that we know from scientists that they are terrified of what is going on with forever chemicals. Yet, weirdly, political parties are just not across it.

Q23 Y ou have talked a lot about the hard evidence and the digging, research and everything. I have a final question. Michael , d uring the program me—which most of us watched — you were tested for PCBs. On a subjective level, how did that make you feel? G oing forward, you are part of the story now. H ow does that make you feel?

I agreed to being tested because I thought , “W ell, I ’ m not affected. I haven ’ t been living in these communities, and I haven ’ t been playing in lagoons , so of course I ’ll do that. ” T hen , once someone i s sitting there telling you that you have 82 different PCBs in your blood, and one of them is the deadliest when it comes to being carcinogen ic , it is shocking. T hen again, when you say, “W ell, what is the baseline here? ” you are told, “W e do not really have a baseline in Britain because we have not got enough research , s o we use the American baseline. ” Y ou then think, “H ang on, can we get the British one , please? ” Once it becomes personal to you , you want to know a bit more about it. Y ou can only imagine what it must be like for families such as Steve ’ s and Michael ’ s and everyone else , where it is incredibly personal , yet the lack of information about it is terrifying .

A lso, to know that communities in the area where I come from were chosen to have this stuff put near them because they could not fight back and because it would get hidden — it would be buried — I take as a personal affront. I ha ve been involved with this now for 10 years , since I first came across this story. I am involved in a lot of different issues , and it all comes down to a basic thing : unfairness. That is mainly what I respond to. I have never come across anything more unfair than this. Communities and families, unbeknownst to them, have potentially been poisoned by this stuff, and it is going to continue. It is very difficult to get anyone to do anything about it. While I have any ability to raise the alarm, push people to do something about it and make sure people’s voices are heard, I will do that, and I will not let go of it.
Q24 Thank you. Lucy and Dan, do you have anything that you want to add?

Just to echo the importance and urgency of this, the lagoon in Cefn Mawr is a really visible symbol: it has an 8-foot fence around it and warning signs that you cannot go into it, and yet it is not legally contaminated land. That really makes you ask questions. That is the visible sign, but there are so many more invisible sites like that. They are affecting us all, and they are affecting our waters. If this chemical were slightly less insidious—if it glowed green and smelled, and if touching it made you keel over within 24 hours—we would be acting very quickly. It is because it is invisible and odourless and sits in our soil—you might come into contact with it and be affected 20 years later—that it is a much more intangible issue, but it is no less urgent.

It is helpful to remember some of those vignettes, which I still cannot believe are true. We have officials who are paid to monitor our poison quota. Britain’s resident population of killer whales will go extinct because of PCBs. Lulu, the killer whale who washed up on a shore, had so much PCB in her that she had to be declared toxic waste. This is really dystopian stuff that is happening on our watch. Think of these sites as taps that are flowing to all of us.

Michael talked about unfairness. There is an argument about geographic unfairness, but there is also an argument about generational unfairness. The latest studies on PCBs and the forever chemicals that are still in production show that 14% of teenagers tested across European countries have levels in them that are harmful or potentially harmful to their health. If we continue to do nothing, we are potentially condemning future generations or at least passing the buck to them. What I see from the future generations is that they are desperate to know more. They are really against personal contamination. They want to be tested, and they want information about what is going on, but they are not being met with enough action.

Thank you so much for coming before us this morning. Thank you for your time. This is such a vital issue. Obviously, this is part of a process for this Committee. We hope that this session has gone some way to acknowledging the concerns that our constituents have raised with us. Certainly, as the local MP in Newport West and Islwyn , I have had many letters since the programme, so thank you for raising the issue.

sessions.iT: National Resilience
sessions.w: Louise Sandher-Jones (HM Government); Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO); Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO); Ministry of Defence; Ministry of Defence

segs.tx: National Resilience Committee
C orrected oral evidence
Monday 7 September 2026
2 pm
Watch the meeting

Members present: Baroness Coussins (The Chair) ; Lord Farmer; Baroness Helic; Baroness Hunter of Auchenreoch; Lord Marland; Baroness Mobarik; Baroness Northover; Lord Oates; Baroness Paul of Shepherd’s Bush; Lord Peach; Lord Spellar.
Evidence Session No. 21 Heard in Public Questions 213 – 2 24
Witnesses

Louise Sandher-Jones MP, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for the Armed Forces ; Ben Fender, Director, Defence and International Security Directorate; Robbie Bulloch, Director, Overseas Territories and Polar Directorate; Brigadier Ben Halsted MBE, Military Strategy , Operations and Commitments Directorate of the Military Strategic HQ , Ministry of Defence; Damian Johnson, Director Homeland Defence and Strategic Threats , Ministry of Defence.
Examination of witnesses
Louise Sandher-Jones, Ben Fender, Robbie Bulloch, Brigadier Ben Halsted and Damian Johnson.

Q213 Good afternoon. Thank you all very much for coming and spending time to help us with this important inquiry. I should remind you that we are being broadcast live; this is a public session. In a couple of days, you will each receive a transcript of the session. That is your opportunity to spot any minor errors you want to correct or any gaps where you wish you had said something but you did not and you want to give us supplementary comments in writing.

Unusually, we have five of you on the panel today. Please do not repeat what somebody else has said, if you can avoid it. Some questions will be directed at either the MoD or the FCDO , while others will welcome responses from both departments. It is extremely helpful for us to have you both here. We have you all for about an hour or so. Mr Johnson , w e heard from you a few sessions ago , so d o not feel that you have to go over any ground you did before because we have that on the record already. Obviously, we have a lot of questions to ask you. In your first answer, if each of you could introduce yourself briefly for the record, that would be helpful.

I turn to the Minister first. My question is about the national conversation — a phrase that is on everybody’s lips at the moment. The strategic defence review recommended that we have a national conversation on defence and security. What will the Government do to ensure that this happens across the whole of society? In particular, what will you do , or what plans do you already have , to make sure that you engage young people in the conversation? We have gone out of our way to try to consult young people as part of our evidence gathering. I am very aware that public attitude surveys on this topic have thus far been with only people aged 18 and above.

I have seen a flavour of what the Government might be up against in this national conversation in the p ast couple of days. I was looking at a particular social media platform, which had 1.5 million responses to the government recommendation ­ so far —it has had a lot of publicity over the p ast few days—about the need to stockpile water and food in the face of the next phase of El Niño. It was quite striking to me that the overwhelming response from th o se 1.5 million young people on th at social media platform was utter mockery, saying, “ W e don’t believe a word of this. The Government are hiding something. Why don’t they tell us the truth? It’s not extreme weather. They’re preparing for war. Why don’t they just come out with it?” That was the flavour of the response, which has provoked my question about what you will do specifically for young people. Obviously, please tell us as well about the broad context of how this national conversation is going to be conducted and planned.

I am the MP for North East Derbyshire and the Minister for the Armed Forces. Thank you very much for doing this topic ; i t is really close to my heart and played a big role in me deciding to stand for election. For those who do not know, I spent a few years in the Army.

It has been clear for some time that we are facing challenges of the future. This is certainly the first time that we have faced them in my lifetime. It is certainly a whole different framing of the problem than I was used to when I was growing up or , indeed, serving. I have responsibility for the national conversation in the Ministry of Defence, as I am sure you are well aware. The overall responsibility lies with the Cabinet Office , but t he MoD has a very important role to play.

As the SDR rightly noted, national resilience is important for a number of reasons. Some of those are to do with the growing challenges posed by climate change, of which we are all very aware — particularly over the summer , with the wildfires we had , for example. We also have challenges from underperforming areas of our infrastructure that pose challenges without any other actor. More and more, we are aware of the threat posed by state and non-state hostile actors. We have a whole range of risks and concerns, ranging from non-state actors in cyberspace to the land domain, across all kinds of different domains. Of course, there is also the info domain. I will come to your wider point about messaging to young people in a minute because the info domain is a really key thing to talk about.

As you are aware, we have already begun a number of endeavours on the national conversation , but it is fair to say that there is a lot more that we need to do. Our big muscle moves are probably still to come. We have the launch of a big awareness campaign coming up in the next few months. For d efence, we have a big exercise coming up next year, which will test a wide range of the MoD’s resilience and reaction s on a scale that we have not seen for a very long time ; t hat is tied in with wider action as part of NATO, of course, with the NATO exercise programme.

I turn to the awareness campaign. This is an interesting one because I tend to find that we can sometimes frame this conversation as though we are introducing it. We are bringing in a topic that most people have not thought about and will react to in a certain way. Certainly, from speaking to my own constituents and people I come across as part of my ministerial duties, I know that a lot of people out there are , in many ways , further ahead than we are. They are well aware of these growing concerns when it comes to hostile threat actors and the other challenges that we are facing. They are waiting and expecting to see the Government take decisive action there .

It is also interesting because this conversation has started in so many different corners of the internet, so many different places and so many different cafés and pubs that it is uniquely vulnerable to misinformation. We cannot be naive to the fact that it will be exploited on Facebook, on platforms that we use and on ones that we do not. I do not use TikTok, but there are all these different platforms that are being used to help amplify misinformation and active disinformation.

That underlines the importance of making sure that we have an awareness campaign that is loud enough and targeted at those different audiences. We need to be able to put forward the truth and the facts to say to people not only , “ W e need to focus on resilience in a way we haven ’ t for a long time” , but some really basic things such as, “Do you have water?” This is very useful for an average power outage. It is important to be able to know that you can rely on this. I found myself with a power cut the other day . To my shame, I did not necessarily have what I needed to make the next day relatively comfortable. This is just simple resilience that everybody needs to have in the back of their heads.

When we look at those narratives, I have also been shocked when I have been speaking to people and they have raised rumours that they have heard online about what something means or does not mean. It is quite shocking to hear some of that , because it has no basis in any actions that the Government have taken.

To come to your point about young people specifically, there are two points here , from the MoD’s perspective. We have a role to play, particularly through our cadet organisation s . As you will be aware, we have ambitions to expand the cadet programme by not only expanding current units but making sure that we have more units, particularly in schools or in places that are not well served by those cadet units. They provide a really trusted organisation for young people where we can have trusted message carriers, if you like, to deliver there. Of course, it is a wider challenge across g overnment ; that is why this is a whole - of - government approach. There is really important work that must be done, both by the Cabinet Office and anywhere that has a touchpoint with young people — education being an obvious one.

It is about not just what we are saying but who is saying it. Again, it is about having trusted message carriers. The MoD has a big role to play there. We have very authoritative voices in d efence when we talk about threats. We have very trusted voices, and we have to make sure that we are using them. Disinformation and misinformation are not being targeted at just the young; they are definitely being targeted across all age groups. These things are a constant fight.

It is encouraging to hear you say that the whole of g overnment , as well as the whole of society , is very important in this exercise. Do your MoD colleagues have anything to add ? No? What about the FCDO? Do you envisage a role for the FCDO in this national conversation?
Yes. I should say that I am the director of the Defence and International Security Directorate

F or years , we have been calling out the behaviour that Russia and other threat actors have been up to in the UK and elsewhere. We see that as an important part of this national conversation. It can be as long ago as the Salisbury chemical attacks to what happened in Leipzig just a few weeks ago. The Foreign Office’s role is often to comment and act on what hostile powers are doing , more than communicating to the UK public, which is obviously an area where the Cabinet Office has slightly more responsibility. We absolutely want to make sure that those things are joined up.

W e are also very conscious that the messages we give our own population are heard by our adversaries and what we say to our adversaries is heard by our own population. One of the things we have been working quite hard on recently is making sure that all parts of g overnment get the tone right in how we talk about, for example, hostile Russian behaviour so that we do not undermine deterrence but , rather , add to it. T his is definitely a conversation that we are part of.

Q214 I fully understand the analysis of the problem, and I absolutely accept the point from the Foreign Office that it has been quite good at rebutting some lines. What I am unclear about is whether anywhere in g overnment is pulling this together in the way that , first, our adversaries do. Russia has been doing it for a century. In China, you have the United Front organisations and all the rest of it pumping that out a round the world. To what extent are we doing that?

By the way, we used to be rather good at that during the Cold War. I am not clear that we have maintained any of that machinery for , first, deciding what the line is ; and , secondly, for expressing it in ordinary terms in order to develop a campaign for people to understand the threat here and in a wider international context. Is there a centre that is actually doing this job?
Is there a national message , as well as a national conversation , in the offing?
Is there a message centre beside that? The landscape keeps changing the whole time, both for defence but also for putting our opponents — and some of their apologists — on the spot.
When you say “ c entre ” , is that as in a specific unit or organisation or as in driving across g overnment?

Just saying , “I t is the Cabinet Office ”, is not enough because it has so much responsibility all over the place ; I am not clear on exactly how that operates. It seems to me that there needs to be interaction and engagement . T hat needs to be driving it out , rather than just being a co-ordination of the good efforts of different departments.

I agree that it needs real heft put behind it because this is taking it to a level that, frankly, we are no longer used to ; t hat is probably fair to say. I c an not comment on where we were during the Cold War, but certainly what we are looking for is to be much more ambitious than we were five or 10 years ago. I certainly see that as my role. As I said at the beginning, this is really important to me. My role is to make sure that we as the MoD are underlying the need and the impetus for this. I appreciate what you have said about the Cabinet Office, but I can see those wheels turning to grip this and take it to the next level. Obviously, we have been through a period of change, but , when we are having discussions about the threats , as we understand them, I feel reassured that we are going to get there.

You referenced what we did in the Cold War. The Foreign Office had the Information Research Department, set up by Ernest Bevin ; th at was controversial , maybe, but it was actually very effective. Denis Healey was one of the driving forces in that department. We had a centre of gravity in the system driving that on. I do not detect any of that now .

Can I add a word on that? One of the big moves that the Foreign Office has made in the restructuring we are doing at the moment is to create a hybrid threats directorate because we recognise that this area needs significantly more resource. We are trying to bring together in one place what we know and are doing on these serious issues.

To your point about working cross- g overnment, from where I sit, this is a very active and regular effort. Communications directors meet very regularly on this agenda. The deputy National Security Adviser convenes people to talk about hybrid threats on a very regular basis. It is an active co-ordination. Certainly, my department is investing very heavily in this. Indeed, it is probably the area where we are seeing one of the greatest amounts of increase in resource and focus here in London.

Q215 Mine is a very simple question. I am very interested in this co-ordinated effort across g overnment. Who is in charge? Which department is it ? Which part is in charge of convening those meetings and making that happen? One of our concerns is that it is not very clear or transparent where the responsibility lies for things. You are having meetings , but whose meetings are they?
The Cabinet Office is responsible for driving it.

Q216 Thank you for coming here today, Minister. I want to touch on nuclear risks , on which t his committee has not really touched. We were advised by the National Preparedness Commission that they are in the “ catastrophic ” category, but it emphasised a very low estimated likelihood: a nuclear accident or major overseas radiation release was estimated at less than 0.2% probability over five years. To my mind, that is probably how the public see it as well. W hat are the reasonable worst-case scenarios for civil and military nuclear risks? How are these perceived by the public, and how should we educate them about them?
Sorry, what are the other risks?
Nuclear leaks from a power plant or Mr Putin getting old and angry.

There is a whole range of risks to do with military, civil and nuclear, be that as a result of an accident or some sort of deliberate activity , that are kept under continual review . Certainly, when it comes to the safety and security of the nuclear capabilities for which we are responsible, a huge deal of effort goes into ensuring that they are as safe as possible and that every risk is mitigated.
How do you understand the public understanding? Do they have any perception of a nuclear risk?

That is an interesting one. I am afraid I do not have the answer to that. I cannot say anecdotally . I have been asked about it before, and I do not know if my perception of the risk reflects the average person on the street’s reflection of the risk.

To my mind, i f there were a nuclear accident or a nuclear threat, it would induce panic , if there had not been preparedness. W hat preparedness are you presenting to the public? Maybe Mr Fender will have a response.

I might point to a couple of examples from Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, where we have had rhetorical threats from Putin about nuclear use and we have seen , even in the last few days , some concerns about the situation at the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Station in Ukraine. On the latter, there has obviously been a lot of planning across g overnment as to what that would mean, and an effort , in our communication on it , to make sure that there is good information out there but also not undue concern about it.

On Putin’s nuclear rhetoric, we are keen to make sure that that is seen for what it is : an attempt at coercion more than actual threats of nuclear use. It is not the right thing for there to be excessive nuclear rhetoric between the nuclear powers about such scenarios. Again, we have tried to be sober in responding to it , while also pointing out what the agenda is : an attempt to scaremonger and coerce rather than , we believe, an actual intent to use nuclear weapons.

Q217 My question is in two parts, but in the interest of time I will ask them both together , so you can pick who to answer which. First, can you tell us how the Government are addressing the international nature of the threat environment through multilateral co-operation, including with our European partners? Secondly, what risks do you see applying particularly to the overseas territories, and how could those risks affect or create wider risks for the UK?

I will briefly address that. The nature of many of the threats we face absolutely does not respect any borders. International co-operation is absolutely vital to face any number of the challenges and threats, be they military or not in nature. Working with partners and allies to understand the nature of those threats and then be able to co-operate in ways to mitigate, prevent or deal with occurrences is hugely important.

As you are aware, we have the “NATO first” policy in defence, which does not mean NATO only, it just means NATO first. We are continually looking at ways to deepen our partnerships with our partners in NATO, be that by working as part of NATO or with bilateral arrangements. For example, we have a strong agreement with Norway—Lunna House—on how we can work more closely together there, and there are things such as the JEF, which is a subset of now NATO countries. This is a huge priority for us. When you look at the risks that the MoD can identify, many of those will be dealt with satisfactorily only as part of a wider partnership. We saw in Ankara this year the commitment that was made to building a stronger Europe and a stronger NATO. I can point to whole other partnerships that we are trying to deepen, but I will not just to save time.

I will move quickly on to the overseas territories ; I will let my colleagues talk in more depth on them . The risks they face can vary greatly from the rest of the UK. In some areas, they will perhaps face greater challenges from climate-based risks. For example, we obviously play a big role in hurricane season in the Caribbean. It is important to make sure that we have that risk understanding for each territory and are able to adjust what we need to have accordingly.

I am Director for Overseas Territories and Polar — and , as of today, also the ocean ; i t is quite a broad remit. I will come in support of that. I understand about the risks, but I want to put on the record that the relationship we have with the UK overseas territories is fantastic for the territories and for the UK. It gives us global reach and a strategic advantage. They are home to many of the world’s largest financial centres. Some 94% of the UK’s biodiversity is to be found across the overseas territories. That is why , on balance, managing those risks is well within the national interest.

As the Minister has said, because of the location of the territories—many are very remote—the climate risks are large. We work very closely with the overseas territories’ Governments in building that resilience ahead of and during hurricane season, in particular across the Caribbean and Bermuda, while also working with some even more remote territories such as Tristan da Cunha , Saint Helena and the Pitcairn Islands to help them respond to any climate emergencies. A very good example of that happened earlier this year . Y ou probably all heard about the hantavirus that spread through five of the territories. The MoD played an absolutely critical role in delivering aid where it was needed to inhabitants of a very remote territory.

There are of course economic risks as well. I have mentioned that there are four territories that house significant financial centres. Making sure that there is resilience there, in terms of both normal economic resilience and cyber security , is an area where the UK can help play a convening role.
Then there is the defence and security relationship, where by the UK is responsible for all the inhabited territories. We are responsible for taking a role there as well.

Just very briefly, you specifically mentioned the financial centres as being a significant benefit, although you said there were some risks around that. What about the risks of those financial centres themselves being used by hostile actors and the reputational risks to the UK around the world?

Absolutely. Both of those are concerns. That is why we have been working very hard with the territories, including registers of beneficial ownership. We are making sure that there is transparency around who is investing and how they are investing . We also work with them to ensure that their domestic regimes are secure against cyber and other hostile actors.

Q218 My question relates to the UK Government’s approach to international frameworks that have been adopted , or are being adopted , by the UN and the EU. How do you assess them? Are there divergences or alignments with what they have produced? Is there anything that we can learn from them?

T his comes back to my earlier point about how we absolutely recognise that these resilience challenges will take a lot of international co-operation, both within Europe and across the globe. We actively engage with partners, be it the UN, NATO or bilaterally, to share those lessons and adopt best practice. Certainly, a focal point of my international activity has been through the lens of resilience.

We work with NATO on civil preparedness, continuity of g overnment and critical national infrastructure because we recognise the importance of that, how it underpins and how we will need to work together, particularly when that resilience might get tested. We are regularly reviewing lessons from exercises or contingencies we face here in the UK, and we also regularly reach out to international partners to make sure we have the right approach to our own resilience and are taking the best practice from around the globe.
Lord Marland has one more question in this section before we move on to a different topic.

I want to go back to overseas territories. I declare an interest as chairman of the Commonwealth Enterprise and Investment Council, and I travel quite extensively among some OTs. You are painting an over-rosy picture . T here are tensions. There is a view among many of the OTs that , if there were a violent issue or an immigration issue, the UK would be very slow in responding to that in terms of its Armed Forces capability. There is a PMQ in a minute on the Falkland Islands, which would be a case in point of how you would respond to that. If you read some parts of the media, they say we do not have a chance and we do not have the capability, but if you read others, they say that we have. I would just like to push you further on that, in particular in relation to immigration issues. Haitian immigration is moving into some Caribbean dependencies.

Yes, certainly, Lord Marland. Just to be clear, immigration is devolved to the territories. Although the UK has an interest and a responsibility in terms of overall security, immigration itself tends to be run by the overseas territories’ Governments themselves. You mentioned—

Sorry, my point was that the Cayman Islands, for example, has a potential very big onslaught of illegal immigrants coming to the country. It does not have the defence mechanism for it and would rely on the UK. The UK did not respond very positively to the last incident that it had.

You mentioned the Cayman Islands specifically. I can tell you that we are working closely with the Cayman Government through our governors. Each of the territories has a governor who is answerable to the OT Government but also to the King.
