I welcome our witnesses, who are from the defence and finance industries, so we are keen to hear what you have to say. The Government have announced £15 billion in extra spending on defence in this Parliament, with the intention to raise spending to 3% by the next Parliament. It would be helpful if our witnesses could introduce themselves, and say where they come from and what their angle is.

I am John Godfrey, the MD for policy and public affairs at TheCityUK, which is a member organisation representing banks, insurers, asset managers and related professional services. One thing that I do is look after our defence and resilience group, which has a membership of about 70 firms, and its aim is to improve the flow of finance into the defence and resilience sectors.

I am Nathan Mathiot, director of policy and public affairs at ADS. We are a UK trade association for civil aerospace, defence, security and space companies across manufacturing and services. Around two thirds of our members have a primary interest in defence. As a whole, we have about 1,000 defence SMEs, if you count it in certain ways, so we represent a significant industrial footprint.

I am Mike Tinmouth, the co-founder and chief operating officer of ACUA Ocean. We are a Plymouth-based dual-use technology company, so we were very much founded for both the commercial offshore sector and the defence and security sector. We build long-endurance robotic systems designed for the deployment of surface, subsurface and aerial assets out at sea, including the North sea and those types of operating environments. We are a team of 30, we are classed as a growth business and we were one of the companies that presented to the former Defence Secretary as one of the potential future unicorns in the UK.

Q897 We have a certain amount of time to get through our questions, so please be concise with your answers. We might have follow-up questions. We want to get through the whole panel and get as much information from you as possible—that would be very helpful.

First, the defence investment plan talks about the different platforms and the new direction we are going to take. Nathan, can you expand on whether the platforms described in there are the right ones? Are we going in the right direction? Do you have concerns, or are you taking some comfort from what is contained in the plan?

What we see in the defence investment plan is a shift slightly away from purely platform-centric thinking towards thinking about the systems—rather than just the warship, it is the data and the AI systems that might be on there, or it might be the autonomous vehicles that are accompanying it. The Navy has looked at moving towards a hybrid navy, and it has made some platform decisions to reflect that, both about where it is going to buy new things, but also about not going ahead with some. Similarly, in the Royal Air Force there is a significant commitment or re-commitment to the Global Combat Air programme, as well as commitments to collaborative combat aircraft, which are going to be autonomous accompanying aircraft to support that. So it is a slightly wider focus.

I think the shift towards autonomous systems as a whole, while not losing sight of the traditional platforms that anchor an overall full-spectrum military offer, is probably the right one in broad terms. If you only look at what is happening in the east and in the middle east, you can see quite clearly the direction of travel. So, overall, I think it is trending in the right direction.
Q898 Mike, what is your view on this, and how does it affect your company?

It is good news for companies like ACUA Ocean. We in the UK are a world leader when it comes to robotics and automation. When it comes to the ability to scale in times of conflict, that will only be achieved through smaller, more autonomous platforms. You cannot spend 10 or 15 years building big, complicated warships. What you need is the ability, at speed and scale, to produce these. We were very pleasantly surprised by the direction of travel.

It also recognises that there is going to be no one size fits all; there is not going to be a silver bullet solution that solves all problems. This is going to be a multi-domain, multi-environment solution. You are going to have a selection of smaller assets and larger assets working together that are operating aerial, surface and subsurface. When it comes to software and robotics, the point is to have that interoperability between different solutions and, we hope, a direction of sovereign capability, where more of those systems are built here in the UK, off a sovereign operating system that will enable us to retain skills, knowledge and control here in the UK.

Q899 Obviously, that sort of sovereign capability is important. It feels like there is a time limit, in terms of how far we need to come in a very short time to feel prepared. Do you think we have enough time to get there, based on your experience of the development time and the work you do?

We are a world leader, but we will not be if we do not invest in UK companies. The clock is ticking and the advantage is slipping away to better funded nations, both friend and foe. From our position, we see advantages. We think this is the only direction of travel, but it needs to be backed by cash, contracts and programmes really rapidly to capitalise on our position.
Q900 John, we just had a mention of the finances. What is your view about the platforms and investment across the industry?

I agree that the reform of the platforms is likely to be helpful. If it adds greater nimbleness and more interoperability, that is very helpful indeed. But the most important thing is if it enables the procurement process to move faster, because this is the absolute problem for financiers. The lack of a demand signal for almost the last two years has meant that the companies one might like to lend to or invest in have in many cases mothballed or given up, and there is nothing to lend against or invest into. So speed is of the essence here for working capital and subsequently for capex.
That is very helpful . T hank you.
Q901 Just to follow up with a quick question, Mike, you said something about the UK losing out to better organised and better funded nations. Which nations do you think are getting it right?

Right now, countries like Germany are putting their cash where their mouth is and are in the process of writing big cheques. The UK has always been very good at doing little £100,000 or £200,000 contracts with lots of SMEs. Germany is taking the different approach of trying to understand where the future capability they need is and writing the £5 million, £10 million, £20 million or £30 million programmes that investors in finance want to see. Once they have the demand signals from the market that there are contracts and there is revenue to be made, it unlocks the growth capital that the industry requires.

Right now, we are performing behind our European allies—the US has always been leagues ahead on spend. The knock-on impact is that if you look at Europe’s growth unicorns and decacorns, we have only recently—in the last couple of weeks—started to see sovereign UK unicorns, with Cambridge Aerospace and Kraken Robotics, whereas in Germany, you have ARX Robotics, Quantum Systems, Helsing and STARK. Over the last two or three years, Germany has been producing them at scale because they have been backed by the big contracts that help them to win and unlock that capital.

Q902 That is very helpful. John, you were nodding along when Mike was talking about the investment that Germany is making. Do you have anything to add? What is your take on the way that other countries are financing?

The only thing I would add, and it goes without saying, is that private capital is globally mobile. It will not sit in the UK waiting for something to happen when there are opportunities in other markets. Perhaps we can come on to how that might be accelerated later but, basically, capital will not sit on its hands waiting for things to happen here.

Q903 We have already talked about some of the reforms that have taken place since the Ministry of Defence announced its reform programme in 2024. What are the most important changes that have happened, if any have? What has not happened?

What has worked in the reform process is still theoretical to quite a large degree. That is partly because those reforms were not all implemented instantly; it has taken a bit of time to get round to building them in. Also, there has been a lack of a demand signal: how do you know whether the new system will work if you do not know if there is any significant amount of money behind it at this point?

But in theory at least—hopefully it will begin to work in practice too—the creation of a National Armaments Director, including staffing up that function and, although it is taking a little longer than one would like, equipping it with sufficient financial and commercial knowledge to engage with our end of town, as it were, has significant potential. Closer engagement between MOD—both the DIAG and the National Armaments Director’s offices—and the City , broadly defined, would make all this work better. That just involves either side travelling five stops on a tube to engage with the other side.

Q904 To jump in on that, that interface—between the MOD, which has the knowledge about the platforms, the kit and the things that go bang, and you who are providing the finance—is absolutely critical . Do you know whether we are at the stage of you actually getting together?

There are meetings that take place. We find that, in relative terms, it is quite straightforward to engage with the military part of the MOD. We are running a series of events in the City called “How we fight”; we have had combined services there, and the Army, the Navy and the Air Force will be coming down. Those are very popular, as the City wants to know more about these subjects.

We have had less engagement with the financial parts of the MOD, which is really because, for the whole time we were waiting for the DIP, the National Armaments Director and colleagues said, “We can’t come out and meet you, because we don’t know what we need to talk about.”

I think we ha ve seen some real progress across the board. There are several different components to this. There is the defence reform agenda that John was just touching on, with the creation of the NAD, the military strategic headquarters and the formation of the Quad. That is all internal structure stuff about how the MOD governs itself, and that is reasonably well embedded, even if not completely there.

Then there is the delivery of the defence industrial strategy. Today is its one-year anniversary, and we have had five defence growth deals launched, five defence technical excellence colleges, and the establishment of the Defence Office for Small Business Growth. There are lots of interesting bits and pieces as well as the UK defence innovation—
Q905 My underlying question was about what you just said: has anything actually changed as a consequence ?

I think so, but not necessarily enough if we want to achieve the ultimate effect, which is the big picture of achieving sufficient deterrence and meeting our NATO commitments. The defence investment plan was an important plank in that. That was great in terms of having a sense of current funding allocations, but the question of the funding road map is very live in the media right now as we go to the Budget and the spending review. It is in translating that existing set of aspirations into a funded pipeline where we hear from our members a degree of frustration, but I suppose you could say that it has only been a few months since that was actually released .

To echo those comments, commercial speed is the thing that has been really lacking. When you have spent the best part of two years waiting for the announcement of the defence investment plan, there is an expectation that thereafter the purse strings will be loosened and there will be a flow of cash. Although there have been some very positive examples, that has not been universal. Now one of the challenges—this is the restructuring part of the conversation—is that we have seen funding allocated to programmes, but those programmes are not able to be delivered because there are not enough commercial personnel in position to deliver them. They are now receiving delays of two or three months while the restructuring—
While you recruit.

While you are recruiting, and while you restructure and rebuild teams and so on. That is one of the challenges of the ongoing changes, and all the back-office staff need to catch up and fall in place.

There are definitely positive signs. I also echo, in terms of positive progress being made, the setting up of organisations such as NSSIF, the UK’s sovereign defence fund, which is an excellent source of venture funding into earlier-stage businesses, particularly dual-use companies. Those are steps in the right direction. Those organisations are very well received, knowledgeable, and located in the MOD, and they can act as that gatekeeper towards future funding and investment, as well as into the MOD and requirements. So there are some real positive signs, but speed in terms of the commercial readiness and delivery of contracts remains the biggest challenge.
Q906 Do you think the defence investment plan has put enough emphasis on supply chain resilience?

Partly. Fundamentally, a balancing act has taken place between the strategic defence review, the defence industrial strategy and the defence investment plan, and between achieving military readiness and dialling up production capacity, while also sustaining industrial readiness as an integral lever of that. There is a bit of a gap there when thinking through, from an economic security perspective, what levers are available to the Ministry of Defence and the wider Government, but I am conscious that you have a cross-section of speakers to explore that in more detail later.

In a sense, the supply of materials is not really a business the MOD has historically been involved in, but it has taken more of an interest—for example, by taking over steel production in more recent years. There is something there, for me, where there is a bit of a gap, but I can understand, to some extent, the primary focus on production capacity at the heart of all these initiatives.

From a purely financial perspective, the problem that we identified in our group, and probably top of our list of challenges, is the funding of SMEs that sit in the supply chains of the bigger primes. Those are typically £2 million to £10 million companies. I t is sometimes difficult to finance those companies for lack of demand signal a nd because there is an expectation of partial or full guarantee. T here i s also a problem with those companies because of the procurement process. I f the procurement process is not visible to the financier in any way because the product is so sensitive, then there must be a way to develop a better way of joining those up — whether through technology or anonymi s ation , t here are mechanisms to do this . T hat would enable us to finance much quicker . A t the moment , a company goes off and wins a contract, e verything goes dark and e ventuall y you are expected to lend against something even though you are not allowed to know what it is or how much of it there i s going to be. That is really difficult . T here are ways to work through that , however, to make that aspect of the supply chain much more resilient.

I will echo and expand on those comments . T o get on my soapbox , s upply chain to sovereign capability is one of the things that British businesses are brilliant at — working with local supply chains and local small businesses. When we were developing our uncrewed surface vessel — a 25 - tonne, 14 - metre , fully capable vessel —a bout 94% of our spend was with UK businesses. That is something that we are really proud of because it maintains small businesses and skills in local communities. W here we are lacking is across the wider supply chain. Everybody is looking for those contracts.

We also need to be investing not just in the resilience of the supply chain, but in things such as manufacturing . Plymouth, where we are based , is home to the UK ’ s National Centre for Mari ne Autonomy . It is a f antastic world - leading location. However, all our manufacturing and waterfront warehouses have been turned into townhouses with beautiful views of the ocean . That is fantastic for people wanting to live in a nice area, but it means that we do not have the capability and capacity to build things where we need to build them . I think that the supply chain needs to look across the entire manufacturing life cycle as well.

F undamentally, we are not going to see businesses investing in what is effectively spare capacity if there is a lack of confidence in that future demand. I t may be that where there is a strategic dependency or concern , the Government should think about minimum demand offer s, or support for “warm production ”, so that we are not turning around in a crisis and expecting that to suddenly ramp up and t here i s a bit of skin in the game . W hat happens in defence is that there are often peaks and troughs . Y ou then have an issue with the workforce going into other sectors and so on, so when the time comes , there i s not the workforce and support to answer.

T hat is an excellent point. T his is where we are seeing dual use being absolutely critical , because it can flatten the peaks and troughs of defence spending. There will ultimately be peace dividends where defence spending reduces in time. T hat is where being able to build and develop with the commercial sector also means that , in the event of conflict, you already have an already - on capacity ; y ou are not building from scratch but are able to grow and scale up from that with the skills. It is an excellent point , and why investing in dual use is key.

Q907 I want to ask an additional question, probably to Nathan. O ne aspect of supply chain resilience that has been causing a lot of concern in recent months is related to the new steel safeguards. Do you ha ve any comment s on the implications you are seeing ? W e are three months into the new steel safeguards being in place . A s an MP representing a lot of downstream industry, I know what I think , but I woul d appreciate hearing what you think.

It is a challenge . W e understand what the Government were trying to achieve with t he introduction of the steel trade measure in July. There was an influx of cheap commodity - grade steel into the UK. Clearly, we want a vibrant steel industrial base here for a variety of reasons. U nfortunately, we have been caught in the crosshairs from an aerospace and defence perspective , with specialist alloys where there simply is not the industrial base , and there is a whole host of issues to do with OEM specifications. You cannot just change from one mill to another. We are working intens ively with the Department for B usiness, I nnovation, S cience and T rade on potential mitigations or exemptions. We are talking to steel industry colleagues as wel l. We will see what the Government feel they are able to do while not undermining their understandable reason for bringing in the trade measure.
Q908 So you are hopeful of tweaks at the review point?

“Hopeful” may be too strong a word, but we are in a live conversation. I give credit to the Government for being open to a conversation and receiving our evidence. The thing is that the shoe has not fully dropped yet because the quotas have not all been used up. We are anticipating a problem. We can already see, from the volumes we know are used by our members across aerospace and defence, and the allocated quotas, that we are going to hit the buffers at some point.
Q909 Mike, my question is very similar to Antonia’s. How easy is it today for defence firms to access the capital that they need to grow?

Very difficult, particularly here in the UK. We have relatively immature defence venture capital compared with places like Germany. Most of the growth capital is coming from the US—and always has historically. This is where NSSIF starts to break the model, because of the role it plays in interfacing with the MOD.

We are also seeing a lot of generalist venture capital firms moving into this space that do not have the background and access in terms of knowledge of defence. This is a stat I always use: in the US, about 56% of venture capitalists are former founders of businesses. They have been at the coalface and built a business. In the UK, it is 13%; we have an immature market. We have a lot of people who are very smart and come from management consulting, accounting and the like, who look at businesses and go, “What’s the risk profile of that?” Defence does not fit. Dual use does not even really fit. Maritime robotics—building giant ocean robots to go out and protect critical infrastructure—sounds risky. It sounds lucrative and exciting, but risky. There is a real challenge.

That is where access to product-market fit and contracts is absolutely key , because that is the big de-risker for growth. There are a lot of people who want to dive in with money when you have all the contracts, but at the critical stage where SMEs need to grow, it is very, very difficult. As a result, brilliant British businesses are starting to move abroad. Just yesterday, I was at ADS and heard that one of our peers in the market is relocating to the United States because that is where the capital sits. We are still struggling with that. Organisations like NSSIF are bridging that, but there is a huge gap, and the UK is falling behind.

Q910 John, you said that TheCityUK has diagnosed part of the problem: the fact that businesses cannot disclose what they are building, or the costs or the finance that are needed. What would TheCityUK like to see the MOD tweak to ease that conversation with the City ?

We have been working on a couple of practical ideas. To pick up on the capital point, we have been working to secure some changes in the standard form of documentation that is used in the venture capital world. That sounds very dull, but it is quite important because some of the standard “agreement to fund” language still carried an awful lot of leftover ESG content, which basically excluded whole swathes of defence. We have managed to change that so that the standard documentation will now exclude UN controversial weapons, but the rest of defence will be explicitly included so that you are allowed to invest in these other things. We think that will help as the new-style contracts replace the old ones. That is one thing that we have been doing.

As I said, the solution to joining finance and procurement more closely together is really a technology solution. It has to be super secure; the banks and funders that are involved must be cleared to the right levels; the data must be anonymised. That is not beyond the reach of technology.

I would put one other thing on the agenda around this: areas where regulation overlaps. One would assume, as a financier, that when a company has won a contract with the MOD, the MOD has done massive diligence to make sure that Mike is who he says he is and all the rest of it. When they come to raise finance, the financiers have to do the same thing all over again—anti-money laundering, know your client and all of that. I think there is a solution, which would be to have what is effectively a compliance passport. Once you have passed the test at the MOD, that should be good enough to at least accelerate the financing process. My sense is that the Financial Conduct Authority would be supportive in trying to develop something of that sort.

Q911 On that point, in terms of non-disclosures and all those other pieces, is there an idea of how much private finance defence firms are missing out on because they are not able to secure finance without disclosing customers and contracts?

It is very hard to come down to a number, but I will just give you a sense of the scale and the enthusiasm east of here, in the City , for funding. If you look just at J.P. Morgan—one bank, albeit a very big one—they have a fund globally for defence and resilience that is $1.5 trillion, so 5% of that, if it landed in the UK, would be pretty much three times the new money in the DIP. The scale depends precisely on the demand signal, but it is large.

Q912 John, you indicated earlier that there is a lot of interest from the City in the kit—looking at it and perhaps even having a little hands-on play with it and all of that . But how is that translating into an appetite to actually invest ? Has that changed? Has the mood changed? Are people more willing to actually put money up now?

I think the appetite is changing. L et us take first the cultural appetite, if you like . Five or 10 years ago , the feeling was, “Well, this is all a bit sensitive . Our staff w on’t like it and some of our shareholders might not like it. I t ’s not part of ESG. ” The Russian invasion of Ukraine has absolutely changed that. To my way of thinking, there is barely any more a question of woke fund managers w ho will not put their money in. It is now the case that investing in defence and resilience is a positive part of the S of ESG , so there’s that. Then you come down to the slightly harder - edged bit of this : am I going to write a che que for it? And, as ever, I’m afraid that brings us right back round to , “Where’s the demand signal? I do need to take a hard - edged commercial decision, but I do n’t have any moral issues with it. ”

Q913 So you think it is less a moral thing and much more a simple, straightforward, hard - headed business decision . You are not seeing the demand signal and then you are judging those businesses that are in defence like any other business .
A bsolutely. As Mike said, people will lend against a contract , but if you do not know whether there is going to be a contract, it is very difficult to lend.

Q914 Last week , the Prime Minister confirmed in the C hamber that the UK is considering joining the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank. I am keen to hear your perspective . What are your thoughts about the UK joining that ?

We are all in favour of it. It is access to more capital ; it is access to more markets and more joined - up thinking. W e see there being very much a pan - European , pan -w estern , allied and aligned nations approach . T hat is where we think the growth opportunities sit for British businesses that are looking to export , and it is where we see international capital — where there is a lack of UK capital — coming in , s o we strongly support that . It is worth noting that it focuses more on growth - stage businesses , so there will still be a gap for earl ier- stage businesses , but we are fully in support.

That was a welcome comment by the Prime Minister. I mostly agree with what Mike said . The DSRB potentially has an important role to play in capital mobilisation , but I do not think we have ever felt it was necessarily a silver bullet . The wider thing that we have all been rabbiting on about, for good reason, is that there are potentially opportunities and sources of capital available , but the central problem is the customer demand signal at the heart of things. With the multilateral defence mechanism that the UK until now has been quite invested in , and the piece a bout demand aggregation , I think that is still part of the equation . I think it is a two - part solution. It is the more the merrier , in some senses . We are broadly in support.

You would expect me to say this from the financial sector perspective, but obviously it depends on what the terms and conditions of joining are, how much capital you subscribe and what the cost-benefit is, essentially. But in principle, I am absolutely in agreement with my two colleagues. It would send a strong signal of financial interoperability as well as operational interoperability, if that is not a hideous mangling of the English language. If it adds to the guarantee capacity that exists in the market, that is a big tick; if it helps us with exports, which I believe it would, that is also a big tick; and it may well increase the volume of funds available and help with the pricing. I am supportive, with the right terms and conditions.

Q915 I have a very quick follow-up. You mentioned the MDM very briefly. Do either of you want to add anything about where you see the gaps with the DSRB versus MDM, or whether they need to be amalgamated?
My sense of it is that they perform different functions, but they could be complementary to one another. I would keep them at arm’s length from one another, frankly.

Q916 I am interested in returning to something you mentioned at the beginning, John. We discussed this a little bit, and panellists spoke about the flight of capital to some places, but I wondered if you felt that there was less of that happening. While there is the ability for capital to move, do we have a strong enough demand signal now that we have things like the defence investment plan and other such announcements from the Government? Do you think it is weak? Do you think it is strong? Obviously, you mentioned that potentially joining the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank would be another signal that would strengthen that. What is your take on where the capital wants to go and how we can retain and invest it?

I do not think we have done enough to keep the capital here at this point. The DIP is one type of signal. The type of signal that my markets are really waiting for is supposedly coming in the defence finance and investment strategy—we are still waiting for that. We always want more detail. We have that still to come, and that may strengthen the signal.

It would be enormously helpful if the Chancellor could do a few things around here to help with the signalling. The first would be to make sure that a meaningful part of the Budget content covers defence. Then there is potentially the publication of the DFIS. There is then potentially a large defence investor summit coming up, we hear—either in November or December—and that is an opportunity to send a very powerful message.

The other half is about co-investment. More needs to be made of co-investment, alongside public finance institutions, whether that is the BBB or the UK National Wealth Fund, or even the National Housing Bank. Basically, if you are talking about dealing with some of the lower-hanging cost items, including military housing and, of course, UK Export Finance, these things all have to sing in a chorus, as it were.
We have run out of time but thank you very much for all the evidence you have provided to the Committee and for your time today.

sessions.iT: Proposals for backbench debates

segs.tx: Backbench Business Committee
Representations : Backbench Debates
Tuesday 8 September 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 8 September 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Bob Blackman (Chair); Jonathan Davies; Mary Glindon; Alison Hume; Will Stone.
Questions 1-2 4
Representations made
I : John Glen
I I : Jim Shannon
I I I : Daniel Francis
I V : David Mundell
V : David Mundell
V I : John Slinger
V I I : Liz Jarvis
John Glen made representations.

Q1 Welcome to the meeting of the Backbench Business Committee where we will be considering applications from colleagues for debates in the main Chamber and also in Westminster Hall. The first debate request is from John Glen for the future funding of our English cathedrals. This is a request for a half-day debate in the Chamber. Over to you, John.

Thank you very much, Chair. I appreciate the opportunity to be here on a matter of significant interest for the country and also Members. There are 42 cathedrals in England. As the MP representing Salisbury and Salisbury cathedral, I am very keen to explore whether the Committee is willing to give us time to look at a recent report commissioned to look into the economic and wider impact of cathedrals in communities up and down the country. I have secured significant interest, with firm interest from about 15 colleagues, but there are 42 in total. We have not chased down all their offices yet, but I am pretty confident that we are going to get a much larger number. The issue of the funding of cathedrals—
Q2 Can I just stop you there? On the application in front of us we only have eight names listed.
The list is growing all the time.
Q3 It would be very helpful if you shared the list with us, for various reasons.
It has grown since the application went in, but we shall put the additional names to you. We will be working very hard to get, I would hope, and being realistic, 25 people there.

It will be an opportunity to explore what impact cathedrals make in their communities from a spiritual and a wider economic point of view. The report points to £235 million of additional expenditure in the economy. T hey also have, across a range of needs, significant capital problems and need investment. There is a real challenge, and it is unlikely that the Government are going to have a massive amount of capital to give. As a former Treasury Minister, I am very aware of those constraints. However, it is an opportunity to fully explore how we can get a wider platform for support with philanthropy and other giving.

Holding it in the Chamber would really help to raise the profile. Obviously, we could get a ministerial response elsewhere but given the numbers that we could get in the Chamber and the wider view, it might stimulate people coming from other faiths with other places of worship to talk about it. You are a great expert on that. I submit that it would reach that threshold and would be a useful debate that the country would also want to hear about.

Q4 Thank you for bringing this forward, John. Obviously, we have a considerably long list for the Chamber. I understand the gravitas of this, but would you consider taking a Westminster Hall debate to get it sooner?
Yes, I would, because I do not want to make the interval from when we had the report published in May unreasonably long, but my strong preference would be to have it in the Chamber.
Q5 Thank you. At the moment, this would qualify you for a Westminster Hall debate, but not a Chamber debate. Could you get those extra names to the Clerks?
I will do that
The Clerks will be in touch shortly.
Jim Shannon made representations.

Q6 Next up is our season ticket holder, Jim Shannon. Jim, you have a request for a debate—in case you did not know, because you ha ve so many applications—for a debate on pulmonary fibrosis and interstitial lung awareness. This is a request for a debate in Westminster Hall.

Thank you very much, Mr Chairman, for giving me the opportunity to ask for this debate on pulmonary fibrosis and interstitial lung awareness. My list is growing as well, but I have the list with the added names, and I will give it to the Clerk. There are not anywhere near 25, but there certainly are 11. That is four people from the Government and then the rest from the Opposition.

Why is this debate needed? September is Pulmonary Fibrosis Awareness Month, and it creates a timely opportunity for Parliament to debate a group of progressive, life-limiting lung diseases. I understand that we cannot have the debate in September because it is too short notice for that. However, if it is possible to have it as early as we can in October that would be much appreciated.

Pulmonary fibrosis describes a group of interstitial lung diseases where the scarring of the lungs makes breathing progressively more difficult. There are 150,000 people in the UK affected and it is one of the most common forms. Fewer than half of those diagnosed live more than five years.

This is a disease and a health disability that has not been fully looked at, so the debate is an opportunity for that. It is very severe, but there are serious gaps throughout the care pathway. Two in five stop treatment within six months because of intolerable side effects. The side effects are gross. Even though you know you have a life-limiting disease, some of the side effects can be unbearable as well. The 10-year health plan and new respiratory transformation partnership have so far focused principally on asthma and COPD, but pulmonary fibrosis and interstitial lung diseases have never been fully looked at.

I am ever mindful of your kindness and generosity when it comes to debates, Mr Chairman. Here is a topic that I think needs to be discussed and I hope that that can happen. There are 11 names. As I said, there are four from the Government side and the rest are from the Opposition side.

Q7 Thank you for bringing this application, Jim. I agree with you that interstitial lung diseases should be included in the 10-year plan. It is a very good application, but you will know that we require an even split between Government and non-Government Members to support the debate. You say you have signatures coming, but at the moment you have only two Labour Members. Can you provide the Clerk with additional names?
I have two more names. I nabbed them this morning—Mark Sewards and Steve Yemm. I will give them to the Clerk.
Thank you.

Q8 Jim, Pulmonary Fibrosis Awareness Month is this month, but clearly we are not in a position to allocate a debate now. Is this an early application for next year or are you thinking of a particular timeframe?

I was hoping this might be a belated application for October. If you don’t ask, you don’t get—that’s how it works. It is my fault as the proposer. It should have been in long before now. The APPG discussed it only over the summer and we realised that September was the month. We knew we were never going to get it in September; we understand that.
Thank you very much. If you could give the names to the Clerks, they will be in touch with you in due course.
Daniel Francis made representations.
Q9 The next application is from Daniel Francis on inequalities in access to therapy for disabled children. It is a request for a Westminster Hall debate on either a Tuesday or a Thursday.

Thank you for having me again, Chair. I am hoping to bring forward a debate on inequalities in access to therapy for disabled children, so that colleagues and I can raise concerns regarding children with neurodisabilities and their families who are facing inequalities in accessing rehabilitation and therapy services in the UK. As I have touched on when I have been here previously, I have some first-hand experience as a parent of a child with quadriplegic cerebral palsy.

I got involved in this prior to the summer. The Member for Harlow was quite involved, but he is now a PPS. NAPA, which is the neurological and physical abilitation centre, is based in his constituency, and he has been working closely with them. They have designed individualised intensive therapy programmes with unique combinations, with a wide range of speech, physical, occupational and other innovative therapies. Their groundbreaking research dives into the imbalance caused by different access levels to advanced paediatric therapeutic care.

I am aware that Members from across the House attended the event that NAPA held here back in June—it was a very hot day—and have an interest in the matter, given the wide range of differences in those therapies across the country. Again, I know that at first hand. For four years, either my father or I did a 118-mile round trip every week to ensure that my daughter could have that kind of service. We went from south-east London to Ingfield in West Sussex, but NAPA offers some of those services.

Families are reporting disparities in accessing services, with provision being determined through a postcode lottery, and hugely through the charitable sector or private therapy. Again, I know from my role as chair of the all-party parliamentary groups for access to disability equipment and for wheelchair users that early intervention could improve long-term outcomes for children with complex disabilities, preventing hospital admissions and pressures on social care systems. Investing in rehabilitation would mean not only investment in the quality of life of disabled children and their families but long-term savings for public finances. Again, I spoke on that in the H ealth Bill last night, and there is very clear evidence on th at matter. I would therefore be grateful if a Westminster Hall debate could be considered and, hopefully, granted.

Q10 You have applied for a Westminster Hall debate, but your application includes the text of a very clear substantive motion. D ebate s in Westminster Hall can take place only on neutral motion s . Would you therefore be happy for us to change your motion to a neutral motion that says, “That this House has considered inequalities in access to therapy for disabled children”?
I would be delighted to accept that request, Mary, and have that rounded debate.

I also forgot to say that, in the last Parliament , there was an all-party parliamentary group on cerebral palsy —there isn’t now— in which Mary Kelly Foy and a former Conservative Member for Blackpool, whose name I forget, were very involved ; I think the gentleman has cerebral palsy. There are recommendations from that APPG’s reports on these matters, and it would be good to be able to talk about them as well.

Thank you, Daniel, for bringing this application ; I think it is really important. I just want to add that I think the economic consequences of not providing timely rehabilitation and therapy services for children are huge. Only the other day, I was speaking to the parent of a primary-aged child who has broken his ankle twice and is waiting for proper orthopaedic interventions . T hat must be replicated across the country , so t hank you for bringing this application.

If you will allow, Chair, a necdotally—as I say, we have heard this evidence in the APPG for wheelchair users—we know that there is clear evidence about that, particularly for children with cerebral palsy who do not weight-bear. My own daughter had half the ball taken out of the socket of her hip three years ago and is about to have to have part of her femur taken out on one side, because her leg has almost come out of its hip on th at side. Those are quite common issues i f you talk to the specialists over the road at Evelina . I am sure that we will be discussing that in the debate — if it is granted.

Q11 You have asked for a Tuesday debate ; i f it is in Westminster Hall on a Tuesday, we need to allocate it to the right answering Department , but y ou have not indicated the answering Department. It could be Health and Social Care or it could be the Women and Equalities Minister— I just want to clarify.
I think Health and Social Care is probably the most appropriate place for it to be.
That’s fine. T he Clerks will be in touch in due course. Thank you.
David Mundell made representations.

Q12 Next up is David Mundell, who has two applications. We will deal first with the application on the global fight against HIV , which is a request for a half-day debate in the Chamber. Over to you, David.

Thank you very much, Bob. I am really here in my capacity as a co-chair of the all-party parliamentary group on HIV, AIDS and sexual health, which is one of the largest all-party groups in Parliament and will , next year, celebrate its 40th year as a group.

As you will be aware, there has generally been a debate in Parliament either around World AIDS Day, which is 1 December, or National HIV Testing Week, which is in the spring. All those debates have previously been very well attended, with a large number of Members from all sides participating.

Within the UK Government’s remit, we have had an HIV action plan in relation to England and quite a significant amount of positive activity. That is why the feeling of the APPG—and my own feeling—is that this year it would be appropriate to debate the global situation . That has been very much impacted by changes in funding , not just to ODA here in the UK but very significant changes in the United States, which has previously been a n important funder of HIV treatment s, particularly in the global south.

It will be an important opportunity to make clear that many of those who are facing infection now are in fact women and girls; it is not the stereotypical gay male community that some people believe is the case. There have been rising rates, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and the middle east, and therefore our view is that the focus of any debate this year would rightly be on the global situation. I believe that there would be sufficient interest in this debate to ensure that there was wide attendance in the Commons Chamber and that therefore it would merit that.
Q13 Thank you, David, for your application . You mentioned some awareness days. Is there a particular date that you would like us to consider?

I tried to get the application in early, and I know you have a very long waiting list, but I had anticipated that the debate would be held in December, because World AIDS Day is 1 December. There will be some other activity in Parliament around that, as always, but proximity to World AIDS Day would be very much welcomed, if the Committee was minded to grant the application.

Q14 You are probably aware that there is a long waiting list for debates. Would you consider having this debate in Westminster Hall, to increase the likelihood of it happening around the date you mentioned?

I would not rule it out, but I think it is a debate that would command wide interest across the House and would merit being held in the Chamber. I and members of the APPG obviously wish the debate to take place, so if those two things were not reconcilable, obviously I would not rule out a Westminster Hall debate, but the preference would be for a Chamber debate, and I think it would both merit that and command the level of support that merits that.
Q15 There is a queue , as Jonathan said. I think 1 December is a Tuesday—is that World AIDS Day?
World AIDS Day is on 1 December, yes.
That might fit with a Westminster Hall debate on that same morning, but we will bear that in mind.
I take your guidance. As I say, I do think it is a debate that is suited to the Chamber, but I take on board what you are saying.
David Mundell made representations
Q16 David, you have a second application.

The second application is by me, with the support principally of Irene Campbell , who is the Labour MP for North Ayrshire and Arran . We would like to have a debate in Westminster Hall on nuclear power in Scotland.

As Members may be aware, under the devolution settlement energy policy is reserved to Westminster, but planning policy is within the remit of the Scottish Government. Over a period of time, the Scottish Government have used that planning policy to ensure that there is no nuclear development in Scotland, which is contrary to the view of, for example, myself, Irene and various other Members. Other people have different views, but it is a very topical issue, particularly as the Government are pressing ahead with nuclear development in England. It is a topic of interest that would spark a very lively and, I am sure, well-attended debate, not least by Scottish Members of all persuasions.
Q17 David, as we discussed in respect of your previous application, there are a great many debates in the pipeline. If we had to prioritise one of your debates, which would it be?

I sort of have two hats on, because I am speaking on behalf of the APPG in relation to the HIV debate. I think that is a very important debate and I would wish that to take place. This second debate is on a very topical, political issue that could be debated at any time. In a timing cycle I think the HIV debate, as we just discussed, is better suited for around 1 December. This other debate could, within reason, take place at any time because I do not anticipate that the Scottish Government will change their position within the short term but—who knows—once we have had the debate they might do so.
Thank you very much, David. The Clerks will be in touch about both of your applications in due course.
John Slinger made representations.

Q18 Next up is John Slinger, applying for a debate on a subject in which we all have a vested interest: the role of an MP. It is a request for a Westminster Hall debate on either a Tuesday or a Thursday.

It is good to be back before this Committee. I seek this debate because I regard the role of an MP as absolutely critical to our democracy. I will talk you through the reasoning. The role has evolved organically over time. It has never been truly gripped, defined or properly assessed in this place, though it has been outside, and as far as I can tell there have been no debates on the role of an MP. There are strengths to that organic growth and some deficiencies, including there being no job description— [ Laughter. ] I note the laughter of hon. Members.

Each MP determines the role as best they can. The public often do not understand our role—how could they—nor do organisations. Nor, quite often, do we. Certainly I do not understand it on occasion. As hon. Members will know, we are under no obligation to ever visit our constituency—although I live in mine so I visit it every week—nor to come to this House, save to swear the oath of allegiance. That is frankly preposterous, I think we can all agree.

There is a grey area both nationally and locally: there are very few formal powers and they apply pretty much only nationally. They are the legislative powers to vote on and to amend legislation, and the powers to question Ministers, to initiate debates or to scrutinise. Of course, we have immense power at certain moments. We may have noticed that when we—those of us in the PLP, at least—determined who the Prime Minister is. That is an enormous power and privilege but the other powers are heavily constrained by whipping.

Locally, no public or private organisation that provides services to our constituents is under any statutory obligation ever to meet us, consult us or respond to us. Of course, they do because they know our status but they are not under any obligation—not even councils are; it is incredible. We have no formal executive power locally to direct policy; we have no resources. Local councillors, for example, do have resources to deploy on issues that they care about. In my area, Rugby borough council is just about to bring in a £3,000 fund for each councillor and councillors on Warwickshire county council each have £8,000 per year to distribute to good causes and to make things happen in their constituency. We have the power of influence, convening, writing, talking and cajoling and that is not insignificant, but it is not enough. That is within the context that we face, which is vital.

If we look at local Government reorganisation and devolution, we are seen as the most senior politician in our areas and yet we hear little else of metro mayors in the current debate. People assume that we have the power and the budget to deploy locally when we know that we do not. People assume that we can improve their area and local services. Of course we can, but the route to doing so is of course highly complex.

As Members of Parliament we end up being held accountable for almost everything that happens in our area. We pick up the pieces of often broken or failing local and national public services, and much more besides. Of course, if I could be so bold, due to our nature as democratically elected politicians, we are incentivised to maximise the appearance of power and minimise the absence of it, which is slightly ironic.

I am seeking a debate to discuss this perhaps most vital role in our democracy, and most importantly to give hon. Members across the House the opportunity to make their suggestions and discuss these issues. They can take it wherever they want: they can talk about the logistics of being an MP, our formal powers, our informal powers and the support we receive; maybe even pay and our package, security and the wider context, as I have mentioned. I want the debate to be about not complaints or moaning but improving the situation, focused on solutions and constructive ideas.

MPs are vital to our democracy, and I believe that our status, power and authority need to be enhanced—not for our benefit, but for the benefit of our constituents and the democracy of this country. MPs must have more opportunities to speak out, and I want this debate to be part of a much wider discussion here in this place, among the various Committees, with academia and others, about revitalising our democracy. Rewiring the state must include improving and revising the role, status and powers of MPs. When I mentioned my application to colleagues, they were very interested. I think the debate would be well supported from across the House, and it is an important and timely one.

Thank you. I would add to your observations that, for those of us who have served in executive roles in local authorities, becoming an MP changes your position from one of making decisions that affect people in the places they live to one of, “Can I bring influence to bear to make a decision?”. It is very frustrating, I agree.
Q19 Thank you for bringing this debate forward, John. Would you want it to coincide with any particular time, or to happen as soon as possible?
As soon as possible, Will—I am not supposed to call you Will, am I?
I called you John, so I started it.
Thank you, Will.
Any other questions? I think we all have an interest in this.

Q20 I do. Thank you for bringing this application, John. I describe myself as a combination of the Terminator and a fairy godmother. That is how I think my constituents see me, but of course, as you say, the reality is completely different. I cannot believe that we have never debated this—is that right, Chair, to your knowledge?
We did check, and I did not find anything, although there may have been some debates that I have not found.
I am sure that if it is accepted, it will be oversubscribed, because you know we MPs love talking about ourselves!

There probably were discussions about this during the expenses scandals, when IPSA was set up, because there is obviously a rationale for that. The Standards Commissioner clearly has an interest in this—as we know, he tried to inflict certain things on MPs—and I think IPSA would have a say on what happens. But you are absolutely right: we have no contract of employment; we have no job description; we set up a small business; we employ our staff, albeit to contracts and within a budget; and there are examples of people who arrived in this place and sworn their oath of allegiance, but who have never been to their constituency or done anything for their constituents, and somehow they managed to get re-elected.
It is extraordinary.
It is. Anyway, the Clerks will be in touch with you in due course about a potential date. Thank you, John.
Liz Jarvis made representations.

Q21 Our final application is from Liz Jarvis. It is an application for a Tuesday morning Westminster Hall debate on improving post-diagnostic support for people living with dementia. Liz, please present your case.
Or a Tuesday afternoon.
We get to allocate only Tuesday mornings and Thursday afternoons in Westminster Hall.
Okay. I am sure that many of us have been impacted by dementia or will know constituents who have been impacted by dementia.

Without wishing to bring everybody down, one in three of us will develop dementia. It is obviously the defining health and social care challenge of our time. Later this year the Government’s modern service framework for frailty and dementia and the first publication of the Casey commission is expected. This would be a timely debate looking at what happens after diagnosis. At the moment, in far too many cases, people are told that they have dementia, and then they get sent home and are left to get on with it. They have to do their own research and find out about everything themselves. However, research shows that if properly supported, they can live a reasonably productive and active life for as long as possible. That is really important.

This debate has cross-party support and would give Members the chance to talk about experiences in their constituencies and to put the case forward for ensuring that everybody in the UK has access to the post-diagnostic support that they need.
Thank you.
Q22 Thank you for bringing this application, Liz. Would you consider a debate on a Thursday in Westminster Hall in order for it to happen in October or November as requested?
Yes, we would consider it, but the ideal would obviously not be either of those.
Q23 But you would consider it?
We would.
Q24 What would be the answering Department? Is it Health and Social Care or is there a different Department?
It is Health and Social Care. I am trying to think who the Minister is now because the last time I spoke about dementia it was Stephen Kinnock, but it is not him anymore.
They have all changed.
Yes.

The only reason I ask is that because if it is a Tuesday morning it has to fit within when Health and Social Care are answering. Thursday afternoon is different and anyone can answer; it is basically a free for all.
Thank you very much. The Clerks will be in touch with you shortly.

sessions.iT: Government priorities for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting
sessions.w: Dr Grace Carrington (Institute of the Americas, University College London); Dr Rakib Ehsan (Policy Exchange)

segs.tx: Foreign Affairs Committee
Oral evidence: Government priorities for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, HC 634
Tuesday 8 September 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 8 September 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Fleur Anderson; Alex Ballinger; Dan Carden; Abtisam Mohamed; Edward Morello ; Sir John Whittingdale .
In the absence of the Chair, Sir John Whittingdale took the Chair.
Questions 1- 18
Witnesses
I : D r Grace Carrington, Honorary Research Fellow, Institute of the Americas, UCL ; and Dr Rakib Ehsan, Senior Fellow, Policy Exchange .
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Dr Grace Carrington and Dr Rakib Ehsan.

Q1 Good morning. In this session of the Foreign Affairs Committee , we will look at the forthcoming Commonwealth H eads of Government meeting in November. I should start by saying that I am in the C hair today because our C hair, Emily Thornberry, is unable to be with us . O ne of our previously advertised witnesses, Professor Onslow, is also unable to be here. I welcome our two witnesses on the first panel . Will they introduce themselves?

I am Grace Carrington, an honorary research fellow at the UCL Institute of the Americas. I specialise in politics and decolonisation in the Caribbean. My last book looked at non-independent states, including the British overseas territories . M y current book project looks more at the relationship with the monarchy, campaigns for republics and debates around reparations in the Caribbean.

My name is Dr Rakib Ehsan . I am a senior fellow at the Policy Exchange think - tank. I was the author of the Policy Exchange report , “ One Family : Harnessing the Strategic Potential of the Commonwealth ” .
Q2 Can I start with the obvious question : does the Commonwealth still matter? Is it still something we should devote attention to? D oes it still have a relevance in today ’ s world?

I n my view, in recent times , the Commonwealth has drifted to the margins of international relations. There is a growing foreign policy tendency in the UK to say that the Commonwealth is somewhat outdated , irrelevant and not necessarily an international arena where British national interests can be amplified

The big thing with the “O ne F amily ” report I authored for Policy E xchange was that it dismissed that view ; rather, it offer ed a blueprint for providing the Commonwealth with a renewed sense of purpose and for the UK playing a leadership role in that. I certainly think that it will be able to achieve that in certain areas, especially educational co - operation. E nvironmental sustainability is a big area, especially when we are looking at small state development across the Commonwealth.

But t hose are the softer , comfort - zone policy areas —t he one thing I really wanted to achieve with the report is to say that we need a Commonwealth that has more teet h. We suggested the creation of a security and defence co - operation forum within the Commonwealth . T hat would help to support member states , such as Guyana, which in my view has faced considerable political aggression from neighbouring Venezuela, especially over the oil - rich Essequibo region. W e are talking about the idea of member states having the potential to have collective military exercises and increased naval co - operation.

T here are certain areas where we traditionally look at traditional alliances, such as NATO , b ut if the Commonwealth wants to have increased relevance within the international system, that will be very difficult to achieve without deepening co - operation between member states, especially in the areas of security and defence.

That is not just about military and naval co-operation; it is also about looking at what forms of modern co - operation we can have, especially in terms of cyber - security. M ember states such as Namibia, Cameroon and Tanzania are exceptionally vulnerable and have very weak cyber - security infrastructure , and t he UK has a sophisticated, Commonwealth - leading cyber - security capability. We are not just looking at those traditional military and naval alliances ; we are also looking to deepen cyber - security . That is essential if we want to allow underdeveloped countries across the Commonwealth to grow and prosper over time.

I agree. A real challenge is to make sure that the Commonwealth seems relevant to the 21st century. The imperial legacies are something that could pose a challenge to making it seem like a modern partnership for the modern age. The UK has a key role: if the UK approaches the Commonwealth from the perspective of leadership, the issue is that that seems much more like the traditional dynamics, whereas if the UK approaches the Commonwealth from the perspective of partnership, collaboration and coalition building, the scope is for a much more modern partnership, with the UK reinforcing that.

One key opportunity for the Commonwealth is to do with climate, coalition building on climate issues and the environment, particularly given the timing of CHOGM, with COP31 just a few days afterwards. That is a real opportunity for the Commonwealth to be a useful forum feeding into COP31.

Q3 Dr Ehsan, can we have the defence co-operation you talked about given the very different views among members of the Commonwealth about who the enemy might be or about particular conflicts and threats?

Absolutely, that is a very important question to ask. Without doubt, as we have seen in recent times, China is looking not just to gain an economic foothold—especially in the African Commonwealth member states—but to develop a military and policing presence, especially in the sensitive Indo-Pacific region. That is where the UK has to be realistic about its role, especially its leadership role, which has to be done in partnership with other countries. India is a critical strategic ally in that sense, as is working closely with countries such as Nigeria, which has considerable potential—youthful potential. Russia making military and defence investments is also an issue, especially in African member states.

It is not necessarily easy—the UK will have to work on it over time. The critical point to make is about the need for a cultural shift. As I said, there is a foreign policy tendency to look at the Commonwealth as irrelevant, but I do not think that we should give up because China has gained such a foothold somewhere, or Russia has made certain investments in military and defence developments. In response to that, as a counterbalance, we need to look to deepen our defence and security co-operation over time. That will not happen overnight, but we should work towards it.

Critically, we should do that with countries that have traditionally been strong diplomatic allies in the Commonwealth. Australia definitely has a role to play—it is also in the Australian national interest—especially with China looking to make developments, contributing to the social and institutional development of Pacific island countries. Recently, China tried to interact with Fiji—it has a policing agreement with Fiji, although I think that Fiji has taken a step back from it. There is also a history of China having that pact with the Solomon Islands in critical areas. The key is for the UK to work with like-minded allies in the Commonwealth to make the Commonwealth over time a counterbalance to growing Chinese and Russian involvement and influence in the international system.

Q4 Dr Carrington, we talked about whether we think that the Commonwealth matters, but what is the view of the rest of the Commonwealth? Do they regard it as important? The heads of the leading members did not turn up to the last meeting.

I think it depends. Looking specifically at the Caribbean, the Commonwealth can be a real opportunity for states to mobilise on vulnerable island states and climate, particularly on adaptation and resilience. It can be a forum for building co-operation and coalitions outside Russian, US and Chinese influence, but it depends, and I think that there is a challenge there to ensure that it continues to be a useful forum. As I said, climate is one issue, given the timing of CHOGM and COP31, where it can be a really useful point of international co-operation, particularly for small and vulnerable states in the Caribbean.

I will just add a quick point. The Chagos islands are very relevant: that was almost a result of the UK, in my view, failing to nurture, build and pay attention to quite important relationships within the Commonwealth. That is very much a gift for countries such as China and Russia.

I agree that China and Russia have made certain developments in terms of gaining a foothold, especially in certain public policy areas and in relation to other Commonwealth member countries. The solution to that is not for the UK to row back, but to actually lean in more to the Commonwealth, see it as a key pillar in its foreign policy interests and try, over time, to cultivate an environment in the Commonwealth that acts as a counterbalance to those growing forms of Chinese and Russian influence in the international system.

Q5 I want to expand a bit on the Chair’s question. I am interested in how relevant the Commonwealth is to the members, given how many members there are and how different all those countries are. Dr Carrington, you have identified that there are shared interests around climate with some countries and shared interests around security in the Caribbean. Dr Ehsan, you mentioned that there are some states where we might deepen our military co-operation. But in every instance, you are dividing up the Commonwealth based on our particular interests in a particular thing or where we have shared values. Those are all effectively separate multilateral groups that you are talking about setting up, so how relevant is the Commonwealth as a collective, given what you have already said?

I think there are certain areas where it is easier to cultivate collaboration and deepen that co-operation across Commonwealth member states. In terms of increasing its relevance, you have to look at the key member states. I will take India, for example: when you look at healthcare there, there are still very significant problems in terms of a lack of healthcare infrastructure in certain parts of India, especially in poorer eastern states. The areas that the Commonwealth could really build on include disease prevention and control—that is a critical area where co-operation could be deepened.

Naturally, female economic empowerment is a very important pillar of the economic development strategy of many developing countries, so the UK can definitely contribute to that by making it an important goal for the Commonwealth. When you look at defence and security, as I said before with, for example, Venezuelan aggression towards Guyana, you have to be very selective about where there are realistic prospects of defence and security co-operation. I am very much of the view that, without any attempts to deepen co-operation in those more controversial areas, I just don’t see the Commonwealth really commanding that relevance and respect within the international system—unless it branches out from those more traditional areas of education and trade and investment.

That is not to undermine the importance of trade and investment; I think that the Commonwealth advantage should be built upon. Having that asset of a shared official language, common legal systems and familiar administrative frameworks is something to really build on. That is a golden aspect of the Commonwealth, but without defence and security, I think it would be very difficult for it to have that relevance.

Q6 I take your point. I guess the UK has a certain romantic attachment to the idea of the Commonwealth, and I am trying to understand whether the Commonwealth has the same attachment. I get that there are areas where we can deepen relationships or work on particular issues, but how relevant is the Commonwealth as a collective to its members?

I think that question depends on whether you are talking about national Governments or the publics across the Commonwealth. The five-country polling I did for the “One Family” report on behalf of Policy Exchange had a very interesting item. It asked survey respondents, “Do you believe the UK does more good than harm in the world?” and the lowest level of approval was among the UK public. It was especially high among the Indian and Nigerian publics, so I think there is a great deal of good will and affection towards the UK among Commonwealth publics. If you are talking about soft power, that is an amazing asset to have. Of course, there could be a difference between the opinion of the Government of the day in those countries and the broader population.

In my view, there has been a growing culture of self-flagellation in the UK, where we have a lack of confidence in what we have contributed to the world, in terms of human advancement and, in general, our moral obligations. I think we have fared quite well on an international level, and we need to make the most of the good will and affection that does exist. India and Nigeria are two huge, very important populations in the context of the strategic future of the Commonwealth, and the UK should build on that and work towards really making the most of and maximising the potential of that good will.

I agree. You mentioned particularly that there are unifying issues for particular regions or countries, but I think that that is the case with any major international organisation. It is the same with, say, the United Nations. With the Commonwealth, there are opportunities for particular regions or groups of countries to unify around key issues and build coalitions. With any major issue, there will always be tensions with other major powers, say, on climate perhaps with countries that are less on board with supporting vulnerable states with climate resilience. But I think that the Commonwealth has a degree of uniqueness by not having, say, Russia, the US and China in it. It offers a unique forum.

As for the attachment, or the particular fondness, that the UK might have for the Commonwealth or the sense of the Commonwealth, it is crucial, for the Commonwealth moving forward, to have a shift in mindset around that and not to focus on the sense of a fondness for the Commonwealth and the shared history. That can often lead to colonial dynamics. It is about seeing this as a useful forum moving forward, perhaps separate from the history.

Q7 I was able to visit Guyana earlier this year with the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association. It was a fascinating visit; we met President Ali there. My experience of visiting the Commonwealth countries has always been that their desire is to deepen and build more strategic relationships with the UK—I agree with everything you said, Dr Ehsan, about the possibilities for the relationship with the Commonwealth. Have you looked at perhaps how the Commonwealth could figure in a more strategic relationship around critical minerals and diversifying supply chains for the UK?

That is something that we considered to a degree in the report. On critical minerals, one thing that we talked about was leveraging the blue economy—blue economic instruments—including looking at blue carbon. What we want to do, in my view, is support emerging markets, so small state islands, and help with their development. Naturally, they have a very small land mass but they have considerable ocean resources.

The UK should work towards leveraging its expertise, especially through the City, and work towards blue carbon, blue bonds and coastal resilience insurance—those are the kind of things that we should really move forward with, especially if we are serious about small state island development. I think that would bring the UK to the fore. The last CHOGM was in Samoa and the forthcoming one is in Antigua and Barbuda. If the UK can really feed into that agenda on small state island development, that will heighten its reputation in the Commonwealth, for sure.
Q8 What is your assessment of how well or badly the FCDO is currently doing at building—

It is hopeless. In my view, there is a situation whereby it is seen as an outdated, moribund organisation, and I don’t think that is specific to the FCDO. Many of our public institutions are seen as some sort of outdated imperial relic. I look at the Commonwealth very differently. I think the smooth transition spearheaded by Her late Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, from having imperial control to the voluntary association of nations, really was one of her finest achievements. That is not something we should neglect.

The reality is that we have attracted new member states such as Togo and Gabon —former French colonies—and I think that that is a real feather in our cap, if I am being honest. The fact that we have Mozambique—a former Portuguese colony—and Rwanda, a former Belgian colony, already in the Commonwealth shows, in a way, that outside former parts of the British empire there is an admiration for the UK in that after decolonisation, more than any other former European colonial power, it has really made an effort to rebuild relationships with former parts of its empire. I think that we should really build on that. You talked about soft power, and that is a critical element of it. I know that other people have a very different view and see it as some kind of outdated imperial relic, but I completely disagree with that.
Do you want to add anything, Dr Carrington?
I have nothing to add on that.

Q9 I want to talk about human rights violations. I know that Commonwealth members sign up to the charter and various declarations, but many members have been suspended or removed as a result of violations in their countries. Do you think that the Commonwealth takes that seriously, or is it superficial in nature? I will come to you first, Dr Carrington.

That is a really good question. I think that it reveals one of the real issues within not just the Commonwealth but international organisations generally. It can be a great opportunity to build consensus around issues, but when it comes to enforcement, particularly around human rights and democracy, it reveals the weakness of the Commonwealth. From a UK perspective, it is important to have a consistent approach and look at how it and the Commonwealth can support earlier monitoring around democracy, elections and human rights issues, as well as early intervention and looking at clearer follow-ups when there are, say, human rights violations. But I think that with international organisations, there is always that issue around enforcement, which reveals a flaw in those kinds of organisations.

There are definitely some enforcement issues. In an incredibly diverse association—I think there are 56 member states now—there will be cases where we feel that there are human rights issues across a number of those member countries. But expulsion is very much a last resort, and engaging with those countries in terms of flagging those issues has to be done in the spirit of the Commonwealth charter, which is ultimately that the members are free and equal nations. Adopting a heavy-handed approach there would not necessarily work—if anything, that could be alienating. It is a very difficult balance to strike, and I think that the UK would be best served looking at those issues, especially female empowerment, across member states. That would be helpful in terms of the economic development of lesser-developed member states.

There are issues in certain member countries in terms of the persecution of religious minorities, and the UK should be a critical friend when it comes to those issues. That has been a concern even when it comes to India, to be perfectly honest. But again, it is a difficult balance to strike because without a strong strategic partnership with India, I do not think that the Commonwealth can move forward very much. In terms of the UK’s position on some of those human rights violations, I think that flagrant violations do need to be flagged, but there has to be a sense that there are countries with certain local cultural customs whose perception of human rights might be different from the liberal, western understanding of human rights. That is very difficult in terms of striking a uniform view on all human rights issues.

The one area that the UK could really work on through the Commonwealth observer groups is the creation of more robust procedures over time in terms of the monitoring of elections—the democratic integrity of those member states. I think that is where you could find the UK exerting a decent level of influence. In terms of flagging every single human rights issue of the 56 member countries, which have very different cultural and social environments, that is a bit more difficult.

Q10 It is a challenge. Coming on to specific cases, if a country is deemed to be more acceptable and has allegedly met the requirements to be readmitted, as in the case of Zimbabwe, what do you think the procedure there should be? Should they be readmitted quite readily, or should caveats be in place?

I think with the case of Zimbabwe, the UK should support long-term readmittance if conditions are met, looking specifically at the Commonwealth charter and making sure that all conditions around elections and democracy are met. More broadly, not just with readmitting but with admitting new states, I think if states can show they do meet those requirements, the UK should support them being admitted or readmitted.

Q11 Dr Ehsan, if I can use another case study, I am contacted quite frequently by constituents in relation to the incarceration of Imran Khan in Pakistan. Do you feel that the Commonwealth could play a stronger role in relation to that? You have referenced the importance of democracy and democratic procedures.
