In so doing, you reduce the severity of a flood spike—you can smooth it off—and you will keep the river flowing during hot, dry spells in the summer as the landscape is still shedding water because it has been retained there. You will probably catch more carbon if there are peatlands in that landscape and, of course, by being wetter and more humid, you will reduce fire risk.

But you have to take a catchment view to be able to do that because water does not know any boundaries. Hydrology needs to be looked at in the context of a catchment. This is not only about ecology; it is about planning and land use planning, and how we line up all the incentives and the tools that we have to encourage people to go in this direction.
Q63 Would you be able to walk through what you can practically do? I think we get the theory, which is why we have the recommendations. What are you practically thinking of doing?

This is one of the areas where our advisory role is at the front. We are not the regulator. We have a small delivery role, which I will come to in a moment. In our conversations on the DEFRA water reform and looking ahead to the next price review—the one that is about to start very soon—our role is to advise on the investment and actions that are needed by water companies to further nature recovery.

A few years ago, our conversations there would mainly have been about the impact of water on protected sites, where there was actual harm being done and an outflow needed upgrading, for example. In the last two rounds, and especially for the next one, we will look at the much broader questions: where do nature-based solutions help and where do they not work? They do not work for everything, so where are they the most appropriate and cost-effective measure? Also, how are we looking at wider water resilience? We have an advisory role to the water regulator and to the Environment Agency about when nature-based solutions work best. We have a small direct delivery role in the work we do with farmers on catchment-sensitive farming and supporting farmers to change land management practices and receive funding for that through things like the higher-tier scheme and capital grants.

As I have just mentioned farming and while we are talking about water, the other thing we are increasingly looking at—we are just kicking off a piece of research with CEH to test that we have enough knowledge on this—is the other side of water quality and what practices could change on farms, on both flooding and water quality. We all know that better quality soil holds more water and therefore creates flood resilience. It holds and stores water, rather than the water washing off. We have seen that especially this summer; the drier soils are more likely to have flash floods. That is a piece of evidence we are starting to really test that we have sufficient robustness in to make sure that that is factored into the next round of the price review. It is not just what the companies do; it is other land management in the catchment.

Q64 I have a question on farming in a second , but b efore we move on from the catchment , you reflected on the challenge of doing this at scale. What can you do to overcome the challenges of implementing at scale ? By the way, if you need any pilots, I am more than happy to host you in Mid Bedfordshire, because there is an appetite for nature-based solutions and to consider the catchment. With huge amounts of development in Bedfordshire, there are real opportunities.

I am not sure we would necessarily call them pilots, but over the years we have gathered that knowledge through the projects we have been involved in. Some of those might not have been labelled a water project—they might have been a nature recovery project—but we have learnt from them which solutions work and which do not. We have learnt it through our work with water companies and, as we said, we are learning it more through our work with farmers.

The other aspect that came to mind when you mentioned Mid Bedfordshire and that we must not forget—forgive me ; I am not suggesting you do— is the urban side of this and the use of sustainable urban drainage and things like that . Water resilience in built development, as well as on farmland, will need to become part of catchment planning.

Q65 Yes, 100%. It is about c onsidering development holistically because unfortunately, at the moment , it is considered case by case. We have classic examples where cumulative impacts of development have had catastrophic effects —b ut I am digressing.

On the farmers’ side , the NFU has raised concerns with us that environmental permitting gives too much weight to the immediate ecological effect of maintenance, rather than the wider consequences if flooding occurs. Do you recognise that problem, and if so, what is the solution?
It has not raised that with us, perhaps because we are not the environmental permitting body.
It is more EA, possibly.

What we are seeing in our conversations with all the farming bodies and individual farmers is a growing recognition of some of the things our strategy talks about— that an environmentally resilient farm is also an economically resilient one, and it therefore contributes to food security. We are seeing more farmers understanding that it is not about nature because they want more nature on their farms, but about nature as a business solution.

Q66 My final question is about budget , because at the end of the day everything is about money . The Minister told the Committee that the new flood funding formula should make it easier for natural flood management schemes to secure funding. Have you seen evidence of that? Are there barriers that remain, from your perspective at Natural England?

It is work in progress. We are working on that m inisterial commitment with the Environment Agency. It is an example of what I said : we are testing where it really is the most cost-effective solution.
These are early days.
Yes, but that commitment is definitely being seen through, and we are part of it.

Let me say one thing about regulation and things that look like they are ecologically a good idea not being that easy to do. It arises, in some ways, from the regulations that have been put in place to stop bad things happening to nature rather than to foster good things happening.

An example I saw recently in East Anglia was Anglian Water seeking to put naturalistic wetlands downstream from some headwater sewage works in remote rural areas — serving maybe 600 houses, so quite small sewage works. It is quite expensive to upgrade them, yet they are causing quite a lot of harm to the rivers. Putting a wetland downstream of the sewage works makes a lot of sense ecologically. However, the regulatory regime does not make that easy because the EA needs to regulate the water flowing out of the pipe at the end of the sewage works, rather than the Perrier- quality water that is coming out of the bottom of the wetland.

T here are issues we could probably work through to make it easier to deploy nature-based solutions. That regulatory piece is one barrier. Another is the extent to which we are not so able to judge risk in relation to a nature-based solution, because nature is unpredictable compared with concrete and steel, the effectiveness of which we can engineer and be far more confident about.
R egulatory and risk-appetite issues do lie in th at nature-based solution space. More work probably needs to be done on that so that we can unleash those solutions more comprehensively.
Q67 I f you had recommendations for this Committee on improving those regulations, would you share them with us?

W e possibly have, and we will continue to. I think you have heard some of that today. It is about thinking about the health of a catchment and the combined impacts on it , not, a s Tony just described, solving a point-source pollution problem that does not necessarily create a healthy ecosystem. A lot of that regulation has been based on human health thresholds, not environmental thresholds. That is part of the advice we are giving to the Government as they think about a water B ill : d o we need to change any regulation as well as the regulators?

Q68 Moving slightly away from one of the areas you discussed as being our most threatening, going from water through to heat and heatwaves—the other extreme—in January 2025, you introduced a protocol for dealing with the impact of drought in your nature reserves and sites of special scientific interest. How has that protocol worked over this summer, and will you make any changes as a result?

On the back of this summer we are doing immediate work, not so much on drought, but on wildfire risk, although, of course, they are related. We are doing an immediate rapid assessment of the fire risk assessments on our nature reserves. They will not just be—if I might call it this—the health and safety version. We are also working together and have pulled together a group of practitioners—ourselves, other ENGOs and other parts of Government—to see what we can learn quickly from this summer. Putting it simplistically—well, we were due to visit Minsmere with the RSPB, anyway, before the fire happened. We visited and used the opportunity to learn a lot more. We saw fire risk assessments that were good enough a year ago but were not good enough this summer because of the heat and the speed at which the fires were moving. Many of us have worked to those same principles. We have firebreaks that we thought were good enough and they simply aren’t.

The second learning we had from this summer is that we need to make the sites more resilient by building in more water, having more variety of vegetation and so on, so that there are more natural firebreaks, more wetland, and not a single monoculture. Even if it is a heathland site, heather alone is not what we need. What we also learnt from the time we spent with the fire service there and when there have been fires on our reserves is that we also need to think about the ability to respond to a fire. We have to assume that more will happen, however resilient the sites are, so can we get the rapid response in? And the third piece of learning is: what do we learn about how best to recover sites after a fire?

Our chief scientist led a piece of work for the Government Office for Science on the impact of fire on biodiversity. The loss of the habitat itself is significant, but the fires also add to risks to water quality because of contamination flooding off the land. The carbon release in the first place and the fact that we have then got dry, bare ground means flooding is more likely. So I think that in some of the places where we have had fires this year, the problems are not yet over.

That was a very long answer, but we have to look at the whole piece. How do we prevent fires? How do we deal with them better? That does not just apply to us; it applies to our partners with private land as well. Both upland and lowland farmers have had the same problems that we have seen on the nature sites. We want to be able to share that learning on what makes land more resilient and what makes responses better.
Q69 Thinking about the areas that have not been subject to fires, but just the heat itself, what impact have you seen on biological diversity, and what are you going to do to try and protect areas?

This goes back to the very big picture to which our strategy is pointing, which is about creating resilience for nature as well as for the human world. We know from previous reports presented to Government some years ago—especially the “Making space for nature” report from Sir John Lawton—that if we wish to have nature flourishing into the future, we need more areas of natural habitat. They need to be bigger, better quality and connected. That is behind a lot of what we try to do at Natural England. That is the big picture, and this is work in progress. Progress is being made here and there, but it is fair to say that the impact of this summer on our wildlife will be profound.

In the summer of 1976, which was not as bad as this one, some butterfly populations were knocked back for decades after that extreme event. This summer, anecdotally—data will emerge in due course—far fewer insects are around. Obviously, some aquatic habitats have been completely wrecked. A lot of ponds and shallow lakes have completely dried up. Fish and insect populations in those will have been wiped out.

When we saw the fire at Dunwich heath, we were told that one place was the location of a population of silver-studded blue butterflies. T hose insects do not move very far at the best of times, and the entire population was wiped out by that fire. How is it going to r ecolonise? Well, the next colony may be some distance away, and so on and so forth. That is now going to drive even more pressure on to our beleaguered natural environment. W e really have to start thinking not only about individual sites and making places hold more water but about landscapes . A s a country we must invest in more , bigger and better - connected natural habitats. W e have quite a lot of tools to do that , and we now have quite a lot of extra reasons to do it, including this climate change impact, which is not only affecting the natural world, but people . B igger areas of natural habitat, holding more water at catchment scale —t hat needs to be the direction of travel.
Q70 Sticking with heat , w hat role is Natural England playing in helping us to adapt to heat ? W hat role can nature play ?
Do you want to talk about Nature Towns and Cities?

Yes. I am conscious that w e have not talked much about people during this hearing so far. I n that helpful exchange , we talked about what we might do to protect nature on more natural sites. T he other area we have invested a lot more in over recent years is what we can do to make urban areas more nature- resilient. Covid was a bit of an eye - opener for many of us, wasn’t it? P eople who have the least access to green space suffer the most . W e have seen quite a lot of data about the inequality of access to green space , and t hat evidence correlates with the people who are most likely to suffer the heat impacts —the communities that are less likely to have green space.

T he Nature T owns and C ities project that Tony mentioned is a partnership between us , the National Lottery Heritage Fund and the National Trust. It is about supporting local authorities to invest in nature resilience in their towns , with more green space, more street trees and more rain gardens, which help contribute to flood risk mitigation . I t is enabling and supporting capacity and capability in local authorities. The reason that matters is that we know that water, green space and shade all mitigate heat , directly and indirectly , but we are also seeing through that programme and the research and evaluation around it that it is benefici al to economic growth, because you are more likely to visit a city centre that has pleasant green spaces , y ou are likely to stay longer and therefore you are likely to spend more. A lot of that is about reinvestment in city centres.
Q71 Is it also about reducing ambient temperature?
D efinitely .
Big time. There is a lot of data on that.
Q72 And that goes for the g reen i nfrastructure framework as well ?
Yes.

Yes. That is a piece of Natural England evidence that local authorities can use to understand where best to target their effort. T hat effort may be the obligations that they put on developers for alternative green space, or i t may be their own investment. Greater Manchester c ombined a uthority was one of the first authorities to use it , and it was used to target where the m ayor ’ s g reen fund would fund community projects to create green spaces and natur e.

W hat that revealed is actually quite an important point in terms of the social wellbeing agenda . T hat work revealed how the people with least access to green space within a short walk of their home were the people who would benefit from it m ost : people on low incomes and people suffering from indices of social deprivation. W e know that access to nature does help with some of the challenges faced by some communities in terms of health and wellbeing . T he benefits gained from green space make a material difference to that , b ut the people who ha ve the least of it are the ones who need it most. T here i s quite a big social question in there about how we expand access to green areas, including in ways that are going to reduce heat extremes and help to mitigate flooding in towns . I t all comes together in the end around the use of green infrastructure in towns and cities in a way that is presently not very strategic in some cases but could be more so.

Q73 You previously mentioned larger space s, and some of them are well connected —h alf of my constituency is in a national p ark —and with all the heat, people are probably going there in even greater numbers than previously , because it is a bit cooler. T hat creates other threats. W e have had fires from wild camping , barbecues and all those sorts of things. H ow do we protect our natural spaces from those sorts of threats?
I think i t is a version of bigger, better , more joined up , isn’t it?

Yes, bigger, better, more joined up and a bit wetter—that makes it less likely to burn. In the wake of this summer, I think there is a major public awareness piece about all this. I think pretty much all the fires, the fire brigades would tell us, were started by people, most of them probably accidentally and some of them deliberately. The deliberate ones are obviously criminal acts, but can we do more to reduce the risk of fires being started accidentally by giving people more knowledge? The alert that went out on the phones seemed to make a difference that weekend. There were fewer new fires that weekend, which I think says something.
We were told today that there was a 42% reduction on the previous week.
There we are. That says something about public knowledge and awareness, doesn’t it?

Q74 You have talked about nature being critical infrastructure that is central to national security. We had the Joint Intelligence Committee report on the national security assessment earlier this year, which this Committee investigated and scrutinised with the DEFRA Minister. What is your assessment of the Government’s response to that national security assessment? Have they reacted adequately and comprehensively enough to the threats to national security from nature decline?

I am not sure that I have seen a response to it. Obviously, it was a cross-Government endeavour to reach those conclusions. From what we know at Natural England, and certainly from what I have seen from other work I have done over the years, there is a very strong set of aligning factors between national security and the state of ecosystems, and that report did a good job of looking at issues of mass migration, political destabilisation, the rise of bad actors and the impact on supply chains. All those things were brought out very well, but I am not sure that I have yet seen a response that sets out the reaction to all that.

Certainly, in what we are doing in the UK, one way in which we can take down some of the risks of damage to ecosystems in different parts of the world is to look after and repair our own ecosystems so that we can rely on them for more of the things that presently we get from overseas, food being the obvious one. Ensuring soil health, water security, pollinating insects and green infrastructure in the landscape to enable it to function in a way that is going to meet our needs is a logical conclusion that we take out of that global picture, but I do not know if I have seen yet a comprehensive piece that says, “This is what we are going to do.” Have you, Marian?

I think that our particular contribution is the one that we have been talking about during this session. How can we, as a delivery body and an adviser to Government, build that resilience? An example of that is the work we do in delivering the Government’s peatland restoration grants. They are a major part of delivering that resilience in upland areas. They help deal with fire risk, flood resilience and water quality. In our first meeting with the new Secretary of State for DEFRA, Dame Angela Eagle, that was what she was particularly focused on: how could Natural England contribute more to building that resilience, security and climate adaptation?

Q75 I am glad you have had that discussion with the new Secretary of State. When we had our discussion, albeit with a now former Minister, my view was that the Minister’s reply did not constitute a full response to the gravity and scale of what the national security assessment said. She referred to specific actions being taken in particular areas and some good work but, like yourself, I did not feel that it was a really thorough reply. That has perhaps given us the impetus to pursue that further.
Indeed.
What would you like to see in such a response?

Our participation in global efforts to halt and reduce deforestation. The UK was a global leader in that field 15 or 20 years ago. We could return there and work with partner countries. I remember us having a very good relationship with the Norwegian and German Governments and being able to take forward plans that turned into quite a big ambition on the global stage. We could re-engage with some of that. Obviously, there is the global biodiversity framework and what we can do to support other countries in the implementation of that.

But as is the case on climate change, there are always big questions about what we are doing at home: what leadership example are we setting in order to show that you can restore ecosystems in ways that are good for growth, good for public health and wellbeing and good for national security? That is where we might be able to really blaze a trail in helping countries to see that that false choice really is a false choice, and that you can restore your habitats in ways that help your country.

There are one or two good examples around the world. Costa Rica is a great example. It has more than tripled its forest cover in 40 years and it has doubled its GDP per capita at the same time, so it has restored its ecosystems in a way that has helped the country to reduce poverty and develop. It did that by taking an approach that is very much reflected in the evidence, but it turned it into policy. It recognised that if it wanted to have secure hydroelectric power, it would have to keep raining, and it would keep raining only if it kept the rainforest—Costa Rica worked out that those two were connected—so it did that. That turned into not only a source of electricity but a source of clean water that did not need to go through a water treatment works because it was coming absolutely pure from the forest. On top of that, it developed a world-leading ecotourism industry, and at the same time it has increased its food exports. Is there an opportunity for the UK to show that kind of leadership in taking nature as an opportunity for national security and development rather than seeing it as an imposition or a distraction, which unfortunately is sometimes where we have been?

Q76 Indeed. It is interesting that you talked about food resilience in your example, because that was a big theme in the national security assessment. What are the principal things that need to be done, from a nature point of view, to increase our food resilience in the UK, given the vulnerabilities of international supply chains that the report highlights?

It is probably about the soil, which, in the end, is sustaining our food supply, and focusing there, as Marian said, in ways that give us greater ability not only to sustain food into the future but to store water in the ground, helping to reduce flood risk. There are plenty of farmers across the country who have now embarked on this regenerative agriculture journey. If any of you have the time next summer, I would strongly encourage a visit to the Groundswell farming festival in Hertfordshire, where there is the most incredible level of knowledge and expertise among practitioners, who are now putting into real effect these ideas about focusing on soil as a means of achieving so many other things.

One thing that you can get by improving natural soil fertility is to reduce reliance on long-distance supply chains for fertili s ers. Access to ammonium nitrate from global markets has gone from being a theoretical thing 10 years ago to now being a real, material factor for farmers. In fact, I heard of one farmer this year who made more money out of selling some spare fertiliser he had than he did from growing crops, such is the volatility in those markets now.

If you were to conduct an investigation into regenerative farming, you could get a great deal of expertise from people who are already doing this. We are advisers on nature, and I think you would get much more wisdom from the farmers who are actually on this journey.

Q77 I intend to go to Groundswell next year. I have one last question. Given the crucial nature of these issues around national security, do you think that Natural England is treated by the Government as a body that is responsible for national security, public health and economic prosperity?

There were some raised eyebrows when we published our new strategy, “Recovering Nature for Growth, Health and Security”, and some people were slightly quizzical. Things have moved on in the short 18 months since we published the first draft of that, and people can now see the connections, but there is work to do in embedding this across the piece.

The piece about nature being infrastructure is where some of this would logically land. If it is about restoring nature for these big national objectives, we will have to put it in a different box from where it currently is, which is a little bit of DEFRA. It seems quite distant from the NHS and what we are doing in terms of defence reviews and everything else. In fact, if you put it in those contexts, it can be of great assistance in enabling us to navigate some really quite big subjects.

Our work transcends a number of Departments that you might not expect us to be working with. As a small example of that, we are doing some work with DWP in jobcentres in the north-east about whether—I should not call it green social prescribing—using nature and having more green space helps to keep people fit and well and therefore more likely to be able to find work. It is partly about people’s health and wellbeing; it is also about their confidence. We did some work recently with a charity that was using nature volunteering to give young people—particularly those who had been isolated during covid in the last part of their schooling years—the confidence to take their first step into the workplace. That idea that nature can also help people’s personal prosperity and resilience is an increasing part of the narrative.

Forgive me, I am trying not to go back 70 years, but having worked in this world for 40 years, I am about to finish, and I am reflecting on what has changed in my working life. I made a comment about this at the beginning, and I might just return to that. The legislation that we work to still assumes that the job is to protect certain places and certain species; it is very much about stopping bad happening, because that is what we needed a couple of generations ago. That is the other thing that, if I dare, the Committee might want to turn its mind to. What do we need in the future? Where do we need to continue to evolve our regulation and our legislation to drive good things, to drive recovery and to drive positive change, rather than just stop harm? We have seen a few bits of that; the Planning and Infrastructure Act takes us that way and Tony mentioned the protected site strategies work that came from the Environment Act.
Landscape recovery, yes.
We would certainly welcome a conversation about what is next to get to a place where nature regulation is driving nature recovery and helping and incentivising good.

Thank you very much, Tony and Marian, for your contribution today and your very fulsome answers. Also, as I said at the start, thank you for the contribution you have made over the course of the last seven years at Natural England and through your careers prior to that. You go with our thanks. We wish you both well in whatever you do next.

sessions.iT: The future of Gaelic Broadcasting

segs.tx: Scottish Affairs Committee
Oral evidence: The future of Gaelic b roadcasting, HC 463
Wednesday 2 September 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 2 September 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Patricia Ferguson (Chair); Dave Doogan; Lillian Jones; Douglas Lumsden; Douglas McAllister; Kirsteen Sullivan.
Questions 40- 93
Witnesses

I : Delyth Evans, Chair, S4C ; Geraint Evans, Chief Executive Officer, S4C ; Deirdre Ní Choistín, Director General, TG4 ; Trevor Ó Clochartaigh, Director , Innovation, Sustainability and Sectoral Capacity, TG4 .

II : John Morrison, Chair, MG ALBA ; Donald Campbell, Chief Executive Officer, MG ALBA ; Margaret Mary Murray, Head of Gaelic Services, BBC ; Luke McCullough, Corporate Affairs Director, Nations, BBC .
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Delyth Evans, Geraint Evans, Deirdre Ní Choistín and Trevor Ó Clochartaigh.

Good morning and welcome to this meeting of the Scottish Affairs Committee, at which we will consider issues around Gaelic broadcasting. I am very pleased to welcome our first panel. Could you introduce yourselves and tell us what your role is? We will then get straight into our questions.
My name is Geraint Evans. I am the chief executive at S4C.
Good morning. My name is Delyth Evans. I am the chair of S4C.
Good morning. My name is Deirdre Ní Choistín. I am the director general of TG4 in Ireland.
Maidin mhaith . I am Trevor Ó Clochartaigh, director of innovation, sustainability and sectoral capacity at TG4.
Q40 Thank you again for being with us this morning. We really appreciate the opportunity to ask you some questions and to learn from your experiences.

I want to direct my first question to Delyth and to Deirdre. Could you both give us an overview of the statutory basis for S4C and TG4 and how they are funded, and perhaps suggest, if you can, what the upsides and downsides of those funding models are?

TG4 is a public service media broadcaster. We were established 30 years ago in 1996, initially as part of RT É , but we have been an independent entity since 2007. Our funding is direct funding from the Exchequer. We have an annual allowance and the funding recommendation is made from the regulator, Coimisiún na Meán . It takes a mixture of the annual statement of performance commitments and the review of performance and public funding to make that recommendation.

The recommendation is then made on an annual basis to the Minister, who brings it to Government for approval. It is announced yearly on budget day—so this coming October, for example, we will know our funding recommendation for 2027. We are different from other broadcasters, in that we do not have multi-annual funding. In Ireland, for example, RT É , the English-language public service media, currently has a three-year temporary multi-annual funding arrangement. TG4 does not.

S4C was created 40 years ago. It was created by statute, so we have a statutory basis. We are funded by the licence fee, not by the BBC. We come under the licence fee, but, as a separate organisation, our funding is decided by Government—the Department for Culture. That is supplemented by an annual programme agreement with the BBC, which provides around 10 hours of programming for us every week. That arrangement stems from the previous situation before S4C was established, whereby the BBC in Wales used to make 10 hours’ worth of programming in Welsh. That arrangement has continued under the current programming arrangement.

We feel that the current system works very well for us. There are clearly big concerns about the licence fee. That is a slightly separate issue, but up until now, the system that we operate under has worked very well. One of the most important elements has been the funding certainty that we have in order to plan ahead . Geraint can tell you more about that; it has been very important.

The second important thing is cross-party support. We have always had the support of all political parties for the existence of S4C and for the role we play in the Welsh economy and in support of the Welsh language.

Sufficient funding is the key for us. That was in the Broadcasting Act 1990, and we were glad to see the Secretary of State reiterate in the Green Paper on charter review that sufficient funding would be an important part of the charter review process for S4C and also for MG ALBA in the UK. Sufficient funding is the important element for us.

What is sufficient is the next question. “Sufficient” for us means more than just achieving the basics; it is about being able to engage with and appeal to wider audiences than the ones we currently appeal to. We are then able to be an economic catalyst for growth across Wales, because we see that for every £1 of licence fee funding we get, we deliver £1.70 in GVA in terms of economic benefit to the UK.

Sufficient funding is the key thing on our minds as we embark on the charter review process. The submission we have made is that we will need, at the very least, a CPI increase on our current licence fee settlement, but we will more than likely need more to be able to engage with young audiences, because of the need to appeal to them on all the platforms that they consume. We are no longer a TV channel; we are more than a TV channel, and we need to appeal to young audiences on all the platforms where they consume their content. That is one of the key challenges going forward.

Q41 Deirdre, you mentioned that you are independent but that the funding comes from Government. Are you and your colleagues involved in negotiations with the Government about funding? Is it agreed cross-party, and is it subject to political machinations? I am interested to explore how that independence works .

The key issue is that we do not have a multi-annual funding recommendation from the regulator or Government. We have cross-party support in the island of Ireland—both north and south—for TG4, and were recognised under the Good Friday/Belfast agreement as a public service media provider in the island of Ireland. The process currently involves an annual request for funding and is based on the augmentation or additionality of the service we provide for our audiences. We currently have large gaps in content that we cannot provide. For example, we do not have adequate funding to provide content for teenagers. We have a children’s channel, Cúla4 , that we established three years ago, but we have a content gap for 13 to 18-year olds , who we cannot provide content for because we do not have sufficient funding.

The current process works on the annual statement of performance commitments as well as the annual review with the media regulator. A funding recommendation is then made to Government. It then depends on the other budgetary pressures and where we perform or how we do on that. We have had incremental funding since 2016, and last year we had a 9% increase in our funding allocation to € 65.4 million, but it is a lot less, for example, than S4C. The European Media Freedom Act has been in place since August last year. That has a provision for adequate, sustainable and predictable funding for PSM across Europe.

To compare the Irish context with the rest of Europe: public service media is generally underfunded in Ireland compared with Europe. We are in the bottom 10 of EBU countries. The public service funding, which would include RTÉ as well, is 0.08% of GDP, in comparison with 0.14% of GDP as an average across Europe. Ireland is funded less than Portugal, on the same level as Malta and just above Romania. For context, that is where we are in terms of public service media funding.

Currently, it is a yearly ask, and it is a lot of lobbying and a lot of meetings with politicians to show the worth of TG4. Generally, however, across the board there is a high appreciation of the value of the content that we provide, particularly for connection with audiences through sport, music and documentaries, and also regarding regional employment. We work with about 60 companies as a publisher-broadcaster. We have multi-annual output contract deals with companies, and part of the remit for that is sustainable employment in a wealth of areas outside the key production areas of Dublin and Wicklow in Ireland.
That is helpful. Thank you very much.
Q42 My question is to Ms Evans and Ms Choistín. How important are multi - annual funding agreements for commissioning content and safeguarding editorial independence?

They are very important in commissioning any kind of programming : i t i s very hard to do that if you only have one year ’ s funding certainty. If you do not mind, I will hand over to Geraint , because he i s better able to talk about the commissioning details .
I have separate questions for Geraint.

Okay. I t is about the point that I made earlier : funding certainty enables us to plan ahead , across all genres. W e work very closely with the production sector in Wales, and it is incredibly important to the Welsh economy to have those jobs in the Welsh language, particularly in rural areas outside the urban areas. For them to plan ahead for their workforce and so on, knowing that there is funding going forward is incredibly important.
I t is especially important in specific genres such as drama and sport . D rama production take s a few years . H aving clarity o n how much funding you have over multiple years—
We will come back to cover that.

I t is key for TG4 that we would like to have a multi - annual funding arrangement. The new B roadcasting B ill, which is currently going through Parliament , has a recommendation that we move from a five - year to a three - year funding model , but it has not actually clarified that it will be a multi - annual recommendation . T hat would be our request. There is currently an arrangement for RTÉ, but it is a temporary arrangement. Again, we see it across Europe: the best-performing examples of public service media, here in the UK but also in Denmark, Germany and the Netherlands, have multi-annual arrangements. The EBU has also shown a strong link between strong democracies and multi-annual funding for PSM. It is very important.

On the difference that not having multi-annual funding makes for us as a minority-language broadcaster, as Geraint mentioned, planning ahead for drama, for example, does not happen within a budgetary year. It takes multiple years and multiple funding sources to produce Irish-language drama, and we do not have that year-to-year certainty on where we will be in the next year and what we can commit to. Currently, we would like to commission two drama series a year, but we are always thinking about plan A and plan B, depending on what our funding is.

There are then inflationary costs and other costs that eat out of the content budget. As a publisher-broadcaster, most of our Exchequer funding goes straight out to the sector. About 74% of funding is spent on content, but without multi-annual funding you cannot plan ahead . You spend half the year trying to get more money for the following year and trying to make sure that you have a zero balance at the end of the year. It is not an efficient way for us as a PSM to run TG4.
Q43 Mr Evans, what benefits has a multi-year funding settlement had for the ability of S4C to plan and invest in Welsh-language broadcasting?

I will centre it on sport and drama. Sport is a key genre for S4C. It enables us to draw audiences from all parts of Wales and beyond, because language is not seen as so much of a barrier: if you want to see a sports event, you will tune into it whatever the language, because you can still enjoy the sport. That enables us to have the rights for things like the Tour de France, international rugby and football, and now even Six Nations darts, which recently did very well for us across all platforms.

With sports rights deals and negotiations, the rights are usually linked to a competition that is multi-year, so you have to have a multi-year settlement to be able to commit to that level of funding. Sports rights are not cheap, but they are valuable and deliver good audience for us. To invest in them, we need clarity on funding. As Deirdre mentioned, drama is similar. It is a multi-year project to get a drama or a film on screen, as we did recently with the film “ Effi o Blaenau ”, which premiered in Glasgow before going on tour in Wales and the UK. That did very well for us.

For those two genres specifically it is very important, but it is also important for things like returning series. If you can commit to a production company so that it knows and has multi-year visibility, it can produce something more efficiently. Going from one year to the next does not enable businesses to plan carefully, develop talent and skills and invest in their workforce—not unless you have that visibility. But I return to those two genres, where it is absolutely key : if you want to compete in the market for sports rights or develop high-quality drama, you really do need a multi-year funding settlement.
Q44 Good morning. Deirdre, how important is commercial revenue, over your public sector funding? Can you give us an idea of the quantum or percentage?

I will not give specific numbers on that, but it is a small additional income for TG4. I do not think it will ever be sufficient for us to rely on full-term, but it is an additional income for our scheduling and allows us, for example, to buy film content and acquisition content to support our schedule. We do not have enough funding to have all Irish-language programming, so we have films and some drama series in English that we buy with commercial income to support our schedule. It is important for TG4, but it will never be a key part of our funding mechanism.

Q45 I accept that, but within that reality, is there a strategic priority in TG4 to grow the commercial element? That would not be to displace any of the public funding, hopefully—you would want to make sure that that was nailed down—but to grow the commercial element of your funding.

There is. It is part of our annual statement of performance commitments with the regulator that we grow the commercial income, but again, the amount is quite small in comparison to the funding we need to provide the services we provide. As a public service broadcaster, we have a remit to provide Irish-language content for Irish-language audiences. It is an additional income, but it is not enough to drive and to deliver key—
No, because you are a public service.
Exactly.
Q46 But what is the nature of the growth in commercial revenue, year on year?
I would have to come back to you with exact figures on that, but it is about 10%, year on year.

Q47 Thanks. The BBC is, by any measure, a challenged organisation. Not the least of those challenges is the licence fee, what it is going to do in future and how it will go forward. How do you quantify and plan for that as a strategic risk within your organisation?

The future funding of the BBC and S4C—which are funded by exactly the same model, the licence fee—puts public service broadcasting at great jeopardy. If there are fewer people paying the licence fee, the income from it will go down. We hear that all the time. We have heard the BBC say quite plainly in this building that the future of the licence fee is unsustainable as it is. The Government need to look at other models, because the licence fee is not going to be increasing at the same level as the costs in the production sector. In much the same way that it is a risk for the BBC, it is a risk for S4C as well.

Our submission to Government as part of the charter review has very much been that we need the same level of funding—and more, if we are honest—because S4C is a very lean organisation. Our budget is about £100 million, but the licence fee collected by the BBC amounts to around £3.8 billion, so a very small proportion of the licence fee comes to S4C. As a lean organisation, it would be very difficult for us to find efficiencies if our income were in any way in jeopardy. It would jeopardise the future of the service and, by doing so, would jeopardise the future of the Welsh language.
That is very clear. Thank you.

Q48 Delyth, I have a couple of questions for you. First, S4C has had a long-standing partnership with the BBC and has been able to maintain its own statutory identity and funding arrangements. How important has that balance between partnership and independence been to S4C’s success? Secondly, has the relationship changed since receiving a multi-year funding settlement that has been funded directly by the licence fee?

The relationship with the BBC is incredibly important to us and always has been. As I said earlier, it delivers 10 hours’ worth of programming to us a week. We share a building with the BBC in Central Square. S4C has three centres around Wales, which is very important in terms of our regional profile, but having premises in the centre of Cardiff, in the BBC building, is also important. We have a very good relationship with the BBC, which we value very much; we also share back-office and technical services with it, which is really important . We have a presence on the iPlayer now, which is also really important . We might come on to prominence, but having a presence on the iPlayer is brilliant for many of our audiences and we value it greatly.

The relationship with the BBC is a good one, and we want to see it continue and develop in new ways. The Green Paper on the licence fee talked about better partnerships, or greater partnerships, across public service broadcasting, and we feel that we are a good example of a partnership with the BBC at the moment .

In terms of being a separate organisation, that is how S4C was set up, and we guard that very carefully. Our audiences think it is terribly important that we are an independent Welsh-language broadcaster—the only one of its kind—delivering content through the Welsh language. That is greatly valued by our audiences. The BBC understands and respects that, but we have managed to develop a very close relationship with it, and we want that to continue.
Q49 Has the relationship changed since receiving a multi-year funding settlement?
I am not sure that it has changed particularly. Geraint might know more about that than me.

I would not say that it has changed anything in particular . For the last five years we have been funded wholly by the licence fee, as well as by the statutory supply agreement, which is the 10 hours a week that we receive from the BBC.

What I would say about that partnership is that the Secretary of State has recently asked the PSBs to work in partnership because the competition that we face is not as much from each other as from the streamers and from YouTube. The iPlayer relationship has been essential in driving up viewing numbers for S4C because of the prominence of iPlayer on connected TVs and the familiarity of the audience with it.

Going into a new iPlayer deal with the BBC, which enabled S4C to go from being a walled garden within the iPlayer to come out into the home page and achieve prominence on that main “New & Trending” rail there, has really driven viewing numbers for us. There was a growth of 25% year on year from 200,000 to 250,000 viewers in terms of monthly active users for us on the iPlayer as a result of that change. Working in partnership with the BBC, as S4C does, is a great example for any other broadcasters.

I know there is a question out there as to whether there should be one PSB player. We can definitely see the benefits of that, if we are realistically going to be able to compete with the streamers and the challenge of YouTube. We may come on to that because that is vitally important for us: the competition is not so much from each other but from the changing viewing habits, particularly of the young users but of all users, in terms of the viewing of streamers and the change of habits towards viewing of YouTube content.
So , in short, the partnership is just as important, going forward, as the multi-year funding settlement, if not more so?
Absolutely, yes.

Q50 Deirdre, we have done the commercial stuff; what about the tax situation that TG4 enjoys? How important is that, and what does that level of concession enable you to do that you otherwise could not?
The tax c redits?
Yes.

We rely on multiple funding sources to produce high-quality content. For example, we work very closely with the Irish language broadcast fund of Northern Ireland Screen. We broadcast the same content a lot with BBC Northern Ireland because the channels are for different audiences, but that partnership works really well .

The tax credits are a revenue-based incentive. Section 481 gives a tax credit for film, drama and documentaries. The advantage of that is that you can get payment in advance on up to 90% of the payment, which helps producers to produce the content. That differs from a lot of jurisdictions, where you can claim that back after production has finished. That is a huge incentive, but the real advantage to us is that it is another funding source for film, documentaries and high-end, high-quality content.

We have another uplift, the Scéal uplift, which is 8%—so that is up to 40% of a tax credit—but it applies only to lower-to-mid-range films; it does not apply to television drama, for example. We are involved in the effort to hopefully change that so that we can include television drama in it. That is part of our lobbying efforts with Ibec’s Audiovisual Ireland.

A new tax incentive was introduced last year for unscripted programming by section 487A. I suppose that is an inward investment initiative from the Government, but we are still working through how it actually works in terms of indigenous productions, and particularly whether there is an advantage for us from that for lower-budget minority language productions. It is definitely already having an impact on inward production into Ireland.

There are other tax credits—for virtual effects and gaming, for example—but all those are advantageous for us as broadcasters, for production companies and particularly for co-productions between producers in the Republic of Ireland and those in Northern Ireland; we can work on the tax credits available in both jurisdictions and the different funding streams from Northern Ireland Screen and Screen Ireland. That has worked very well for us for high-quality content such as “ Crá ”, which was on the BBC iPlayer and such a huge success that it was then broadcast on BBC Four. That all came from working with the tax credits from both jurisdictions.
It sounds like it is essential, then, for the breadth and quality of what you are producing. Is it too much to say that without those tax credits, there would be things that you could not do?

Without those tax credits, there are a lot of things we could not do—our films and high-quality drama, for example. They are one of numerous funding sources that we have for the content we make. For example, we had a film, “ An Cailín Ciúin ”, go to the Oscars in 2023; that would have benefited from the tax credit. Last week, IFTA selected one of TG4’s films as Ireland’s entry to the best international feature film category; that is our fifth film since 2021. All of those films would have benefited from the tax credit.

Again, those high-end projects give status to TG4 and the Irish language and bring new audiences to us who would not necessarily engage with television content but will watch the films in cinemas. When they hear, “Oh, this has been selected as Ireland’s entry for the Oscars,” they think, “I’m interested in knowing more about that.” It is brand and status building, but ultimately, without those funding sources, we would not be able to produce that kind of quality content ourselves.
Understood. Thank you.
Q51 Mr Ó Clochartaigh , I will come to you now. I am sorry: you have been sitting quietly and waiting, but you will get your chance now.

How important have the Irish language broadcast fund and the Sound & Vision scheme been in expanding Irish-language content generally, supporting independent producers and strengthening the wider Irish-language media sector as a whole?

As Deirdre has explained, the funding sources for most of the production companies tend to be a tapestry. They are trying to find money from different pockets and supports. It would be wrong to think, though, that the money is just about producing audio - visual content that is going to go on screen, because behind all those efforts there are also training initiatives and seed funding. There are also schemes to develop writers and directors and shadowing schemes to bring crews through and to train new talent. Those are vitally important.

The ILBF in the north is one of our strongest partners, and the training and sector capacity building that it has been doing over the years has meant an increased number of production companies available to work with us as well as the staff and people who can work on the productions—and it has brought those to a much higher level.

This is important to share with the Committee: you have a very important role to play in creating the space for this type of work to happen. We are 30 years old this year; my role is around innovation, sustainability and sector capacity, and we are looking forward to the next 30 years. We are trying to build the new cohort of people and companies that can create content for people who speak Irish and increase those numbers. Unless the legislation gives the space to do that, you cannot build in that way.

As Geraint mentioned, it is also important that we look to collaborating transnationally. Really good collaboration has happened over the years: for example, I spent my first years in TV production as a director on the soap opera “ Ros na Rún” . When that started, we borrowed lots of people from “Pobol y Cwm” to come over, because we did not have people with the relevant experience at the time. We brought them in as heads of department, but local heads of department shadowed with them and so grew up through the system.

It is important to take into consideration the sector capacity building that needs to be done. It builds the regions and the cultural and creative sector for us outside Dublin and Wicklow, which means that people can stay at home, work in their own areas, raise their families, send their kids to school and spend their money in the local area; that has always been a huge argument that we have made with our funding submissions. That element of what we do cannot be underestimated. It is the same for all of the broadcasters here, because we need to work together to fight the challenges and get those eyeballs from the people who are looking at Apple, Netflix, YouTube and others, because that is where the competition really is. We need public service media at the forefront in all of these efforts.
That is very helpful, thank you.

Q52 Can I ask a general question to either Trevor or Deirdre? Forgive me, because I cannot see it in our papers; I have the information in relation to the Welsh language. Can either of you tell me what percentage or proportion of people in Ireland report having any skills in the Irish language? What percentage can actually speak Irish?

In the last census in 2022, 1.8 million people said they spoke some level of Irish. But in Gaeltacht areas , for daily Irish speakers, the figure is down to about 66,000 per year. There is then another cohort of about 500,000 who say they have a good level of Irish, or who can speak Irish very well.

We have to create content and cater for all those different types of Irish speakers. We have the core daily Irish speakers in the Gaeltacht and we also have the 1.8 million, primarily because Irish is a compulsory subject in schools up to leaving cert. It is the first official language of the state and the constitution, so we have official status for the language. However, there are multiple layers of fluency and ability within that, and TG4 caters for all levels of speakers.

The number of speakers should not be equated with the audience, because the audience includes not only all the people on the island of Ireland but those abroad in the diaspora, through the player. All of our content is accessible to a much broader audience through subtitling or whatever, which is very important in the international sense.

Our content is available internationally on the player, and it grew by 22% last year. Some 215 countries and territories watch TG4 content on the player, so people worldwide want to watch Irish-language content.

Q53 Before I ask a question, I want to declare an interest: my wife is part-owner of a small independent TV company, but I do not consider that to be a big enough reason for me to exclude myself from the session today.
Geraint, you mentioned iPlayer and streaming services. How much are those changing how you are operating, working and reaching people with the Welsh language?

We all know that the numbers of people watching traditional TV or linear television are declining, but what we are seeing is a real growth in our digital platforms. We have our own player, S4C Clic , and we have a presence on iPlayer that does really well for us. Again, it is about the familiarity that the audience has with that platform.

Also, we now commission specifically for platforms such as YouTube, TikTok and even Instagram, because we know that very few young Welsh speakers actually engage with social media content in the Welsh language. Around 80% of Welsh-speaking young people use social media in English only, and that is because of the sparsity of Welsh-language content on those platforms. So we now deliberately set out to commission. We recently commissioned a vertical drama, which means that you can watch it on your phone on TikTok, and we have gone back and commissioned a second. We can see that that is the type of content that is going to get young people watching Welsh-language content on a regular basis.

That is also the kind of content that means we can compete with the other challenges out there. We know that, according to the recent Ofcom “Media Nations” report, around 60% of Welsh people watch YouTube on a weekly basis. Again, that is the competition. It does not mean that they are watching YouTube content; maybe they are watching content from other PSBs on YouTube, as well as all kinds of other types of videos. We commission specifically for that platform, because we know that if they are spending so much of their time there, the Welsh language needs to be there.

S4C was established in 1982 due to public protest in many ways, because people wanted the Welsh language to be on the most popular media of its time if it were to survive. I have since described this as a battle on several fronts, as it is not just a battle for the future of the language on television; it is a battle that needs to be on YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, as well as on the other players that we have.
Q54 If we look at the demographics of your viewers, what sort of age ranges are there? Is it a complete mix, or is it an older generation? How does it pan out?

It is a real mix. Around 60% of the viewing of our audience aged between 16 and 44 is purely on the players. They spend more and more of their time watching our content on Clic or iPlayer, rather than on traditional linear television. The older audiences are still watching on linear television. In terms of the future of the language, we have to think about the younger audience—by young, I mean under 45.
I’m old, then!

That is how we term the younger audience. It might be parents with children and so on who could be consuming Welsh-language content, and we want that to be a part of their lives. We need to commission carefully and to establish that we have rights, so that we have a longer rights window for our content on things such as BBC iPlayer. That way, our dramas can be on there and people can tune into them. T hat is all part of the new strategy that we have, which is again about being more than a TV channel. We have to cater for audiences on whatever platform they are consuming their content.
Q55 How much new content—excluding sports and news, which obviously cannot be repeated—are you producing every year?

Basically, for 52 weeks of the year we have a live schedule, with original new content from 7 o’clock to 10 o’clock every evening, which is pretty much all new content commissioned. We still need to serve that linear TV schedule, but we are increasingly finding that that schedule needs to have a longer tail: it needs to be able to be viewed by people for a longer period of time afterwards.

The number of hours commissioned by S4C is significant. I can come back to you with the figure; I have not got it at the top of my head. Sustaining a volume of content to maintain a linear TV schedule but also the shorter-form content that appeals to younger audiences is all a part of what we need to do now to be a modern public service media organisation, not a public service broadcaster.

Q56 You mentioned that sport is quite a big thing for you. How are people watching it? Excuse me, I do not know—do you have to listen to it in Welsh, or are there options to listen to it in English as well? How does it work?

It depends on the rights holders and what they will allow us. Very often, we have successfully gone into partnership with streamers such as Amazon or TNT, which may have a contract for a sport that they will show on their pay TV service. We have gone in and negotiated with them to get some free-to-air rights to show that in the Welsh language only on S4C. Those streamers do not deem that as competition, as if they were selling those rights to, for example, BBC or ITV, so that has proved to be very effective for us.
However, for domestic sport, we occasionally provide English - language commentary as well as Welsh - language commentary where rights allow, and that has been very popular with audiences in Wales.
Q57 Has the Media Act 2024 implemented the recommendations from the independent review conducted in 2017?

Pretty much, yes. In Euryn Ogwen Williams’s report, there was a clear desire for us to be moving more into the digital space and creating a digital hub. Since then, we have developed our own digital news service, which is an in-house service by S4C, working again in partnership with the BBC. We are increasing the amount of commissioning to platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and so on, and are increasing our social media team, who are repackaging content from linear TV and getting it out on those social media platforms. There has been a clear drive there.

The report also stated that we should be getting our funding from the licence fee and multi-year funding as well. Many of these recommendations have already been implemented. The other one was that the board should become a unitary board, which it is now, with Delyth as chair.

That concludes our questions to the first panel. Thank you for your time this morning and for being so open and frank with us; it has been very helpful to our inquiry. Thank you for coming along to London today.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: John Morrison, Donald Campbell, Margaret Mary Murray and Luke McCullough.
Good morning and welcome to our second panel. May I ask you all briefly to say who you are and what you do ?
M adainn mhath —good morning. I am Luke McCullough , the corporate affairs director for nations at the BBC.
I am Margaret Mary Murray. I look after the BBC’s Gaelic - language services, BBC ALBA, which we operate in partnership with MG ALBA, and BBC Radio nan Gàidheal .
I am John Morrison, the chair of MG ALBA.
M adainn mhath . I am Donald Campbell, the chief executive of MG ALBA.
Q58 Thank you very much, and welcome—welcome back to some of you, as we have had you here before on at least one occasion, or perhaps more in your case, Mr McCullough.

My first question is for Mr Morrison. MG ALBA has called for parity with S4C in funding and in its statutory recognition. In practical terms, what would that look like for Gaelic broadcasting, and what specific changes would be needed to make that happen?

In terms of parity, we look for an equivalence of treatment. I do not think that we are in the position where we are looking for the same budget that Welsh has , but we would like to see, for example, when documents come out relating to broadcasting from DCMS, a couple of additional words in Welsh and Gaelic . That would be very welcome because sometimes, as we have seen even recently, Gaelic is not mentioned in very important documents that are looking forward to the BBC charter.

We were happy to see the Green Paper mention the sustainability of MG ALBA. Sustainability is key for us, as I am sure the Committee is aware. I notice that you have actually used some of our own words, that we are in real jeopardy, and that cannot be overstated . Our budget was frozen for 10 years, so its value has dropped by about 45%. That trajectory is unsustainable for any organisation or company. We are looking for equivalence in both legal terms and in the treatment of Gaelic and Welsh. Obviously, we are also looking for an increased budget.
Q59 And how would that help you to improve what you deliver for broadcasting?

It would be transformational, because one of the first things we did when I came in was get EY to have a look—Ernst & Young, in old-fashioned language. EY did an analysis that showed that, effectively, our budget should be double what it was at the time because it had fallen so far behind. It said that, if we had kept up with inflation, we would have created an additional 300 or 350 jobs. Most of the jobs we have created as a result of production have been in the h ighlands and i slands, which badly need jobs. For example, we have a media centre in Stornoway that is now one of the biggest employers in the whole of the Western Isles.

The demographics of that are fantastic , because you see young people who have gone away to college or university, and they come back because they can have careers. Trevor mentioned the importance of sustaining communities, and that is vital. So we do all that. Then, in terms of broadcasting, it allows us to do the ordinary things that every other TV channel does. We are now down to new content every week of just over 20%—21 %, or is it 23 %?— which is not a TV channel . If we slip below that, we can see audiences go away, particularly young audiences because , like everybody else, they are consuming Netflix and Apple TV . With BBC ALBA , u nless we have new content, they go away. We can see that in the weekly figures.

For example, one big thing that we did, and would like to do more of — I am sure you will ask us about the risks associated with spending all our drama budget on one big production; the board sat with the image of eggs in a basket — is that we took a calculated gamble that a big production in Gaelic could actually raise the profile of the channel and the language. We are delighted that happened, because “An t-Eilean ” was watched by 2 million people—more than 2 million now , because of the iPlayer. However, it also won best drama in public sector regional television in Europe, and also best programme in regional television in Europe, which shows you that there is no dearth of talent nor of storytelling ability. W e would love to do more high-profile drama.

If you think about it, we spent our entire budget for a year on a four-part series, and we would love to do more of that. In other programming, one of the previous contributors spoke about big gaps. There are big gaps in our schedule as well. We would love to do more programming. We would love to do more digital because, as we heard earlier, that is where the youth audience is going.

F or example, with our LearnGaelic and SpeakGaelic , which have been hugely important and have been welcomed by audiences and learners of the language, we now have nearly 50,000 people signed up to Facebook and learning Gaelic online. We can see that they are staying with us for over 20 minutes, which shows they are actually savouring the content. On Instagram, we are heading towards 110,000 followers, again showing the way that young people are consuming the content. We would love to do so much more than that.

In terms of finance, there was a figure that emerged in both the House of Commons and the House of Lords that said that MG ALBA spent £420 per G aelic speaker while S4C spent £260 per Welsh speaker. Honestly, we looked at that figure and were bemused by it . W hen you look at the budget that Wales ha s and the budget that we ha ve , how do you slice and dice th o se figures to come up with that figure ? W ho has done that ?

W hat we found was that if you add all the sums that go into Gaelic broadcasting and then take the lowest number of speakers, which is those who are totally fluent in Gaelic — 69, 000 or 70,000 — then you get that figure. T he latest census showed that the number of speakers of Gaelic had actu ally gone up to 130,000, which is a doubling in ten years. BBC ALBA has played a critical role in that alongside Gaelic - medium education.

Also, i f you are going to do that calculation, that is the least helpful figure for us , because every week 360 , 000 people in Scotland tune in to BBC ALBA— 360,000. Then you look at the figures. I seriously ask the Committee to look at that figure with a fairly jaundiced eye, because we think it is flawed.

Q60 I was going to ask you a little bit more about the issue of parity and the numbers of speakers but, t aking your point about that particular figure, was it calculated in the same way for S4C, or do you think it ha s been calculated differently?

I do not know. We do not know, unless you have depth of knowledge, Donald. C ertainly , if you take S4 C’s budget and MG ALBA’s budget — even when you add the BBC — it is very difficult to calculate how you can get to that figure. I think it is by taking the lowest number of speakers, the highest amount of money , i f you add the money that we receive at MG ALBA, and then add ing in the BBC contribution . T hen you get a figure divided by the lowest number of speakers. But the lowest number is people who use the language daily. We then have the same number again who are learners , a lot of whom are approaching fluency now and have shown by their interest that they want to continue.

T hen you add in the 360,000 people who tune in every week. I f you look at when we do the really high - end productions , which we would like to do more of, more than 2 million people watched “An t-Eilean ” . I do not know exactly how it was calculated.
Q61 What is the annual budget? What i s the actual figure? I can see the figure for the Welsh and Irish.
W e were working with £ 13.4 million , a nd it was stuck there for about ten years. L ast year , we got an uplift of about £ 2 million , so o ur annual budget is £ 15 million now.
Q62 Where does that come from?

That comes from the Scottish Ministers. T he way I ha ve described us previously is that we are like the orphan child of British broadcasting because everybody loves us ; w e were set up by Westminster ; w e are regulated by Ofcom ; w e have a very valuable and productive partnership with the BBC ; we ar e funded by Scottish Ministers , b ut somehow, somewhere , we fall between the stools . W e need somebody to take charge of where we are going and mak e sure that we have a proper settlement.

Q63 Mr McCullo ugh, S4 C currently has a multi - year funding settlement and TG4 is also hoping to secure multi - year funding. W hat would the benefits be of multi - year funding for MG ALBA and BBC ALBA ?

I t is interesting to go to that question on the basis of what Mr Morrison has just been saying because, of course, we have both MG ALBA funded by the Scottish Government and BBC ALBA—t he BBC ’s channel — which is funded by MG ALBA and by the BBC through the licence fee. T here i s the funding that MG ALBA brings to the channel, and there i s the funding that the licence fee brings to the channel. When the channel started in 2007-08, as the Chair will remember from her previous life, the BBC invested £4 million of licence fee funding and there was investment through MG ALBA from the Scottish Government, which, as the Committee has just heard, has got stuck for some period of time .

In that same period of time , despite the BBC’s revenue decreasing in real terms by over £1 billion, investment from the BBC in BBC ALBA has gone up by more than inflation. If you applied the inflation rate to that £4 million original investment, you would get something like £7.5 million. We now spend £10 million on BBC ALBA and then further investment on Radio nan Gàidheal , BBC Online and so on.

There is no less certainty of the BBC’s investment in the channel than there is in any other BBC service. We treat our investment in BBC ALBA exactly the same as we would BBC One, BBC Radio 2, Radio Scotland and Radio nan Gàidheal . There is the certainty of licence fee funding for all that we do, to an extent, but, as Mr Doogan was saying in the previous session, there is a real challenge and a threat to that licence fee, which probably impacts multi-year anything.

The licence fee settlement as it is at the moment ends in August 2028. We are in the slightly strange position where 93% of the population of the United Kingdom use the BBC every month, but only 78% of households are paying for it. There is a large and growing gap between the number of people who are paying for their public service media, including BBC ALBA and BBC Radio nan Gàidheal , and the costs of providing them. The real threat is around the sustainability of funding generally to all the BBC’s services and no service is exempt from that. I would say that the BBC’s contribution to BBC ALBA has been more than steady. It has been growing. However, we entered that as a partnership model, and it is vital that the partnership as a whole continues to grow and have some certainty.
Q64 Mr Morrison, can you give any specific examples of projects or investments that would be easier to pursue if MG ALBA operated within a multi-year funding framework?

If you take “An t-Eilean ”, the high-level drama, for example, that rarely fits neatly within a financial year. Therefore, it would be easier to plan ahead for high-level drama. The other important element for our viewers is that we like to think of ourselves as the home of women’s football. At BBC ALBA, we show a lot of women’s football and it has been fantastic for the game and very good for the channel as well. However, sports rights are negotiated over a three or four-year period. This comes very high up the risk register for the board when we have to say, “Do we commit to this?” The answer is, “Yes, we want to commit to it, but we have no guarantee that we can fulfil that commitment without the multi-year.”

There is a risk there. It would bring security for us, but it is not just for MG ALBA; it is for the people who work for us. It is the jobs that are involved in showing these games on TV. Women’s football is one of the fastest growing sports in the world. In Scotland, BBC ALBA’s coverage of it has contributed to that, but it is not helped by not having a multi-year deal.

Q65 Mr McCullough, since 2017 BBC ALBA has been regulated through the BBC’s wider operating licence rather than a distinct service-specific framework. Has the move to a broader BBC-wide regulatory model strengthened or weakened protections for Gaelic-language broadcasting?

Ofcom’s operating licence for the BBC is as strong a regulatory footing as any. BBC ALBA is regulated in exactly the same way as BBC One, Radio Scotland, BBC Radio Wales or any of the other linear services we have. The operating licence makes a number of clear provisions for Gaelic, which I think are really helpful . In terms of BBC ALBA, it determines that there will be a weekday evening news programme that is provided entirely from licence fee funds. It is broadcast live from Inverness every evening in the studios there. The operating licence also provides for a news review programme at the weekend and, beyond the BBC ALBA conditions, for learning in Gaelic.

Our learning provision, yes, exists on BBC ALBA, but also in our partnership SpeakGaelic and the Bitesize service that we offer for children and learners. There is provision for regular news on Radio nan Gàidheal through the day and for Gaelic content on the BBC website, particularly the news content, which again operates primarily out of Inverness, Stornoway, Portree and Glasgow, although also through journalists based in the Scottish Parliament.

The regulatory system therefore underpins all that, but it also allows creative freedom for us and those who co-commission with us. Margaret Mary will be able to talk about our content decisions but, working with our partners, in the licence we need a bit of freedom to stay where the audience is. If you get too prescriptive and have very specific licence conditions, you end up moving quite quickly away from perhaps what was the intention at the time that the licence was set. If you look at the charter 20 years ago, for example, which came into force in about 2007, it did not envisage BBC ALBA or iPlayer, and yet within about 18 months, both those things existed and became absolutely part of the weft and weave of the culture of Scotland and the UK.

I think you need a framework that not only sets the minimum requirements—particularly around how we serve as journalism and tell the story of Scotland to itself—but allows for creative freedom and the ability to make editorial decisions that move with the times.
Q66 What opportunities does the BBC charter review present to update and strengthen the long-term sustainability of Gaelic-language broadcasting?

In our BBC response to the UK Government’s Green Paper, we said how important the languages that the BBC operates in remain and how important we see them remaining in the future. Obviously, like everything else, that requires sustainable funding for public broadcasting and for the BBC as we move into the future, but I would expect the charter to underpin the fact that we have services in Welsh and in Gaelic, with that freedom to respond at the speed that the audience needs, and perhaps also to give a nod to the other languages that we work with.

I know that this morning the Committee has heard about Gaelic Irish in the Republic of Ireland, and about Welsh. The BBC also works with the Northern Ireland Screen broadcast fund, which the witnesses earlier mentioned, to produce content—Government-funded via Northern Ireland Screen—in Ulster Scots and in the Irish language, in Northern Ireland, sometimes working in Irish in partnership with TG4, who you heard from earlier.
In Cornwall, we are working—again in a partnership model—with Cornwall council. They have helped us invest in a “Learn Cornish” podcast , and we present the news in Cornish on BBC Radio Cornwall.
