One of the points that I routinely made on the P ermanent Secretar ies’ version of the National Security Council was that we were not always that good at joining up the international and domestic . E ven the interface between the national security infrastructure , the domestic infrastructure and the international economic infrastructure has not always been as effective as it needs to be for a genuinely operationalised— to use your word — join - up of a of a strategy.

I would support the c ommittee recommending to G overnment to sharpen up their ability to engage across all the different types of approach that the UK can have — not just defence , diplomacy and development, but more broadly. I would seek to prioritise that. W e are not trying to do that on everything, but we are trying to do it on the issues that matter most to our country’s future. I would have a very clear hierarchy of interests about what that future depends on. Clearly, the peace of our nation and our ability to withstand a ttack from an enemy ha ve to be right at the top of that list.
Lord Houghton of Richmond: Perhaps we can hear a quick comment from Olivia and then Richard.

Olivia O'Sullivan: We are good at writing strategies and doing long PDFs— I have worked on that in g overnment myself — but not good at implementing them. That is an absolutely correct diagnosis. Some of that gets to what Matthew said, which is that we have had a lot of churn in leadership. N aturally, leaders want to look again at strategies. The two things that are like stick s of rock as problems to the British Government are what Matthew said about struggling with long - term strategic thinking and struggling with going from writing strategies to implementing them.

It is a good moment now, following the aid cuts and with , potentially , Ministers and a P rime Minister in place for the remainder of this p arliamentary term , t o start thinking about the difficult nuts and bolts of implementation . O nce the F CDO is through its restructure , n ow that the aid budget has been cut in the way it has , it will be a good moment to start thinking about whether we have any of these issues that we have been pointing out — where we have legacy seats or are part of a multilateral institution but we are not adequately resourcing or are not clear on what we want out of it , and whether we should , therefore , refocus . That would be very sensible. I will stop there , because I am mostly agreeing with you and what others have said.
Lord Houghton of Richmond: Richard , any comment?

Richard Gowan: I am not well - placed to comment on Whitehall process. I would simply make a small point, which is in line with Matthew’s call for us to be focused. I think that the UK sometimes gets a little bogged down in initiatives. Ministers want to come to the UN. They want to sit in the Security Council or the General Assembly and often they come with a personal initiative. I recall that there was one a few years ago about defending faith at some part of the UN system. T o be quite honest, those initiatives tend to take up time , take up diplomatic energy and fizzle. I do not think that they contribute to the focused national strategy that everyone here is talking about. So , maybe it is not about having fewer seats but about using those seats in a slightly more parsimonious way around the multilateral system to achieve key national goals and not pursu ing “ nice to have ” initiatives that do not really contribute that much to the big picture.

Q76 Baroness Blackstone: I want to come back to the issue of v alues and interest s . At the beginning , Sir Matthew, you said there was no trade-off between the two. P erhaps I could start with you, Olivia, because you have not commented on that so much , but c ould you be brief , so that I can ask the other two to come in , to o? I n this contested world that we now live in , should we spend more time and effort on promoting our values ? It could be on human rights, the rule of law or any other area that you want to pick out.

Olivia O'Sullivan: W e should but, to pick up on Richard’s point, we should be cautious of the tendency to launch initiatives and to be declaratory about this without adequately considering the power and influence required to back up a defence of those values. That requires an effective multilateral strategy, precisely because of the trends that we have been talking about. The US is currently adversarial towards parts of the system — the US national security s trategy referred to lashing its sovereignty to institutions that do not have America’s interests at heart.

We have a greater distribution of power in the world . Some 50 years ago , t he G7 represented a significant proportion of global GDP a nd now it is much lower. There are other countries that are less practised . “L ess practised ” is perhaps the wrong phrase; they have less of the habit of using the multilateral system and multilateral institutions to deal with problems or regional issues. We need to understand that shift and get good at understanding the ways in which levers and processes are maybe slightly different from what we are used to . We are used to investing a lot in multilateral institutions and systems. T hose are very important, but there are probably other things and other forms of diplomacy that we need to understand better in order to adequately stick to and amass the levels of power and influence that we would need to defend our values.

There are different ways to ask this question , b ecause in foreign affairs it also means that you sometimes have to deal with countries that do not completely share your world view in order to pursue a shared outcome. We always need to consider doing that a nd , in a world where there is a greater distribution of power and there are more influential regional actors , you need to conside r coalitions of folks who are not as like-minded as the peo ple we a re traditionally used to working with or who do not as habitually work in the multilateral institutions that we are used to work ing with. It is just a question of balancing and understanding the ways in which the map of power is changing in order to do precisely what you said, which is to defend those values. Sorry, that was not succinct. I apologise.

Richard Gowan: First, I am afraid that the verb is “ defend ” rather than “ promote ” . W e are at the end , sadly, of the period where countries like the UK are able to use forums like the United Nations to promote liberal values around things such as gender equality. We are very much on the defensive now and the priority is to hold on to many of the norms that we buil t up and not allow more conservative powers to eat away at those norms. It is very important for our international profile and just for the principles themselves that we continue to defend the causes that we believe in.

I fully agree with Olivia that there will be times whe n we have to balance that with working with countries that do not share all those principles. I mean, very frankly, there are now policy areas at the UN on which we are closer to China in our understanding of what is necessary than we are to the US. A l though we are clearly not going to agree with China on many issues, es pecially around human rights, where there is common cause we should think about how we pursue that common cause with Beijing.

Finally, it is also worth remembering that it is not just the liberal principles of the post-Cold W ar era that are under attack ; w hat is really under attack today is Article 2 of the UN charter, which prohibits aggression , defend s sovereignty and defends territorial integrity. For a lot of UN members, after Russia’s aggression against Ukraine and the US operations in the Middle East, the big question is whether we can band together to defend those basic principles of the international system . We are on the defensive on a lot of levels.
Baroness Blackstone: Sir Matthew, last word?

Sir Matthew Rycroft: I agree that we should be careful about how we pursue our values. We should be able to engage with literally every country in the world, even those w ith which we fundamentally disagree about those values , but we have to know what those values are and be absolutely clear about what they are before deciding tactically how much to talk about them. To use an analogy, if an individual leader says that they are open to challenge a nd then the first time that they are challenged they demonstrate through their behaviour that they did not like that challenge at all , t he ir credibility would be shot , that is the end of their credibility as a leader. S imilarly, a nation that says, for instance, that it supports , as one of its core values, the international rule of law , human rights or whatever , and then demonstrates through its actions that it is not consistent in th ose value s , ends up with no credibility at all. W e have to decide for ourselves wh ich core values matter more than anything else to us and then uphold them.

Q77 Lord Bruce of Bennachie: I wonder if I could explore how our bilateral presence can inform our multilateral priorities. This is directed to Sir Matthew. I was there when we achieved 0. 7%. I was there when the multilateral reviews were instituted. I saw the United Nations agencies very sharply reacting to the pressure that was put on them , b ut that was because we were the world leaders , but we are now nowhere in that sphere. That is a tragic shame and I weep for it , b ut that is where we are. T he consequence s of that are the merger of DfID and F CDO , which was very disruptive ; the continuing cuts in staffing , with a 30% cut on the Foreign Office going through ; and the systematic withdrawal of our presence across the world.

M y argument is that we were told that the cuts in aid meant that we did not need so many diplomats on the ground , but is not the truth that we need just as many to do a different role — much cheaper —to make sure that the UK both projects our values in countries where we have connections and informs ourselves about their wishes ? O ne of the concerns that I have about what we are doing is that we might be more interested in how our equals want to reform the system, rather than the aspiring countries looking to us as to how we can shape it. If we do not have a presence on the ground, we are not going to be able to be informed. I just wonder whether you feel that that is the case. O n the basis of that, would that make it easier for us to say that that will be a factor in helping to shape our multilateral priorities, because we better understand our partners?

We just had a group of New Zealand MPs here and I wanted to ask them about this , but time did not allow. We have several British island realms across the Pacific, but we almost ignore them. We have almost abandoned them. They are very small, but strategically China is all over them , as it is all over Africa and Asia, and we are not there . My question is: do we not need to have a presence in reasonable numbers , cost-effectively, to ensure that the UK both informs its values and feeds back what the aspirations are of these countries? That might give us some degree of leadership in the world. I am goi ng to come to you, Richard, but I wonder if I could go to Sir Matthew first.

Sir Matthew Rycroft: I very much agree with that point, Lord Bruce. In a nutshell, diplomacy is more cost - effective than development, and development is more cost - effective than defence. O ne of the reasons why the aid cuts are so short - sighted is that they will end up costing us a lot more in the long run, because somewhere or other , where there has been a reduction in not just UK aid but American and other types of aid, there will be consequences at some point. We do not know how or where or when, but at some point something will happen around the world — whether it will be a bit like Co vid, 9/11 or something else, we just do not know. With the benefit of hindsight, in the future, we will look back and realise that those cuts to the aid budget were counterproductive to our own national interests, very selfishly, as well as for the countries involved. Among the most powerful voices for reversing those aid cuts have come from the defence world , where they can see that development is more is more cost effective than defence. I would add that diplomacy is even more cost - effective than development. F or a very small amount of money, you can have an effective diplomatic service.

The UK still ha s an effective Diplomatic Service, including in New Zealand , b ut it is smaller and more stretched than it has been. I would hope that this c ommittee would strongly push the Government to ensure enough investment in the Diplomatic Service, including in things such as language skills, expertise on the United Nations and other things, and the ability for people to really get under the skin of countries, which is what diplomacy is all about, not to promote and tell them what to do —to go to Richard’s earlier point —b ut to build those relationships and alliances with them so that they choose to do things that we would be comfortable with them doing.

Olivia O'Sullivan: I have a lot of sympathy for the Government i n that resources are not limitless. I think we need to invest more in defence and trade - offs need to be made. But we are also at a time when, as a whole range of people have recognised , there are more emerging, active, influential middle powers in the world ; our relationship with the US is becoming very difficult ; and understanding those increasingly influential powers well , their aspirations and what they want, should be a feature of our diplomatic strategy and a feature of any strategy for multilateral reform, because we will not achieve any of that on our own. W e need to understand what other countries which share some, even if not all , of our goals want t o o, because it is only coalitions of member states or countries sharing a similar outcome that can push for these kinds of reforms or outcomes that we seek —w hether that is coalitions outside institutions or within institutions . Y ou need that kind of connective tissue between countries.

I t is an interesting feature of the UK strategy that we have sought to build deeper relations in the Indo-Pacific , a nd one aspect of that has been to seek observer status at A SEAN . M y colleagues and I at Chatham House looked at this a bit for some work we did on the UK’s Indo-Pacific strategy. J ust joining is step one — step zero. You need to understand an institution, the way countries and member states within it interact with it, what they want and what their aspirations are , to be effective. S o I agree that it would be a mistake to just say , “W e are a member of lots of multilateral institutions ”, almost like an insurance policy against cuts and withdrawals elsewhere. You need to invest in your diplomatic understanding , your knowledge of those institutions and the countries within them to achieve the things that you want.

There has been a lot of talk about middle - power diplomacy and coalitions of middle powers. To do that effectively, you need to understand those middle powers and what they want, and make sure that you actually have shared interests with them . O n our own , we a re not going to get Brazil , South Africa , India or other countries to join us in serious joint diplomatic efforts unless we have a significant investment in understanding them.

Lord Bruce of Bennachie: The 30% c ut s currently going through the F CDO are a drop in the ocean compared with the aid cuts. I mean, to me this looks like a really false economy. It is not a big goal and we are not going to have the people on the ground. I just make that comment. How do we use our bilateral presence to inform our multilateral priorities? I s that a legitimate part of it? H ow do we determine those multilateral priorities independently of that , as well as alongside that?

Richard Gowan: I would simply make the point that very significant decisions regarding the multilateral system are not always made in the big multilateral centres. China, for example, is very good at using its bilateral relations with Ministers in capitals in Africa or Asia t o override what ambassadors are agreeing in New York and Geneva. I am sure Matthew experienced this. You can negotiate something with the African group in a UN centre, but then China will simply go country by country to the P rime Ministers and F oreign Ministers of the states involved and get them to change position. T he only way that the UK can push back against that sort of bilateral pressure is if you are on the ground, if you are in those countries as well, and if you have relationships with those P rime Ministers and those F oreign Ministers. I t is absolutely essential that we retain strong bilateral relationships, because otherwise a lot of our multilateral work will be pulled apart by China and others going through different routes.
The Chairman: Lord De M au l e y has an important question to ask you.

Q78 Lord De Mauley: We have moved into the area of financial realities . B udgetary restrictions within our Diplomatic Service will necessarily entail some hard choices about which institutions, initiatives and program me s the UK can and should prioritise. In your view, what are the three most critical policy areas for the UK when it comes to multilateral engagement? Can I start with Richard Gowan , please?

Richard Gowan: We have to retain focus on peace and security. I think we have to accept that we are going to get less out of bodies such as the Security Council than we once did. But , in a dangerous world, it is important that we retain points of contact , such as the Security Council , with our rivals . T hat is number one .

Secondly, Matthew referred to the fact that the UK has a long history of investment in humanitarian agencies , a nd that is one area where there is a proven track record that international bodies can deliver in a way that no one else can. S o we should definitely continue to invest politically and with resources in humanitarian assistance.

T hirdly, climate change has gone down the agenda politically in multilateral forums over the last few years since the Glasgow summit , b ut as we are all experiencing these horrible heatwaves, I think that we know that climate change is going to go back up the agenda. T here i s actually quite a lot of work to be done reforming the international architecture for addressing climate change , a nd we should be investing in that now. So the three things are peace and security, humanitarian aid, and climate change .

W here I think we should be very cautious and possibly ask whether we can disengage a bit is some parts of the development architecture, because some parts of the existing multilateral development architecture are effective ; t here are others which are probably no longer fit for purpose . T hat may be an area where some economies really are possible.

Olivia O'Sullivan: The question is about which groupings of institutions we should prioritise . I would say a word about trade and economic governance , n ot least because it is such an area of contestation and volatility . China’s role in the global economy , China’s use of subsidy, the US really shifting from what previously was consistent support for broadly open and free trade , I think that is a shift on both sides of the aisle in the US, and it has made parts of the WTO deadlocked and a real space of contestation.

The second question we should ask is : what can we do about that? It is good that the UK has signed up to the alternative dispute settlement mechanism in the WTO. There are also things we could be thinking about with groupings that we are either close to or members of , such as the EU and CPTPP, about the future of global economic governance. I t requires a nuanced take on what we can actually achieve within the institutions, but on the issue , it is an area where there are a lot of countries outside of the US and China wh o really need a clear direction of travel and way forward. I am slightly drawing on some work by my Chatham House colleague, Creon Butler, who ha s written about the future of trade and economic governance in these terms.

I agree that the humanitarian and development agencies is an area. T rade and economic governance, I think, is critical because the UK is very exposed to open trade , it is this space of contestation and volatility and great power competition, and it is likely to really expose us to shocks if we cannot get it right. On humanitarian and development , there is a slightly different logic . T o pick up on what Richard says , w e have a lot of expertise . It is critical : we are likely to see more shocks from climate and more conflicts in the world, and there are things we could do that would be very effective as a leader of reform and pushing for effectiveness.

There should be some p riority around global public goods that we are concerned are being neglected. Climate is one, global health may be another, given the way that the US is increasingly withdraw ing from its hegemonic role in underpinning those things. I would tentatively pick those areas. I would not envy the task in g overnment of thinking about what we then do not do, because inevitably there i s an interest in everything, but we should also try to think about what we do not do. That is where I would start in terms of priorities.

Sir Matthew Rycroft: All the priorities mentioned so far find their place within the sustainable development goals framework, which is unsurprising because everything is connected to everything else. That is a framework for a holistic approach to all international action. The problem is that there are 17 of them, not three, and underneath the 17 there are 169 targets. Fortunately, they are summarised by five, and they all begin with P. Within the five, to answer your question, I would pick out the following three: the first is peace, which was Richard’s first point; the second is planet, which was Richard’s second point; and the third is prosperity, which was Olivia’s first point about the international economic architecture. The fourth and fifth P’s are people and partnerships, which you could argue underpin all of that. I would go with those three Ps as my answer to your question.
The Chair: Are there any areas that need new organisations?

Sir Matthew Rycroft: Technology moving so fast is a good example of how the whole world has to come together. We have to use some form of UN framework to regulate artificial intelligence and other things that will come next. On the whole, our ability to get our multilateral act together is slower than the tech revolution, so, if there were one additional area that this committee could push for focus on, in my view it would be technology, specifically the architecture to bring together competing worldviews on governance of AI and so on, so that there was a way for the whole world to choose between the US, Chinese and other approaches. That is much easier said than done but I hope that, with a bold initiative, our next Prime Minister could build on the success of our current Prime Minister in that area.

Q79 Baroness Prashar: My question is about the machinery of government. As you know, several departments engage with the multilateral organisations, and our previous witnesses have said that the approach of government departments is rather fragmented and there is no strategic direction. You have served in three different departments, Matthew—is that your experience? How can we get co-ordination up to speed to meet the new challenges?

Sir Matthew Rycroft: That is an ongoing challenge, and I very much agree with the thrust of the question. I mentioned earlier that I did not mind where the co-ordination hub was, provided that we had one and it was effective. As a general rule, the role of the Cabinet Office is to co-ordinate, so that is the obvious place. The problem is there are different parts of the Cabinet Office. Even within the secretariat part, normally one bit does national security-type things, another bit does domestic and quite often a third bit does international, economic and/or European issues. All three of those have to come together because everything is connected with everything else. People in this country feel the real impact of international issues through what we would call domestic issues, in our economy in particular, or through other pressures on society in the UK. It is an important job for civil servants to do all that joining up. I see that the Foreign Secretary has an initiative to explain foreign policy in terms of how it impacts British people, which is commendable, and I would encourage more of that. The short answer to your question is: Cabinet Office for co-ordination and the Foreign Office for leading on the international aspects, the diplomacy and the development, but bound in with the whole of the Civil Service, not just the national security-facing parts.
Baroness Prashar: Olivia, you were in the Cabinet Office. Do you have some views on this?

Olivia O'Sullivan: I broadly agree. It has been a positive trend that the Government have built more of a hub for trying to think coherently about national security at the centre in the Cabinet Office. Since the creation of the National Security Council back in 2010, it has been staffed up more, with a bigger national security secretariat in the Cabinet Office. That is helpful because you need a brain in the middle to bring in all these touchpoints, not just from the FCDO but from the trade department, energy security and net zero and the Home Office. As we mentioned earlier, many of these departments deal with and touch on the multilateral system. If there were to be a co-ordinating brain, and that is a good and important thing, then that growing hub in the Cabinet Office is a good place to for it to be.
Baroness Prashar: Richard, do you have anything to say as an observer?
Richard Gowan: No, I defer to those who have been on the inside. I do not have anything to add.

Q80 Lord Lamont of Lerwick: We have heard very little criticism on the whole of multilateral institutions. One can be a believer in multilateral institutions but at the same time believe that they should be subject to examination and criticism. I wonder whether Matthew would tell us what view he takes, for example, of UNESCO. One witness told us it is not worth pulling out for the sake of pulling out, but the United States has twice withdrawn from UNESCO—not just once but twice—and there have been arguments about the cost effectiveness. Which institutions do you think could be subject to some pruning or criticism? Surely this is something that should get our attention, not be swept under the carpet.

Sir Matthew Rycroft: It absolutely should. I very much agree, Lord Lamont, and I think the UK should position ourselves as the permanent member of the Security Council most in favour of reform, not just of the Security Council but of the whole UN family. That is a relatively low bar, because most of the other permanent members are not at all interested in reform. The UK should make a virtue of that and, from a position of broadly supporting the international structure, should absolutely demand radical reform. The parts that are least effective in terms of cost effectiveness include UNESCO, UN Women, UNFPA—some of these things may no longer exist but they did when I was ambassador to the UN, and they generally scored at the bottom of that DfID review that we have already discussed for their ability to deliver the outcomes that matter most for the UK. That should be our lens: we should be insisting on reform. If the institution is unable or unwilling to reform quickly enough then we should leave, not in a fit of pique but because we have finite amounts of resource and we should spend them in areas that we think will do the best collective good, including for our national outcomes.

Lord Lamont of Lerwick: Some of the American critics have referred to some parts of the UN machinery becoming politicised, particularly on human rights. One does not have to agree with all they say, but is there not some point in this and some merit in their criticism of human rights organisations within the UN?

Sir Matthew Rycroft: Every part of the UN is politicised in some way or another. One of the challenges for the current Secretary-General, whose term is about to end, is that 10 years ago, when we selected him, and that was at the time that I was there, there were great hopes that he would be the reforming Secretary-General, but he had to be the Secretary-General for all 193 countries, and a good number of them, including the two most important countries, did not want the same sort of reform that we wanted. As a result, sadly, he has a poor track record of reform in his time there. He has done wonderfully on lots of other things, but he has not reformed the UN family as a whole quickly enough or radically enough to keep up with the demands.
The Chair: As someone who once ran an international organisation, I know that it required 9/11 to get any form of reform into my organisation. We hope that we do not have to do that again.

Q81 Lord Alderdice: Olivia, do you think that the British public see multilateral organisations as connected to the UK’s national interest in their lives? If not, is that a problem? Is there a need to raise greater public awareness of multilateral organisations?

Olivia O'Sullivan: That is a good question. I would not want to get out beyond my expertise in terms of polling data or focus groups on what the public think. My instinctive answer to that question is that it is probably not at the forefront of people’s minds. Any work that we do on foreign affairs in general suggests that, in and of itself, people do not tend to prioritise it, but when things go wrong they do.

There are a lot of reform priorities that we have named in this discussion today. To the previous question, there are plenty of criticisms to be made about duplication, inefficiency and poor performance in the multilateral system. The top focus of the UK Government should probably be to improve that and to improve our strategic focus to make sure that multilateral institutions are enabling us to achieve our diplomatic goals. In a way, the proof of the pudding should be in the eating in terms of the public’s engagement. To me, getting the public interested or excited about the UN particularly is perhaps less material than being really clear about the things that we want to achieve in the world, and that these institutions are a channel for that. That is my personal view of that kind of thing.
Q82 Lord Darroch of Kew: I hope that Matthew will be allowed to answer the previous question too, as it is quite relevant to his time in New York.

Next year, 2027, sees the appointment of a new UN Secretary-General and, as it happens, the UK’s chairmanship of the G20, so this is a two-part question. First, how much influence can we exert over the choice of UN Secretary-General, and how exactly do we exert that influence? Secondly, on the G20, what is your assessment of the value of that grouping? In a broad sense, if you were advising the British Government, how would you say they should use the presidency of the G20 next year?
Richard Gowan: I say to Lord Alderdice that, as someone who was young once, I am glad that I spent none of my youth thinking about the UN, and I would not want to inflict it on today’s young people.

As we understand it, the race for the Secretary-General remains very open. The US does not have a preferred candidate, nor does China. The UK should engage quite actively in vetting the current candidates and, if necessary, looking for alternatives. The UK can then get very close to whoever is chosen and essentially hold that person’s hand, offering political advice and ideas on reform through their first 100 days in office and beyond. The next Secretary-General will need precisely the expertise and the ideas on reform that have been somewhat lacking, frankly, inside the UN system of late. The UK, if it can get close to the successful candidate, can probably whisper good ideas in their ear. There is a real demand for change in the system, and accessing the next Secretary-General is a good opportunity to drive that change.

The G20 is not what it was back in the late years of the first decade of this century, but it matters a lot to many of the middle powers that Olivia has referred to, as a space where they can have a voice on international trade, climate, and other issues. From talking to colleagues from Brazil, South Africa and elsewhere, I know that they really hope the UK will organise a G20 that listens to their priorities—after this year’s US presidency, which is clearly not going to be particularly sympathetic to the concerns of the middle powers. There are already quite good contacts beneath the surface between the UK and some of those middle powers about what the G20 should be about in the UK. Looking at questions of sustainability, fairer financing and addressing the concerns of the global majority is a good opportunity for the UK to show both leadership and respect for other countries in the multilateral system.
Lord Darroch of Kew: Chairman, is there a minute for Matthew, just because he was part of the UN that chose Guterres last time round?

Sir Matthew Rycroft: Selection of the UN Secretary-General is my “Mastermind” specialist subject, but I will do a very short version. It happened in 2016 and will be happening again this year in order for the new person to start in January next year, 2027. The UK is well placed as a permanent member of the Security Council to ensure that the Security Council recommends to the General Assembly the best possible candidate to reform the UN, and to influence the process that increases the chances of us finding that person.

I would be strongly against any regional rotation. Lots of countries think it is the turn of one particular continent or another, but that narrows down the pool of brilliant candidates. I would actively encourage female candidates, as we did 10 years ago, because otherwise you are discouraging half the world’s population from putting themselves forward—there has never been a female UN Secretary-General before. I would ensure as much transparency as possible so that the candidates were really tested, not just on their manifesto but on how they would deal with the real challenges ahead. We did a bit of each of those things 10 years ago, and I hope the UK can lead the way in doing even more of them this year.

The Chair: Sounds good. In fact, the committee has been invited tomorrow to meet one of the candidates—the ambassador of Guyana, Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett—who is in London. The committee has been asked to meet her at very short notice.

I say to Richard that I am the same age as the United Nations: it was born in 1946 and so was I, and so was Donald J Trump. You will have to draw your own conclusions from that. Anyway, we are deeply grateful to all three of you, because you have imparted a lot of new and good information to us in our search for what to recommend to the British Government that they should do about multilateral institutions. Thank you so much for attending.
[1] Post-meeting note: witness clarified that the metals-related body the US withdrew from was the International Lead and Zinc Study Group.

sessions.iT: Trade in a turbulent world: how should the UK deploy its trade instruments?
sessions.w: Pascal Lamy (World Trade Organization)

segs.tx: International Agreements Committee
C orrected oral evidence: T rade in a turbulent world: how should the UK deploy its trade instruments ?
Thursday 9 July 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Lord Johnson of Lainston (The Chair) ; Lord Anderson of Swansea; Baroness Anelay of St Johns; Baroness Blower; Lord Boateng; Lord German; Lord Hannay of Chiswick; Baroness Lawlor; Lord McDonald of Salford.
Evidence Session No. 6 Heard in Public Questions 52 – 60
Witness
Pascal Lamy, former director-general , World Trade Organization.
Examination of witness
Pascal Lamy.

Q52 Good afternoon, everyone. I am extremely pleased to welcome Mr Pascal Lamy to this committee. As you know, the International Agreements Committee monitors all of the treaties and agreements into which the UK enters. We are currently doing a specific inquiry on what we call “ t rade in a turbulent world ” . Many perceptions of free trade , the acceptance of multilateralism and so on have clearly been eroded over time — specifically , in the p ast two years or so —and direct changes from nations across the world that assumed that multilateralism was set in stone , including our own, are now looking to distort that.

Our questions are around the future of multilateralism and how the UK should react; and , second ly , how the UK can use different trade mechanisms, such as M o Us, bilateral agreements or less formal agreements to ensure that we can trade globally . We want to look at the ramifications in relation to our ability to scrutinise proper agreements and whether they are the sorts of thing we should be doing to promote trade and economic growth.

Having followed your extraordinary career since I got involved in and became interested in politics aged 16— that is quite a few years ago now—I look on you as the father of the modern trading system. I ask you to be quite expansive in your opening thoughts , in terms of what has gone wrong in the p ast few years. When you retired from the WTO, you may have thought that you had created a wonderful system that would last for eternity, but the friction seems to have started almost the day after you relinquished that position.

My supplementary, more philosophical , question is : why do you think that nations fundamentally do not like free trade? I say that in the sense that everyone says they like free trade, in the same way as they say that they like going to the gym, but , when it comes down to the realities of having open economies and so on, they find it a lot harder — particularly when stresses are placed on them , as they are today , with wars and other significant issues . T hey relinquish their adherence to the principles of free trade and multilateralism. Did you see that as far back as when you started in the European Commission, and do you see that going forward? Again, we welcome you hugely and look forward to your responses today.

Good afternoon , everybody. Thanks for inviting me to this discussion and for the small list of big questions that you sent me. If it is okay with you, I will take them not exactly in the order you suggested ; I will look at the UK side of things at the end , after we have looked at the global frame, and maybe regroup one or two questions.

I will start with the big picture . Y ou are absolutely right: the world trade scene now looks very different from what it was 10 or 20 years ago, when I exercised various institutional responsibilities in that field. What has changed? Overall, what has changed is the balance between geoeconomics and geopolitics. Since the 1980s, we have been living through a period of rapid globalisation where , for some time, geoeconomic developments, views, beliefs and achievements have superseded the normal bias of geopolitics and turned into tensions, rivalries and conflicts. Some thought that this was the end of history and that the benefits of geoeconomic integration would for ever balance the evil side s of states as cold monsters.

What factors have changed this balance? The main underlying factor is the growing geopolitical and geostrategic rivalry between the US and China , which has permeated their view s of what opening up trade brings in terms of benefits and challenges. We have also had episodes such as Covid, which revealed the fragility of a number of supply chains, which were the way in which globalisation expanded in connecting production systems through not just end products but components. In terms of the balance between “ just in time ” and “ just in case ” , “ just in time ” used to be the priority but , in a number of cases , it is now “just in case” .

There are also a number of social impacts of rapid globalisation, at least in the western world, which have impacted the ideological sense that opening up trade was the way to go . Not everybody was 100% convinced of that at the time , but there was a large consensus— notably, it is now dented ; in my view, that is unsurprising—in a place where the social system that buffers the Schumpeterian impact of the Ricardian division of labour, as in the US, is pretty weak.

Of course, w e also have other developments that play in different directions. The main one remains technology, which has always reduced the cost of distance in human history. We have now reach ed a stage where the cost of distance is at zero with digitalisation, which plays in a way that formidably favours the international exchange of data, services and value addition. There are probably a few million Indian doctors who are now ready to enter the global market of telemedical diagnosis, but there is a much more fragmented regulatory landscape on things such as data ownership, localisation and protection — not to mention the different views o n where AI is going.

This has been accompanied by two dynamics that were already there at the beginning, 10 or 15 years ago. The first is the US distancing itself from the WTO and its disciplines. We all know the saga , with the US progressively putting in doubt then paralysing the dispute settlement system, which is a main instrument of the WTO. Th at system has been replaced by another one for those who want to work with that — not the US . O f course, there is also the extraordinary rapid development of the Chinese economy , which is now huge— I will come back to that — in today’s world trading system.
Mr Lamy, we are trying to turn your volume up so that my colleagues and I can hear you clearly. Perhaps you could move closer to your microphone.
My sound is now at the maximum, I think.
Thank you; that is much better.

Q53 Mr Lamy, thank you for your evidence. The last time we met was in South Africa 20 years or so ago. In many ways, your periods in office, both in the EU and in the WTO, represented the high watermark of globalisation and the belief in it . We know from the experience of South Africa that globalisation has not risen everyone’s boat. In South Africa, the accession of China to the WTO meant, in effect, the destruction of what was a very successful clothing apparel industry. We have seen globalisation have an impact on communities elsewhere in both the developed and the developing world. As a result, people have suffered. There has been an upsurge in popularism, which is totally opposed to free trade. How do you answer the question of globalisation and the impact of free trade on disadvantaged communities? How , in any event , do we begin to rebuild confidence in the role of multilateral organisations in relation to trade?

Thanks very much for the question. That was exactly the point I was making: the attitude vis-à-vis open trade and globalisation has been dented by the social impact of globalisation in some quarters — mostly in the United States of America, which plays a big role here .
It has also affected the north-east of England , as well as South Africa and many other countries all over the world.

I totally agree. I am among those who believe that the Brexit vote was influenced by these developments. In a way, the UK is a bit of an exception because it has a reasonably comfortable , European-like welfare system as compared to other continents. However, w e should not treat our western European/UK perception that the world has changed as the dominant view. First, we have to look at the numbers. The reality is that the volumes of international trade are still comfortably growing; this includes in 2025, which was not the best year for the geopolitics of trade, as we all know, because of the US. Secondly, overall, if you attend the General Council of the WTO, where countries are represented by their ambassadors, or a conference , where countries are represented by their Ministers, you see that an overwhelming majority of developing countries still want globalisation to go forward.

I bring this caveat or nuance to the notion that things are transforming : t hey are, but not to the point of questioning globally the benefits of open trade or the general political attitude, even if there some costs or vulnerabilities have appeared . We have a series of problems —I can give you a short snapshot of how I see them — but , overall, we should understand that our little western perception may not be the way in which others in the vast majority o f this planet see things.

Wh at are the problems? I will explain them in a reasonably simple, but inevitably provocative , way. Looking ahead, there are four problems . We have a small problem, which is the US. We have two middle-sized problems: first, the way in which the WTO is organised and works; and, second ly , th e touchy interface between opening up trade and environment al protection. The big problem, on which I am very much focus ed now , is China.

In my view, t he US is not a big problem; it is a US problem. If the US surrounds itself with a 10% tariff fence for the years to come, it will have to pay the price, and we will all compensate the small part of market share we lose in the US by opening more with others, which is what we are all doing. I do not see Trump as the guy who will start the revolution in globalisation and turn it the other way around, whatever he proclaims.

The middle-sized problem is long-lasting ; I underlined this when I was the European Trade Commissioner and the DG of the WTO . T he organisation of the WTO itself —that is, the balance between the secretariat and the members — is wrong. It does not work efficiently. There is not enough trust between the formidable technical capacities of the secretariat and the member states. As a result, agreeing on something that is inevitably of a fairly technical nature takes too much time , using procedures that are way too protracted.

The other middle-sized problem is the trade and environment nexus. The Institut Jacques Delors in Brussels, which is one of three that I co-ordinate in Paris, Berlin and Brussels, has worked a lot on this, including in tabling the first CBAM template. The problem progressively permeates both sides and , at the moment , there is no proper solution. This is a key issue because we need a clearer strategic stance overall on where opening up trade benefits the environment, notably through proper specialisation . Conversely, the increase of transport, with the fact that steel is transported and exchanged more than other commodities, is an issue. On that, I will stop there for the moment.

Finally, in my view, China will be the big problem for some time to come . That is for two reasons . The first is its importance in international trade, notably in manufacturing. China produces 35% of world manufacturing and exports roughly more than half of that, which is a huge proportion as compared to the past. A s everybody knows, I am a big believer in the benefits of open trade, provided that the distribution of the benefits is done properly . This not a global or WTO issue; it is much more of a national one. I am a big believer in the benefits of opening up trade because I believe that, if I do some things better than you do and you do some things better than I do, we have a rational, Ricardian, Schumpeterian base interest in trad ing . I have always believed that and still do , b ut, if China gets a comparative advantage everywhere along the manufacturing , supply and value chain, we will have a big problem. With the notion that comparative advantage is what we have to foster in order to create efficiencies, if China has comparative advantages stemming from its political regime, its capacity to subsidise, the size of its market and the formidable investment it has made in education and innovation — stemming from where it was 30 years ago , producing T-shirts and shoes , to being at the frontier of artificial intelligence now— we will have a problem.

This problem shakes the WTO system, which is based on the notion that opening up trade is good because comparative advantages can play. The moment comparative advantages start not to play any more, the ideological basement of WTO is shaken. I speak as a European; pardon me for that. In my view, the UK is and remains part of the European system; the details of this participation, whatever they are, are important for political reasons, but , globally speaking, the UK remains a European country in many ways . We in Europe a re competitive vis-à-vis all countries on this planet, including the US, but we are not competitive with China any more. T his is the problem we have to cope with.
That summary was extremely helpful and well put. We have a few more questions ; we have around half an hour left.

Q54 Mr Lamy, do you agree that, since you stepped down as director-general 10 years ago , the world trading environment has become more complex , with more subsidies , China , more protectionism and less consensus? These are the problems facing your successor. Is the WTO more inclined to help countries find a way around problems rather than confront ing them ? Is this forced pragmatism good for world trade? I think in particular of the recent tariff changes made by the USA . A re you among those who are inclined to think that they are incompatible with the WTO system?

I totally agree; we have already mentioned that the world is different now . The WTO is about opening up trade and reducing obstacles to trade in a rules-based way that provides economic agency , notably to those countries that want to expand their operations by penetrating national markets other than theirs with a stable, predictable and litigable system. This is still valid. We have to consider whether the disciplines enshrined in the WTO rulebook , including the fundamental principle of non-discrimination , are still fit for purpose in a world where China has become what it has become . Th at is the real question for us all.

When we believe that China does not play by the rules, we can use the disciplines of the WTO to impose anti-dumping or countervailing duties. We can use a series of instruments that target either the sector or China. I am not saying that we should do this tomorrow, but we probably need to start think ing about something much more powerful : a China-specific safeguard clause. In WTO terms, th at is a sort of atomic bomb. A priori, it is not compatible with the WTO rules because safeguards, which are allowed by the WTO disciplines, work only when they are erga omnes. I f you want to limit the flood of imports into your own country, y ou cannot target one country; you target imports from everywhere. This is where there is an issue around WTO compatibility .

Again, the notion of WTO compatibility deserves a bit of thinking at a time when the fundamentals of why we have these disciplines are based on comparative advantage. There are also different ways to keep trade open, whether bilateral or regional agreements. There are softer instruments than properly negotiated , treaty-enshrined free trade agreements, but we have to look in two directions: at diversifying how our economies can benefit from open trade when our national operators exploit a comparative advantage abroad; and at looking again at the rulebook on the conditions that would be fit for purpose given what China has become.

We all know that a large part of the Chinese extra presence i n export markets has to do with a macroeconomic imbalance in China, in that what it invest s and produce s is much bigger than its domestic consumption. Chinese leadership has been saying for 15 years, “ We want to pump in more domestic consumption ”, “ We believe in dual circulation” , and so on. Th at has not worked. If you look at the latest projections for Chinese macroeconomic strategy in the next 10 years, it is still about investing and producing more, as well as moving more to wards the frontier of technology. This is a political strategy that needs to be questioned , but I do not think that the Chinese leadership is ready to do that by itself; we and others have to try to create the necessary pressure on this front.

Q55 Pascal, what a pleasure it is to be talking to you again, many years after we started discussing these problems in quite different contexts, and to have your wisdom available to us in this study that we are undertaking. Perhaps we could move a little away from China, about which you have spoken extremely interestingly and at some length, and on to the other big problem that you identified : United States trade policy. How fundamental are the challenges faced by the World Trade Organization from the Trump Administration? Are they, to use a rather overworked phrase, existential? Or are they something that, when President Trump is no longer in the White House, we could find better ways of managing than we are just now ? How resilient is the overall system of rules-based trade to the challenge of President Trump, who appears not to have studied the “ most favoured nation ” provisions when he was at business school? Is it possible to preserve the structures that were established in the GATT then carried forward into the WTO?

Thanks, David, for th at question ; it is good to see you in good shape. I will answer your question very bluntly and frankly: Mr Trump is not a serious problem for world trade. I take the view that , for many reasons , he is a serious problem for his country , and, o n geostrategic issues, when he keeps saying that Greenland should become American, he is a problem for us.

Although he believes in tariffs and believes that administering trade from the White House desk is the way to go, this is totally hyperinflated. The US represents 13% of world imports. If the remaining 87% keep their head s cool, which is what they are doing so far, we will not see a destabilisation of the system. It means de facto that the US has left the WTO — not de jure but in reality. It will not leave the WTO de jure for the simple reason : the WTO administers the trade - related intellectual property agreement, which protects intellectual property in international trade. If the US were to lose this guarantee, you can imagine the impact it would have on its economy.

That is where we are. For disputes with the US, the WTO has disposed of the dispute settlement system, although, as I have already said, another system that works reasonably well has been promoted by the European Union and a few others. So t he Trump trade issue is not existential. Will another Administration not led by Mr Trump go back to where we were 20 years ago? No. We have already seen , during the Obama and Biden Administrations , a distancing of the US from the WTO, the basic reason being that its number one problem is China. It believe s that, today, the WTO system does not properly address the problems that the US has with China.

I would rather be on its side here because I also believe that, today—th is was not my view 10 or 20 years ago—as things stand , the WTO does not properly address the Chinese problem . I will not enter into the technical details but this is not least because the WTO ’s discipline on subsidies is extremely weak — much weaker than when you look at the procedure requirements for questioning whether a Chinese subsidy is impacting your own competitive position. The US is not the problem; the way in which the WTO’s disciplines ar e structured is becoming a problem. To answer your question, David, the way forward is to make a number of the WTO ’s disciplines more flexible.

Q56 Thank you, Pascal, for this session. It has been fascinating so far and will continue to be so . In listing the four problems, you mentioned the US, how the WTO is organised, the trade and environment nexus, and China. We have heard about two of those problems . What about the way in which the WTO is organised? I grew up in politics thinking that, as a body, the World Trade Organization would ensure that countries negotiate with each other and shore up how the rules-based system happens and continues , but t he rules-based system is being chipped away. Members of the WTO ha ve undertaken the option to revive the negotiation function by introducing smaller plurilateral agreements among like-minded groups, as we heard in a recent ministerial meeting. What is your view of that process? Does it have a future?

Yes; it is part of what I call flexibilisation. The problem with the WTO is twofold. First, it does not work efficiently , as compared to other international organisations. The source of that is the mistrust between the members and the secretariat , which remains after decades. The secretariat and the DG of the WTO are not powerful enough in the system, given how decisions are taken.

Let me give an example. If the DG or the secretariat of WTO believes that there is a problem that should be fixed by negotiating an amendment to agreement A, B or C, this is just not possible. There is no authority for the DG or the secretariat to say, “Ladies and gentlemen, you have a problem. We believe that this problem can be described as such. Here are a few options to fix this problem. Now it is up to you to decide”. This simple way of working is not available . That is the first part of this.

Second ly, there is the rule of consensus, which is very much like unanimity , in a way . There are normally differences between consensus and unanimity, which is why the plurilateral way is to be open. It exists by the authority of the members, which, collectively by consensus, for some time , have allow ed a plurilateral trade regime among themselves that is more open or more regulated than with others. At the moment, this has resulted in very few plurilateral agreements , although t here is a well-known one on public procurement. We see that in the judicial system, and we saw it at the last WTO military conference. When countries get sick of waiting for others to agree to go plurilateral , they just do it. In my view, t his is a way to transform part of the reality. If members do that, on top of what can originally be done bilaterally, I will support it .

Q57 Mr Lamy, I am very interested in your last answer. It brings me nicely on to my question : apart from the unilateral direction, what does the WTO need to do to promote services trade in today’s world of financial services, digital , telecommunications, professional services and mobility? What steps would you propose, and how realistically do you think could you achieve them? That is the first part of my question ; I will give you my supplementary , too . Are there lessons to be learned from any of the other trade deals we have seen, such as the CPTPP, on financial services or professional services — or , indeed , the US-Mexico-Canada deal?

That is an excellent question. Obstacles to trade in goods are tariffs and subsidies; obstacles to trade in services are regulations. If you compare goods to services, goods are more regulated globally than services . The problem in opening trade in services is reduc ing obstacles to trade, as always.

In this case, the obstacle to trade is a regulatory discrepancy. For instance, the real issue for the financial services trade in the EU, the UK and the US is the potential regulation of capital markets. If you look at the problem of hormone beef, the issue is the discrepancy in what is deemed healthy in the US and what is deemed healthy on our side. If it is about pesticide residues in flowers, the issue is the same . We have to move to either more regulatory convergence in services or mutual recognition, which is like regulatory convergence with an added layer of trust : “I believe that you have good reasons to do it this way. Please believe that I have good reasons to do it that way . D oing it your way or my way will not prevent us exchanging services” . That is what we did in the European Union with the internal market.

The question— it is a tricky one— is: what is the right body to lead to regulatory convergence in many areas? This is complex. P ersonally , I believe that more should be given to the International Organization for Standardization . It is not a well-known , first-rank international body but , in reality , it plays an enormous role in the streamlining of regulation, certification and labelling. The real question is : should we promote regulatory convergence or mutual recognition? Yes. Can we do that efficiently with the system we have today? We are not there yet; we have an infra-capacity.

For instance, I have been working for some time with the Institut Jacques Delors to see where we are on artificial intelligence today , in terms of convergence that would allow the exchange of AI - processed systems in future. We are far from having the necessary convergence capacity . There is a discrepancy between our level of globalisation and our capacity to keep moving forward because of administrative and regulatory reasons. You have the CPTPP, of course . You have the whole WTO system, and then you have regional and bilateral systems. As you go to more specifical ly open trade, in my view, the CT P PP is the best standard available today to cope with what you have in mind , as compared to other systems — leaving aside the internal market of the EU, of course, which is something very specific.
We now come to our last question.
Q58 Thank you very much, Mr Lamy. You have given us a very broad perspective on all your thinking. Y ou have talked about the fact that things will move, change and evolve—
I am sorry, madame, but I cannot hear your sound.
Perhaps I should speak closer to the microphone. Is that any better?
Yes .
Great. Can the current trade rules evolve to adapt to or accommodate measures such as carbon border adjustments or industrial subsidies without undermining core principles such as non-discrimination?

That is the key question on the nexus between trade expansion and environment al protection , which I mentioned at the beginning. My answer is yes. Carbon border adjustment s —I was one of the intellectual fathers of the European one when we started working on it in 2019-20— are one way to reconcile trade expansion with the problem of differentiated carbon pricing in different countries. In theory, global market capitalism has a simple solution to this tension: a common price for carbon. We all know that, unfortunately , this is pie in the sky. If we all agreed to price the externalities of our production system properly , we would not have a problem. We are not there , though, so how can this relationship be better addressed than where we are now?

This is a forum problem. The WTO has its Committee on Trade and Environment , but many developing countries believe that that is not the place to discuss these matters. If you look at the Paris Agreement, the UNFCCC system has some trade-related components, but developed countries believe that COPs are not the place to discuss trade . Hence the initiative that Brazil took at Belém last year, of which I was a part, to create a side forum that is not the WTO or the COP but an informal round table to find something of a proper balance between what is and is not allowed in the name of protecting the environment through trade restrictions , it being understood that , in many cases, open trade is good for the environment.

If Saudi Arabia stops buying its wheat on the international market, it is good news for the environment and water. It is not a one-sided equation but , for the moment, we have a forum dispute between north and south. As we know, for understandable reasons, north-south relations permeate environment governance — at least, the bits and pieces of environment guidance that we have — enormously . This is where we have to move forward. It is , again , an area where the UK and the continent share the same principles and ideological vision. There is no difference between the UK and the continent on things like this.

T his may be my final point, if that is your last question . T he way forward is the Mark Carney-like equation : the plurilaterals or the variable geometry in how trade regulation and trade disciplines are created and administered. Unfortunately, as the C hair said at the beginning, we are in a world that is inevitably more brutal, more turbulent and more fragmented . W e have to find ways to navigate this via variable geometry and more flexible rules. Th at is necessary. I still believe that , overall, at the end of the day, given the benefits of trade opening up and many countries being able to exploit comparative advantages domestically, that is the way to go.

Q59 I have a supplementary question o n the dreaded Brexit, which we rarely speak of around this table . Y ou were the European Trade Commissioner . S omething went wrong in terms of the UK’s perception of the value that we got from trade with Europe. This is slightly personal but what do you think went wrong? How important is a realignment or a new framework operating with the EU , in terms of our own trade benefit s ? We can do dozens of bilateral treaties with New Zealand — a country I love — but the reality is that the biggest trading partner in the world is on our doorstep. My first question goes back to the philosophy of what went wrong , in terms of how you were doing your job in the sense of the belief in the benefits. Secondly , what would your advice be for this committee when looking at a relationship with European trade? I am not suggesting that it was your fault, but you know what I am asking , in that sense.

I suggest that what went wrong wa s the UK’s political chemistry. I have worked in European institut ion s for many years, and this has been a bit of a problem for reasons that are too many to list. My sense is that the UK political system derailed at some point and that that made the difference on this unfortunate, in my view, day. Is it the end of the world? No. Again, I fundamentally believe that the United Kingdom remains a European country with European values, European systems and a European vision of the world, framed by geography, history and culture.

The question now is : how can we live in this situation without damaging the UK economy too much? The cost of Brexit for the continent has been zero , economically speaking . The cost of Brexit for the continent has been losing the clout of a major European country in the way the world is shaped, including in foreign policy or geostrate gy . The first issue can be addressed , as can the second. The first issue can be addressed if the UK , nolens volens , remains aligned on the EU standards.

The big problem for the UK in leaving the European Union was not leaving the Union or the customs union but leaving the internal market. We all have to remember that we only got rid of the borders in 1992 when we had enough of a convergence in how we administer our markets to suppress borders. Inevitably, leaving the internal market was re-establishing a border, and the cost of the border is all the higher as there is the reality , or a suspicion , of misalignment in the rules you administer for goods and services.

On this, the solution—I am not saying that it is an easy equation for a British politician— is staying aligned while not having one’s say on the standard, which is not a comfortable political position. On the other side, experience has shown that , when it is about really serious things, such as Russia invading Ukraine, the fact that the UK has left the European Union has not prevented what really matters : working together in the same direction with the same willingness , in this case to defend our Ukrainian friends from Russian aggression. This is where I would put the answer to your very complex question in an inevitably sketchy way. Trade-wise, there are many simple ways for the UK to remain aligned with the European Union so that the inevitabl y negative consequences of Brexit are limited.
Baroness L awlor definitely want s to ask a supplementary question. We have two minutes left.
Q60 Mr Lamy, that would involve accepting EU law, which was one of the big problems for the UK. Do we take laws made elsewhere , o r do we make our own laws in our own interests?
Please answer in one minute, Mr Lamy.

You are absolutely correct, which is why I say that the only rational, pragmatic solution — remain ing aligned — is an uncomfortable political position. You have to choose between either paying the price, which is pretty high, or suffering this uncomfortable position. To be sketchy, there is a good way to do that. You can still proclaim to those in the EU who do not want things to be decided by Brussels that fox hunting is administered by UK law but not pesticide residues in flowers, the hormone content of beef or the way in which the European trading system for emission permits works , because this is where it will cost you a lot.
Does that include mutual recognition?
Absolutely, if there is enough trust on both sides: “Y ou do it your way and I’ll d o it my way ” . This is complex , but it includes mutual recognition in cases where there is a level of trust.

We have come to the end of this fabulous session. I am so glad that many people on this committee have had a chance to work with you in the past. This is my first interaction with you . I am extremely grateful to you for your wide-ranging discourse on the situation that we in the UK face in terms of world trade , the US , China and so on. I extend an invitation as the Chair : if you are ever able to come and meet us in person in the House of Lords, we would be privileged to have you with us. In the meantime, on behalf of all my colleagues, I thank you very much for your time and for what has been an excellent session.
Thank you, Chair. M any thanks for your questions and attendance. I am ready for more, for reasons you obviously know about .
Thank you ; we are much obliged . Have a great rest of your day .

sessions.iT: Convention on the Manipulation of Sports Competitions
sessions.w: Moses Swaibu (GameChanger360); Madalina Diaconu (University of Neuchâtel)

segs.tx: International Agreements Committee
C orrected oral evidence: Convention on the M anipulation of S ports C ompetitions
Thursday 9 July 2026
11 am
Watch the meeting

Members present: Lord Johnson of Lainston (The Chair) ; Lord Anderson of Swansea; Baroness Anelay of St Johns; Baroness Blower; Lord Boateng; Lord German; Lord Hannay of Chiswick; Baroness Lawlor; Lord McDonald of Salford.
Evidence Session No. 1 Heard in Public Questions 1 – 9
Witnesses
Moses Swaibu, former footballer, f ounder and CEO, GameChanger 360; Dr Madalina Diaconu, Associate Professor, University of Neuchâtel.
Examination of witnesses
Moses Swaibu and Dr Madalina Diaconu.

Q1 Good morning, everyone . T hank you very much for joining this inquiry into the Council of Europe ’s Convention on the Manipulation of Sports Competitions, which is better known as the Macolin convention; it is p articularly relevant in the light of all the major sporting fixtures that are going on at the moment around the world.

I am pleased to welcome on behalf of the committee our two witnesses today . Moses Swaibu is a famous former footballer and now the founder and CEO of GameChanger 360 . He brings to this meeting an extremely high degree of understanding of the problems around match-fixing , which he encountered , and of how we can solve them. T hank you very much for being with us in person ; i t is extremely good to have you with us.

Join ing us online is Madalina Diaconu, an a ssociate p rofessor at the University of Neuchâtel, who has made it her business over the p ast few decades to build a high level of expertise . She has contributed significantly to the drafting of this treaty and has a very good understanding of the legal ramifications of such treaties. I thank both of you very much for joining us.

My first question is for M oses . Can you talk briefly about your experience of match-fixing, which you have been open about, have written books about and talked about, and the broader systems behind it, both as a footballer and since ? I know that this point will be developed more in our discussion but how do you see the relevance of this treaty? Y ou have been a great advocate , since the situation some years ago, of removing or reducing corruption in sport. Is this treaty a useful way of going about that? Again, thank you for joining us ; we look forward to hearing your views.

T hank you all for having me. Before I start, my journey into professional sports started when I was 16. I was a young boy playing for my school at the time. I went for a trial with Crystal Palace at 16 years old; th at is relevant to the conversation we are having today. I have had no education with regard to frameworks or how to deal with certain issues.

Going from attending a state school in Croydon to going into an elite environment was quite a shift and a change in terms of geographical location —that is, where I come from and t he community . M ore importantly , I was going into an environment of mentors, structures, big brothers and discipline. Although I had that framework, I was well endowed to adapt to scenarios. I was travelling from London Bridge to East Croydon every day in a generation where there was no social media. Stylistically, i t was very much an old - school way of navigat ing through London at that time. It was not until I left Crystal Palace and moved to Lincoln City at 19 that I had my first real interaction with life and society outside London. I was 19 years old in professional sport, experiencing different elements of culture and different teammates.

One thing that was quite common was not really know ing or understand ing what people we re going through. A teammate introduced me to the world of match-fixing for the first time at Lincoln City . I t was a word I had never even heard of. At the time, I knew that it was morally wrong ; I was 19 but , more importantly, I just wanted to play football. Years later, I found out that he had a gambling addiction and everything else, but , at the same time , I did not have the power or confidence to go to Chris Sutton, my first team manager, and say, “ Hey, the teammate who introduced me to match-fixing is the captain ”.

So, in the first instance, I turned around and said , “N o ”, but there were no reporting tools in place for me to approach anyone confidently in the club and say, “ Hey, I think we have a problem ”. B ear in mind that there was € 60,000 in a changing room in Northampton. Years later, I was let go by Lincoln City . I dropped down into lower-level football, and th e structure that I once had at Crystal Palace was gone ; it was non-existent.

In m y second interaction with match-fixing, a gain, a teammate approached me and said, “ Look, we have a game coming up . M ore importantly, do you want to meet these match - fixers? ” G o ing back , in 2011 , you will have seen that there was a scandal around players who were caught up in a match-fixing ring moving to Australia. Two years later, I got caught up in the same ring . So, the second time, w e went ahead and fixed the game.

That was my first real introduction to highly organised crime. As I navigated this journey , at each and every layer, this criminal syndicate took me in like a child, if that makes sense . It built the same mechanisms that are used in sport : teamwork and togetherness. That is how a lot of the manipulation is carried out in the wider world and why it is relevant today . It is about the nuances of manipulation and its mental and psychological effect . It was not violent or dangerous, but I believe that systemic change and frameworks are needed. A top-down , bottom-up approach is needed; that goes to your question on the Macolin convention .

If you look at it from an international point of view , with all the countries potentially ratifying this convention, there is not enough system at ic influence from where we are today in the digital world —a world where young people are the future of this nation and these countries. More importantly , fundamentally , this should be taught in the school system as early as physical education in primary school . W e can look at manipulation and ask, “W hat does it mean to be integral and have integrity? ” That is very important, but that framework is not robustly designed. You can see from what is happening in the Premier League and , currently , the World Cup that the word is, in my humble opinion, a tick - box exercise. However, in the UK, we have the opportunity to establish something across the board that includes stakeholders and policyholders as well.

To answer your question on where society sits today , are we moving with the times or are we still thinking as we were 20 years ago? What I see —Dr Diaconu will attest to this — is that we need to include different stakeholders, different mindsets and different people , and act as sport does. Sport is free for everyone, especially football. It is a community- based game where the language should be colloquialised. It has culture and influence. We need to look at prisons and other systems and ensure that, where there is football or sport, people are involved . W e need to consider the weapons that we now have in this digital space. For example, there are cryptocurrenc ies, technologies and different areas where criminal influence r s live in our society. I believe that we are in a position of strength and that, to move forward, we need to take a practical look at what this all means.

On the Macolin convention , we need to ask questions around the cultural influence from these countries , because that kid living in Portugal in a f avela and that kid living in south-east London are playing the same game , but it is a completely different mindset demographic. If we look at case studies and research, how much data and information are we getting to understand human behaviour, including reporting and risk? Within that risk ecosystem, we can build a framework. For example, if you have a young Moses Swaibu at 18, look at his background, his family, and his siblings : w hat were the influences around him that shaped this opportunity for crime and corruption?

A s a supplement, I should declare my interest , which is relevant to the debate. I am on the board of a data business , and the systems it is building are now being used by polymarkets and prediction markets. I do not think that there is a conflict of interest there.

T he point is that the idea of broadly fixing a match at 1-0 is history. Now , we are looking at very specific in tra- match points where people can bet on whether someone will get a red card half way throu gh, whether they kick the ball from the halfway line or whatever. As you say, it is interesting that the focus should be as much on the big multinational criminal syndicates as on the players themselves , such as the vulnerability of a 17 year-old player being offered huge amounts of money in a junior football league.
