Do you think that something such as the Macolin convention or what the UK is doing is enough to support the players in a cultural sense? Do you feel that, in English and British football , there is an understanding now, as compared to what there was when you were first approached 20 years ago?

I am going to be really open with everybody in this room . H onestly , I believe that it has got ten worse. If we look at the likes of Polymarket , a lot of these commercial companies are for - profit companies . When you look at companies such as EPIC Global Solutions , as well as mental health a wareness and the NHS, you have to strip everything back. How does one view crime? W hat are the laws behind this crime? I n 2013 , I knew that, if we were caught , we w ould be penalised . However, I did not know about the criminal element and the likelihood of getting a conviction if we were tried for bribery .

Before we get to the likes of Polymarket and data , you have to understand the negative effects and the psychology of what actually happens in sport. Say a player ha s broken his leg . Say t his player was once a top-tier star but he is now in prison . Say another athlete now has an opportunity to play for Crystal Palace ’s women’s team . It can be about whether a sport is underfunded.

You also have singular sports . I t is not just football : look at tennis, too . If you look at this through the eyes of the criminals, you now have one of the biggest open markets across Asia pinpointing Polymarket where you can bet on literally anything. The fact is that they exist. They are enabling young children to gamble and bet through ads and technology ; more importantly, they are being faced with algorithms where they cannot pay for their college and education. Once we look at amateur sports, we realise that 99% of these athletes drop out into this ecosystem. Not everybody comes from a family or background that can enhance them .

Although the Macolin convention may see oversight at the top, I believe that we also need to build from the bottom and meet in the middle. I believe that , under the framework, you will have more people coming forward to report, much more awareness and more regulated commercial companies. These companies must ensure that they are doing the right thing on compliance and risk . It is about making sure that mitigation is fully understood by everyone in the UK if there is , say, a breach of integrity or an issue with betting and gambling. It does not affect just football ; i t affects the entire country and its reputation, and it goes far beyond access.
Thank you very much. Lord Boateng, you may want to direct your question to Madalina in order to give her an opportunity to introduce herself.

Q2 Thank you, Mr Swaibu, for your important evidence. Professor Diaconu, Mr Swaibu has indicated that, in his view, the situation is getting worse. Do you share that view? Do you also take the view that we are seeing the problem change in its nature in some ways —that is, shifting into new regions and sports, and through more highly sophisticated methods? What is your take on this issue?

Thank you for the question and for the invitation here today. I totally agree with Mr Swaibu. In the p ast 20 - something years, we have seen, experienced and been able to measure through studies a certain increase in the phenomenon of match-fixing— or competition manipulation , as the convention calls it. I would say that it is getting worse in the sense that the phenomenon is amplifying. We are obviously now facing globalised trade , with an extraordinary increase in online exchanges ; Mr Swaibu talked about this . I t is now possible to access this kind of service from anywhere and at any age, and to be able to pay , not to pay or even to defer payment. It has become an increasing problem.

Is it changing in nature? Yes . As Mr Swaibu said, and as I can confirm , we have many studies that show this. In the p ast 15 , maybe 16 , years, we have seen a tremendous increase in the infiltration of organised crime into match-fixing . We know that , nowadays, we are no longer talking about the small fixes that have always existed in sports : this team talks with the other team, this player talks with the other player , and they agree to fix either the match result or some micro events during the match. Obviously, that is a serious crime , but it is overall less serious and less dangerous if we compare it to the situation that we know of today: the infiltration of organised crime syndicates. We know that this is a fact and that it is one of the main reasons why countries need a top-down approach. This is where the Macolin convention comes in, because no single sports organisation or sports betting organisation can fight international organised crime syndicates. That is a job for law enforcement and international co-operation in this field , which is precisely what the Macolin convention does.

Let me give you my personal commentary on the Macolin convention. I t is a very Swiss convention , all in all , because it does not aim for the stratosphere , like other conventions of its type. It does not create any new supranational bod ies or p roceedings. It does not aim for the stars ; i t stays very close to the ground. Th e convention was made through co-operation between different stakeholders, sports, sports betting and law enforcement authorities. It was made to benefit the everyday work of law enforcement and of the people on the actual field. A gain, it is a very Swiss convention . Staying close to the ground is the best way of tackl ing this phenomenon.

F inally , in one of your other questions, you asked whether we have seen any increase in certain markets or in certain sports. Fifteen years ago , I would have said that, globally, it is mostly football, cricket and tennis that are affected by this. I would also have said that the most deregulated markets, the Asian markets, were a point of concern. Nowadays, I would answer that all sports are concerned. Lately, w e have seen match-fixing scandals in sports that are much less susceptible to this kind of phenomenon, such as darts , chess and skiing. We also know that it is happening everywhere , not only in Asia and Europe .

I have been told that there has been a 92% jump in recorded cases of suspicious football matches in Africa and that, i n North American and c entral American football, the expansion—a 42% surge—has been fuelled by a considerable increase in the unregulated online sports gambling industry. Mr Swaibu, is that your experience ? D o you recognise those figures?

Yes, I am aware of those figures. I will go back before I go forward s . At the time of our match-fixing , the technology was nowhere near where it is today. They were able to use spread bets , algorithms and mathematics for the performance o n the pitch . The technology could not tell you how a player was breathing, what was being said on the pitch or the way they we re moving. All of these indicators signal those vulnerabilities and can now penetrate markets in territories such as Africa at the click of a button. So, although there has been a massive increase , and everybody has smartphones and mobile phones, the new match-fixer s are in plain sight . T hey live in society. Law enforcement has not been able to grasp the cusp of what that advancement looks like. In my humble , independent business, we have no conflicts of interest in the work we do ; w e are not tied to any entities or any illegal betting or regulated companies.

In hearing this evidence and these case stud ies , we need to understand that this is a highly organised syndicate that is built on the ground. If you have not had that experience and you have not been on the ground, it is hard to comprehend where those numbers are coming from, bearing in mind that we now have international borders, immigration and migration being mixed into and mingled with these communities.

Another way of looking at your question is : how do you tackle the 1 million people now using illegal betting online? Those numbers are very much strategical ; they are there in black and white. At the same time, how do we go behind the net and understand , to Madalina’s point about the Macolin convention , how we can add law enforcement and intelligence ? I believe that that would really strengthen this treaty moving forward , a s well as having a singular independent unit that could focus specifically on the area you have just spoken about.
T hat is a very good point. Lord Hannay, some of your question has been covered already , but you may want to expand on this principle.

Q3 I ndeed. Y ou have both , in fact , begun to answer the question I was going to ask : h ow significant is cross - border activity and international organised crime in fuelling the manipulation of sports competitions ? I s international co-operation — that is , co-operation between countries and Governments — required to tackle it ? That is the first part of the question.

The second part relates specifically to Britain leaving the European Union , which meant that we were cut out of some law enforcement co-operation activities with the European Union, such as SIS II and other instruments. I am not too sure where Switzerland stands on that; it is probably still included because it is part of the single market. C an you say whether you think that the UK being cut out of some law enforcement co-operation activities is hampering the effort to prevent cross-border crime , which both of you have already referred to in your answers ?

Thank you very much for your question, which is right on point. I will start with the first part of your question, to which I feel closer. You ask ed about the increase of online trading in match-fixing and the implication of organised crime. As Mr Swaibu and I said at the beginning , we know for a fact that organised crime syndicates are behind a large number of match-fixing schemes nowadays . This is obviously the most dangerous situation out there in the field of match-fixing .

We know for certain that there is an increase. A few years ago, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime released a publication, on which I was happy to participate, where we measured—as much as this can be measured, of course—the implication of organised crime syndicates in match-fixing. We found tremendous infiltration. This is somehow logical because match-fixing offers a golden opportunity for these syndicates : they can not only access this market easily, as Mr Swaibu explained, but make high profits immediately .

More importantly , some crime syndicates can at the same time launder the illegal proceeds of other, even more serious crimes. I am talking about cases of crime syndicates being involved in drug trafficking, human trafficking—especially that of young girls—and money laundering. This is a way n ot just to gain undue advantages and profits but to launder the proceeds of other horrific crimes. Undoubtedly, this issue can be tackled effectively only through international co-operation. Criminals do not stay in one countr y, as we know— they travel , benefit from and profit from this new , open world in which we have lived in for a few decades now— so the law enforcement response must also be international.

On the second part of your question, to which I feel less close , I can answer for Switzerland. As you know, Switzerland is not and has never been part of the EU, as the public voted in the early 19 90s to stay out. However, we participate in every aspect of the EU internal market not just economically but socially, culturally and in terms of law enforcement. We are not in the same position as the UK is after leaving the EU.

Although this is not my main field of competence, I humbly suggest that , in my view, the UK would probably benefit largely from the ratification of the Macolin convention in order to implement or be able to access some of the measures and instruments that it lost by leaving the European Union. For example, in operational situations where international co-operation and information exchange with law enforcement in EU countries are needed, or when a person needs to be apprehended abroad, the Macolin convention has very useful provisions. Obviously, the EU would also benefit from the UK’s presence in these instruments.
Let us move on to the next question, which will be asked by Baroness Anelay. Sorry, Lord Hannay, do you have a supplementary question?
It is not a supplementary; I just want to hear Moses Swaibu’s answer to my question.

I would add that, although I am from and live in the UK , it is important to understand that , in my case, one of the reasons why I changed my life, decided to move forward and chose to bring awareness to this subject was an ex- M etropolitan P olice officer. He worked for the FA’ s Integrity Unit and literally held my hand on the day I came out of prison. He helped me understand and break down stereotypes by saying, “ Okay, I know you ’ ve done this and are a part of this, but how can you help and assist us as we move forward? ”

You will find that officers who have left the public sector and now work in sport— this is specifically for the UK—understand this world better than anyone because they are on the front line. They have 20 or 30 - plus years ’ experience of dealing with organised crime and international borders. On Madalina’s point, these former officers or superintendents have helped me understand how th e landscape looks from international borders. I nclud ing a group of privatised officers with specialist experience in the areas of organised crime and money laund ering would definitely help and assist the Macolin convention, but I have not seen that happen yet in the UK.

Once you understand the landscape and geography of how criminality and prison culture articulate themselves in different areas of sport, you can better understand the robust structures that need to be put in place from the ground up. W e are looking at it from the highest level but, at the same time , it is about finding a medium to understand, “O kay, if we ’ re based in the UK, and we have migration and immigration, how do we now close that gap in the net and have specialised officers who could assist on the Macolin convention under that framework? ”
W ere the crime syndicates in t he match-fixing with which you were involved national or international?

They were international. During my career , I was approached by three different syndicates. The main syndicates still have a big, global ised foothold in this world of manipulation and have not changed in their practices ; t hey use the same systems and approaches but , with current technology , things have become more digitalised. You need to understand that it means that you need different types of collaborators and individuals who understand that network far and away beyond myself. Even though I am very much at the epicentre, I also know the sweet sciences—if you want to call them that— in terms of how this network operates , moves and manipulates.

Q4 I would like to build on what Mr Swaibu said . W e have been hearing about the changes in cultures and technolog ies , but you just said that the collaborators are still there and are finding different ways to move forward in illegal terms. T hinking about what Mr Swaibu just said about how collaboration actually opens up the market for illegal operations , do you think that the main problem lies principally with sports organisations themselves, with athletes and officials individually, or with the sports betting industry?

I will start by saying that everybody has different interests in sport . FIFA acts differently from the IOC and the Premier League acts differently from the National League . This creates a real challenge: how do you understand where rules and regulations lack openness and transparency? If you look at an athlete coming from Africa or Asia, they are not even aware of the rules because it is not their primary interest. When we look at training and education at that level, you have only a few hours or minutes to interact with staff and players to h elp them understand the rules and learn what they can and cannot do. In this evolving landscape , where sport is pumped into a commercialised model , we now have to deal with different territories and countries facing the same issues in various ways. H aving that collaboration is important for us as a whole .

One really positive thing about the Macolin convention is that , when I first engaged with it , I sat in front of all these judges and helped them understand what this look s like from a legal point of view. If there is a breach or someone is penalised, these people must be brought to justice. I went to prison and had that experience . A ctually, we can be much more preventive rather than reactive. We have the Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974 . I t is about making sure that , across all levels , these stereotypes are understood and broken down into new systems and new words , so that people understand why it seems scary and people who might say , “ I don ’ t want to come forward and say anything ”, know what is going on.

As Madalina will show, although you may be based in Switzerland and be hyper-focused on one element, there is also a massive international network that is focused on the next 10 to 20 years. If we do not catch up with that curve, we are going to fall far behind in establishing th e se levels of collaboration. I strongly believe in and advocate for this being built into systems and education. That is very important. It has taken me almost 10 years to establish GameChanger 360 just to get it right. It should be a tool for sport, Governments and the ecosystem to identify where a problem is.

In my opinion, it is a problem of culture: if you do not have cultural and emotional intelligence, how are you meant to understand people’s minds and psychology? Groups such as the NHS can help with gambling and betting harm, and I know that the PFA and the FA have S porting C hance and other clinics, but how do we present and promote more people com ing forward and using this international treaty to set a precedent? Again, in my humble opinion, the UK is the home of football and is definitely the home of sport. Being able to fly that flag at the highest level would help everybody else understand how far ahead we can become.

Following on from that, as Mr Swaibu said, we have people who are coming from other countries with different cultures and are perhaps not as educated on these laws. C an you , Dr Diaconu, give a view on the responsibility of sporting organisations and officials ? W hat depths have you seen them go to in trying to ensure that they are up to speed on assisting new players who, after all, come here not really knowing what the future for them is?

I agree with Mr Swaibu that the problem lies everywhere and everyone has a shared responsibility —that is, sports organisations , with their athletes and officials, but also the sports betting industry and law enforcement in general.

I am confident in answering this question because , for the past two decades , I have been working an international sports organisation, namely the International Olympic Committee. I am also a member of UEFA’s disciplinary committee , and we tackle this very seriously. I have worked with law enforcement such as Interpol and Europol , and, as an active barrister , I have worked for athletes, defending them against match-fixing accusations and , dare I say , exploiting the grey zones where they exist.

With this view , I can confidently say that the responsibility lies with every one of the stakeholder s . That is why th e Macolin convention has the potential to be so useful : it is the first time a convention re groups all the stakeholders around one table. We are talking about not only the sports world but the sports betting world , which is a different universe , as well as about law enforcement, which we have spoken about previously.

You are absolutely right that it is not about just the aspect of prosecution , which we have talked about a bit more in the past few minutes . The Macolin convention tackles three important aspects , and it has a 360-degree view on the phenomenon.

First, it tackles the question of prevention and education, on which we have already touched. The Council of Europe has been creating instruments in the past few years to help all the countries that sign and ratify the Macolin convention . It will provide them with access to all these resources and tools for prevention and education, such as hotlines and direct access on the field or in changing rooms with the players and their families, whatever the ir culture and wherever they come from. Secondly, from a legal standpoint, it concerns prosecution and sanctioning. For these reasons, the Macolin convention is the exact instrument that we need to give us , for the first time, a real chance in tackl ing the phenomenon of international match-fixing effectively at an operational level .
Q5 You have spoke n about having all the stakeholders around the table. Are you happy with the response of the sports betting organisations?

The Macolin convention is a work in progress but , personally, I am quite happy with it because we now have not dozens but hundreds of sports betting agencies, regulators, and operators around the table. They have all agreed to sign a memorandum of understanding and to share their data, their suspicions, patterns and system alerts in live time, whether those are here, in Taiwan or in Argentina. This is the operational co-operation that I was talking about, right on the field and very close to the ground. I am happy to say that basically all of the regulated sports betting operators and agencies have joined this effort. Ob viously , it will be a bit more difficult to convince illegal betting operators to do so, but chances are that this is a live instrument tackling everyone for the first time. It offers a 360-degree view on gathering information from the field, betting operators and law enforcement. That data could be solid information, such as someone ’ s criminal record, or it could be a simple rumour or system alert that pops up on someone’s system.

Let us take a true scenario involving a match in the UK and a player from Brazil. By coincidence, hundreds of bets were placed in Brazil on a small event : a yellow card for a player . Such an event does not prejudice the result of the game ; b ecause of this, the player does not have the impression that they are betraying their team or coach. These small events are what we call micro-fixing. Without the Macolin convention , it is virtually impossible for UK law enforcement and UK sports authorities to access information from Brazil—they can access some parts of it but not all it—and of course, in the end, the criminals walk free.
That is a very apt point.

Q6 I have two questions ; t he first is for both of you , while the second is a supplementary for Professor Diaconu alone. I start with the question to you both. You have said that the phenomenon is getting worse despite the existence of the Macolin convention . W hat value does UK ratification of this convention add in tackling the manipulation of sports competitions ? In your personal experience, would these measures have made a difference in past cases with which you are familiar?

I strongly agree with your point. What is fundamental here is that we have all these measures but things are getting worse. Clearly, something is not working. When we strip away the fluff —pardon my French— and put it in black and white, we have a problem that is not getting any better. In order to make that problem either go away or improve, we must strip everything back to its origins.

In my experience, athletes today are more sophisticated and intelligent but are still not aware of the rules. They do not know what the Macolin convention is . I f you ask a 15 year-old living anywhere in the world, “W hat is the Macolin convention?”, t hey are not aware of it . Why? T here is no social media or public awareness. As I keep saying , it is structured as an instrument of law and understanding for a certain demographic, audience and generation. Match-fixing is getting younger, but our solutions are old and outdated. With respect to the UK and the landscape we currently sit in, we have a massive opportunity to ratify this treaty and build those structures in terms of what this is going to look like for the next generation of athletes , helping them make the right decisions.

However, before we ratify any convention— many of which I believe are tick - box exercises —we need to think about what this actually looks like across the whole ecosystem. Are we tackling the problem of social media? I have not heard anything today around solutions for that. Are we talking about how to develop structures into other areas where we can include other stakeholders? If you look at charities that do an amazing job around gambling and awareness, these people are right on the front line in terms of understanding what that landscape looks like.

I know that I may be a bit direct but , at 37 , I am still having to learn the next version of, “ Okay, I ’ m getting older, but am I using different tools and different elements to understand this world? ” The issue is not necessarily just for law enforcement, police, Moses Swaibu, GameChanger 360 and the Macolin convention; i t is a societal issue because sport is played on the streets. T ake the World Cup right now : everybody is talking about it and wants to be included. Are we creating the right awareness and intelligence around it? That could be as simple as a campaign. A campaign can affect the masses better than these legal structures that nobody understands because , without any athletes, none of this happens. My message to the Macolin convention , which does a great job, is that there is still much more that needs to be done for the future. In the coming years , we need to include the relevant people in the conversation as well.

Let me ask my supplementary question. Dr Diaconu , you were eloquent about what the convention c ould do regarding prevention, education, prosecution and sanctions. A range of countries have already ratified. There are a lot of theoretical benefits from this co-operation, but is it actually making a difference?

Thank you for clarifying the question and raising the opportunity for me to say, “Y es , i ndeed ”. I will try to answer your supplementary question quickly . The Macolin convention has been around for a while now and is starting to be ratified by more countries — hopefully , by even more in future . So h ow come the phenomenon we are talking about is still here and increasing? I can answer with one of my favourite historical examples. I have recently been able to consult an extraordinary document that you hold in the UK. It is in the library at the University of Oxford and is a papyrus from upper Egypt from , I believe , 26 7 AD . It is the first known match-fixing agreement in the world— at least , until now.
You must get a copy of it for the report.

It is an extraordinary document. It was created by a notary public and signed by both the athletes and their parents. Legally speaking, it is a perfect document and an extraordinary piece of history. To me, that is necessary historical background . It shows that we have been fighting competition manipulation for the 1 , 700 years since that papyrus was written —o r, as King Charles might say, just the other day.

Does the convention work? I believe that it does. If we compare it with recent history, the Macolin convention really has the potential to be a game - changer on the field. I am not talking about the stratospheres here; I am talking about what happens on the pitch.

There is one element of this convention that we have not talked about yet: Article 13, which speaks about national platforms. Perhaps we could talk about it briefly now. It simply mean s each country participating in the convention set ting up a centralised national hub or database. All of the necessary information is stored there and made available to everyone else live. For example, a prosecutor from Birmingham, a sports person from Brighton or someone from Scotland — any body who has information that is useful for a match-fixing case— can feed such information into th e database , which is accessible on both a national and international level so that it is efficien t .

The good news is that the UK already participates and already has a national platform ; it is quite effective , in my view. Like many other countries that have signed but not yet ratified the convention, the UK uses a sort of anticipated application of the convention, if you like. Obviously, as a lawyer, I believe that it is much better to have a confirmed legal base. So, in the UK, things are already being done, but more could be done. More instruments could be accessed, especially in the field s of prevention and education.

Briefly, to convince you of that—or at least try to—let me take Spain and Belgium as two examples of countries that have experienced the Macolin convention fully after ratification. Lately, t here have been some very successful operations in both Spain and Belgium with the help of Europol and Interpol. Some very large mafia syndicates have been taken down — syndicates that were responsible for hundreds or thousands of match-fixing events not just in one country, but throughout the world. Belgian law enforcement and the Spanish police were able to access these marvellous instruments provided by the Macolin convention to wrap things up and put everyone behind bars.
Forgive me but we need to move on to the next question as we have around 10 minutes left and I want to get everyone in.

Q7 The convention was concluded in 2014 but did not come into effect until 2019. Many countries have signed but not yet ratified it . Are the deficiencies in the convention , which have been pointed out by seven countries , leading to hesitation and delay ? Is there a feeling that it could be improved?
Perhaps you, Madalina, might want to answer this question since it is more specifically about the regulatory environment.

As you rightly pointed out, the convention was opened for signature in 2014 and entered into force in 2019, when the first five countries both signed and ratified it . Since then, we have seen a decrease in the momentum of ratification. Quite a few countries have signed , and we now have non-European countries, such as Australia, Morocco and Brazil , participating. We know that it is a really important tool outside Europe, as is its purpose, but it is true that there has been a loss of momentum in ratification. The reasons for that are diverse ; I do not believe that there is a single explanation for it. It also has to do with the very different regulatory and democratic landscape s of each country.

Let me take Germany as one example . Germany was one of the countries that signed the convention immediately in 2014 but only now, as we speak, is its P arliament on the way to ratifying the convention. Just like the UK, Germany has already been participating in most of the instruments of the Macolin convention—a gain, though, it is anticipated application of the convention — and more countries are going to ratify soon.

Also, at the EU level, there has been a secret de Polichinelle, as we say in French, which is a secret known by everybody: the Malta lockdown. Malta put a lot of effort into trying to delay as much as possible the signature and ratification of the Macolin convention by EU countries. This was for a specific reason : Malta is one of the largest providers of online betting in the world , so the convention has implications for that industry, which is important to the country. It is a well-known secret that this was one of the primary aspects of the dela y in the convention ’s ratification process.
If you were rewriting the convention today , in the light of experience, would you make any changes?

I would change only one thing, but it is a formal matter rather than a material one. I would make it a U nited N ations convention. I would not change any of its contents ; I would just make it clearer that this is not just a European convention and is already open for signature and ratification by most countries in the world . However, when I travel to other continents, I sometimes get the feeling that legislators do not feel attracted to the convention because they believe that it is strictly European. It is true that sport is still very Eurocentric. Most sports that we now call international a re actually European, and 99% of international sports bodies are European. There is a bit of global reluctance toward s the Macolin convention because of that, so , if I had a magic wand, I would change the umbrella of the convention — but not its content.

Q8 Dr Diaconu , you have already talked about national hub s—y ou have talked about a lot of the things in my question, actually— but do you think that the UK has the right policy, regulatory and enforcement structures in place to implement this agreement effectively? I should say that I also have another question for Mr Swaibu.
Please keep the answer quite brief because we are coming to the end of our session.

I believe that the UK already has most of the instruments and all of its authorities in place to participate effectively. As I said previously, the UK already participates in the Group of Copenhagen, which is a select group of countries that have national platforms co - operating with other s, so t he UK is in the top tier when it comes to the application of the Macolin convention . As I mentioned previously, this convention does not aim to create new bureaucracy, build new structures or make things difficult ; it aims to simplify what already exists to the maximum and to assist if there is a need for national improvement.

Mr Swaibu, both you and Dr Diaconu have talked about education and training. You talked about it happening as early as primary school, although, in your first answer, you also talk ed about the fact that you had a sense that match-fixing was morally wrong. When you talk about education, are you really talking about young people having a sense of right and wrong and being resilient in order to stand against things that they definitely perceive as wrong? I do not think that there is space in the curriculum to spend a lot of time on this convention specifically.

I will correct myself : I was talking about the fact that everyone does physical education. W ithin that, integrity is not just verbal ; i t can be shown through body language or picking up cones. These soft skills and assets serve as a deterrent, repelling potential manipulation or corruption. It comes down to who you are inside. In my own dealings with professional sport at an amateur level, those things come down to knowing how important the environment is : the kitchen staff, the kit man and all these people who make up England , make up these teams and make the world love sport. That version of education is very nuanced . I t does not take a lot of time and effort; it just needs to be reinforced. As we go through a lot of these areas, it is about making sure that the right structures are in place and tick the right boxes, to be honest.

I read in the documentation that sports academies have to teach the Macolin convention . I do not know how specific they are but , if you go to Chelsea ’s youth academy , you are obliged to be taught that match-fixing is illegal. As you said, you knew that it was wrong when you were doing it. The specifics of the convention do not necessarily need every reinforcement. Am I right, Dr Diaconu, th at it is a component of the convention that this has to be implemented by sports bodies and sports academies as well?
That is correct.
That is v ery helpful.

Q9 This is a bit of a sweep ing- up question . A part from all the things you have mentioned, what else could we do? What is your priority for new actions through either the convention or the United Kingdom’s own measures?

L inked to that , I have a specific question for Dr Diaconu . First, I must declare my interest as a member of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe. What has been the role of the monitoring body of the Council of Europe? Quite clearly , it has a monitoring role and a monitoring body. Has it been doing sufficient work to make sure that this convention is operating properly internationally?

I can answer that briefly. T echnology is su fficient and important. One thing you will find in using proprietary data to train new models is that you can now click a button to change languages and build frameworks for that level of understanding. Whether you are really good at academic work or more practical, it builds a robust structure for who you are as an individual.

With all these messages and the Macolin convention 's national platforms, to my knowledge, those systems are now being implemented in different ways. It is just about improving the technology and that inclusion for the convention on a mass scale. In my experience, the Macolin convention is doing the right things structurally and continuing to improve those models. The answer, for me, would be hyper-focused on technology and solutions , as well as understanding that great information can come from good datasets. Feeding that good information and data in , and mixing it with the right compliance and regulatory solutions , will enhance things and make for effective change.
Would you like to make a closing comment, Dr Diaconu?

I will try to give my answer in 30 seconds or less. You asked about th e role of the Macolin convention’s follow-up committee, which exists and works a lot . It actually do es too much for my taste . I am not sure whether that is the answer you were expecting but , yes, it is a very active follow-up committee.

For now, its follow-up is limited to the countries that have signed and ratified the convention. We hope that it will do much more work in future as more countries come and participate in the Macolin convention , but it is already doing a lot of work. For example, a few years ago, it tried to enlarge the definition of match-fixing to cover even more offences than were initially included in the Macolin convention . It is doing a lot of work, and I hope that it will do more in future.

T hank you very much indeed. What a fabulously useful session. Madalina, thank you for joining us from Switzerland. Moses , I speak on behalf of our whole committee when I say how appreciative we are of the journey you have taken. The fact that you are now here giving evidence is of great credit to yourself.
Thank you very much.
Thank you very much for the invitation.
Thank you again, Madalina; we will see you soon. We will now stop the recording.

sessions.iT: The Humanitarian Situation in Yemen
sessions.w: World Food Programme; Médecins Sans Frontières; Noha Yehya

segs.tx: International Development Committee
Oral evidence: The Humanitarian Situation in Yemen , HC 553
Tuesday 14 July 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 14 July 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Sarah Champion (Chair); Janet Daby; Tracy Gilbert; Monica Harding; Alicia Kearns; Noah Law; Brian M a thew; David Mundell; James Naish; Sam Rushworth; David Taylor.
Questions 1 - 6 3
Witnesses

I : El-Khidir Daloum , Country Director, Yemen, World Food Programme; Konstantinos Psykakos, Deputy Programme Manager Cell 5, Médecins Sans Frontières; Noha Yehya, Gender and gender-based violence specialist.
II : Dr Richard Barltrop, Visiting Senior Fellow, Middle East Centre, London School of Economics (LSE); Helen Lackner, Associate, SOAS Middle East Institute.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: El-Khidir Daloum, Konstantinos Psykakos and Noha Yehya .

Q1 Chair : This is the International Development Committee’s one-off session on the humanitarian situation in Yemen. As a C ommittee, we repeatedly come back to this topic because the humanitarian situation out there is truly horrendous. It has been going on for over a decade, and unfortunately it gets very little attention . T hat is partly the short attention span of the media . They like a crisis and this is an ongoing protracted disaster. I t is l argely hidden, as this session will show , because it is very difficult to get current information into the public domain. All that said, we are very fortunate to be joined by a number of witnesses today who we will separate into two panels. Mr El-Khidir is here in the room but o ur other witnesses are virtual. Mr El-Khidir, could I ask you to introduce yourself and your organisation, please ?

El-Khidir Daloum : T hank you very much, honourable m embers of the International Development Committee. It is a great honour and privilege to stand in front of you today . I am the representative of World Food P rogramme in Yemen. We have been working in Yemen for over three decades and are honoured to have a long-lasting partnership with the UK Government and p eople. I am really grateful to be here with you.
Q2 Chair : For those people who do not know, could you explain what the World Food P rogramme is and what it does around the world?

El-Khidir Daloum : The World Food P rogramme was established in 1963 and stands to achiev e zero hunger. The sustainable development goals ha ve identified the second goal of achieving zero hunger and WFP stands for that. WFP operates in 84 countries. It saves lives . S aving lives is basically a humanitarian response and we work on survival, feeding people and addressing hunger to prevent the worst outcomes . At the same time, we work on the development side ; w e call it changing life. It is about addressing the root causes of hunger. We translate those root causes into positive programmes such as resilience, food systems, and school meals , and so on .

In addition, WFP work s in enabling the humanitarian space, especially agencies , to deliver humanitarian response in hard-to-reach areas where access is limited . WFP provid es logistic support , such as the logistic cluster , when there is an on-surface demand for agencies that are not able to deliver . T hat is across the world. WFP is the leading agency trying to address most of the famines that happen in the world , which happen as a result of climate , conflict , or the outbreak of diseases. Those are the main reasons for famines and crisis.

I have to mention that, because of the volume of the humanitarian response, WFP is often perceived as only a humanitarian agency. Yes, we are the largest humanitarian agency in the world , but we also have a developmental side.
Q3 Chair : Are you part of the United Nations?

El-Khidir Daloum : Yes , w e are part of the United Nations . I n any country you will find agencies called resident and non-resident agencies. WFP continues to be a resident agency because it is operational and work s deep in the field. You will find us in the capitals , but you will also find us closer to the people we serve.

Chair : WFP is one of the best values for money on public record ; y ou are one of the leanest organisations. I have seen you on the ground and w hat you are able to do is remarkable. Thank you for everything that you and your colleagues do. We can now turn specifically to Yemen.
Q4 Janet Daby : What is the impact of food insecurity in the current conflict in Yemen?
El-Khidir Daloum : I want to start with the trajectory. In the last decade, Yemen has gone through a very challenging moment.

Until 2015, the World Food Programme ’s developmental programme was the major component and humanitarian programme was the smaller one. As a result of conflict, we have reached a situation where 50% of the total population of Yemen is food insecure. That constitutes about 18.3 million people. Further, 3.5 million are acutely malnourished, 55% of children are chronically malnourished, and 5.2 million are internally displaced as a result or war or the climate crisis. It has affected boys and girls. About 3.2 million children of school age are currently out of school.

I started this role on 5 March this year. I have travelled in the southern part, under the control of the in ternationally recognised go vernment, where I met the IDPs —internally displaced persons—and refugees, and people who are affected by climate and conflict. I have to say that it hit hard. Any conflict is hard for women, children, and the elderly. Those are the three categories that have been hit hard.

We have also marginalised communities in Yemen, called Muhamasheen in Arabic. Those Muhamasheen, or marginalised communities, have paid the largest price. I want to give you an example of what will happen to the household when hit by crisis. Whether this crisis is as a result of climate change, conflict, or outbreak, the first thing the household will do is cut meals. Three will go to two , and two will go to one . If one, it will go to the quality of the food they take. The quality is going to be compromised. As a result, malnutrition will happen. They will then try to borrow from their local community. Everyone will know what you have in terms of assets, so they will not give you more than the value of your assets. When you then go for the third strategy, which is to sell your assets, you will find that the terms of trade are not in your favour. You sell all your assets and are not able to pay your debts, so you will be indebted. When you reach this stage you have only two options ; to stay in the land or to leave. If you stay, you will be malnourished and the whole issue of a declaration of famine could happen. Otherwise, you become an IDP. That is why , as a result of that push factor, there are 5.2 million IDPs. Th at is the situation in Yemen right now .

Q5 Janet Daby : That is quite shocking to hear and very concerning. In terms of the long-term impact of malnutrition and Yemen’s stability, how do you perceive its ability to recover and improve? What are your thoughts around that?

El-Khidir Daloum : One thing I have learned from my humanitarian work over the last 35 years — 10 of them in the United Nations and 25 in international NGOs —is that you have to be optimistic in this sector. There is always hope. Yemen was not dependent on aid, especially humanitarian aid , until 2015 . That will tell you the story that you focus on resilience , food systems , and the value chain . Yemen is rich in three food economy zones : agriculture, livestock, and fishery. I f we work hard with support from the UK Government and others, and we have examples of WFP working in resilience , then all those food economy zones can turn around the lives of the people. We have operational research to show that whenever you invest $1 in resilience, it can save between $3 to $7 during times of emergency or shocks. These are examples of how Yemen can easily go through recovery programmes. We have a number of recovery programmes that have been successful and paid back in terms of turning the lives of the people around and created hope for marginalised groups.
Q6 Monica Harding : The rates of disability in Yemen seem to be very high as a population. Why is that?

El-Khidir Daloum : Disability in Yemen is sometimes the result of war. Some is the result of immunisation coverage being very low . We also have an issue of stunting . R ecently I went from Yemen to the western coast and about 40% to 60% of kids were stunted. Stunting has a lasting effect, especially after the age of five but s ome nutritionists say after the age of two. It is e ither the conflict , the polio coverage not being as good as it should be —but that has now been improved —or i t is the result of a chronic malnutrition situation, especially the stunting form of malnutrition.

Q7 David Mundell : A re there any resources or attempts to pursue food security initiatives to ensure th at the Yemeni population can shift from this dependency model to a more self-sufficien t model?

El-Khidir Daloum : Yes; this is not only WFP ; there are other agencies. I can give an example from the World Food P rogramme. We worked with farmers in Mukalla in resilience —w e call it resilience programmes —and w e provide them w ith agricultural inputs and approaches to agriculture. We also engaged them in the value chain ; how they can be in aggregation. A number of them come as associations . T hey then link them to the market , and they sell their commodities to the market. We have help ed them to bring back a lmost 3,000 hectares of land. It is now active. M y deputy was there recently . I was not in M u kalla, but my deputy was retained by M u kalla ’s govern ors . T hey have reached this situation and w e now would like to work in the Bab -el -Mand e b Strait . W e are trying to work with a fishery association to bring them together and try to link them to the market. They are mainly producers but they are not linked to the market , which is the biggest issue. It is th e transport, connection, and cold chain systems ; a l l these things together.
Q8 David Mundell : W hat are the main barriers to tackling food insecurity? Have you just set out what you see as the main barriers to tackling it , o ut with the conflict itself ?

El-Khidir Daloum : T he agriculture , livestock , and fishery food economy zone s are the most vibrant food economy zones. In these zones, people should be well off. W e need to ask ourselves why they are not well off. The main reason is that between the production , value chain , and the market there are many aggregators. They are not able to sell their products at the right time. For example, if they have fisheries they have no cold chain for it. If they have fruit and vegetables, they have no cold chain for it. If they produc e milk, they cannot link to the market . Th at is one thing. The other is to group themselves into proper associations. They study the market and become one group. Instead of having many mediators between them and the consumers, you minimise the mediators and they c an engage directly with consumers. The more they engage directly with consumers, they more they will be winners. The consumers will be winners. The economy in total will be a winner.
Q9 David Mundell : Do you think that is achievable?

El-Khidir Daloum : It is achievable because our experience in Mukalla has demonstrated it. To give you another example, we are working on something called home-grown school feeding. In the past, we have brought food from the UK, the United States, Australia, Canada, and different places and distributed it in the schools to attract more children. We have now introduced something called home-grown school feeding. If you are in agriculture, we link you with the agriculture food economy. Schools buy from local farmers instead of from outside. It is the same for livestock and the fisheries. We found that, once linked, it stimulates the local market. The UK Government gave us funding for cash transfers during the humanitarian assistance. We have a study that shows that w hen you are providing assistance in kind, it will stimulate in the local economy by only $1. For ever y $1 in cash , the local economy will be stimulated by b etween $1.7 and $2.5. It is a humanitarian response but it will have a lasting impact on the local economy.

Q10 David Mundell : Y ou have essentially been talking about the southern part of Yemen and what is happening there. How or to what extent are you or others able to operate in the northern Houthi-controlled territories?

El-Khidir Daloum : As I stand in front of you, 38 out of 73 of my beloved colleagues are detained by the Houthis for doing the noble job of delivering humanitarian assistance to the Yemeni people, irrespective of where they are and under which authority they are controlled. That is the situation we are in.

I would like to say that we are not operational there . T he Secretary-General took the decision about the UN post in the north for two reasons. First, it is because of the 73 detainees. Secondly, it is because of limited humanitarian space that respects international humanitarian laws and the humanitarian imperative. Having said that, World Food Programme and other humanitarians work with all people i r respective of where they are and who they are. It is not going to dictate our work for us. For the time being, we are in post.

The situation in the north is not good. I do not have a high level of confidence to speak about it because we do not have ground colleagues who can provide us with the data. Generally, when I talk about the 18.3 million we have information on, they are not only in the southern part of the country but are also in the northern part under the Houthi authorities.
Q11 David Mundell : D o you feel you have an accurate picture of the food insecurity position in the north?

El-Khidir Daloum : We have an estimate. The estimate talks about 18.3 million. Out of them, about 12 million are in the north. These remain estimates. As long as we are not operational, WFP cannot speak with authority on how bad the situation is in terms of malnutrition and food insecurity.

Q12 Chair : Mr El-Khidir , can I send my solidarity to your colleagues ? Detaining international humanitarian workers is a clear violation of international law. I am disgusted that it is going on and deeply sorry for the individuals , their famil ies, and the wider humanitarian family. I wonder if I could just pause and bring in Noha and Konstantinos. I know we have some problems with the connection. Konstantinos, can I ask you to introduce yourself and your organisation to us, please ?
Konstantinos Psykakos : I work for Doctors Without Borders, Switzerland. One countr y we are operating in is Yemen, along with other colleagues of MSF in the country.
Q13 Chair : Noha, can you introduce yourself and your organisation to us, please?
Noha Yehya : I work as a gender and GBV specialist for a national NGO.
Q14 Tracy Gilbert : Can you tell me what unique challenges women and girls are facing today?
Noha Yehya : T he problem in Yemen is that, in the south and the north, women are exposed to violence and used as a weapon.

One big problem women and girls in Yemen are facing is our laws and institutions. They give us no way to protect ourselves or to find safety. No law in the country bans discrimination against women. Marital rape is normalised and never considered a crime. Even getting a basic legal right such as inheritance is a battle for a woman in Yemen. To make it worse, there is adultery law in Yemen , or Zima law as we call it. If a woman who is exposed to rape tries to report or file a case against the rap ist then she might be prosecuted for adultery unless she can prove that she was raped. This cannot happen in Yemen. If she is not imprisoned for adultery, she might be exposed to an honour killing. Under the laws in Yemen, if a male in the family kill s his mother, sister, or daughter for adultery then it is only one year in prison or a fine. This exposes women to a lot of risks.

There is also a total lack of accountability everywhere in Yemen, north and south. It is kept alive by the m ahram rule. It is more in the north than the south, but every woman who needs to travel needs m ahram . It means that she needs to be accompanied by a male or get permission f rom a male to move from one place to another. This is a kind of violence because women who are exposed to domestic or gender- based violence cannot go and seek services. It is the same f or service providers. Most service providers of specialised services for gender - based violence are women. If they cannot travel or move freely to service provide rs then services will be stopped and women will be exposed to more violence. T here is also a stigma issue. W omen cannot always speak out about v iolence or their expos ure to violence by a male abuser because it is known and normalised . E ven if a male is an abuser, he is also the protector. She cannot speak about this , o therwise she will be considered disobedient.

The n orth and s outh have different dynamics. When we look into the violence against women, it is hidden everywhere and is equally in the n orth and the s outh. In the n orth, we have a serious issue relat ing to the security of women. It is Zainabiyat , which is a female force. In the n orth, t he Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedoms documented between 1,400 and 1,654 cases of violence against women. T here are also testimonies f rom prisoners who were recently freed from prison that say Zainabiyat facilitated all kinds of violence against the women in detention. Zainabiyat i s the one monitoring women working in the field s of GBV , protection , and humanitarian field s in general.

No ne of our colleagues or researchers can even speak about gender-based violence. That is why some colleagues , who were supposed to be here today , could not join ; t hey are based there where are different dynamics. In the s outh, there are armed groups that can do whatever they want to do to expose women to risk or violence. There is no clear mechanism or way to appeal for any support for women . I t is also difficult because of the divided ministries and armed groups that are connected to the Government and different political parties. It is a bit chaotic in the s outh.
Q15 Chair : C ould I bring you back to a point you made earlier? You spoke about Zainabiyat . Could you tell us what and who that is?
Noha Yehya : It is a female force.
Chair : A female force?

Noha Yehya : Yes, it is a female police force formulated by the Houthis in order to monitor and detain women because of the culture. Men cannot touch or monitor women so t hey created this group in order to control women and make sure they keep their mouths shut. They cannot speak because they are reachable and can be detained.
Q16 Chair : You said in prison s , the Zainabiyat were carr ying out violence against women?
Noha Yehya : Yes . T hey facilitate the process by a ll kinds of v iolence you can imagine , which I prefer not to talk about.
Chair : Could we bring Konstantinos in to talk about it from a medical perspective?

Q17 Tracy Gilbert : If there is anything to add, that would be great. Are you aware of any protective funding or dedicated programmes designed to aid the needs of women and girls facing these circumstances?

Konstantinos Psykakos : B efore starting on dedicated prog rammes to address those needs, I have to complement what my colleague Noha ha s said. In the no rth, especially where women are already deprived of access to health care and with the pause over the past month that the administration had to face in the n orth of Yemen, those limited services are already extremely scarce. They are already hindered and access to them put s them more at risk as we speak. Where you had a network of PHCCs that would be able to screen and identify women at risk and refer them to appropriate secondary health facilities for support and to provide services, they are now even scarce r . Women already have barriers and issues to access at a local level , let alone when they have to cover further distances to reach that access to care. Keep in mind the context ; t he restrictions are many. A year or so ago , we were relying on other partners in the vicinity to provide those needed services. Today, we are very worried and raise d the alarm that we might not se e the majority of those cases access our facilities or the care they need for the matter at hand.
Q18 Tracy Gilbert : Are you aware of any reserve funding or any projects that are trying to exist in either the north or the south?

Konstantinos Psykakos : A s my colleague has already said, the north and the south have a different reality. In the south, while you have the availability of funds, it is more about feasibility and implementation on the ground . T o what extent the efficiency of it happens and is applie d . In the north, we are facing a more c hallenging environment where restrictions and barriers exist for different re gions . F unding has been scarce but, even if it is available , it needs help and support to be implemented on the ground. We can elaborate further on this specific point.

Q19 Chair : While I was researching for this session, I was shocked to discover that three women are dying in pregnancy or delivery daily, which in June of this year was the highest maternal mortality rate in the Arab region. A re there any specific programmes to encourage training and the support of midwives and doctors specifically around sexual and reproductive health rights?

Konstantinos Psykakos : On that matter, I can tell you that there were a lot of activities at a primary healthcare level that would engage with the communities, through the modalities of the Ministry of Public Health and Population , to train TBAs in the traditional delivery system of the community in Yemen. We were trying to train the communities to refer to the PHCC for stabilisation and treatment if possible , or at least timely referral to a secondary healthcare facility where antenatal care could be followed , when they identify early complications.

Y ou have already mentioned the 2025 numbers . Alarmingly, i n 2026, we have a different problem that insinuates the situation has been exacerbated on its own . W e do not see as many cases anymore . Th is has led to the conclusion that, if the trend continues, women have lost access because the support to the primary healthcare level has been reduced drastically due to the UN pause and other reasons.

Those women do not have the means to access secondary health facilities. Of t he ones we received in 2025, 40% of cases were late arrivals to the hospital hence complicated cases. If there was a system in place, we would be able to treat them earlier and with fewer complications .

I can share this experience myself because I was in Ad -D ahi, Hudaydah two weeks ago. I was visiting one of the primary healthcare centres we are supporting to refer to another hospital in Hudaydah , Al-Qanawis . It offers maternal care and sexual and reproductive health facilities . The team mention ed that in 2025 they saw cases referred to Al-Qanawis , but until June 2026 they have seen far less cases. I do not think we are in a situation where we have trained the communities enough to deal with complications at local level with the means that they have. T hose women have lost access , or it has been severely hindered and p robably will be hindered further in the future the more we progress in this timeline.
Chair : That is chilling.
Q20 Janet Daby : Noha, I was thinking about female children, teenagers , and young women in terms of their mental health. What protections, if any, are in place for them?
Noha Yehya : Do y ou mean services for them?
Janet Daby : Yes .

Noha Yehya : Since the war started, the percentage of early marriage s has increased sharply. G irls less than 18 years old are getting married or getting pregnan t before they are ready. This has increased mortality among the children and exposed the ir health to a lot of risks.

UNFPA , through national NGOs , is running some health facilities. Due to the pause in the north and a lack of funds, almost 70% of these protection or health services ha ve been shut down, which means women are now left behind . They cannot seek services . T hey cannot access case management, psycho - social support through the protection centres or safe spaces , and they cannot get the health services needed. They are exposed to unsafe abortions and childbirth , which can cause a lot of issues for them. This is one of the biggest challenges that we are facing; many services have been shut down or are on the edge of being shut down.

UNFPA is trying . It asked for $ 71 million this year to ensure that services c ould be sustained and continued. Unfortunately, up to now, only $ 9 million has been received and used by the partners for the implementation of sustaining some health facilities and safe spaces . Out of 103 safe spaces in the north, now only eight are operating. You can see the variance and t he massive need .

Q21 Brian Mathew : Konstantinos, I want to take it to a higher level now b ut want you to dig down. I will ask you three questions in one . W hat is the current state of healthcare in Yemen? How does MSF meet those needs? W hat are the long-term implications of those needs not being addressed?

Konstantinos Psykakos : What is the status of the current health state of Yemen? In north and south, we have different situations and the same in parallel. What do I mean ? In Yemen, people are in need in the north and south . The Ministry of Public Health and Population and PHCC level s are in need of support, technical supervision , and more knowledge on the ground to support them in mov ing forward and address ing those needs. The difference is that you have more resources available in the south compared to the north , as in the past year more funds have been concentrated in the south rather than the north. That is the big difference. It is the same needs but different . The south has the funds, tools, and NGOs to operate and move ahead with whatever needs to be addressed at a health level. The north has been defunded and isolated. Its needs are still the same though and will accelerate in the months or years to come. That is what we anticipate as of today.

T o connect the first point with the third point : what do we foresee in the long term if those needs remain unattained? In any given country where the health needs of the population remain unattained, we do not expect this part of the population of the country to be able to recover themselves or enter any trajectory other than one of prolonged humanitarian disaster need or the prolonged management of outbreaks . T here are no more outbreaks ; i t is a regularised situation that we are manag ing week after week to address those needs but without being able to outpace th e curve. W hen it comes to the north, w hat we at MSF are trying to do is keep a modus operandi that can reflect the needs of the population in a versatile way and address outbreaks and emergency response s because the humanitarian landscape has changed.

M any NGOs were able to collaborate and co-ordinate their responses before. W e now need to keep a focus on how we can better address the needs of areas , k eeping in mind that we have already reached our maximum capacity in terms of operations over the past years . O ur further growth is not a matter of financial support but it is a matter of the feasibility of having a wider operation.

W e are collaborating with ICRC — International Committee of the Red Cross, the other actor in the north of the country — to be able to have maximum efficiency and not overlap in geographical areas. For the south, we are attending to different health needs in some areas because we have activities and programmes . B esides focusing on malnutrition or paediatrics, we are also focusing on activities for the migration population that cross es from the Horn of Africa to the south of Yemen to reach the rest of the Arabic Peninsula. Tha t is another population in need ; i t is not a Yemeni population but they have needs.
In the meantime, in the same modality, we are try ing to engag e with other actors to avoid the duplication of activities and to maximise the geographical coverage.
Q22 Noah Law : The needs you have described persist at a time of global aid cuts. To what extent are you confident in your own organisation’s funding in the years ahead?

Konstantinos Psykakos : That is the question. If I had the answer today, I would be able to organise my operations for the next five years. Every year dictates the next one. Today, in the north, you have a different situation. It is not only the funding cuts that are global. We experience it in every country ; i t is not only a reality in Yemen itself.

What we see in the north of Yemen is that it is not only the global funding cuts ; i t is also that decisions have been taken to restrict any little funds that might have remained . If there is a ny willingness for those funds to be injected in the north, there is no facilitation for those funds to find their way north . For MSF or ICRC, we can navigate t hings such as a l ack of access for UN H AS f lights and i mportation, and flagging a terrorist organisation of Ansar Allah, the de facto authorities , to deliver activities and services to the people of the north , but o ther NGOs might not have the same capacity. It might create an activity of fear about operating in the north . It is not only a matter of global funding cuts that we see less services on its own , we see other effects and additional pressure s coming to the northern part. In the south, it is as we said but the north and the south share different realities in some ways.
Q23 Noah Law : Noha, h as your organisation specifically been hit by UK aid cuts?

Noha Yehya : Of course. My organisation is one of the biggest organisations providing gender-based violence and health services for women and girls in Yemen. W e are one of the biggest recipients from UNFPA and a few other donors. With the UK cutting the fund , 70% of our services have been shut down including health services or safe spaces for women and girls. It means that women cannot reach these services and the consequences will last for a generation. Women are exposed to psychosocial stress and violence , which will be passed to their children. It will increase poverty and the consequences will be difficult. Cutting the fund now will not stop violence ; i t will only stop the help for women in Yemen. That is what is going on now.

We are trying with our resources to downsize the interventions or services , but that means we have more than 6,500 women on the waiting list. In the n orth, 2,300 are on the waiting list for safe spaces and t o get some psychosocial support . T his is the only door open for women seek ing services ; i f we shut it down, w e will face a lot of consequences. One is structured violence , which will not be easy to address later. We are destroying the structure of the community by leaving women exposed to this violence and not provid ing any support for them. Girls will be deprived of schools. Poverty will add stress to women and their families, which will increase domestic violence. It is a cycle. If we d o not find a way to restore the services, we are destroying a community and we will not be able to fix it easily.
Noah Law : That is incredibly disturbing to hear.

Chair : Noha, it sounds like you are describing hell and it is getting worse. I hope that the international community hears what you are saying and a solution is negotiated fast because it take s away future potential —

Noha Yehya : C an I add something ? T h e international community, by cutting fund ing , is adding another kind of violence against women in Yemen , especially in the north. W e are punishing them for being in places where the Houthis are. We do not give them money or services because they are there. It is heartbreaking and, I am sorry to say, unhumanitarian .
Chair : I agree.
Q24 Noah Law : Can I make a quick clarification, please ? How much of what you have described is about cuts versus the restrictions that Konstantinos referred to earlier?

Noha Yehya : There is a restriction of access but, for the national NGOs, we have our own way to provide services for women. We are an experienced organisation and we have been there for decades. We are using informal trust an d personal relationships to ensure that we have access to women and provide services in any way. We are always sensitive to the situation and know how to reach women. Restrictions are difficult ; they take time and expose our team to risk. Our team and national teams working in humanitarian areas , especially in GBV, are exposing themselves to risk at a level no humanitarian in any other country would accept. W e do not have any protection from the state or humanitarian actors. We do not even have policies to protect our staff. We are implementing partners. Not all donors or organisations can provide us with this kind of protection. We know our ways. For years, we have been working with restrictions , but the restrictions do not mean that we will not find a way to do our job.

Q25 Sam Rushworth : Can I ask one question that is off script? Noha, th ank you for talking with such candour about some really challenging situations people are facing. You have talked about some services that are being provided to women to relieve suffering. Are there also any civil society level forms of resistance ? T o what extent is it possible for women to organise and challenge Government around their rights in this space?

Noha Yehya : I t is not easy. It has exposed them to a different kind of risk. Y ou can consider me an example. Because I was talking about so many issues in an online meeting , I am out of my country, under stress, away from my family , and cannot go back . This is the risk we are facing if we speak out , but it does not mean that women will stop speaking out. We will find a way. Things will change. We will keep negotiating. Despite all the problems that we are facing in th is situation, we manage to negotiate with the Houthis. We find a way. For example, they do not want anyone to talk about GBV. We can talk about economic empowerment though ; we can provide services for GBV . It is a matter of knowing the context, having the language to talk with Government and authorities, and the trust level between civil society and the authorities. It takes a long time to get approvals , but in the end we get the approvals.
Q26 Sam Rushworth : I want to change topic now and talk about humanitarian aid access. Would you mind setting out what you see as the main barriers to humanitarian aid in the area?
Noha Yehya : Humanitarian aid access?
Sam Rushworth : Yes.
Noha Yehya : In general or for women and girls?
Sam Rushworth : You can speak to both.

Noha Yehya : I n general, there are different dynamics in the n orth and the s outh. In the n orth, we have the Houthis and we need a lot of approvals. They ask for details ; s ometimes they try to force us to provide the name s of staff with their addresses and mobile number s — private information — in order to give us permission to implement. We do not do it. It is a problem that might delay implementation of some activities in the field. As for physical movement, as I mentioned earlier, for access to women and girls we now need m ahram. This is one of the biggest challenge s . Women cannot move around to either get a service or provide a service unless she is accompanied by a man or get s written permission by a man so that she can move freely or provide services. At the country level for other humanitarian actors, they are usually requested to provide a list of the beneficiaries, which is against humanitarian principles. No one can provide this i nformation. T here are also sensitive areas in Yemen, both in the n orth and the s outh . T hey can give you permission to work there, but you will be monitored. You can be force d to hire among your team people who you know are monitoring your work.
Sam Rushworth : If I understand it correctly, it is more difficult in the n orth than in the s outh but not impossible thinking about —
Noha Yehya : It is more difficult in the n orth definitely than the s outh. In the s outh, we have this armed group that is also doing these things , not in Aden but in some other governorates.

Q27 Sam Rushworth : It is not impossible to get humanitarian assistance in, but the effect of monitoring is severe. I n terms of your organisation, how does that sense of being constantly monitored impact on you ?

Noha Yehya : As I told you, we are all monitored. All the women who are working in protection and in GBV are monitored. It is a matter of how clear you are with the authorities. If you provid e full details about what you are planning to do and necessary information then it may take long er . It might take a lot of mutual trust. It might need a lot of personal relations between some authorities in order to manage and get permissions to implement. It is not an easy way. It is the only way many national NGOs ha ve to implement , but i t does not mean that we compromise o ur humanitarian principle s . It does not mean we are trying to work against these principles. As nationals, we always find a way to negotiate it. We are Yemenis at the end of the day, either north or south.

Q28 Noah Law : T o come back briefly to the question of the UK’s impact , y ou mentioned that your programme is one of the main implementations of the FPA. T o what extent do you believe the UK is responsible versus the broader global cuts to that programme ? Does the UK have a very specific role and contribution that it is failing to meet?

Noha Yehya : T he UK can advocate and provide funds to Yemen. It can support a diplomatic process for peacebuilding. It can do a lot. By providing funds to us, and I will talk about women and girls , you are helping the community in other ways. You are helping the peacebuilding process. Without wom e n empowerment and the inclusion of women, we cannot talk . W e cannot speak about genuine peacebuilding. There is no real peacebuilding. I f we want real peacebuilding, we need women to be part of the transitional justice. If women are excluded because of this violence , cannot get services , be empowered or be included , then this will not help the stability of Yemen. The UK and FCDO can do a lot of things to support Yemen.

When we talk about locali sa tion, the majority of organisations that work in the north are national NGOs. The UN was in both north and south, but it was forced to move its operation to the south. Only national NGOs have been left behind in the north , trying to fight and not collapse due to the lack of funding. N egotiating and returning operations of the UN to the north will help national NGOs respond. It will improve the f unding situation in the north as well .
Q29 Noah Law : A re you mainly feeling that hit through the fact that UNFPA has been cut? I s there anything the UK can do to fill the void?

Noha Yehya : Help us to respond diplomatically and financially. This is what we need . I f I say only financially, it does not mean there will be stability. W e can work on stability diplomatically and financially .

Q30 Sam Rushworth : Noha, t hank you very much for those responses. I am conscious of the time and what we still need to get through. This is a question that I am going to pose to our other participants. It is about the protections in place for aid workers. El-Khidir, could you share your experience of what protection is in place. Konstantinos, is there anything you would like to add on this topic before I com e back to the C hair and move on?

El-Khidir Daloum : T hank you very much. Aid workers are at the front line and are always there. We are tr ying to do everything under our duty of care for the people who work and serve and the people we serve. We are very conscious of the transfer of risk, including to co-operating partners. Even when we are working with international or national NGOs or civil societies, we are try ing to do our level best.
