Someone has already mentioned interpreters; in primary care, there is a standard that, when you are working with an interpreter, you have double the length of the appointment. That has never been applied to maternity services, and that cannot help with developing those relationships.
Q36 Do midwives need to return to case holding so that they have a better relationship with their patients?

On the return to case holding, we strongly recommend putting your efforts into strong continuity during the antenatal period and the post - natal period w hen it comes to organisation, particularly around midwives . Y ou should be able to organise it so that a midwife does the same clinic on the same day every week—it should not be that difficult—and then sees the women back at home. We are not recommending intrapartum continuity. That was attempted, with great efforts, after “Better Births” in 2016.

Q37 I will move on to the questions that I am supposed to be asking—that just struck me as one of the things going on. You have talked about the need for Government action to ensure clinical capacity and escalation pathways, including at weekends. Is that possible, given the other pressures on maternity at the moment?

What we found, again, was huge variation across the country in terms of seniority of cover, particularly out of hours. In some places, it is about the availability of senior—and senior can mean very senior residents or consultants. Often, where you had patchy coverage, particularly out of hours, when you looked at the workforce, these trusts had difficulty staffing their rotas, as a minimum. Baroness Amos spoke to that in terms of the geographical challenges that many of the trusts experienced, in terms of not just their demographics but recruitment at midwifery level and doctor level, and also in the allied specialties that are required.

Q38 Very quickly, you talked about the NHS workforce plan, and it is probably too late for us to influence that. But given the cost of training for an individual, do you think that midwifery training is currently an appealing thing for a young person to go into, particularly given the pressures?
I will hand over to my colleague.
Sorry, I didn’t hear the question.
You talked about the need for more people to come through. Given the cost of training for individuals and the pressures in the system, do you think that a career in midwifery is currently appealing?

I would say we still have some of the best midwifery education in the world, which is regulated by the NMC and delivered through very high-calibre training courses in HEIs and other places. There is no shortage of people wanting to be midwi ves, despite all the publicity and all the pressures they are well aware they will be entering into.

You are probably asking the wrong person, because I am from Wales, where, if you train for an NHS position, the Government pick up your tuition fees. It is not in the report, but I would strongly support that. We need to be supporting our students and looking at all the variety of ways to train individuals.
Q39 Is retention the problem, rather than recruitment?

Retention is absolutely a problem. We need to make changes. The retirement age for NHS staff coming in now is 67; we need to restructure careers so that we can give them longevity. We need good preceptorship programmes to support our more junior staff. There is a peculiar issue with—
Q40 So w hat do we need to see in the upcoming workforce plan?

In the workforce plan, we particularly need to look at careers for midwives, so that they can progress into specialist roles but retain a clinical, hands-on component. Maternity is a safety-critical service that runs 24 hours a day, seven days a week, but at the moment many of our senior midwives finish work at 5 o’clock . U nits are being staffed out of hours by relatively junior staff, who are excellent but need support. We need to restructure those careers to support our junior staff and give postgraduate training to midwives, which is currently more or less completely lacking.

Q41 Baroness Amos’s report notes that 67% of midwives are experiencing burnout and 65% of doctors are at risk of burnout. I should declare an interest: I used to work for the GMC and work on the national training survey. Last year, it found that 63% of trainee doctors in obstetrics and gynaecology had a heavy or very heavy workload, compared with 42% across the rest. What can be done to support our trainee doctors and midwives, just to make the training pathways safer?

In terms of that general support , one thing we say in our report is that it is important to look at the range of our expectations of our doctors and midwives to make sure that there is sufficient time for them to do the things we want them to do—particularly around the areas of listening and tackling racism, discrimination and so on—and that sufficient time is built into rotas and appointments. What you have at the moment is a system where everyone is expected to meet standards and to have long conversations in very short periods of time, which puts pressures on the women and families and on the doctors and midwives.
Q42 So where I started is where we should end: the pressure on midwives and doctors is leading to a breakdown in the doctor-patient relationship, which brings up safety concerns. Is that correct?
Yes, in some instances.
I am sorry to say that we have to end this first panel. I am grateful for your time.
Examination of witness
Witness: Donna Ockenden.
Q43 Welcome, Donna Ockenden. It is such a pleasure to have you with us; thank you very much. I am just going to get cracking.

Your report was heartbreaking to read. I cannot even imagine what you went through, but more especially what the families will have gone through in its preparation. What were some of the challenges that you faced in pulling it together, and what choice things are you very keen about? It was a massive report, talking to thousands of families, but what does it boil down to in the end for you?

It boils down to two very similar things: lack of listening to women and families, but also lack of listening to staff, and that is where Nottingham was different from Shrewsbury. Some of you may have seen my presentation to the taskforce last week, where we showed that what staff on the ground were saying was almost identical to what women and families were saying.

Secondly, it is really important to say that we all have to be born and, at some point, we all die. We were deeply , deeply shocked when 18 families came forward to raise concerns about after-death care; that opened up a new avenue that I never thought my team and I would have to go down. That is now, I hope, leading to national work.

The pressure that ordinary staff on the ground are under on a daily basis is really important as well. We spoke to more than 830 ordinary staff on the ground—midwives, obstetricians, anaesthetists and so on. There were disappointing numbers of former senior leaders who came forward. But those staff that did come forward—really brave midwives, obstetricians, support workers and so on—described years upon years of raising concerns right up to board level and being disregarded in the same way that women were.

Q44 Of course, several police investigations are under way. We will have to be very careful in our questioning that we do not stray over that. You will have seen an intervention by the former Secretary of State, Wes Streeting. He wrote to us to say that we should be using our privilege to name and shame, but also calling in front of us, some of those executives who refused to give you evidence. Do you think that is a good idea and something we should look at? Perhaps even more importantly, what was missing from your report as a result of them not giving you evidence? What did you hope to hear from them that you feel might not have been reflected in your work?

I think there is a difference between staff on the ground , who are living the reality of, in most cases, trying to deliver the best care they can , and then executive leaders . I would stress that these are recent , former executive leaders , and I want to be really clear that all the executives at the trust came forward as requested. Clearly, there is going to be a difference in focus , because a recent , former executive leader is going to have been responsible for the leadership of the trust, hearing staff concerns and hearing concerns from women and families . So there would have been an extra strand of information that we would have wished to get from those former leaders , but that we did not.

I am grateful, Chair , that you mentioned the police investigation , so I do not think that I should comment any further on who may or may not have come forward, because I am still awaiting police advice on that.
Q45 Understood. We will leave that alone.

You will have seen that Jim Mackey put out a 10- point urgent maternity plan following the publication of your review and then the Amos review, which was more or less co- concurrent. Did you speak to him about the plan? Do you think the plan is the right one? What involvement did you have?
I was not told about the plan until it was out there on Radio 4 and so on.
Q46 Now that you have seen it, do you like it? Is it along the right lines?

What I would say, and I have said this very clearly since my report was published, is that we do not have the luxury of time now. The current conversation, as I understand it, is that the taskforce is going to take up to six months for an action plan. What I would say, having heard from thousands —and I mean thousands— of families and colleagues on the ground across all the professions since we published on 24 June, is that we know what we need to do to improve on perinatal safety. So I did urge the Government to move at pace. We set out a really comprehensive suite of immediate and essential actions — I do not use the word “ recommendations ” , by the way — agreed by families, royal colleges and so on back in 2022. There was partial introduction , even though the then Secretary of State—
Q47 What has happened? Let us be really frank about it. Why has that not just been implemented wholesale?

My honest belief is that, had we maintained the Secretary of State at the time, the right hon. Sajid Javid MP, I think we would have got there , because he took an enormous amount of time to understand what my team and I were saying. We will all remember that there was a lot of churn and change at the top. I think I am now working with or for my 12th Secretary of State for Health since 2016, which is obviously of concern. Whenever there is that change, there is a risk that we lose our way, even though we know what our way needs to be.
So the chopping and changing—
Doesn’t help.
It doesn’t help. I will pass over to Dr Beccy Cooper.

Q48 As I said to Baroness Amos, I represent Worthing in Sussex , and you are due to commence a review in October with the families in Sussex . University Hospital s Sussex has obviously taken on the recommendations from the Amos review and has looked at your Nottingham review. There are over 100 recommendations from both . It is on a 100 - day sprint for the Amos review. What is your review going to bring to Sussex ? You said you have spoken to so many people and are seeing similar patterns— horrific, tragic patterns. For the families and teams in Sussex , and the other reviews that are going to happen as well, can you talk about the additionality of those reviews?

An Ockenden review — there are hundreds of people behind me in my team, by the way — has two purposes. First of all , it is to find answers for families that they may not yet have had , but equally something we have done in the last three years in Nottingham is talk to huge numbers of staff . I can tell you that University Hospitals Sussex staff are already coming forward in large numbers to say, “ Can we talk to you and your team , Donna? ”

In terms of the last three years , and this will be rolled out in Sussex , w e did not just hand Nottingham a great big purple report . We had bi-monthly— every two months — learning and improvement meetings where we fed back to the trust the things we were hearing from their own staff and from families that they needed to do , and then we looked at their evidence on an ongoing basis. I can say with confidence that Nottingham has put in place a lot of the learning throughout the process ; it is not about waiting for three years for Ockenden to finish her work. As you are a local MP, I am sure we will be in touch on a regular basis. I want to reassure Sussex and Leeds MPs about the way we do things.

Q49 I asked Baroness Amos about recommendations in her review complementing the recommendations that will doubtlessly come out of your Sussex and Leeds review and previous reviews. Do you see large areas of overlap and complementing recommendations for the trusts and for letting families hear about improvements?

Yes. Having been in and around perinatal services since 1989, which is a very long time, I think that we often know what we need to do, but we simply do not get on and do it. That is one of the issues that we face at the moment—albeit I still think it is absolutely vital that staff on the ground get to have their views heard. We will work very hard with UHS staff on the ground. Families deserve answers. There is something about the system that means that parents are waiting years for answers and staff voices are still silenced. We have to get that right.

Q50 Baroness Amos said earlier that the taskforce will have the job of prioritising what they go after first, second and third. Paulette has just left the room, but she and I sit on one of the expert reference groups that will feed into the taskforce. What should be feeding into the taskforce as the top priority that we should be going after? We need to do it all—t hat was made clear, and I am sure you would agree—but what is the top priority in your area?

There are priorities that are interlinked. First, listening to women, families and staff on the ground is one. That is absolutely vital and the golden thread, but we will not achieve that until we have a comprehensive perinatal workforce tool—I am a midwife and a nurse, but it is not about midwifery and nursing—that tells us what we need. We know that we have gaps across many rotas, including obstetric rotas, and we have vacancies in midwifery and neonatal units that are under significant pressure.

I do not believe that we have ever had a perinatal workforce tool. That needs to be funded, so you might say to me, “Where’s the money?” We are already spending vast of money on compensation for harm when none of the money in the world will bring back what families have lost or compensate staff for the moral injury that they suffer on a daily basis. I have heard from hundreds of doctors and midwives—hundreds—in the last four weeks saying, “We don’t know how much longer we can take this.” I have heard obstetricians saying, “I am not sure now, Don, that I can actually complete my training,” and midwives saying, “Is tomorrow going to be the day I hang up my uniform for the last time?” Time is not on our side, Chair.

Q51 Good morning. I would like to focus on accountability, because I understand that your review highlighted the impact of poor organisational culture and leadership. What does accountability in this space mean to you?

It is about truth-telling, hearing and taking the action that one is in public office for. There has to be a sense of responsibility. If we take the aspect of after-death care in Nottingham, there has to be accountability for what happened to those families. It is myriad things brought together under one umbrella.
Q52 Does the lack of accountability in organisational structures in itself lead to some of the failings that we have seen?

I think it has. For example—this is in the report—50 midwives and maternity staff wrote to the chairman of the board in 2018, and they did not get a response, so they tried again in 2019. They were so worried that they told the board that babies would die in 2018, but nothing was done. In 2019, in Nottingham, an inquest got halted, which is really unusual. The coroner read out that letter to be supportive both of the families and of the staff on the ground. That is an absolute failure of accountability.

Q53 We heard in the previous panel from, I think, Christine Ekechi on the question whether you can have outstanding maternity services in a poorly performing trust. I think the answer was that, if you can, it is despite the system, not because of it. It is about the leadership at trust level rather than necessarily within a maternity service itself. Would you echo that? Is it about addressing poor leadership at the very top of trusts, or looking more at where the maternity services operate?

I think it is both. I know of some outstanding maternity units with outstanding leaders. Having been around as long as I have, I know of many outstanding board leaders, but if we take obstetrics and midwifery now, I know many brilliant consultant obstetricians and consultant neonatologists and they are saying to me, “We do not want these leadership positions.” I spoke to a doctor last week who said to me, “Maternity governance broke me. I had to walk away.” Leadership is there on the ward, on the day, interacting with women right up to board level and then commissioning level. There should be seamless leadership literally from ward to board.
A clear line of sight through?
Absolutely.
Q54 Why are they refusing to take those kinds of leadership position? Why are they saying that they do not want them?

The pressure. There are insufficient resources. To be clinical director of obstetrics or maternity governance, if you are very lucky, you may get one day of time, which is in no way sufficient. In some trusts, they are given half a day of time. These leadership positions are not respected. As I say, it breaks colleagues, which is really worrying.

Q55 In your report, you said that it was of particular concern that many of the issues were already known and that there had been several attempts to flag them throughout the years. Is the current regulatory framework fit for purpose?

That is a really good question. We have seen, throughout the duration of the Nottingham report, some improvement in the relationship between the main regulators, the General Medical Council, the Nursing and Midwifery Council and families, but that has been hard-won. It has been hard work, if I am honest. I am confident—I met with the GMC, NMC and CQC yesterday—that we are going to start the Leeds and Sussex reviews in a different place, with the regulators on the front foot, but I am going to speak as I find, and it has been extremely hard work to get to this place. It has taken three years of concerns raised by families and by me. I think we are in the last chance saloon. We are going to push really hard to get this effective relationship between families and regulators for Sussex and Leeds. I am pretty confident that we can, but I will have my eye on it, believe me.
Q56 Why do you think the regulators have not really performed in this space up until now?

It is really interesting. If we take Nottingham as an example, because that is the place I know best and am most up to date with, there were lots of opportunities for regulators to understand. HM Coroner in Nottinghamshire is really active. There were lots of inquest verdicts where negligence was ruled and deep concerns about the care, yet the regulators were not aware of those cases. I know that HM Coroner invited the regulators on multiple occasions to attend inquests. There were significant lost opportunities.
Q57 Is it how they operate? Is it because they are not taking a proactive approach or looking at the system as a whole, or is there something else going on?

I think they have not, to date, but there have been some very honest conversations between families and regulators, and myself and regulators. I see that we have green shoots of recovery, but I will be keeping a very close eye on it for the duration of the Sussex and Leeds reviews.

Q58 I am always interested in where the accountability lies in a healthcare system. For a constituency MP and service user, it is quite hard to see people who are often paid a lot of money seemingly fail upwards in their career progression within a system that fails and continues to fail. I do not want to go into the individual level because there is an ongoing police investigation, but it feels as if you are saying less that there are individual failures of leadership and more that the system itself is not set up to support those leadership roles to be effective. Is that right?

It is both. We are all accountable for what we do. From the minute I open my eyes in the morning, I am accountable for the work that I do. All of us in public service in the NHS, whether we are in a leadership role, the midwife on the ground or the obstetrician on the labour ward, are accountable, but I do not think that the system as it is currently set up supports staff to be always able to do the best they can and deliver things the way they want to.
Q59 What would you change in that space?

The key issue is that we need to look at why we are allowing so much maternity harm—we are talking billions of pounds—to happen in this country and why we are allowing so many staff to feel damaged by their everyday working life, and say, “The tide has now got to turn. It has to turn.”

Q60 We have heard a lot from Baroness Amos’s review and your work about the failure to listen to women and families. The previous panel touched on what this means practically in consultation and conversations about birth choice and how it can be affected. I want to focus on what it means systematically because of time, though if you want to add anything about how to build that into decision making in clinical practice, we would be very happy to hear it. Do you have thoughts on how patient and family voice can be embedded more systematically within trusts, unit decision making and governance arrangements? Is that something you think needs to happen?

Yes, absolutely. Among the thousands of families that we spoke to, there were countless illustrations of women, husbands and families not being listened to. That can be a time issue, without a doubt. Not having time to care is really important, and we have to be honest that it is a daily feature of life in perinatal care in this country. Again, it is about resetting the ship. We have heard that these things were happening in Morecambe Bay, East Kent and Shrewsbury. We still have not done enough to turn that ship around.

Q61 Are families and parents often represented on trust boards or in their governance arrangements? In my experience, many of the governance boards tend to be older or retired people. Are there peer groups or family groups right from the top in governance arrangements of trusts or units? Are they embedded in peer-reviewing the unit for family-centred practice? As well as hearing the mother and family’s choice about their birth, is the voice of families and parents reflected right through how trusts are run?

We had contact with families over a three-year period in Nottingham. As women and babies are now discharged so early from maternity care, sometimes it was up to me and my team say to the trust, “Are you not aware what has happened to Mrs Jones or Mrs Ali? Do you not know that she is at home struggling with the most appalling health problems?” We did make some differences. We had to set up an escalation pathway in Nottingham for families’ urgent care needs, whether it was brain-injured children or mothers needing colorectal support, that the trust was completely unaware of.

We have seen some real improvements in Nottingham in terms of engagement with the local communities. However, when I got to Nottingham late 2022, I said, “How do I meet with the Roma community? How do I meet with the Jewish community? How do I meet with the most disadvantaged women?” and got a blank face in response. I had to go across the city and the county and find those groups for myself, which I have done. I have reintroduced them to the trust, but they were not in the best place at the start of this review.

Q62 Are there any systematic approaches that you have seen that work well? A trust board is probably worried about their A&E times and their bed occupancy rates, and they are under huge financial pressure. It sounds like quite a fundamental change is needed in the risks that they are looking at, who they are hearing, and how they are speaking to people to get their feedback.

What I have found in my years and years of working with community groups, listening to women and listening to families is that the NHS almost needs to turn itself on its head. People say, “Well, women over there are hard to reach,” which they absolutely are not; if women and families are asked, they will give freely of their experience. They will engage and put huge effort in, but there is a tendency to say, “Over there—hard to reach.” That is not a phrase that I will use at all.

Q63 Where people have turned it around and where they do listen, is there anything they specifically do? Is it making sure there is time on the board agenda? Is it having a representative for midwifery? Obviously, there is normally a chief nurse role, but is it having a specific midwifery voice at trust level? Is there anything that particularly works in hearing the staff and patient voice?

I spent many years—more than I can count—as a chief midwife. The relationship between the chief nurse, the chief midwife and the medical director is absolutely vital. I have seen many settings where that works very well.

It is also about ensuring that the services on the ground are resourced. It is important how much we in the NHS expect women and families to do free of charge. Some of the Nottingham families have virtually worked full time supporting community engagement and making sure that they liaise with other families who often would not be heard. We are not resourcing that at all for those families.
Q64 More resource and peer support should be a focus for us?
Yes. It is very poorly resourced.

Q65 You said a moment ago that staff feel damaged by their everyday working lives. There is clearly a crisis in staffing levels across many of the settings that you have reviewed, including Nottingham more recently. I note that a recent Royal College of Midwives survey published last month showed 77%—more than three quarters—of those who responded did not feel that their team or unit was safely staffed. That is something for us all to worry about. Some 93% felt that staffing levels affected the quality of care they were able to provide for women and babies. That is extremely shocking, and presumably that is at the base of why circumstances such as those at Nottingham arise. How do we overcome that? How do we attract the right people into post and attract sufficient numbers of them to be able to support each other?

There are a number of issues here. There is recruitment, but there has to be retention. I talk to midwives and doctors on a daily basis. If they are doing a 12-hour shift, they do not even have time to go to the loo.

The big issue is that we do not have time to waste—we have to develop that perinatal workforce strategy that tells us, “These are the number of obstetricians, these are the number of obstetric anaesthetists, and these are the number of midwives.” Until we do that, we do not even understand yet what we need. That cannot be tolerated any more.
Q66 Does that need to be mandated?

It was an immediate and essential action from Ockenden, not a recommendation. It was something that we worked on with all the royal colleges—midwives, obstetricians, anaesthetists and so on. I am a midwife, but it was not about me being precious about midwifery. It was about saying that maternity is not an island and there is a big team of people who are required to deliver safe care. I do not think we have done enough towards that yet, but I am confident that the royal colleges were absolutely involved in the drafting and crafting of that immediate and essential action.
Q67 Is there now a mandated framework?
Not as far as I know. I was at the taskforce that the ERG uses last week. I do not know what the outcome was from that, but I was really clear—
I think that the taskforce is meeting this week, so it feeds in.
Right. I was really clear that we do not have six months to wait.

Q68 Is that in relation to the number of antenatal and post-natal beds? Are they sufficient in number? In many settings, it seems that often women are discharged in antenatal circumstances when perhaps that is unwise, simply because there are insufficient beds.

Yes. I saw it in Nottingham, but what I hear from all my colleagues in Newcastle down to Cornwall is that, as one real doctor on shift last week said, “We are trying to deliver safe care with at least one hand tied behind our back,” because they have not got sufficient neonatal cots. The infrastructure was lovely in 1998 or whatever.

Maternity and perinatal estates are also of vital importance. I spoke to a doctor not very far from your constituency and he said to me, “I was doing emergency drills and I had to take my junior doctors out on the patio by the bereavement suite and hope that the suite wasn’t needed, because I did not have anywhere else to take my resident doctors to train them in emergency drills.” That was last week.

Q69 The report that you produced obviously had some shocking and extremely distressing cases. It is very difficult to say, but in how many cases would you say that that was driven not just by an attitude and a way of speaking to patients, but by the pressure of inadequate staffing levels?

Inadequate staffing in Nottingham was well known by the board—and there have been multiple iterations of the board—going back at least to 2010. Staff were raising concerns going back to that time, and parents started whistleblowing in 2016. There were many years of inaction. However, we also need to be clear that there was a cabal of people in that unit who led the way, and both staff and families said a small group of people were allowed to infect the unit. Again, staff on one—
Q70 Are we talking at the clinical or leadership level?

Within the division—it was both. “Infect” the unit is a very strong word. However, staff and families both said it without ever having talked to each other in the middle. I think that behaviours play an important part and poor behaviour that was tolerated definitely played an important part. It is important to say that staffing was a long-term and known board issue with no action.

Q71 In terms of the Government’s response and the proposal to invest £10.6 million into the recruitment of additional band 5 midwives, band 5s are paid at £31,000. Are you going to attract the right kind of people with the right capacity into that post with pay at that level?

As I understand it, band 5 midwives are very newly qualified. I know from my experience in Nottingham that when one invests in large numbers of newly qualified midwives, you have to have the preceptorship support programme because they are very, very junior.

I have seen some good practice in that. After Shrewsbury, University College Hospital in London invested in what it called Ockenden-retention midwives—I checked recently and these posts are still in place—where very senior midwives are there literally to hold the hands of and support newly qualified midwives in the first year to 18 months of their career. I then hear from elsewhere in the country that midwives are put under quite a lot of pressure to get their band 6 competencies. I do not think that the good practice I have seen and heard of is by any means rolled out across the country.

Q72 In the past, to become a midwife you would become a registered nurse and then do your midwifery as a postgraduate. A lot of experienced midwives believe that being trained simply as a midwife and working in the more limited clinical perspective landscape has created less capable midwives, given the range of complexities that they may be presented with. In your experience, does that sound reasonable?

I trained in the olden days: nurse first, midwife afterwards. I think there is room for both. I would very much like to see more registered nurses, perhaps with ITU or surgical experience, join midwifery. We need to look carefully at the training programme currently offered to qualified midwives as a stand-alone profession. They do not have that nursing background, but I think there is room for both.
Okay, thank you. I was looking for your facial response when the issue of Dr Kirkup and the Amos review came up, and the issue of natural birth ideology was under discussion.
That is someone else’s question.
Q73 If you don’t mind, may I ask this? Given your perspective across a number of inquiries, would you say there is an issue in relation to non-clinical groups campaigning for such things?

In Nottingham, we used the phrase “normalisation of deviance”, where we found significant evidence that women who were no longer normal were being denied the care and treatment they needed. That is the phrase that we used—“normalisation of deviance”—and sadly there are lots of examples of that with tragic outcomes in Nottingham.

Q74 You have read the Amos review and heard the evidence given today. There is clearly a lot of agreement between you and Baroness Amos in the review. But when The Standard approached you, you said, “I don’t see anything that we didn’t already know, that hasn’t already been spelled out very clearly.” Do you think the report adds anything significantly, and how do you see it playing out and interacting with your reports and reviews?

Having spent decades in and around maternity care, this is now my second inquiry, and Sussex and Leeds will be my third and fourth inquiries. I think that what we have amassed over many years has been a vast amount of knowledge on maternity and neonatal care that we simply have not acted quickly enough on. If I had been shocked—I did read the Baroness Amos report from cover to cover, burning the midnight oil—I think probably I would not have been doing my job properly, because a lot of what was in there, as we have said, is very similar to Dr Kirkup’s previous work in East Kent and Morecambe Bay and in my Shrewsbury review. So, I think that is the issue.

Q75 I pointed out that there were a number of areas of agreement in your reports. Were there specific areas where you felt the recommendations were not helpful, something you would not recommend or where you did have disagreements with Baroness Amos’s report?

I mentioned the normalisation of deviance to your colleague. We definitely saw that in Shrewsbury, and we very definitely saw many women being denied the treatment that they needed, with tragic outcomes.
Q76 Why do you think you were able to pick that up, but Baroness Amos—

I cannot answer that question. I know what we did. We had interaction from 2,511 cases and we heard from so many staff on the ground who said , “W e were under pressure to discharge : ‘Get them out the door .’” And then the re were the appalling behaviours that you may have seen on a recent BBC programme . E xtremely rude things were written on whiteboards in labour wards . Basically, there was this culture of “get them out the door ”. There are many issues, but staff told us and families told us , and y es, we believe them.

Q77 One recommendation that Baroness Amos made was about doctors working on site at weekends. You said that that would not make a difference —“a bsolutely not ” was your phrase . Why were you so clear that it would not make a difference ?

Again, we h eard from very many obstetricians in Nottingham , and my team heard from people in places ranging from Newcastle right down to Cornwall . These are d octors who will be on their labour wards today and on the weekend. And what all these colleagues and the hundreds of colleagues who have contacted me since are saying is , “We are spread so thinly on the ground. Where are these people going to come from? ” I get midwives telling me this on a daily basis . M aybe it will be their day off tomorrow. They will wake up tomorrow morning —they are in these famous WhatsApp groups for when the unit is short - staffed and they say that day in, day out, managers are saying, “We know you have a day off today. Is there a ny chance you can come in?” or “You have mandatory training tomorrow . B ring in your uniform because you probably won’t spend the whole day training. ” So , the pressure that staff on the ground are under is deeply concerning.

Q78 To drill down a bit more into the denial of caesarean sections, which you saw very clearly in your report , that may be down to clinical reasons or to id eological reasons. Your report suggests very clearly that it was ideological. If we as a Committee are trying to make recommendations , but we have on the one hand your investigations and reviews , which say, “This is definitely a national problem ,” and we have on the other hand Baroness Amos ’s review , which says, “Well, i t isn’t,” how do you back your argument up? What evidence should we be looking for to ensure that we can support what you are saying? W here can you point us?

I would point you to “ Intrapartum Care” , which is the l abour chapter and gave lots of examples, the “A ntenatal Care” chapter, the chapter on women ’ s voices and the chapter on staff voices. That ’s Nottingham. Shrewsbury is now four years old , b ut there was significant evidence there. Of course, Dr Kirkup is a very well - respected colleague . He has done East Kent , and he has done the Morecambe Bay report , which goes back to 2015.
Q79 I know you can’t predict this, but would you be surprised if similar pressures and issues were in , for example, the Sussex area , which you are about to look at ?

W e will have to wait and see , but yes, I have spoken to women who have used all four units in Sussex and increasing numbers of staff are coming forward. The jury is out, so to speak . W e will approach our work with absolute diligence , and we will ensure that women and family voices and staff voices are heard , reported and acted o n.

Q80 On the Amos review, do you feel that the six - month timeframe, given that it has told us nothing that you had not already said somewhere , is the right timeframe or do you think it should try to do its work faster?
Do you mean the taskforce creating the action plan?
Yes.

I have to speak as I find , and I have said that we don’t have the luxury of six months . And that is an action plan by the end of the year. How long does it take , once the action plan is out and Christmas and everything is done , to then get that implemented? If we were to look at how many midwives will hang up their uniforms in the next six months , how many doctors will decide they can ’t do this anymore and how much harm potentially could be caused , I would say that we do n’t have six months to create an action plan. That would be my view.
Q81 On the question of a statutory public inquiry, which has been picked up by a number of families across the country , what is your view? Valerie Amos ’s was in the negative.

I think it w ill be important for the Committee to listen to famil y view s, and I did ask them if they were able to attend , as you had requested me to. I understand where families are coming from. The vast majority of families that I have known , over decades , say that they want two things: they want not only answers, but assurance that what happened to them will not happen to anyone else. Where they are left sitting at the moment is that not enough has been done to give them that confidence, so I fully appreciate where they are coming from.
If I had to press you for an answer, do you back it or not? Baroness Amos was a no at this stage. Is the jury still out, on balance?
The jury is still out. I note that the Secretary of State has said he is not taking anything off the table.

Q82 This has been interesting. Thank you for your work. It is extraordinary and very important. To come back to the action plan and maternity commissioner, I get the sense that you feel that the action plan could be written in a week.
I think it should be done by now.
Q83 A week since your report and Baroness Amos’s, and you think it should be done by now. Given your experience, why do you think that the Government think it needs to take six months?

I do not know, because as I explained to Dr Cooper, throughout the Nottingham report, we were meeting very senior NHS leaders, we were meeting the trust and we were keeping them informed of our findings—we will do that throughout Sussex, too, I promise you. That is probably the reason why I would say, “Why are we saying we need six months to write an action plan?” There was enough knowledge—
Q84 And the money behind it, maybe?

We are spending the money already—we have to be really clear that we are spending the money on the cost of harm, not that that can ever compensate families for what they go through. I am sure some very clever economists somewhere could say, “We are spending this on harm. How do we turn that back around into better care?” I am not an economist, but I am sure there must be a clever will and a way somewhere.

Q85 As I mentioned—we have talked about this already with Baroness Amos—the Government announced that they are going to create this maternity and neonatal commissioner role. I think you have said that you do not want to take on the role yourself—
I haven’t been asked!
Q86 If you were asked, would you take it on?

Well, I think we would have to understand more about what the role was and what resources underpinned it. First of all, a maternity commissioner has been asked for in multiple reports, going right back to Baroness Gohir in 2022 and further, so this is not the first time around the fence.
Q87 It has been agreed, though, hasn’t it?

Yes, it is probably the first time it has been agreed. Clearly, we would have to understand what the powers were and what the infrastructure was behind it, because I do not think that one person can fix everything.
Q88 Do you see a world in which—with the appropriate infrastructure, resources and powers—it would be helpful, or not?
Potentially, yes.
Q89 Would you be more interested yourself in helping to do that if all those things were in place?
Well, I have quite a lot on at the moment.
Q90 I think that brings it to a close, but I will restate it: you do see a role, properly resourced, for the maternity commissioner.
Potentially, yes. I think I would want to know more about it.

Q91 My last quick question is this. We are going to have six months—we have major comments on the length of time—for the plan to be developed. The commissioner would come in only some months after that, even. W ould that make the job more challenging, or is it still doable?

My understanding is that the request is for the commissioner to co-chair the taskforce—I think that is what I heard today, and that would be a good thing—with the Secretary of State. I guess every effort would then need to be made so the commissioner was not responsible for introducing work they might not have had influence on. That is one reason why we need to move at speed and at pace with this action plan.
Q92 Because it is statutory, which is a good thing, it can take a bit of time. It is going to be brought in with the Health Bill, and that is not going to come to its end for a few months.
I think time is not on our side.
You could have a plan next week, but a commissioner might not be in place for another eight months.
Exactly, and that is a concern.
Q93 So we need to bounce ahead, even without a commissioner. Then the commissioner is going to come up and say, “What have you been doing? You’ve got it all wrong”—or not.
I don’t know. We will have to see.

Q94 We heard from the last panel that it was suggested that the commissioner should have the power to compel the creation of new datasets and so on. What other powers is it critical that the commissioner has—powers that might, for example, be written into legislation? Can you be specific about that, so we can recommend it?

Yes. I was really moved to hear all the discussion in the House about the Hillsborough law. It was really moving. I do think that compelling people to speak is really important. The role has to be resourced. The fact that it is on a statutory footing is really important, but the structure underpinning it has to be given considerable attention.
Q95 Who it is accountable to, and so on?
Absolutely.
Thank you very much.

sessions.iT: Pre-appointment hearing with the Government's preferred candidate for the Chair of the Financial Reporting Council
sessions.w: Dame Jayne-Anne Gadhia

segs.tx: Business and Trade Committee
Oral evidence: Pre-appointment hearing with the Government ’ s preferred candidate for the Chair of the Financial Reporting Council , HC 540
Tuesday 14 July 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 14 July 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Liam Byrne (Chair); Antonia Bance ; Chris Bloore; John Cooper; Alison Griffiths; Leigh Ingham ; Charlie Maynard; Mr Joshua Reynolds.
Questions 1 - 6 2
Witness
I : Dame Jayne-Anne Gadhia, Government ’ s preferred candidate for Chair, Financial Reporting Council .
Examination of witness
Witness: Dame Jayne-Anne Gadhia.

Q1 Welcome to today’s hearing of the Business and Trade Committee, which is a pre-appointment hearing. Dame Jayne-Anne Gadhia, you are very welcome; thank you for coming along today and for supplying the Committee with the background questionnaire that we issued last week.
Why don’t you kick us off by telling us why you want to be chair of the Financial Reporting Council?

First of all, thank you very much for having me, everyone. Thank you, Chair, for inviting me here. I am getting to the later stage of my career. I started off in a business that was then called Ernst & Whinney , it was such a long time ago, where I trained to be a chartered accountant through being an auditor. In many ways, it feels like I have come full circle in my career.

Accounting, auditing and corporate governance have always been important for me. During my time at Virgin Money, where I was the CEO for a number of years, we acquired Northern Rock during the financial crisis. It was quite clear that there were a number of governance issues that were leading towards the problems Northern Rock had, so I have also seen the importance of good corporate governance. This felt like very much the right thing to go for, based on the skills and experience that I have had over the years.
Q2 So the appeal is the opportunity to use your skills?

The appeal is that I understand, I think, what the FRC is trying to achieve. As you know, I am also the lead non-executive director at HMRC. As I get to the later stage of my career, I am enjoying working more in public businesses than I am in corporate businesses. That is where I would like to be for the years ahead, so I hope that this will be something where I can add a little bit to the public agenda as well as use my experience and background.
Q3 What is it that you think the FRC is trying to achieve?

Growth and regulation, so good, safe business that reports transparently. The UK is well known for sound financial reporting. That is important for incoming investment and for shareholders, and we have to have that platform at the FRC and in UK business to make sure that we can grow. Supporting the agenda of safety for the public interest and growth for the economy is something that I think we can play our part in.
Q4 What experience have you had in your career that means that you are especially well equipped to deliver on those objectives of the FRC?

I think that because I was so involved with the financial crisis, I am able to see the balance, if you like, that we need to achieve as a system and as a country between regulation, commerciality, growth and risk to come to a good outcome. It has always been something that really interests me.

To give you a little story about the Northern Rock years, I had set up Virgin Money with business partners back in the ’90s. RBS bought my business—the Virgin business—in the very late ’90s, and I stayed at RBS for a number of years before going back to Virgin in 2007. Of course, it was in summer 2007 that we first started seeing the cracks in the system where Northern Rock started to fail. Because I had run a mortgage business at RBS, I was setting one up at what became Virgin Money; Richard Branson was a trusted individual in the system at that time, and it felt to me as if we could bring something to help at the very beginning of the financial crisis with Northern Rock. We became the preferred bidder, and as a consequence, although I had not been responsible for the problems at Northern Rock, I could see where the problems came from. That led to a lot of close work with a number of regulators, the Bank of England, the Treasury and obviously with the business itself before, in the very end, post-crisis, Virgin Money acquired Northern Rock. Working out how all those different stakeholders work together was very important to me, and that is something I can bring to the FRC.
Q5 What from that experience crystalises something you would bring to chairing the FRC? I was not clear what lessons you were distilling from that story.

It is important to listen to all stakeholders and make sure that you are independent. That is of course important for the chair of any significant business, but particularly for an organisation that is in the public interest in this way. It is important to be clear on what you stand for. The problems with Northern Rock came from a lack of clarity about good purpose. Managing risk is really important—I learned that from Northern Rock—as is having good relationships with the Government, the regulators and your stakeholders to make sure that, as we drive forward on the regulatory agenda, it is something that is not being done to people, but being achieved collectively in a positive and constructive relationship.
We will get into the crisis that we think bedevils the accounting industry in a moment.

Q6 The role that we are talking about today is envisaged to be a commitment of about 10 days per month. You are currently the chair of OVO Energy, Shakespeare’s Globe, Ozone API, Moneyfarm, the audit committee of the Tate board of trustees and the Economy Honours Committee , as well as being the director of several other organisations. How will you find the time?

Certainly, in my non-executive career, I am as busy as I was in my executive career—and that is how I like it. It is an honour to do that and a privilege to be busy and to be in the thick of things. That said, I could not take on this role if I were not standing down from a number of the roles you have just identified. My 10-year term comes to an end at Tate on 17 November. It is a matter of public record that OVO Energy has been sold to E.ON. Both of those chair roles have been extremely enjoyable, but quite a heavy lift. I have also finished at Ozone, which is one of the ones you read out. There have been a number of changes, or upcoming changes, that mean I am happy to say I can manage this role within my timeframes.

Q7 That is still seven director or chair roles that you would hold, in addition to being the chair of the Financial Reporting Council. The Financial Reporting Council is 10 days a month; there are only 24 hours in a day and only so much you can do. Do you reckon those other seven roles work together with this? For example, how would you link being the lead non-exec director at HMRC and being the chair of the Financial Reporting Council for conflict of interest purposes, as well as just in terms of time?

Starting from the time perspective, I have been doing the independent non-executive director role at HMRC for a number of years, alongside all the roles you talked about there. I do not think I have ever missed anything important for HMRC, because it is important that I get involved with everything that I need to be involved with. You ask a busy person to do something, and you make sure it works.

I am very fortunate to be supported by an excellent assistant who manages my diary; I would not be able to manage my diary on my own because of that business. It is important that I have that, so from a time point of view I have no concern that I will be able to give the time required to the FRC to do what needs to be done. I can make that commitment to this Committee. I understand the importance of that and have no concerns about it.

From a conflict-of-interest perspective, I have spoken with both the permanent secretary of HMRC and of course the FRC about it, to make sure that everybody agrees there is no conflict of interest, and none of us see a conflict. This was something that I understand was reviewed by the DBT when I applied for the role. Everyone agrees there is no conflict there, not least because in a chair role you are not involved with the specific detail of some of the key cases, and certainly not in the world of tax.

It is important, from an HMRC perspective, where the board is mainly operational, and from an FRC perspective, that we are clear on the strategy and the role of the board, rather than the role of the executive. That means that, from a conflict-of-interest point of view, I am happy. If ever anything were to arise that appeared to be a conflict of interest, clearly the FRC and HMRC have rules that mean I would be able to recuse myself, but I do not anticipate that happening.

Q8 You said that you have someone who helps with your diary, which is incredibly important in that respect. How will you balance emergencies that require your immediate attention within the FRC with the other seven important roles that you hold? How will you balance those and be there for the FRC when you are needed on last-minute occasions?

The fact that we can do that online through Zoom or Teams is so important these days. That gives us a much more stretched timeframe in terms of the hours that we can give. I will always be there when I need to be there, either in person, which is always my preference, or online if need be.

Q9 Are you planning to stand down from any of the other roles that you have? You have mentioned OVO Energy, Ozone and the Tate’s board of trustees. Are there any others that you are planning on standing down from or departing?
Certainly there are some where I will be timed out.
Q10 Can you confirm which ones those are?

Not in public at the moment, because I have not said anything to those boards, but I will be managing my portfolio in order to make sure that I have the time to be as committed as possible to the role we are talking about.

Q11 As Mr Reynolds said, this is a 10-days-a-month role. You will still hold seven posts. That is only just over one day per role. We are pretty concerned about the overload. What more can you say to put our minds at rest?

Some of the roles, as important as they are, take up much less time than that. Mr Reynolds, you pointed out my role as chair of the Economy Honours Committee, for example. That meets four times a year, just to be clear. I am the director of a US business. I go to the US three times a year and I am there for two days. Obviously, there are calls between those meetings, but these are not roles that require me to commit 10 days to anybody else, if you see what I mean. They are in the diary, very structured and very manageable, and there are roles where I am not chair. From an FRC point of view, the time commitment is something that I am very happy to commit to.
Q12 Good afternoon. What do you see as the biggest problems inside the FRC’s brief, and what do you most want to get fixed?
Before I answer that question, I should say that I have not started yet, and I have known that I am being considered for this role only for the last week or so.

Quite clearly, there has been huge change at the FRC. So much of it has been positive, so we should definitely applaud the fact that the organisation has changed and that the profession has changed along the way. As I understand it, the quality of audits that are being reviewed has improved significantly over the last few years. I think it is important from an FRC point of view that that continues—that we continue to change, to challenge ourselves, to be better and to hold the industry to account for constantly improving audit. That is very important.

Q13 Could I ask you to be a bit more specific? Can I ask where you stand on various things and you can say whether you want to see them changed or not? Is putting the FRC on a statutory footing something you want to make happen or is it low down the priority list?

I think that is also high on the priority list. The reason for that is, of course, that it will give the FRC the opportunity to ensure that its funding comes in and that it has access to data on a statutory basis, whereas at the moment, as you know, it is on a voluntary basis. Giving us that platform is important, and it is definitely something that I will want to follow through on.

Q14 On audit reform, we have had the Kingman and Brydon reviews. In 2024, the Government said that they would go forward with audit reform and now they are not. Does that matter? What problems are presented by not going forward with audit reform?

I have given that quite a lot of thought, as you would imagine, and I am fortunate to come in with clarity. I know that over the last several years there has been a lot of talk, not least in this Committee, about the importance of audit reform. I know that my future colleagues—if I were to be appointed following this meeting—are disappointed that that did not happen. However, we are now clear that it has not happened. I think that focusing on what the Government have committed in terms of following through on a statutory footing is something that we should be following up on.

I am also very clear that despite the fact that we have not had audit reform, the work, the role, and the delivery of the FRC have continued to improve. As a consequence, I hope that that means that we are getting the balance right between regulatory burden and growth. Going forward, we can use what we have done to achieve that so as to consistently improve.

Q15 I have three more. On information powers, it is goodwill-based, which seems not good. Then we have the definition of public interest entities, and how they can only be public, not private, which seems like a problem. Finally, we have the accountability of company directors, which your remit covers only if they are inside the accounting profession rather than anybody. All three of those things seem really suboptimal. Which of those is in your crosshairs? Is it most, all or none?

I have spoken to some of the team about all of them, but obviously in the last week, I have only scratched the surface on those. They are all important to resolve, or to discuss and take forward, but I would not be able to comment on that now.
Q16 What do you think about competition in the industry? We have the big four. How are you going to encourage competition in that market?

There was a recent article in the FT on this exact subject. It reminded me that when I started off in my Ernst & Whinney days, we were the big eight and, as you say, we are now down to the big four. Making sure that the big four are delivering to an excellent quality continues to be important. I accept that when we change auditors, you have a small population to choose from. Nevertheless, let us make sure that that population continues to be as excellent as it is. Let us then also make sure that we are helping the other audit firms to be top quality too.
Q17 How would you do that?

I think that the method of the FRC now, which I agree with, is setting the rules, supervising and then enforcing. Those three points continue very strongly. There is also building strong relationships with stakeholders, which is something that the chair role should do.

Q18 Has the market share been concentrating or spreading relative to those big four? My impression is that they are getting a higher and higher market share, so that is not working sufficiently. Therefore, we need to do more. What would you suggest we need to be looking at?
I will have to get back to you. I can probably write to the Committee about that afterwards, but I could not answer that question at the moment.

Q19 When we look across the Kingman, Brydon and CMA reviews, we can see literally hundreds of recommendations that have been made by those three reviews that the Government have not actioned or implemented. Which are the most important outstanding recommendations that you would prioritise for action?

I was talking to Richard Moriarty about the Kingman review over the last couple of days. I might get the exact numbers wrong, but he pointed out that of the 83 recommendations, I think 56-ish applied to the FRC and we have done 55 of them. There are a lot of recommendations that have been followed through. It is the Kingman review that I have looked at most.

All those reviews have contributed to the improvement of quality and, without a shadow of doubt, they are all taken seriously. We should not think that because certain parts of them have not been established in legislation that they are not being taken seriously and that they have not had an impact on the way in which the organisation has been run. They absolutely have. The Kingman review in particular has been something that, as far as I understand, my hopefully future colleagues have taken very seriously and have used as a basis for the quality improvements that they have achieved over the last few years.
Q20 Which of the outstanding recommendations would you prioritise for action?
I do not know at this point—as I say, I have not been involved yet. Do not forget that I am not appointed yet; I am subject to your appointment.
Q21 Our advice, not our appointment.

If we look at some of the scandals that this Committee has reviewed over the last four or five years, starting with Carillion, what were the lessons of the Carillion crisis that you drew and how does that help you to think about the role that you have got to play at the FRC?

Carillion was a number of years ago now, although of course it still comes through—not least, most recently, in the fines that have been applied to some of the accountants there. From an audit point of view, there is a definite view that the auditors involved there—I think it was KPMG—have really learned the lessons from that and have done a very serious review of what went wrong. As a consequence, they have taken a massive step forward and are to be complimented on that.

It is very important that we continue to insist on transparency for the board. The board felt that it did not have transparent information at Carillion to make decisions on. I think the role of directors is super-important in overseeing that.

It is important that we, as the FRC, are really clear on corporate governance; I think the update to the UK corporate governance code has been very helpful in the last couple of years. It is very clear on what is required for audit quality. Building relationships with the important auditors—the big auditors and the small ones—to make sure that the quality of audits continues to be great is also important.

However, we should not think that regulation is going to solve every problem. The executive and the board of course have a duty to make sure that they are fully transparent—in the Carillion case, I think transparency was in question—and that directors of boards are clear on their role and accountability for a failing business.

We are never going to stop businesses failing, but I think that what the FRC can do is to put in place transparency and reporting requirements that mean that, in good businesses that are well audited, we can see where those failures are likely to be.
Q22 Do you think that the FRC has now put in place sufficient reforms to prevent another Carillion?

As I understand it, from the people I have spoken to, the lessons learned from Carillion have been very deeply felt and thought about, and remedial action has been implemented where there has been any weakness.
I do not think that anybody would say that we could stop another corporate failure. In a sense, I feel that, in a healthy system, we are bound to have failure as well as success. I do not think our—
Q23 Audit failures were at the heart of why Carillion failed. Surely we should be trying to prevent audit failures.

Of course we should try to prevent audit failures, but was it really an audit failure that was at the heart of it? I think we will find that the accounting department and the business itself created the information that was presented to the auditors. Yes, we want a better audit, but we also want better business.
Q24 Do you think that the audit profession has now made sufficient reforms to stop a repeat of the audit failures that helped to bring down Carillion?

I think we have made progress in that direction. For all regulators, we are never going to get to a place where you stop everything failing. However, I think you put in place what you can see for the future, you learn from the past, and you ensure that everybody understands what their roles, obligations and accountabilities are in the process.
Does that mean it will stop all failures? Nobody can say that. Do I think we are in better shape than we were when Carillion happened? Absolutely. I have had assurance of that.
Q25 What is the key unfinished business?
For the future?

From the Carillion scandal, we drew lots of lessons. We have had these reviews that John Kingman, Brydon and others have conducted. I am still not clear enough about what the priority reforms are that you think need to be driven through the UK audit profession to ensure that we do not have a repeat of scandals such as Carillion.

As I say, only yesterday I was talking to Clare Thompson, who is the SID at the FRC, and she was making the point that with the board and the executive there is constant review of lessons that we have learned, and consideration of how we can move in a direction that is going to be helpful, to make sure both that we are appropriately regulating and that the regulatory burden is not preventing growth. We have to get that balance right.

I think we are constantly learning, as I think all organisations and regulators are, not least in a changing world. Mr Maynard, you asked what I think are the key things for the future. Of course, AI is one of the key things for the future. That will change business and the audit profession, and we need to think about how that will affect the way in which we regulate and the way in which business reports.

Therefore, my answer, Mr Chairman, is that I think we have learned a lot of lessons and I think there will be more lessons for the future; we need to keep ahead of it, and we need to keep on iterating to make sure that regulation is fit for purpose.
Q26 But you cannot specify precisely what lessons and reforms you would champion as the chair of the FRC?
Not at this point, when I am not appointed yet.

Q27 Okay. How will you persuade the Government to put the FRC on a statutory basis? They have promised that a succession of times under different Administrations, and they have failed repeatedly. How will you make sure that this time is not just a repeat of that?

I don’t know that I can make sure of it, but I will certainly be making sure, when I speak with Ministers, civil servants and the people who can achieve that, that they understand how important it is. I think they know how important it is.
Q28 It cannot be that important , because they have decided to defer it repeatedly. It looks like they are trying to avoid doing it.

I have not been involved with that until this point. As I understand it, they are hoping to find a way of getting it on to the legislative agenda, which as you know is very full, and I will be encouraging them to do so.
Q29 What is the case that you will make to them? What is the argument that you will give them for why this is important?

There will be more than this, but there are two key points out of the statutory footing, as far as I understand it. To Mr Maynard ’ s earlier point, it is about making sure that the funding for the FRC becomes something that is required rather than asked for , and that information is shared by everyone, because it is a statutory requirement. I nevitably there will be some organisations at the moment that do not pay their way and do not give the information that is required . It is important that we have a system where everybody participates equally to get an equal outcome.
Q30 Is the FRC underfunded today?

I looked at the accounts, which were published this week, as you may have seen. It has an income of roughly £69 million, and it has a positive out-turn of about £3 million. I would say it is financially stable, but not richly endowed.
Q31 Do you think it has sufficient resources for the tasks that it has?

As I said, I have not started there yet. It has 460 staff, of which 70 - plus are in Birmingham, I think. That feels like a good-sized team for what we have to do, and I am delighted to see that it is on at least a stable financial footing and building reserves rather than the alternative.
Q32 Does the FRC have the right powers to seek information today?

To be honest, I do not know the answer to that question. I think that comes through the FCA; as I understand it, we have a good , close relationship with the FCA in order to achieve the information that we need.

Q33 When the FRC came before this Committee in 2024 , it said that there were two priority areas of reform. One was statutory funding, which you have just referenced, but the second was that an effective regulator absolutely had to have the powers to obtain information relevant to its work. Did they oversell that case when they came before us in 2024?
I think both the funding and the access to information will be part of the statutory footing that is required ; I do not think there has been any change there.
Q34 So it should have more powers to seek information?
Yes, under the statutory footing.
I mean, in your view.
Yes, for sure—so that it is equal and so that everybody knows what they have got to provide and that it is a legal requirement for them to do so.
Q35 At the moment, the FRC does not have powers to require information as part of its investigations. Is that a change you would seek to prioritise?

Yes. I think it is important that anybody has access when they investigate things, just as we have access through F O I s as citizens. As we look into important events, it is important that we get access to full information where possible .

Q36 Could I just take you back very briefly to the question about competition in the audit market ? The FRC put out a report in December, which was marking its own homework and congratulating itself on what a great job it had done. The reality in that report was that the big four — Deloitt e, EY, KPMG and PwC — still held 40% of the audit engagements for public interest entities. Do you think legislation would help the challengers? Could you seek legislation from the Government to help those challengers to get a bigger slice of this?

It is not something that I have even thought about at this particular point. As somebody who consumes audit services in my corporate life, I can see some of the problems with the peak of the big fou r, b ut it is something that I will need to talk about further with the team.
Q37 It is something that you are certainly going to look at?
Oh, definitely yes. I am sure it is something we should look at.

Q38 The thing that we have heard time and again here today is balance . Businesses often argue that regulation imposes costs , and investors argue that strong governance underpins confidence. You were at RBS, and we saw what happened there , arguably as a result of light - touch regulation ; things went very pear - shaped and very south very quickly there. I think you have personally spoken about your situation at RB S , where I think there was an issue with insurance products . I think you were very concerned that a lot of businesses were reliant on PPI , and you felt that was a bit of a smoke - and - mirrors situation, but you did not feel empowered to do much about that. How do we get this back to balance? How do we get the balance right? It is going to cost a lot of money. You are very entrepreneurial. You have said you want to see growth. How do we do that without stifling people — with enough rules but not too many ?

Gosh, you take me back quite a long way with some of the stories that you have pulled out — all of which are entirely accurate. I will address them as we go. The issue with PPI , which I have talked about previously , is that , before it was obvious that it was a big issue , RBS was making quite a lot of profit through PPI . I do remember raising that with the deputy chief executive and asking whether that was right . His point was , “ It may not be right , but we can’t be the first bank to change it. ” That was much more of a stock market point than a regulatory point at that stage.

You could argue that the regulators should have seen that , and I cannot comment on that , but t hat was the point that I was making . When I was at Virgin Money , I did not permit Virgin Money to sell PPI as a consequence of that. I think that business leaders have a responsibility to know what is good and what is bad and not to do bad things , if you see what I mean . Regulation should pick up on that , but nevertheless, I do think there is a requirement there.

As far as RBS is concerned, it is really interesting that you mention light - touch regulation —I think you mean t that the external environment , perhaps , was light touch on regulation. To start with, I thought you were talking about the internal environment there. The thing I often say about RBS— forgive the vernacular here — is that it went bust with all the risk boxes ticked green . There was so much process of regulation that I am not sure there was enough thought about risk.

I think that it is really important that we get to a place where we do not believe that an organisation of any sort is okay because the administrative processes mean that the risk box es are ticked, which is why I think the FRC has done very well with this. I think we need boards to be asking, “ Is the process right ? W hat ’ s the process telling me about the risk profile of my business, and what does that mean for the way I engage with regulation and run the business going forwards? ” I may not have explained it terribly well, but that has been a recent change , which has been well accepted , that the FRC has put into practice.
Q39 Do you think the FRC has got the balance right between growth and regulation , and that one can go hand in hand with the other ?

Without a doubt. I am really sure that growth and regulation can go hand in hand, but I do not think it is black and white. This is why I mentioned earlier that I think it has to be constantly iterative. Without getting myself too much into trouble with the Bank of England and financial services regulation, we are sort of seeing that now .

Before the financial crisis, quite clearly there was a problem with regulation, one would assume. My chair at the time —this is just by the by e , because I always thought it was interesting — was Sir Brian Pitman , who used to run Lloyds Bank, and he always said that the reason why we had a financial crisis was because no CEO knew what a CDO was. I thought it was such a nice way of putting it. You have to understand your business , and that is why I think, back to the earlier point , that having good, fair and transparent reporting is really important.

We then had the financial crisis and there was so much work going into the question of, “So what could regulation do better? ”. As we now know, we are starting to move away from, “ Have we overdone it a little bit , given where we are? Can we pull back? Should we do different things with bankers ’ bonuses ?”. Of course , the regulators are trying to work out , given the learnings from the financial crisis, where that appropriate regulation is. I am really supportive of the way in which that is reviewed.

That is why I am really positive about the culture at the FRC . As I say, I have only known that I had been put forward for this role for the last week or so, but, in talking to people, their constant point is: “We need to keep iterating. We need to keep learning. We need to understand what the industry wants. We need stakeholder engagement. We need to make sure that regulation is appropriate and proportionate.” At that point, as long as we can get there, transparency is what will enable us to grow. Stating the blindingly obvious, before the financial crisis, growth had been super successful, but we didn’t half lose it very fast. I think getting that balance right is something that every regulator has to work on all the time.

Q40 You have obviously had extensive executive and non-executive experience across a number of different industries—importantly, many regulated industries. I am really interested in something you have touched on at a high level, but perhaps we can go more deeply into it: what are the principles that will guide your decisions on whether reducing regulatory burdens conflicts with maintaining confidence in UK markets? If we can focus on the principles that will guide you, that would be great.

Now that Mr Cooper has taken me back to my RBS days, you have made me think of a different story from a little bit later. In my experience of regulated businesses, it is definitely true that executives tend to be negative about regulation—not universally, but obviously it is always a tension. I remember a situation at Virgin Money; I cannot remember the exact point, but there was some new regulation that had come out from the PRA, I think, and my risk team came in to see me to say, “These rules are completely mad. We definitely can’t adhere to them.”

Partly because of the work that I had done through the financial crisis, my view had always been, and continues to be, that regulators do want to do the right thing and we should be looking for the outcome that they are trying to achieve. But sometimes the process of getting there can be a bit clunky. I remember taking home this new consultative document, or whatever it was, over the weekend, reading it and thinking, “Oh, I can see that you could read it the way my team have read it, but I can actually see that the regulator is trying to get to this point.”

I am very clear that all regulation should be focused on its outcomes. We should not have processes that people find time-consuming and burdensome. As we look for lighter-touch regulation, if you see what I mean, that can be a way of releasing or reducing the burden, but nevertheless achieving what we want to achieve. I felt that we were able to do that with the financial services regulator .
