Q41 As chair, what instructions will you be giving to both your non-execs and your executives? You will obviously have the CEOs and CFOs of different businesses under your purview. How will you get them to see your point of view?

Well, it might be more about me seeing their point of view, if you see what I mean. For me, I really like when complex things can be explained simply. I am somebody who will say, “Why do we want to do that? We are doing that for what purpose?”

Sometimes it is hard for people to explain the reason they are doing things, but provided that people can explain the reason that we want to achieve something, whether that is in any business, through regulation or indeed through any stakeholders, I think it is much easier to align. We know that communication can be difficult, and people can miss each other and complicate things through a lack of clarity. So I hope that it will be through a clarity of purpose and outcome.

Q42 Going back to the point about maintaining confidence in UK markets, if you felt that the regulatory burdens were actually conflicting with that, what signs would you be looking for and what actions would you be taking?

I think it would mainly come from stakeholders. You have to listen really hard as a regulator, because I do think that good businesses, good auditors and the profession, on balance, want to do a good job. It is incumbent on the regulator to listen to those stakeholders and understand where they feel there may be too much burden, and then to test that objectively so that you can come to a place where the oversight is appropriate for the challenge and the objective that we are trying to achieve. Building good relationships with stakeholders would be my particular role in that.
Q43 Before we move on to the next question, are there any other core or personal principles, or a business raison d ’ être , that you would have at the centre of your approach?
You make me think of the Nolan principles, which I think are really important for anyone in this sort of role.
I was not trying to guide you to that.

I know you were not, but that was the thought that popped into my mind. I think it is important to do everything that we do with openness, transparency and integrity to achieve the right systemic answer for the country.
Q44 How can the FRC contribute to economic growth while maintaining robust corporate governance?

As the regulator that we are, I do not think the work of the FRC in itself will contribute to growth; it is, of course, businesses that contribute to growth. The work that the FRC does will enable business, and does enable business through its reporting, to show why a business is thriving, successful and appropriate for investment.

That is where the FRC really makes sure that growth is at the heart of the agenda. Good reporting of good businesses brings in investment and protects shareholders. That is what we need in the UK for growth—shareholder confidence and incoming investment. That will come to businesses that are well managed, operating well within the umbrella of UK corporate governance, and transparent in their successes.

Q45 Obviously, the Government have taken a judgment not to pursue audit reform because they are worried about the impact on growth. It is fair to say that has provoked some outrage from the ICAEW, the ACCA, the Chartered Institute of Internal Auditors, the Association of Financial Mutuals, the Building Societies Association, the Quoted Companies Alliance, UK Finance and the IfG. Did the Government get the call wrong?

W hen you have an FRC that is functioning and a Government who are trying to manage the balance between regulation and growth, I can see why it may not be appropriate at this time for additional legislation to be passed. Would legislation be something that would help? Possibly. Are we operating effectively without it? I think we are.

Q46 On the point about competition, the CMA was obviously very clear that the level of concentration in the audit market was a problem. It is not just a problem for the private sector; it is a major problem for local authorities. The CMA recommendation was that FTSE 350 companies appoint two audit firms, one of which should be from the non-big four. The Government have now resiled from implementing that. Did they get that call wrong?
I am afraid I cannot comment on that one.
Q47 If that CMA recommendation is not pursued, what are the best ways to foster greater competition in the audit market?
That is something I would like to work on with the board and the executives, and perhaps we can come back and report to you on that at the time.

Q48 You were just talking about the proportionality of reporting. Loads of companies in my Witney constituency and beyond are saying, “We are drowning under reporting requirements.” What is your perspective on that in terms o f proportionality , and what would you like to see the FRC doing to try to drive down unnecessary reporting, as opposed to it being a one-way street in the other direction?

I hope I get this quote right, but I was talking to someone about this yesterday, and they pointed out that the recent stewardship code enabled people to reduce the reporting they had to do under the stewardship requirements by 25%. It is something that the FRC is very alive to and—again, to my point about iteration—is working hard on.

I have a particular view that going through an annual reporting cycle is a very good discipline for businesses and enables them to understand their own business. That might sound slightly odd, but it is not just about presenting yourself to the world; it enables people to take stock and think about what they are doing in comparison with their peers. The vast majority of the reporting I have done in my time in the private sector has been positive and constructive.

Now, could we take out some of that burden? Should the remuneration report be 30 pages or whatever it is? I completely agree that perhaps it could be more concise. By the way, please don’t take that as a specific thought from me; it is just an example. Can we constantly be more concise? Yes. But do I think the burdens are harmful? Often, for a healthy business, they can be a good way of looking at your business.

Q49 Just thinking about money, although resources and capacity have been touched on a little already, I am looking at a table that says that in the 12 years from 2012 to 2024, the total budget went up three and a half times, and the headcount went up four and a half times. I am jumping ahead a bit, but the financial sanctions went down three times, and non-financial sanctions went down by 40%. We are spending vastly more money to do something that, at least to my mind, is not materially different from what happened 12 years ago. I just don’t understand why we have a headcount that is four and a half times bigger and a budget that is three and a half times bigger. Do you have any perspective on that?
Not specifically, although I might challenge your perceived assumption that you can measure a regulator by the fines it puts out.
Q50 We will come to that in a moment. Why has the budget gone up three and a half times and the headcount gone up four and a half times?

I don’t know the specific answer to that question, but I imagine that it is to do with supervision. There has been a lot of work to improve the quality of audits, and I hope the fact that the quality has improved is the reason why the negative outcomes have reduced. As I say, I don’t know, so I am just going on the way that you have described it. I hope I am seeing an organisation in which further investment in resource is proven to be reducing the problems that the regulator is trying to solve. That is certainly a way to look at it. When I am there, I will have a look, and hopefully that will be the case.
Thank you.
Q51 Could you outline the kinds of circumstances in which you would be prepared to disagree publicly with Ministers?

I would hope that communication and relationships would be sufficient for disagreements to be behind closed doors. I have no problem disagreeing with people if I believe that is necessary, but I would hope that it could largely be achieved, if it happens at all, behind closed doors. That would be the most effective and constructive way of dealing with anything. If your question is whether, in extreme circumstances, I would be prepared to disagree where I think it is necessary, I believe I would, but my preference—like everybody’s, I think—would be to do that privately.
Q52 Okay. What other steps do you think might be necessary to protect the FRC’s operational independence from Government?

I think you are right, if you are pointing that at the chair. It is important that the chair is independent, and I think I am known to have an independent spirit and mind. It is important to me that it is clear what the purpose of the FRC is—that goes for any organisation I work with—and that we hold very clearly and strongly to the stated objectives, the strategy that has been published and the objectives of the organisation. The role of the chair is to make sure that that is the case. If it is the case, and if any incoming information is contrary to that, it gives us an opportunity to push back and explore it further.
Q53 Can you describe a scenario where Ministers might want to do something that you regard as unfortunate and unwise, and could you tell us how you would handle that?

I have worked with Ministers, and I am pleased to say that I can’t think of any circumstances when I felt uncomfortable engaging with them and finding a constructive path forward. I can’t summon up an example at this point.

Q54 Let me give you an example from the CMA. The Chancellor has issued a growth duty to regulators. The CMA’s principal statutory duty, however, is to protect consumers and to conserve and promote competition. Sometimes those two things are in competition with each other as ideals . We could easily foresee a situation where the Government asked you to water down audit standards because they are a “burden on business”, but the result is that investors are kept in the dark about accounting malpractice. How would you deal with that tension when it arises? It feels to us as though it is bound to arise.

There are two things. I do not believe we have a Government who would be satisfied with accounting malpractice, but let us assume that might be a risk. I t is then entirely consistent with the answer I gave to a previous question : as long as we are clear about our purpose, which is top-quality reporting, good standards and transparency, I would of course be very motivated, in every sense of that word, to push back and stand independently to ensure that we are issuing quality statements.
Q55 Even if the price is a public spat with Ministers?

I would always prefer to avoid that. However, if your question is, “In extremis, would you go there?” then of course. If I had to protect the quality and independence of the organisation, I would reluctantly feel that that would have to be the case.

Q56 First of all, thank you for being here and putting yourself forward . Co ngratulations on being nominated. It is a very impressive CV. When I told a group of high school children that I was coming to do this this week, they immediately asked, “Is that like the BBC and HBO drama series ‘Industry’?” I said it probably was not going to be quite like that, but they were very excited about what I was coming to do.

Obviousl y , the performance of the FRC is what we are really here to discuss, as well as how you can take that on. Investigations are averaging 33 months to complet e . Should the target be a lot lower, and do you foresee being able to make that happen ?

I would have to find out why it is taking that length of time. I did not know that was the average length of time for an investigation to close. Although I cannot give you a specific answer, my modus operandi, if you like, in all things is to say, “ Let ’ s try to do this in a sensible length of time .” F or a number of reasons , we need to ensure that people remain acutely aware of the importance of that work, and over a long period that may drop away—I do not know. That is important.

It is also really important that teams are actively engaged in resolving issues. I do not know why it takes that length of time to resolve some of those complex issues. Again, we are back to balance, aren’t we? Do it properly, but do it in the right period of time. That is something that, of course, every organisation wants to look at.

Q57 On l earning that the average completion time is 33 months, is that something that concerns you, or is it something that you would want to dig a bit deeper into to find out why it takes that long?
Certainly, and thank you for raising it. I will certainly dig more deeply into it and find out what that is about.
Q58 In terms of your first term, what would you most like to be a measurable improvement? What would you like to be able to say about , “Right, that is what I achieved”? What would be on that list?
It is important for all regulators to be trusted, isn’t it?
Q59 Crunchier, measurable improvements.

Measurable improvements? The risk register is important. It is published in the annual report and accounts which , as I said, came out earlier this week. It would be good to see positive, constructive progress against a number of those risks, including cyber-security, which everybody is, of course, looking at.

Without a doubt, AI, as I mentioned earlier, is also something I am sure we will look at during my first term, and I would like to be able to see the progress we have made internally and externally on that. Who knows? It may very well be that we go back to Mr Bloore’s point and look at the time that it takes to resolve cases. Let me come back to you with KPIs when we have agreed them.

Q60 There is the FRC’s statutory footing; there is changing your information powers; there is making private companies, as well as public companies, PIEs; there is making company directors, whether accountants or otherwise, accountable to you—you have not named any of those quite clear goals. Are there any of those on which you think, “Right, well not that one or that one, but that one and that one, yes, I really want”?

My a pologies. I thought we had discussed all those. I agree with you that all those are important and key for the FRC, and not just for my term—they are what the FRC is going to be working on for the foreseeable future. At the moment, I cannot prioritise them without talking to the board and the executive. Having not started yet, I would not know how to prioritise them at this point.
Q61 Is there anything else you would like to say about your vision for the FRC that you think we should be aware of?

We have touched on most of it. It is an important regulator. It is important for it to be a trusted regulator. It has made significant progress since Carillion and the Kingman review. It has good relationships with stakeholders. To the earlier points, like all organisations there are obviously new things to do, whether on the statutory footing—that is absolutely important—on AI, or on the growth of trust. I will be very proud of work on all those things as part of the FRC.

Q62 You have mentioned AI several times. I am also particularly interested in your reference to cyber-security. You know as well as I do that we have had problems getting the boards of a wide range of businesses to really engage with that. How do you think the FRC can lead on that through audit processes or other types of leadership?

Again, I am speaking without knowledge of what the FRC does at the moment in this particular area. It was interesting to see it in the FRC’s accounts. All leaders should model the way and the FRC, as a leader in reporting, has included it in its annual report—that is important for all organisations. My own experience of audit firms is that they are very focused on cyber-security; that should continue. I would be disappointed if every board in the country is not considering cyber-security on its own merits for the board’s business. As I said at the beginning, although of course the FRC is the regulator of corporate governance and reporting, businesses themselves have the responsibility and accountability to make sure that they are safe, and that very much relates to cyber-security.

If there are no further questions, that concludes this hearing. Thank you very much indeed for appearing in front of us, and for answering all our questions so comprehensively and with such candour. We are grateful to you. The Committee will now meet in private and conclude our recommendations.

sessions.iT: Deterrence in an age of Russian aggression
sessions.w: Rachel Ellehuus (Royal United Services Institute (RUSI)); Sir Adam Thomson (European Leadership Network (ELN)); Armida Van Rij (Centre for European Reform (CER))

segs.tx: Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy
O ral evidence: Deterrence in an age of Russian aggression , HC 338
Monday 13 July 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Matt Western (The Chair); Lord Arbuthnot of Edrom; Lord Boateng; Liam Byrne; Sarah Champion; Mr Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi; Lord Godson; Lord Hutton of Furness; Lord Jack of Courance; Mike Martin; Lord Sedwill; Baroness Tyler of Enfield; Lord Tunnicliffe; Lord Watts , Sir Gavin Williamson .
Evidence Session No. 5 Heard in Public Questions 4 8 - 54
Witnesses

Rachel Ellehuus, former US Secretary of Defense Representative in Europe, Defense Advis er, US Mission to NATO; Armida van Rij, Senior Research Fellow, Centre for European Reform, Senior Non-Resident Fellow (European Security and Politics), Chicago Council on Global Affairs; Sir Adam Thomson, former UK Permanent Representative, NATO .
Examination of witnesses
Rachel Ellehuus, Armida van Rij and Sir Adam Thomson .

Q48 We now return with our second panel of the day. It is our third session on deterrence in an age of Russian aggression. I invite our witnesses to introduce themselves. Perhaps I could start with Armida.

Thank you, chair, and it is an honour to be here. I am a senior research fellow with the C entre for European Reform, based here in London and a non-resident fellow with the Chicago Council on Global Affairs. I work on security, transatlantic relations and NATO issues.

I am the director - general of the Royal United Services Institute — RUSI —and have been for about a year and a half now. Prior to that, I was at NATO as the Secretary of Defen s e representative in Europe, and I had a long career in the Pentagon as well.
I am a senior associate fellow at the European Leadership Network and a former British ambassador to NATO.
Terrific . W e are going to start with some questions around our relationship between EU and US NATO allies. Baroness Tyler is going to kick us off.
Q49 I wanted to start with a quite general question to get your view on how valuable NATO summits are. D o they actually help with driving change within the alliance? Armida, would you like to start?

I can kick off, although I am very conscious that we have got a former UK ambassador to NATO here. Under normal circumstances — I will elaborate in a minute on w hat I mean by that — NATO summits are hugely valuable. They are an opportunity for leaders to come together , hash out in private any potential issues that there might be and make progress on big decisions. S ome of the previous NATO summits we have seen did that. T he 2022 summit set the new strategic concept, which was a major turning point for the a lliance. The 20 23 summit hashed out the regional plans , which, again, was a major turning point. T hen , the 2025 summit set out the new defence spending pledge of spending 5% on GDP. Those were all significant summits. We can get into this in more detail later, but the difficulty of doing this in the current moment with a US A dministration that tends to flip - flop, putting it mildly , on their stance on European security is that then these summits become about managing President Trump and the transatlantic relationship rather than actually making progress. I will leave it there.

I would agree with that. When you look at the summit declaration, it is no accident that it ends with a rather vague statement that says, “W e look forward to our next meeting ” , but it does not say exactly when that will be. I think that is a quiet attempt to get away from this new habit for the last five or six years of having annual summits. I agree with A rmida that under normal circumstances, it can be a useful way to drive progress, because otherwise , NATO is only meeting at the Minister of Defence or Minister of Foreign Affairs level. You really need heads of state and Government to be the ones signing up to things , such as the NATO plans, a new strategic direction on Russia or support for Ukraine, because that is the only way you can be sure that the implementation and the execution of those will happen across national Governments . On t he habit of annual summits , Trump A dministration aside, it just does not allow for the same type of preparation along the national delegations , a nd it becomes all about the optics , politics and so-called deliverables, rather than doing the work that it takes to implement what was agreed.
Adam, with all your experience, I am sure you have views on this . So, c ould I turn to you?

Yes. It is not just that a summit allows leaders to come together to do business and to put their stamp on NATO decisions. It is also a whole institutional process. The setting of a date for a summit s ets the rhythm of work for the alliance across its hundreds of c ommittees for the intervening period. I t is a forcing event : a llies have to come to conclusions and agree language because their leaders are about to meet. So , summits are extremely important , a nd if we are not going to have them on a fairly regular basis because of US uncertainties, then we need to find some other mechanism to do that. That is not saying they have to be annual, but I think you need them at least triennial.

Thank you for that. You have all made the point about the annual summits. J ust to clarify that, do you think NATO would benefit from having fewer , and indeed shorter , summits in future? Adam, can I go back to you?

​​ ​ I am not sure they can be much shorter—I think the Ankara business was conducted over no more than three hours, compared with three days in the good times gone by—but I do not think they have to b e annual. T he focus on President Trump and the uncertainties about his commitment to the a lliance are somewhat damaging . I t would be perfectly possible to skip it in 2027 and return in 2028.
​​ ​ Thank you very much . Rachel and Armida, would you like to come back on that point on frequency and length?

​​ ​ Just to agree with that , plenty of work needs to be done on implementation, whether that is on the defence industrial side, carrying forward a real strategy on Russia or laying out a plan to help Ukraine become more integrated into the alliance. All th e work behind the scenes th at Adam alluded to takes a lot of energy , and if everybody is spending their energy preparing for that next annual summit, that does not allow the real grunt work to go on behind the scenes. The political guidance that is due in the first quarter of 2027 will take a lot of energy and effort, and I would rather have that energy and effort spent there.

​​ ​ I just add that there is some concern within NATO that if we were to now shift to bi e nn i al summits , or even less frequent ones , that would send a message to Russia that we cannot hold these summits on an annual basis because the y are a display of disunity. However , everyone can see the optics of having to manage the political leaders at the moment , s o you can ask yourself : which is worse?

Q50 ​​ Lord Arbuthnot of Edrom: ​ You are all expressing concerns about the uncertainties arising out of the current US Administration. Is there any role for the UK, with its purported special relationship, to play in trying to heal or mend this? I should have declared my interest , first as chair of the Thales UK advisory panel and secondly as a member of the advisory board of RUSI. Rachel, would you like to go first?

​​ ​ Yes, t he American will take the pain for the team. I appreciate the traditional role that the United Kingdom has played in trying to manage not just the United States but the European Union , sometimes even playing a bridging role between the two . F or better or worse , you have seen President Trump get very fixated on certain ideas, whether it is the fact that Spain is not pulling its weight in the alliance, that the EU is a competitor to the US and taking away jobs, or that he has to have Greenland. U nfortunately, the United Kingdom has been caught up in that at the political level . It started with Iran and has continued with some of the delays around defence spending and technology, where the UK has rightly tried to diversify its relationships , grow closer to Europe and create more domestic and European options to counterbalance the tension in the relationship with the United States.

A t a political level, there is certainly not space for the current P rime Minister , and I wonder if there is space for a future P rime Minister or Government . W here the UK can play a very skilful and strong role in managing the US is behind the scenes. You have a lot of leverage and a lot of cards to play , and y ou bring a lot to the table in terms of defence industrial co - operation, including on the nuclear dimension. The US cannot get those Trident missiles out the door without the co - operation of the UK ; t he price just goes up , as do t he timelines. Similarly, on the intelligence side, you bring a lot to the table that is undervalued.

I would recommend that that influence role is there, but that it happen s behind the scenes rather than at the political level, because we have a P resident who is very focused on certain themes and certain victims to blame when things are not going his way.

Armida van Rij: ​ I add that it is useful t o think of the US as not just President Trump and his A dministration , with all the different factions within that , but the country as a whole . It is about not just managing the next two or two and a half years , or whatever is left of this A dministration , but managing the relationship beyond that . I t is clear that the US is on a trajectory of long - term structural change, where Europe is less important to it and the Indo-Pacific is more in favour—although that is perhaps a bit less clear in the actions of this particular Administration .

I suggest that the UK could play a much more significant role in trying to influence the US as a whole , not just going through the political system in D C. Following the mid - terms in November , for example, there will be quite a significant turnover of C ongressmen and Congress women coming in who will likely be a bit younger and will not necessarily have very good or well - formed views on NATO, the transatlantic relationship or Europe. T here is an early opportunity for the UK and other European Governments to get in there early and have those conversations with those new Co ngressmen and Congress women.

As well as going through Congress, the UK could—I think it does this a bit already—engage much more closely at the political level through U S states and through the governors. All of this is indirect influencing . I acknowledge that it is not direct ly speaking into Trump ’s ear but, that way , we spread the UK’s web a little more broad ly than just going through DC and the A dministration.

​​​ ​ I would like to build on both those comments . I agree that the UK is very unlikely to change President Trump , so Rachel is right that there are roles for the UK behind the scenes , and I agree with Armida that the US is much more than just the P resident. But I think there is also a role for the UK in the diplomacy of European collective defence. The United States ’s n ational defence strategy has signalled clearly —this was in evidence at Ankara, to o—that Europe is expected by the United States to take primary responsibility for at least the conventional defence of Europe. I believe there is a role for the United Kingdom, working with major NATO allies, particularly Germany and France, in shaping what that means and what the future governance of European collective defence should look like. That works with the grain of US concerns, but it is also a really important political requirement for Europe.

​​ ​ Thank you. For m y other question , c an I start with you, Sir Adam? Should the UK , and European NATO countries generally , try to ally ourselves more with the United States ’s policy goals? If so, how would we do that in light of the absence of consultation and a proposal relating to Greenland that we might find rather difficult?

​​ ​ S tepping back for a moment, UK and European policymakers have to assume that the problems they encounter with the United States are not particular to this A dministration but are a reflection of a longer - term trend that is unlikely to change. It m ight get better at intervals, but toxic US political polarisation is now infecting U S foreign policy, including security policy, towards Europe for the long term. That says to me that the United Kingdom and other Europeans need to work with the present US aspiration to have Europeans take much greater responsibility for their own collective defence . T hat cannot safely happen in a rush, as you have heard in previous session s. Europe will remain very reliant on US critical enablers for quite a long time to come , s o any European approach on collective European defence needs to be done t ransatlantic al ly , as far as possible.

But there is scope for talking not just about greater European burden sharing , higher defence spending , a more coherent European defence industry and procurement , but about the political dimensions of this. Is Europe prepared to embrace the American desire that it should take primary responsibility for conventional defence ? The answer is p robably yes b ut , in that case, wha t are the next steps? What is the road map for that, and is long-term US nuclear commitment to the alliance—the nuclear umbrella—something that European leaders, including British Prime Ministers, believe in their heart of hearts will actually be there in a crisis? Europeans need to be starting a conversation, including with Washington, about a more European nuclear deterrence as well.
Thank you, that is very helpful.

I would like to flip the final question that Adam just posed on its head : is the US comfortable with Europe developing its own defence industrial base? F or decades we have received very mixed messages on that , and we continue to receive mixed messages on it from this Administration as well. Part of the reason for that is that the US defence industrial base is dependent on foreign sales. There is a possibility here to meet somewhere in the middle where we build where we can the capabilities that will take a longer term to develop in Europe , where we can already scale up production , but things or systems that are more exquisite that we need on shorter timeframes we can continue to purchase from allies, including the US but also South Korea and others. However, we also need to acknowledge the industrial production challenges within the US itself, where , following the conflict in the Middle East, it will take a very long time to receive a number of key capabilities like Patriot missiles. We need to make a n either / or decision but we need to be aware that there are constraints on any decision that we make.
But having our own strong industrial base is part of our deterren ce posture, is it not?

Absolutely. I continue to believe that we need to be able to stand on our own two feet , while acknowledging Adam’s point that this will take time. We cannot have a gap in our deterrence because we do not have the right capabilities to be able to deter.

I will just say that there is a difference between overdependence and interdependence. Interdependence is actually quite healthy, not least because it builds resilience in our supply chains, in our economic infrastructure and in certain capabilities that might be in short supply. Americans do not think about NATO every day. When you live in Europe, you are just so close to the challenge that you are you are seeing it on the news and really thinking about it. The closer you are to the threat and to the eastern front , you are thinking about it on a daily basis , but there is almost a public relations job to explain to the US public the value of NATO and a strong Europe that takes primary responsibility for its own continent and its own region so that the US can focus elsewhere, whether that is on taking care of some of the problems of political fragmentation and economic inequality that exist there, or whether it is to allow the US to focus more on the Indo-Pacific or, dare I say, the Middle East, which seems to have taken up quite a bit of bandwidth.

W hat we have to correct is that overdependence where there are no alternatives for Europe, and the minute that Starlink is turned off you are left without any satellite intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capability. I was reassured at the NATO summit to see some concrete steps to reduce that overdependence and create more options. The one that is most striking to me is the decision by NATO allies to choose Saab’s Global E ye surveillance system rather than the Boeing E-3. That is a strong signal that there are good, solid European options , and that NATO as a whole is willing to diversify beyond US options.
Q51 The NATO treaty was signed a very long time ago. How robust do you think the articles are now, in light of everything that we have seen over the last few years?

I have been really impressed by how, when you read that treaty, you can really find what you need. It is like kind of like the US Constitution : there are little nuggets built in there. Everybody focuses on Article 5, the collective security guarantee that an attack on one is an attack on all , but Article 3 talks about the fact that the first line of defence is national defence and making sure that each individual ally is spending adequately and taking care of its own homeland and is ready in any front - line scenario conflict.

Article 3 is very resilient , and there is even flexibility in the way that Article 5 is written so we do not have to have it as a single point of failure where not all 32 allies want to come to the rescue of another ally in a scenario where there is an attack on one of them. We already had one example of that on 11 September, when the US was attacked. Yes , we want the image of political solidarity of all 32 allies saying , “An ally was attacked , that is unacceptable and we stand by them ”, but the response was up to each individual ally. In the treaty there is the optionality to provide political support or — with military, political or economic support —to go beyond what NATO can agree at 32. That is important because we talk a lot about the tripwire scenario, where Russia tries to take a small bite out of one of the Baltic states or somewhere else, and then that is the single point of failure for Article 5 and it is the end of the NATO alliance. I completely disagree with that because — to your question —there is a lot of flexibility in the treaty whereby you can maintain the political unity that is needed and then allow for a varied response.
So you are suggesting that little green men in Tapa in Estonia would be met by political unity at 32 , but then only countries A, B, C and D — chief among them America — would respond militarily ?

In that particular scenario , the correct military response would be a front - line response. R ight now there are US forces forward positioned in the Baltic states and Poland , so I think they would be part of that regional response. Any scenario you can imagine starts small but then builds , so, at least initially, if there is an attack on one ally then we do not want all 32 rushing in. You would get that regional response built up by reinforcements further down the line. However, we have to control our messaging . In particular, I see a lot of press stories suggesting that even one boot over a NATO border would cause the entire alliance to collapse , but we have seen that that is not the case.
We have already had that with drones.

We have had that with drones. There is another example of the flexibility in the treaty in Article 4 , which allows for allies to consult and determine the nature of their response and whether Article 5 is actually necessary .
Adam, do you agree with Rachel that the founding fathers of NATO were wise in building in sufficient flexibility to deal with the unprecedented situation that we find ourselves in ?

Yes. They may not have envisaged it all but they left us with great flexibility, which is tremendously helpful . I want to underline Rachel’s point by comparing the 14 articles on roughly two sides of a piece of paper that are the Atlantic Charter for the North Atlantic Treaty and the Treaty on European Union, where you get to the collective defence clause at Article 42.7. The NATO treaty is a completely different creature and, because it is so short and general, it leave s great flexibility for the alliance.

One to you, Armida: we have spoken quite a lot about the Europeanisation of NATO as America steps back — which it has been trying to do since Obama’s pivot to Asia , so there is nothing new here —but there are a number of political obstacles, not least between different European allies. Is there a role that Britain can play to help that greater Europeanisation of NATO in overcoming some of those political difficulties?

Sure. I also want to comment briefly on the previous two questions , if that is okay . The point that Rachel made about reinforcements coming is key . Currently , the assumption in the NATO plans is that the reinforcements will come predominantly from the US. The question is whether they will actually come —that is a big question mark. I point to Germany , which is in the process of putting a brigade in Lithuania . That relates exactly to the point about essentially putting a tripwire in a front - line state but also therefore directly implicat es Germany itself should a “ little green man ” scenario or something like it happen. That is an important signal to be sending as well as direct military capability .

On the Europeanisation of NATO, the UK’s policy for quite some time has been “NATO first”. That is the entire premise of its defence policy—understandably so, especially since Brexit. The UK, and I say this as a Dutch-Italian national who speaks regularly to European counterparts, is still very much looked to as a military leader within Europe.

We see that also in Starmer’s approach in building the coalition of the willing for Ukraine alongside France. There is a question about how long some of those political leadership initiatives can last with potential political changes in some key European countries like France from 2027 onwards , but there is a challenge around the UK’s spending and actual military heft. You will know this better than I do, I am sure, but by 2030 Germany will have spent more on defence spending than the UK and France combined, which really does shift the equation. Now, spending does not equal strategic culture, nor does it equal readiness and capabilities—
Willingness to use force.

Exactly. The risk taking, the appetite, all the things that I think would still come more from British leadership and French leadership. But we need to acknowledge that things are shifting, so there is a real question for the UK Government: where do they want to be? And, if they want to lead, they need to be able to put money where their mouth is.
If SACEUR is not American, what country provides SACEUR?
That is a great question. Those are the kinds of things that are very much—
A one-word answer.
Okay. Historically, it should be Britain.

It will be Britain. If it happened tomorrow, it would be Britain. First, the French are still outside the integrated military structure, and then there is Britain’s coherence with the nuclear side of things. Given the overlap between nuclear and conventional, you cannot have a country that sits outside of the whole package running operations. It will not be Germany, because it lacks the strategic culture and the readiness. It might be spending a lot but, for good historical reasons, it has embedded its entire defence planning system and capability procurement choices in NATO, so it cannot run NATO as it is still trying to build its own strategic culture. So it would be the UK if it happened tomorrow, but let us hope not.

I think it might be Britain first, but I think it would rotate. The chairman of the Military Committee at NATO is chosen on merit, and it would be perfectly possible for Europeans to find the best man or woman for the job when the term of its predecessor has come to an end.
I will make one comment. If it is to rotate, that provides a problem, does it not, because you need a framework nation that other nations are going to plug into?

Q52 Ms van Rij, if I can come to your good self, given the new US Trump Administration’s considerable shifting of priorities towards homeland defence, the western hemisphere and the Indo-Pacific, there have been greater calls for more European leadership within NATO. What more do you think the UK can do, particularly within the E3, to further advance and encourage European leadership of NATO?

The E3 has been a very useful political forum, and it would be good to see it connected much more closely to actual NATO ministerial forums as well. I would also not dismiss the E5, because that brings together the key European defence industrial countries. Doing more with the E5 rather than the E3, and connecting those to political decision-making formats within NATO, is a useful mechanism.

This is a bit sensitive, and it is difficult to see this taking place within NATO at the moment , but within the NATO defence planning process there will need to be a reassessment of which countries take on which capabilities. That process will start from 2027 onwards, I believe. The UK should be leading a conversation that takes a hard look at and makes an honest assessment of what the US will actually provide, perhaps even working—on an assumption that, beyond the critical enablers, the US may not provide anything beyond that—on what the Europeans can be doing. The UK can be leading that conversation within NATO.

I have a few thoughts on UK leadership of any Europeanisation in NATO. Something you discussed in the last session, but it is worth repeating, is that the UK is one of only two European nuclear powers, and it is the only one that has committed nuclear weapons to its allies since 1962. It does not make enough of its nuclear role in Europe. As doubts grow about the US nuclear umbrella over European collective defence, the UK should be at least as brave as President Macron in talking in fresh ways about what the UK’s nuclear dimension can do for European allies.

Given our strong relations with Ukraine, there is a space for the UK to provide leadership on the emerging debate inside the alliance about a European way of war and how to keep that interoperable with the United States, while doing things a bit differently from the US. I have spoken previously about the importance of clearer European political leadership on how parliamentarians can look their constituents in the eye and tell them that they still know how to deliver European collective defence when we now have doubts about US commitment.
Q53 I have a couple of questions about Ukraine. Is there anything more the UK should be doing within NATO to put more pressure on Putin to come to the negotiating table over Ukraine?

There is not much that NATO can do to put pressure on Putin or Russia. First, there is no longer a NATO-Russia Council, so there are no longer direct communications between the alliance and Russia beyond some last-ditch emergency communications lines at the Secretary-General’s level. Secondly, they do not have the right tools other than deterrence. What deterrence signals to Russia and to Putin is “Do not go any further”, and that is NATO’s job number one. Helping Ukraine to stay in the fight and helping Ukraine to become very integrated into NATO, even short of membership, is something they can do that creates a deterrent effect.

Bringing Putin to the negotiating table needs more of a political and economic lever. We have seen individual allies try to compel Putin to come to the negotiating table through more precise sanctions—I think you had a hearing on that several weeks ago—to try to cut off some of the capabilities and components that allow Russia to stay in the fight militarily.

I think individual allies are giving what they can in terms of both direct military assistance—at the summit we saw a commitment of €70 billion for the next two years, which is not nothing—and the EU’s loan mechanism. That sends a strong message to Putin that the EU and NATO are here to stay by Ukraine’s side for the near future. But that is simply as an alliance. They simply do not have the political levers to create the conditions for a ceasefire and bring everyone to the negotiating table.
Is it more military, diplomatic or economic pressure? I am not quite sure which ones you are saying we should focus on.
I ask you to keep your response very brief. Apologies, but we are expecting votes in a few minutes’ time so would like to complete this session before then, otherwise it might get a bit messy.
As with most military conflicts, you can only get so much progress on the battlefield and then it is actually diplomatic efforts that will bring it to closure.

Yes, it is the diplomacy. We need all the pressure that we can apply to Russia through sanctions and in other ways, but at the moment there are not the incentives for Russia to come to the table, at least as Putin sees it. The war in Ukraine is at least as much about Russia’s relationship with Europe and NATO as it is about Ukraine. There is scope for British diplomacy, probably with the E3, to make this more interesting for Putin.

I agree with Rachel that this is perhaps more of an economic discussion than a NATO discussion at this point, but there are things we could be doing. One of them is for European countries to stop buying gas altogether. The other one is that we are heading into tourist season, so we should be taking a look at tourist visas for Russians who are still visiting Europe. In helping Ukraine, we should be doing much more to facilitate joint ventures between the UK and Ukraine—for example, by taking another look at banking regulations, which are currently making it very difficult to get loans in the UK, and it continues to be difficult for Ukrainians to get visas to come to the UK for those business ventures. Those are tangible things that could be done to support Ukraine.

I have a question about peacekeeping forces. As you know, the UK is committed to deploying forces, in the event of a ceasefire, to Ukraine, as are some other countries—the coalition of the willing and so on. How credible do you think that peacekeeping force is going to be without US capabilities like air cover or missile defence?

Not very credible. Before I sent any country’s forces into Ukraine, I would want to understand what the rules of engagement were and what exactly were the terms of the agreement. We had a period almost a year ago when there was quite a lot of detail about freezing the conflict along current battle lines, allowing for a buffer zone and then coming to some sort of an agreement with the Russians about exactly what would happen in terms of a consolidated response, including from the United States, if it went past those established rules of engagement and red lines. However, I do not think we are there; all that has fallen by the wayside, so I do not think a peacekeeping force on the ground before we have a ceasefire and a political agreement is where we are.
More work to do there.

Q54 I want to ask you what we need to do better in the UK to open up the conversation with the public really about defence expenditure and what is going on in other nations that you would strongly recommend that the UK look to for best practice.
To be honest, I think the UK is really behind on that front compared to some other western European countries, quite a bit. There is no public conversation at all.
A year, two years or what? What about the Dutch ? Give us an example.

Yes, the Dutch are very far ahead. Part of the impetus for the Dutch was that they hosted the NATO summit there last year. In the run-up to the summit, the Dutch MFA, together with the now-disbanded public diplomacy division of NATO, hosted a series of events called “NATO through the Netherlands”. Essentially they hosted theatre shows in the equivalent of the Royal Albert Hall—not LSE or King’s, but cultural institutions—with Ministers of Defence and high-profile journalists. Those events were sold out every single time, and they went through the entire country. We could do much better to engage cultural institutions to better tell the story of NATO. We could use popular figures to mobilise some of the support around it. We have got the Royal Family running around who all have a role in the Armed Forces in this country, so we could use them much better. We should be developing curricula in schools, not to scare people but just to make them understand.
I would be most grateful if any of our witnesses wish to write to the committee on that topic. That would be greatly appreciated.

That concludes today’s session. I thank the three witnesses for their time. As anticipated, there has been an interruption, but I think we have been through as many of the questions as we needed to. Thank you so much for your time today. That concludes our second panel.
