South Korea has a red-lighting approach to data sharing as opposed to our current green-lighting, so there is an assumption that you would share data. Singapore has a system whereby, as long as you have a reasonable rationale, with seven criteria, you can see the data, so it is a much more seamless flow, and I think that the UK needs to follow that model. Otherwise, as we saw in Covid, you have the ridiculousness of the DWP wanting to give payments to vulnerable people, but the DH not being allowed to tell them who the vulnerable people were.

Q194 Building on what you have been saying, we have had evidence to say that there really should be a middle layer between the strategic level and the operational level, so that you have the intelligence services on top, with COBRA, and then you have the police and emergency services, and the private sector underneath. You have touched on this. Should there be a middle layer? I was just thinking today that, for instance, drones are a big area. I am involved in prisons, which have drones above them the whole time, and nets to catch them. Would it be wise to have a middle layer that would just advise local services that the hostile activity that could be seen would be sudden drone warfare and, therefore, “Be prepared. It probably will not happen, but just be prepared”?

The test of any layer, especially an additional one, should be whether it is making the response more co-ordinated and faster. If you were to map out the layers that we already have in terms of local government ( which, we assume, is about to be handed more powers ) local resilience fora, government departments and local and up to national emergency services, you have an architecture that is already multilayered. The focus needs to be on the connective tissues between those layers, and those sinews need to be exercised, stress-tested and improved.

There is absolutely a place for expert evidence at parts of those layers, and the Cabinet Office has a role in bringing those experts to bear. I would suggest that local resilience fora, if they were working well, would also do that. I am not convinced that an extra layer beyond those that I have already set out would be additive, but I would be interested to see what it would look like in an exercise.
Mr McGuinness, you looked a bit cynical about the idea of a middle layer as well.

I had three quick thoughts. I worked for many years in the Middle East, in the foreign service. There was a category of state in the Middle East—I will not say which—when I was serving there, which were referred to as dawlat al-mukhabarat, which are intelligence states, where the intelligence service is at the core of and are the titanium endoskeleton of those states. We can think of which they are. You could argue that Russia is one, with the Chekists at the core of it.

I am really unnerved at the idea that we have a structure, at the top of which are the intelligence services, given that we have to deal with a whole variety of things that may happen to us, which our enemies are seeking to exploit. We are dealing with natural hazard, and one of the characteristics of Russian hybrid warfare technique is that you exploit things that are happening, rather than causing things to happen. The tools that we have for responding to everything are part of our hybrid warfare response.

The intelligence services provide us with a tiny bit of information and framing that can be helpful for strategic decision-making. One of the answers to your question is that it seems to me that, in the private sector—and, in particular, in almost every organisation now that is data-enabled—it is your ability to bring together and analyse, increasingly using artificial intelligence or Agenticly, although that is a bit cutting-edge, all of that data to form a view on what is happening to you, of which the really sensitive parts may be very small.

One of the risks of our conversation here is that we are backward-looking, with a way of doing business that is behind us in the private sector, including, incidentally, in the energy sector. When I worked with major American energy providers, their knowledge of what was happening within their networks, or how everything was running, far outstripped what we seemed to be able to bring together, so there is an issue there.

On the middle layer, I would note two things. First, no one has said the word “devolved”. When I used to convene a National Security Council resilience committee, I had with me representatives of the devolved Administrations, as well as all of the government departments and relevant arm’s-length bodies, which was quite a large meeting, as you can imagine, that would do something around resilience. We have to think of the devolved Administrations.

As a final thought for you, it seems to me that both the National Cyber Security Centre, which has some structural issues, and the National Protective Security Authority are significantly under-tasked and held to account—in other words, “What are they meant to do for us? What do we expect of them?”—and underresourced as a result. In terms of giving them the resource and holding them to account, it does feel to me that a body like the National Protective Security Authority, possibly not in MI5 but somewhere else, should have a more significant role in closing that gap between local resilience fora and what happens at the top in terms of preparedness.

What has been said makes a great deal of sense. You gave us notice of that question, and I had difficulty dealing with it. I did not really know what it was aimed at. What has been said rather demonstrates that we should structure it differently. In the end, we want two things. First, we want a lot of trust between those who are involved. We have to learn to give trust to each other. Secondly, we want something that operates fast, so having something multi-layered reduces your speed.

Q195 Thank you very much for coming, and for this conversation. My question involves the supply chains, at every level. First, do you think, based on your experience, that the private sector is sufficiently concerned about the key risks that Paddy has so eloquently laid out? We did a little war game, and there was a strong belief that the supply chains would be robust and would work, almost regardless. You had to make the scenario incredibly favourable to Russia before people started to accept the threats and risks.

We know that it is a national conversation, and there is some government action towards solving that issue, but do you think that, generally, from your experience, there is enough understanding in supply chains on two issues? One is the general health of the supply chain. While they own great chunks of infrastructure and manage a great element of our national resilience, there might be vulnerabilities in their supply chain that they are keeping quiet about. As a committee, we think that that is now probably highly likely. Therefore, do the Government give enough guidance to these private sector entities on how they should and can behave with their own supply chains, some of which are very exposed to people who may wish us harm?

There seem to be two questions there. First, do the Government give enough guidance on the risks? Does corporate business take notice of it, take it seriously and act? On the first, it is patchy. In some areas, we do quite well. The NCSC is an excellent organisation and a very good development from GCHQ. Is it active enough? Could it do more? I believe so. How would it do it? One of the criticisms that I have of our discussion of the cyber security Bill that is coming forward is that it virtually ignores the private sector. It brings it in insofar as corporate suppliers of service providers will now be regulated, but the fortunes and the security of the private sector in companies such as JLR, which has had a nasty experience, are ignored.

The Government are now introducing something called a pledge. I do not think that this is the game. We want industry to be much more organised, in the way that banking is. That is to say you have a very close relationship between the regulator, or the Bank, and the banks themselves. It is a relationship of confidence. That does not mean to say that they do not get a nasty rap over the knuckles from the Bank of England from time to time. Nevertheless, this is a co-operative relationship.

In banking, you can imagine that it is pretty close. I do not suppose that all industries need to operate like that, but banking is one that has competition, so they have managed to make it work. It should be looked at as a means of infiltrating into the corporate sphere more earlier advice from the NCSC than is the case at the moment. I would like to see a real change there, which does involve creating structures. Those structures, it seems to me, can and should be funded by the private sector, but the counterpart is that the Government then take them seriously and feed them really good info that they get.

The corporates themselves get information, and the whole system is stronger when the corporates are also feeding in, so it is both necessary and possible to create a situation in which both parties perform better. That is to say that the Government give more information and the corporates take the thing seriously. It is a habit of working and a habit of mind that you need to develop.

My experience of companies is that they are patriotic. Apart from anything else, they stand to lose if they are not well informed. They know that they are vulnerable. I do not think that there is much unwillingness to come forward in order to be more secure. It is very often a practical problem. Companies should be made responsible for the security of their supply chains. That is where it lies. The big ones do have to take care of the smaller ones. The smaller ones need better access. This comes back to the distribution of information. It is possible to make this system cohere while maintaining the separate roles of the parties, and to attain a much higher level of confidence in our level of security.

This was a question that we asked in government about resilience of supply chains. We felt that there was not enough bandwidth or resource being devoted to understanding the supply chains as they relate to the critical risks on the risk register, and that is work that should be done and expedited. I am aware that you have heard from the National Preparedness Commission, which does some of that work, and there is a role for experts to be brought in.

The proof point is that, when we did need a supply chain in terms of ventilators during Covid, the question that went out to business was, “What is the supply chain? What can you do?” That was a success and there was, as Baroness Neville-Jones says, a patriotic response, but we perhaps need to be a little bit more strategic for the next crisis and the critical risks.

There is more guidance and the developments are welcome, but it is very much self-service. It goes to the cultural point that we might come on to discuss in terms of feeling a shared purpose, in that business, private citizens and the Government have a shared responsibility for our resilience.

I noted Rishi Sunak’s comments about the Covid bailouts at the weekend. Without commenting on that, it speaks to the culture that businesses can abrogate responsibility, to some extent, to government, but cyberattacks alone cost the economy, if you believe KPMG, £14.7 billion a year. Together, we have to work out a way of getting to a culture where we prioritise resilience more because it needs to be that shared endeavour. Government could push a lot of their offer, such as the UK Resilience Academy, which offers world-leading training. People come from all over the world to be trained there, but how many of our businesses are aware of that offer and are putting their people through it?

Q196 Are there any particular measures that you think the Government should be taking to support SMEs in particular, whose sustainability might be more precarious than the big multinational companies and that find it harder to afford some obvious resilience measures such cyber insurance? How can or should the Government be focused on helping SMEs?

That is a wonderful question, because they are a significant source of vulnerability. As we hear, not least from their representatives, it is a particularly difficult time for them to find the space, investment or time to do these additional things. The role of insurance is potentially very significant.

For SMEs, thinking about my role with Pool Re, there is very poor take-up of terrorism insurance or cyber insurance. It is between 5% and 7%. If you have a big drive, you might get another per cent. It does feel as if, when you get below a certain size, there should be a standard insurance packet that you receive as an SME, which, incidentally, other companies will have an interest in. In other words, they will have an interest in SMEs functioning, and the Government have an interest in it too.

That would also drive preparedness. If one thinks of preparedness, response and recovery, the one that we tend to neglect is recovery. We do a certain amount around preparedness, and place requirements on businesses to do stuff. We do a lot of work on response, and so do businesses, because they think, “We will respond to this crisis”. Recovery is the thing that really kills you, and it particularly kills you in an SME, when small amounts of money can make a really significant difference. Having insurance set up to support instinctively, with a degree of automaticity, SMEs that have certain categories of risk eventuate would make a material change.

On the question of supply chains, any serious business is getting a deeper and deeper knowledge of their supply chain. Some of that is technology ‑ enabled, because it is easier to map them now. Interestingly, it is easier for outsiders to map them as well. By that, I mean regulators and others. One sees this in, for instance, something such as CFIUS in the United States, or the Investment Security Unit here, which can look down a supply chain and say when they hit something that it does not like.

On the whole, our high-performing providers, such as the food retailers—the supermarkets—do not want the Government coming and advising them how to optimise their supply chain, because not only do they feel that they can do it, but they also say, “We did it for Covid, so we know that we can do this”. Stuart Machin from M&S would probably say, “Even when I had a major cyberattack, there was still food in my stores, I still turned over, and I was still reasonably well performing on the stock exchange”.

There is a thing about thinking about which sectors need to change their game and where the significant vulnerabilities are, and it is possible for the Government to map those out and have a dialogue in those areas, rather than doing something that smears across otherwise profitable and effective businesses that we should leave to get on, because they have a motivation to get their supply chain right.

Can I just check, before Lord Oates comes in with a quick supplementary, that you do not all have to leave on the dot of 12.30? We have three more questions to get through, which we would like to ask you.
Can I say something about SMEs just before we leave?
Yes, but can you just tell me if you can stay after the dot of 12.30?

Yes, I can. There are organisations called CRCs. I am afraid that I have forgotten what those letters stand for, but they are regional organisations for business. They are led at the moment by the police. There is also something called a ROCU, which is avowedly about cybercrime. I do not think that they are very high-powered, but they are a basis on which to build regional dissemination of information to SMEs that do not have time to come to London every other day.

I would like to see a greater spread of guidance and help out to where the SMEs really are. I am pretty clear that, if you convene a meeting for info, people will come. That is one of the things that we should try to do. I have forgotten what the other point was that I was going to make, but do not worry. Regional help is quite important, and perhaps Manchesterism can be the solution here.

Now that we have said that we are going to stay after 12.30, I can say one more thing, which is that one of the features of what banking regulation does with the larger end of the financial industry, because it has a long tail and you can get into many more funds and insurance firms and other things that are not as secure as the big banks, for instance, is that it has picked up and is using methodology from the aviation industry.

CBEST is a testing of the resilience of banks in the round to breaking point. What they end up with is a definition of when McGuinness Bank fails. They do not walk away. They go all the way until the point at which they say, “Then you fail”. That is not a common feature, and there is also not really any blaming.

I want to offer the committee a word that is a feature of resilience work, and especially cyber, and that is “blame-storming”. Something happens and you all gather around and think, “Who is to blame for this? Who got this wrong?”, rather than resolving the issue. I would suggest to you that there is a lot of coverage of the moment of a set of generative AI vulnerability mapping tools, such as Mythos or ChatGPT 5.6, which are really causing concern in business, partly because they do not have access to them, so they do not know what the consequence is.

I note commentary from the National Cyber Security Centre and from the Department for Science, Innovation, and Technology of a plan to have a national look at vulnerability. What they will highlight is notional vulnerabilities on networks. All devices, including the phones in your pocket, your computers at home, your routers and everything else, live with vulnerabilities. All distributed network systems are risk-managed. Unless they are the nuclear firing chain, they are not perfectly secure.

We are at a really interesting moment where, if we are not really hard-minded about how we do this, there is going to be a new tool that illuminates apparent vulnerability, and we are going to blame-storm. The effect is not going to be to improve our security, but to improve our costs and the difficulties that you have in communicating public to private, or central to devolved government, et cetera.
You have remembered your second point.

I have. It is about insurance, which is an important part of the coming picture. Perhaps you are going to talk to the insurance industry. I have two points about that. It is fairly new, and there are still a relatively a small number of companies that have taken out insurance. Part of the problem has been that this is new for the insurance industry, and it has had to develop models. They are not particularly easy to develop, so it is also partly a learning exercise for them.

The time is coming when we do need to think about whether you need to have a licence to drive, and you are only part of the system if you do have insurance. That is quite hard at the moment at the SME level, but, as you go up the line, the whole business of having an insurance policy, which is then closely linked to how you report on your state of security to your shareholders and so on, is all part of a corporate way of behaving.

The insurance companies are also very helpful in getting companies to set up a proper recovery routine, which most companies fail to do in the absence of having an incentive of that kind, which is likely then to make their premium reasonable. There is some very useful progress that can be made on reducing the level of vulnerability by getting people to have blocked some of the risks that they are otherwise not taking notice of.

Q197 Some of this has been covered, but it is related to this illusion on the banking system. You have the stress tests, but you also have the capital adequacy requirements about the capital that has to be held against it. Is there some sort of parallel in terms of the private sector that is critical in a national emergency situation, whereby you had some risk assessment of their supply chains and required them to do certain things on the back of it? That seems to have driven a lot in the banking sector.

What you are saying, in effect, if I am translating that through, is, “What about the regulator?” Of course, the regulator is emerging as an important force in cyber, because the Government are putting the regulators in as a major piece of control machinery. It may well be that, in the course of wider resilience, we will find the regulator appearing in recovery. It is certainly a possibility.

It raises obvious questions, because the Bank is not just a regulator. It is a guide. It is a protector of the industry. It is all sorts of other things, so the relationship with the Bank is much fuller than companies would like to have with a normal regulatory body. It does raise the question of, “Where does the regulator fit in?” It seems to me that, when you do have a serious recovery, it is almost inevitable that the regulator will be part of the outcome, because they are going to be the one that levies a fine, if there is one.

It is partly, as I say, about ensuring that those CNI providers have appropriate governance and auditing structures baked into their systems, which are secure by design, and that they have metrics. The GovAssure framework can be applied to assess where they are in terms of their resilience, and then the question is whether the measures in the cyber security and resilience Bill can be brought to bear to hold people to account.

Paddy’s point about CBEST is a really good one as well, because, under NIS2, there is something about testing the assumptions, whereas, in our Bill, as currently proposed, the plans have to be there, but there is nothing to mandate that they are tested at all.

Baroness Neville-Jones touched on something really important. The Australian Cyber Security Centre was given a role to assist industry and found that it could not do so. The Department of Home Affairs set up a cyber unit to do something about it. Something different has happened here. As I go about, with business, looking at the way in which they are regulated, there are really strong points in Ofcom, Ofgem, Ofwat and the FCA. There are some really significant technology figures operating within that, managing technology risk, some of whom have a workforce that is working with their clients to improve preparedness, response, and recovery.

Hidden beneath the surface of our regulators, there are little strong points that are dealing with the most egregious difficulties that they have by sector. Some sectors have significant egregious difficulties. Some—one thinks of telecommunications—are somewhat more used to this and more part of the collective effort. You do not want to lose sight of that and put all the responsibility on NCSC, but, at the same time, we should reward the regulators for what they are doing behind the scenes.

Q198 Thank you for coming. I am a relatively new Member of the House of Lords, and this is my first committee that I have sat on. I have to say that I am incredibly reassured by your wisdom, expertise and experience, so thank you very much.

I am not so reassured on the whole of society’s awareness. I do not think that they are even aware of the notion of resilience or preparedness. There is the Government’s Prepare website, which is perfectly good but nobody knows about it. What are your views on what we communicate to the whole of society and how we communicate it, especially in this new landscape of influencers? People know an influencer more than they know a national broadcaster. They know the name of that person. What are your views on where we should now go in this, but without following the Denmark model, which is perhaps too extreme?

You have touched on a really significant point about how the Government communicate. One has to communicate where people are receiving. I noted that the Government are not terribly happy using TikTok, when a very significant proportion—more than half—of the British population has a TikTok account. It is madness. They do communicate and they are present there, but, because we have got ourselves all tied up in a knot about the Chinese having access to data, we are somehow not using the main source of information and news that the younger generations have, so we have to balance that somehow. There is a really interesting communications point, and it does feel like Government are behind the curve on that.

I want to claim credit for almost everything. I very much enjoyed being the senior civil servant who faced Oliver Letwin as he did all of his shaking of the system to try to make resilience higher up the agenda when he was Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, and that was a great effort by him. Even he found it difficult to get to the point where we would put out advice of the kind that Sweden, or any of the Nordic or Baltic states, or the Poles, would put out about what is expected of you in your home, or how you should prepare yourself and the rest of it, or, indeed, to have alerting systems through GSM.

We have made progress on that and we do now have alerting systems, but we are not yet at a point when we are talking fully enough about this, and there is a reticence about it: “We must not spook the public”. The public will not thank us the day after a really bad thing happens to them when the Government have not bothered telling them something that the Government know, or have not said it clearly enough. If you want to alienate the public, that is the route to it, so there is a major communication task to be done.

There is then a thing about consistency of communication going down from central government through the locality. Again, I go back to my thing that it cannot be that it is solely or mainly people in uniform who communicate about risk. It cannot only be the Armed Forces, the Ministry of Defence, the police service or the fire service. They must communicate, but everyone must communicate about it.

I do not disagree with the challenges on the channels question. That is absolutely right, but, before that, there absolutely are cultural permissioning and messaging challenges. Having launched the national alert system and the new website, the battles that we had internally to talk about those mechanisms were intense. There is a culture within government and, indeed, wider society that people do not want to hear about these measures.

Whether it is British stoicism, fatalism or exceptionalism, we do not seem to be able to have a national conversation on a sensible level about the level of threats that we face and what we should do about them. That conversation has to be led by the Prime Minister and senior Ministers. Long before it is led by influencers, the media or the Army, it has to come from the top. We have to strike a tone so that Ministers feel able to be honest without fear, frankly, of political attack, because these issues transcend politics.

As a final observation, I find it extraordinary that we live in a country where, last year, there was a poll that suggested 50% of young people would not fight for their country, and yet, at the same time, on our continent, we have young people, some of them conscripted, fighting because their land is being taken, and their livelihoods and their lives are under threat. We have culturally got to a situation where, as a nation, we can indulge in the fantasy that somehow we are immune or naturally resilient, whereas we have to recognise the immediacy of the threats that we face around our immediate neighbourhood, not just in the wider world.

Your question is one of the most important ones facing Government. We have a deadline. That deadline is what NATO says about the threat to us. It put a date on it of 2030. What are we now? 2026. That is not a lot of time to bring about a much more informed public that is also not content but understands and is supportive of what is being said to it. Those are all quite big tasks.

Part of the problem is that not all the work is being done. There is quite a lot of work to do on resilience to put some of it into law. We do not have a resilience Bill. When are we going to have one? Secondly, partly because of that, the Government do not know what they want to say. Are they going to launch into the question of a national service of some kind, or are they going to treat resilience as strengthening the CNI? They absolutely have to have a goal. They have to decide what picture they want to paint. That is a very big question.

The first thing that has to happen, it seems to me, is a dialogue inside the Government. They need to decide what it is it that they are trying to do. Then I agree, absolutely, that it needs to be led by the Prime Minister. If I were doing this, I would start with the threat and involve people other than the Government—people who are respected in our society, including the corporate sector—to talk about the world that we are entering. They can mix it with all sorts of other things that people are interested in, such as AI. Get the yeast going of what the issues are and, out of that, it would then be easier to identify how far to take the debate in things that are more sensitive.

I do think that we need to raise the question of some kind of national service. On the whole, we would be wise to make it voluntary, but there would be takers. I do not think that this is an impossible task, but it is an important and a big one, and it needs to start now. We do not have a lot of time.

I am loath to, but I disagree with Baroness Neville-Jones, and I disagree in this way. In my experience, in particular with business, a threat-based conversation results in them looking at the specificity of the threat and then making a judgment about whether it is likely. A service-based conversation—i.e. “You must continue to deliver your service”—makes them think about being resilient.

I am rather in favour of focusing on what we expect from citizens, businesses and different levels of government in terms of continuity, regardless of the threat or hazard confronted. We will end up, therefore, with common solutions, which may reflect Russian interference, a weather event, civil disobedience or whatever it is that is causing the problem, and a common approach to it. If you do threat-based things, people say, “Yes, that is not very likely and probably will not happen to us”.
I think that you have to have a reason when you want people to do things.

If I can just make a small practical suggestion on this point, it is that the Government, when they go through their exercising programme, publish something around the outcomes of the exercise, and an action plan for how they are going to address the deficiencies that they have found through that exercise. I participated in Operation Mighty Oak, which exercised a national power outage. That was extremely illuminating for where the vulnerabilities would emerge first, and there were huge lessons learned.

I understand that there are obviously things that cannot be said in public around those exercises, but there is much more that could be said, which, again, would contribute to the national conversation , as would hav ing some metrics that people could be held to account to through parliamentary processes.
Thank you. We are going to move on. We have already touched quite a bit on cyber security , but Lady Winterton has a very specific question.

Q199 Thank you all for the fascinating evidence. I am particularly interested because all of you will have worked with a close eye on the legislative framework, if not devising the legislation itself. First of all, I wanted to ask whether you felt that the cyber action plan and the cyber security and resilience Bill were up to addressing the severity of the threats that we face. I am very aware that Baroness Neville-Jones has said that she feels that it ignores the private sector, and Ed thought that it was a bit lacking in terms of accountability, but is there anything else on that?

I also wondered whether you have any sense of whether the legislation that we have in overall resilience at the moment is confused or whether it should be streamlined. Again, Baroness Neville-Jones mentioned the resilience Bill. A question that I always pose is whether we are sure that we need to legislate for everything, given that Governments do have a tendency to over-legislate. Should we be doing more without legislation?

On the cyber Bill and the cyber action plan, I have already said that my main anxiety about the Bill is the fact that the private sector does not appear. What I do not want to do is impose obligations on it for the sake of it. What I want to see happen is much more partnership with it, and information flow both ways. That is my main concern. It should feature in the Bill, and I would like to see some structures created to enable that to happen.

On the cyber action plan, I suspect that my companion is going to disagree with what I am about to say, which is that I have to confess that I find it slightly odd that DSIT finds itself at the centre of regulating and designing the structure. In my view, DSIT is a department that certainly has a big job in promoting science, technology and innovation. I am less convinced that it is the department that should set up and monitor the structures, and deal with the problem of other government departments and the lead government department. It seems to me that it is much more naturally a central government function and would sit more naturally in the Cabinet Office, where I suspect resilience is going to be. I do not think that we are going to now change the locus of the national risk register, the Amber Book, and all the things that go with the foundations of resilience.

Where there is a great deal more policymaking, even if you do not put it into legislation, that needs to be either done by Government or adopted. The National Preparedness Commission has done a great deal of excellent work. Quite a lot of it is pretty oven-ready and it would not be difficult to profit from all of that. The Government can make some quite quick progress in some of the areas, and they certainly do need to, because we need a government resilience agenda, which, at the moment, we do not have. That should be located in the Cabinet Office, alongside government departments. The Cabinet Office should not do everything, but it is inevitable, when you have several departments involved, that you are going to have to have the Cabinet Office there as well to make sure that everybody is participating, coming back to the old problem.

I am not suggesting that we now try to change what is happening in DSIT. That design has been passed by the House of Commons, and we must let it go ahead. It is not where I would have put it. Nevertheless, let us make it work. It is a hard read, but, if you look at the detail, there is a lot of detailed work that has gone into it. People really have thought about it. You can see the homework that is going to have to be done, but it is there, and so I am very reassured by that.
What about the over-legislation part of Lady Winterton’s question?

I was thinking about that. It will depend on how much you think you need to be able to oblige people to do things, as distinct from relying on their voluntary co-operation. I do not think that all detail needs to go into law, but it seems to me that the spine of people’s obligations probably does need to be there. They have to be able to justify these actions to their shareholders, because it involves costs, so there does need to be some legislation. The point about not over-legislating is a really good one, and I am in the same corner on that.

The answer to your core question about whether it is adequate to the severity of the cyber threat is no. I was responsible for the second half of one cyber security strategy in the national cyber security programme, and the first half of another one. It is never a good sign when you have a set of strategies and then you change their name into something else by calling it a plan; it is a bad sign.

I have had to sit in front of the Public Accounts Committee and give an account of how we spent the money, and we spent some of the money well. In terms of the National Cyber Security Centre, we are in a better place than we were previously. We have a focal point and the rest of it. It is not what we hoped it would be, and I fear that it is overmatched by what we are dealing with now. I do not know why we think that the action plan will be any different than the previous three strategies. It may be; it may not be.
It is very detailed.

It needs close interrogation as to whether it will deliver something. The Bill is tactical. It is a globbing together of things. The reality is that what happened to us in this country last year, with multiple major cyber events caused by the ease with which ransomware attackers could attack, but also by the complexity of the systems that were being operated and which needed to be shut down, revealed a very great deal about the problems that we have. I do not see that the Bill is materially going to change that, and I have some misgivings about some aspects of the Bill.
It does not ban ransom payments, but I think that it needs to.

I disagree, but, on the question of overregulation or over-legislation, I would say a couple of things. First, if you run a listed company, you have a fiduciary duty. Something that disrupts your business impacts directly on your duty within the company, and on your interest and your purpose. That is the best driver for getting listed private sector companies, or those privately owned with investor funds within them, to innovate and to do what you require. Additional legislation, in my view, is probably unhelpful in terms of complicating that duty.

In the cyber space, I see a critical role for regulators. One of the most interesting things when you are a senior civil servant and working with regulators, where you want a business in particular, or part of society, to do something, is what I call Al Capone powers. If you are a bank and the Financial Conduct Authority writes to you and says, “It would be really nice if you did X”, you tend to think you might do X.

In particular, if the PRA writes to you, my word, you would think, “Hang on a minute. We would like to remain being a bank. We might take account of their views”. That is far more powerful than clauses in an Act, which then become a subject of an internal self-licking lollipop interaction between those who hold to account and those who are held to account, which is what very often happens.
That is not in the Bill.

No, but we are talking about whether we need more legislation, and I am saying that I do not think that we do. We need to think about what mechanisms exist already, which is a very British thing to do, that allow us to achieve our outcome. They exist, and we want to use those rather than unnecessarily spending a lot of your time putting together things that do not result in an improvement in our resilience. If our rubric is that we wish to be more resilient, you can have any number of Acts, if you like, but, if it does not ultimately result in improved resilience, you are probably making things worse.
The Government are scared to use sector regulation.
Hold on, Lady Neville-Jones. Let Mr de Minckwitz get a word in between the spat here between you two.

I would agree with Paddy that the answer is no. We have spent years now warning about a challenge that is growing. In terms of the capability of AI models, it is growing exponentially . T he barrier to entry in terms of perpetrating cyberattacks is lowered, and the severity and regularity is increasing, so the threat and risk picture is moving to the left pretty rapidly, but the Government’s ambition is moving to the right.

I do not want to be alarmist or shrill, but, in the Government’s own language in the cyber action plan, they are calling for a ‘ radical shift ’ and talking about the scale of the challenge, but then, in the next breath, taking the 2030 target for government organisations to be resilient, which we were criticised for saying was not ambitious enough, and moving it to the right.

Paddy talked about that time to exploit. That has moved from nine months in 2022 to nine hours today, and that is only going to decrease. As Paddy says, there were 204 significant cyberattacks last year, which was more than double from the year before. I do not think that we would bet against that doubling again, so I have to say that we need to take it more seriously.

In terms of whether there is too much regulation or legislation, we should ask ourselves whether the voluntary approach worked. You talk about a fiduciary duty in the private sector, and yet we see cyberattacks costing the economy £14.7 billion a year. The public sector is not, of course, included in the Bill. It is extraordinary for the Government to ask the private sector to be statutorily responsible for a standard that it is not prepared to impose on itself, while, in the same breath in the cyber action plan, admitting that GovAssure and the voluntary approach has not succeeded in the Government and public sector meeting the appropriate standard.

I hope that, in the time that is left in the Bill, it can be toughened up, particularly in terms of the private sector, and both the exercising and the sectoral scope. I note that Andy Burnham, in his op-ed this morning , mentioned the JLR cyberattack . I think we mentioned that earlier this morning, and yet, of course, manufacturing is not in scope at the moment, so there is more that could be done.

Q200 I have the final question. You have been very clear and vocal in your thoughts about some of the changes that we need to make. What one recommendation would you make to the Government about preparedness and resilience? What is the thing that keeps you up at night or the one thing that you want us to take away from your thoughts?
Just one.
I want some firm resilience proposals from the Government. Note that I said “proposals”, not “law”.

I would advocate a fuller role for the insurance industry. The Government make a mistake of thinking that they must do things. While the Treasury may wish to deny it, the Government are the insurer of last resort. We saw that during Covid and, my word, we wasted an enormous amount of money making payments to people who maybe were not even people or did not deserve them, and we did not have a mechanism for doing that.

We are excellent in the insurance sector in this country, dare I say. I always think “world-leading” is an indicator of something that is going to go wrong, so I am not going to use that term. None the less, we are excellent in the insurance sector, and we have a history of innovating, with Pool Reinsurance, around significant breaks in the market. I am not saying necessarily that what we should do is pick up that model and just expand it, but there is a really interesting opportunity to think about how we structure ourselves so that insurance gives us channels, drives preparedness, and builds the resilience, response and recovery industry that we want, which it does when there is assured payment.

We see it in the cyber area. You end up with people who will respond and help you recover. It can drive excellence. It can reinforce small and medium enterprises with assurance through specific insurance. It has a potential, outside government, to give us a structure that gives us a measure of the risk and how resilient we are. It is very difficult for the Government to order that. We have excellent risk management, whichever direction it is, just a couple of miles away.

My recommendation would be for the government to talk about it : to be honest about the threats that we face, and to make a virtue of the measures that we are taking to mitigate and respond to them. As we have said, the only people who can start that national conversation are the senior members of the Government. That would be my one recommendation.

Thank you. We made it to the end of the list of questions. Your evidence has been immensely helpful. Thank you so much. We appreciate your time, including the extra time. We will ponder very carefully everything that you have said, including the things that you disagree about and the things that you agree about. Thank you very much.

sessions.iT: National Resilience
sessions.w: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government; Department for Culture, Media and Sport

segs.tx: National Resilience Committee
C orrected oral evidence
Thursday 9 July 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Baroness Coussins (The Chair); Lord Farmer; Baroness Helic; Baroness Hunter of Auchenreoch; Lord Marland; Baroness Northover; Lord Oates; Baroness Paul of Shepherd’s Bush; Lord Peach; Lord Spellar; Baroness Winterton of Doncaster
Evidence Session No. 18 Heard in Public Questions 1 80 - 1 89
Witnesses

Zainab Agha, Director of Resilience and Recovery, Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government; Jonathan Martin, Director for Project Delivery and Major Events, Department for Culture, Media and Sport.
Examination of witnesses
Zainab Agha and Jonathan Martin.

Q180 Good morning and thank you very much, both of you, for taking the time to come and help us with this important inquiry. I should remind you that this is a public session. It is being broadcast live. You will both receive a transcript of the session in a couple of days’ time. If there are any small inaccuracies that you need to correct, that is the time to do it. If you suddenly think of something you wish you had said, we always welcome supplementary evidence in writing if you think of anything.
We have a lot of questions to ask each of you. Before you give your first answer, could you introduce yourself briefly so that we have that on the record as well?

It seems to me, and it has been reflected in a number of the submissions of written evidence that we have seen so far, that the resilience action plan is seen to be heavy on response and recovery but rather light on planning and preparedness. I wondered whether you agreed with that or could comment on that. What are your views about how preparedness and resilience are linked at national and local levels, including through the regional forums, and how gaps might be bridged between those two things?

Zainab Agha : Thank you to the committee for having us today. I am director for resilience and recovery at the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. The UK resilience action plan sees the local resilience forum in England as a critical part of the resilience system, bringing together local partners and expertise in planning for, responding and recovering from emergencies. It also underlines the importance of partnership working, both with the local resilience tier in England and with devolved Governments in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

MHCLG, so my team, provides the central role in linking the national and local together across the resilience cycle. This means, especially in terms of planning and preparedness, that each local resilience forum in England will have a dedicated resilience adviser, who will work with them on planning and preparedness—for example, making sure that there is development of local risk assessments aligned with the NSRA risks. They will work with lead government departments in bringing together local resilience forums and lead government departments to prepare for certain risks—for example, we have a local-national energy risk planning group—as well as making sure that local partners are part of exercising. As a recent example, Exercise Pegasus, which was an exercise for pandemic preparedness, involved all 38 local resilience forums and was a very useful exercise in strengthening the local and national joins.

We will do the same in response and recovery. Members of my team act as government liaison officers during a response, making sure that there are joins between the local and national and identifying, for example, where you might need sharing of mutual aid across local resilience forums, or indeed where chairs of strategic co-ordinating groups, which are the local response structures set up, need to attend COBRA, again to strengthen the national and local join.

The resilience action plan acknowledges where things need to be strengthened to strengthen that function. There are a number of actions we are taking forward on that, including a new LRF partnership assurance framework and peer review model, which adds to the work that we currently do to assess local capabilities, again from a planning perspective—I can go into more detail on that—as well as improving data sharing and the commitment we have to clarify the role of strategic authorities and mayors as well. There are a number of actions in that and we will continue to deliver those.

Jonathan Martin : I am the director of project delivery and major events in the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, which does not actually include the title “resilience”. That probably is a reflection of the fact that we are not a national security-focused department, but I have responsibility for co-ordinating resilience and incident response within the department as well.

We would echo the points around saying that we have seen a genuine shift evolve within the Cabinet Office and the wider structure to start thinking about some of those social policy departments and get us engaged much more. As a department, we are a very strong convener of positivity across the piece, in terms of saying how we are able to convene our sectors to support this work. A lot of what we are doing is trying to create that kind of national story, with a cohesive and confident narrative within it, which we see in a lot of what we do, and recognising the cultural capital side of things within that. That is where we take this point around not just the response bit, but trying to look at how you strengthen those institutions locally, regionally and nationally as well.

Could I follow up quickly? We have been told, I think by the Cabinet Office, that the Government’s intention is to establish a strategic resilience forum. I wondered, from both your departmental points of view, what that needs to have written into its constitution, if you like, to prevent it becoming another talking shop. If there is going to be a strategic resilience forum, surely it needs to have specific responsibilities and accountabilities. Would you agree with that? What is the way to do it?

Zainab Agha : The commitment to the national strategic forum will add to the number of forums we already have that bring together different partners at different levels. For example, we have quarterly meetings with all the local resilience forum chairs in England. We bring together a wider set of local resilience partners twice a year, which includes voluntary and community sector and businesses. Then we have various other forums at different levels that do the same.

The intention of the national strategic forum is to make sure that we have a forum where we are sharing situational awareness and strengthening that information flow between all the partners that are there in the resilience space. The resilience action plan clearly recognises that our response across the UK is a whole-of-society response. We need to make sure that we are enabling all our wider partners to contribute and support the delivery of resilience forums. That would be the intention of the strategic forum itself. One main aim from my perspective would be to make sure that it recognises the flexibility that we need to be able to respond to emergencies of various different scales. It needs to recognise the principle of subsidiarity, which means that most of the response to emergencies will be led at a local level, where they have the most expertise.

Jonathan Martin : I would echo many of those points. The main thing for us is that shift where this is not a national forum that is dictating to a local level. It is one that is understanding how you can do the interfaces better and connect people in a more effective way. That feels like a positive step forward, as opposed to the kind of central diktat of, “You must do it this way”. How do we improve the pipelines of information? How do we ensure that we are genuinely reaching all the different levels and helping to connect any that are not in the right space for that?

Q181 Following on from your question, Chair, the Cabinet Office also told us that DCMS is engaging with the VCFS—the voluntary, community and faith sector. Can you give us some progress on that, please? What are you doing in terms of funding? Also, what information gathering are you doing for the vulnerable people and those providing assistance?

Jonathan Martin : I will come back a bit more on that. We are producing a VCS protocol, which will help make sure that those linkages are being made with each LRF and the VCS sector. We are working with them to ensure that that information flow goes through, in terms of the importance of getting that right.

At the regional level, those voluntary groups are plugged into the local resilience forum. It is really important that we do that and make sure that we have that clear interface with the formal emergency responders and are not duplicating effort when people are going through. People from the voluntary and community sector are quite often the first to arrive on the scene. It is important that there is an effective use of that skill set and an understanding of what they can and cannot do as we go through. We are keen to make sure they also have a role in national decision-making and are able to feed in really clearly within that.

We are funding to the tune of about £2.5 million. There is a tender under way at the moment to support the civil society infrastructure piece. That funding replaces the grant that is currently held by the Voluntary and Community Sector Emergencies Partnership . . That will be staggered over three years, so it is not huge amounts of money, but it enables those civil society groups to share views and insights and collaborate with government on resilience, to strengthen that knowledge and understanding and the interaction between different voluntary and community groups, and to build on and develop approaches to utilise the role that civil society can play at a local level within that space.

Zainab Agha : Shall I come in on the data sharing? From my engagement with local resilience forums, I understand the challenges that they have in discharging their responsibility to identify and hold data on vulnerable people, as well as maintaining updated lists on voluntary and community members who can be deployed in emergencies, because of the compatibility between different systems and need for data sharing protocols. Cabinet Office last year published guidance for local resilience forums to be able to identify and support vulnerable people, including data-sharing protocols. The Information Commissioner’s guidance has been really helpful in this regard, which makes it clear that data sharing in emergencies, where there is serious risk to life, is completely fine.

Centrally, where we have information on vulnerabilities, we will share with local partners. Recent examples include any information that we held on people who were coming back to the UK as part of the response to hantavirus or who were being repatriated as a result of the Middle East conflict.

MHCLG funding in the past has also been used by local partners to develop tools, which were really great to see. Cumbria LRF in particular has developed a tool using property data to identify vulnerable individuals. In the south-west, LRFs have done something similar, where they have used mapping software to identify vulnerable cohorts as well as deploy resources to them. We are very interested in using those lessons to strengthen the local resiliency as a whole. I have some dedicated team members in my team who are thinking about how we best do that, working closely with Cabinet Office on the tools that it has, so that we can make sure that we are plugging in that information nationally and locally.
Lady Paul wants to go into further detail about the local resilience forums.

Q182 You have answered or alluded to some of these questions, but we would like to dig a little deeper, given the importance of the local resilience forums. I wondered about the long-term funding for the forums and what the role of the trailblazer programme was within that?

There are a couple of other subsidiary questions. We are slightly concerned about, or have some interest in, what the boundaries of the local resilience forums are when you consider potential changes to police forces, issues around, as you have already talked about, maybe further devolvement to local mayors and the different structures that exist in Scotland and the way that they have responded there. We are interested in that. We are also interested in how you mobilise the private sector, particularly around exercising, as there is no obligation to do that.

Then I have a general question, if you do not mind. I realise that there are a number of questions. How would you characterise the level of preparedness among the local resilience forums? We put a lot of emphasis on them and they are a very key component of our response. We would like to get a sense of how prepared you think they are for the variety and the number of events taking place all at the same time.
Zainab Agha : I will take these in turn. Apologies, this will probably be a long answer.
I apologise for how much there was.

Zainab Agha : On funding in particular, in line with the committee’s report from 2021, MHCLG now provides direct multi-year funding to strengthen LRFs’ core co-ordination role. So since 2021-22, MHCLG has provided around £34.5 million to LRFs and has committed to £30 million, so £21 million core capacity funding and £9 million approximately for trailblazers, for the next three years, so LRFs have the certainty to plan. This averages around £180,000 per LRF.

Two and a half million pounds of funding has already gone to the trailblazer programmes that you mentioned. They are part of the stronger LRF programme committed to in the UK resilience action plan, with funding going to Cumbria, Manchester, Northumbria, London and Suffolk. That is testing how we can strengthen leadership accountability and integration with different models. I am very happy to go into some of the emerging learning that is coming from the trailblazers. Our intention is to make sure that that plays into how we strengthen the system as a whole. The MHCLG contribution is part of the overall contributions for LRFs, with LRFs also getting partner contributions and in-kind contributions. That makes up the totality of local resilience forums.

On the boundary question, the strength of local resilience forums, as I see them, is the fact that they bring together local partnerships with local expertise to respond to emergencies that reflect challenges and risks as they apply to areas. As an example, south-west LRFs cover predominantly rural areas with high levels of visitor economy and will be thinking about impacts of severe weather and coastal flooding. North-east LRFs will be thinking about the critical national infrastructure they hold in their patch. The LRF model allows that flexibility. As Jon said earlier, those local insights shape responses.

One strength of our current model is that it is able to flex to respond to the scale of the emergency. For example, the recent outbreak of MenB involved Kent LRF only. For the heat-related emergency that we had last month—you could say we are back again, although not quite emergency level yet in technical terms—we were able to convene affected LRFs in a response co-ordinating group, so bringing together a different configuration of LRFs. In some cases, such as the response to the Middle East, we brought together all LRFs to share situational awareness. The current model helps to flex and scale up.

In the UK resilience action plan, we have already committed to clarifying the role of strategic authorities and mayors. We are engaging with strategic authorities, taking learning from the model that is there in Scotland and models that exist in other countries, such as the US and Finland, to make sure that we are strengthening and clarifying that. That supports the regional lens.

We are mainstreaming resilience considerations into reviews, including the review of police boundaries, keeping in mind, of course, that we also have changes to local government as a result of local government reorganisation. There have been changes to integrated care board boundaries as well. At the moment, the geography is no less creative. As an example, Cumbria is one LRF where there is a broad degree of alignment between council, police and fire geographies. In contrast, Thames Valley LRF, I believe, encompasses one police, three FRSs and 14 local authorities. Already we are talking about a very different geographical pattern as far as LRFs are concerned.

You asked about whether we include private sector in exercising. Local resilience forums will include private sector in some of the training and exercising. There are some good examples in London and elsewhere. Dorset LRF does the same in some of the responses to its risks. There is more that we could do to make sure that there is more consistency in that approach. That is something that we work with lead government departments on, as well as making sure that, when we are engaged with local areas, that is something that is there.

On the level of preparedness, we have different processes to assure ourselves of that, which include doing seasonal preparedness twice a year. That is basically where LRFs self-assess themselves against their level of preparedness. We work with Cabinet Office on local capability assessments, which look at the level of preparedness that is held at local level, aligned with NSRA risks and national capabilities. As I said, we will be rolling out this year a local partnership assurance framework with a peer review protocol, which is designed so that we are bringing challenge into the system and building on the expertise the sector holds itself to assess that.

Jonathan Martin : That was a long set of questions. Our main engagement point in all this is the voluntary and community sector and ensuring that they are woven into that local resilience forum route. We have some really good examples, including around Southport and other areas, where they have done a really good job in doing that. We tend to find that, where they are most used to engaging in crisis and being able to respond, they are much better at engaging and knowing who their local responders are. We only tend to step in at those points where it is not working or there is something in the response that needs a bit of clarity in terms of how the voluntary sector is engaging.

We do a little bit as well around understanding what the skill set is. You cannot predict exactly what skill set a volunteer is going to turn up with. The Red Cross and others that you will have heard of bring a wide variety of everything from search and rescue through to managing support mechanisms effectively and crowd management for local events and engagement. For us, that weaving in is the really significant bit. That is certainly the bit that we are looking to make sure happens much more systemically, including through the protocol that I mentioned earlier.

Q183 My question is primarily focused on you, Mr Martin. We heard evidence from the Finnish ambassador that they have 50,000 shelters for a population of around 5 million, and many of those are in sports facilities. Obviously they are on the real front line. I wondered whether you could tell us a little bit about how the Government go about recruiting cultural and sporting organisations to provide a network of community hubs and emergency information centres and shelters.

Jonathan Martin : I should be open at the start that we do not actively go and recruit those organisations in. The reason we do not is that they are quite a fragmented and diverse group, so there is no overarching network to pull them together. The other reality is that it is that local-level engagement that is probably quite crucial on there. The local planners will know where their cultural infrastructure is much better than I would and how to make use of that. We will come in and intervene if there is a problem or challenge within that. We are working across those in the implementation of new legislation, such as Martyn’s law, to make sure that they are fully engaged and aware of what the responsibility is. We do not have a direct role in recruiting.

The evacuation and shelter bit is a policy area owned by the Cabinet Office and I know that it is engaging across the VCS and others, looking at some of this area. That process is something where we should be focusing on that local tier to be able to understand and connect all the different local areas and spaces that can provide support. We saw a lot of these institutions stepping forward during Covid and being vaccination centres. We saw an amazing range of activities that libraries provided in terms of response, in getting key worker status during the pandemic but also looking at how they can support people to get on the NHS app and at a much wider group of responsibilities, as well as that cultural integration and being a first port of call for a lot of people coming into the country. We are keen to ensure that we can support that, but we do not have an overarching programme to recruit those individual organisations.
Do you, the Cabinet Office or somebody in government have sight of where all those shelters are and who is providing them?
Jonathan Martin : I do not at the moment. The Cabinet Office may do. I might have to come back to you on that one.

Zainab Agha : Shall I come in and add something from a local perspective? This is a good example of the work my teams do on the national and local join in preparedness. My teams will work with LRFs to encourage the identification of rest centres and shelters. A good example of that is the work that Wiltshire and Swindon LRF has done, which has set up a protocol for emergency information centres across the country in the event of a national power outage. It has done that thinking on the back of some innovation funding provided by the department. That is an example of that. As Jon said, given Cabinet Office’s role in being the lead government department for mass evacuations, we will identify where there are concerns at a local level that cannot be addressed at that level and escalate that to Cabinet Office to see whether there is more national support needed.

Q184 Sticking with the broad theme of command and control, how do you feel the local government system, which you have outlined very clearly this morning, and the central government responsibilities come together? We have heard that there is quite a lot of good practice in the devolved Administrations, whereas in England, generally, there is not as clear a regional structure. For example, we are not just dealing here with climate and other emergencies. We are also talking about national emergencies.

Specifically, you talked about Exercise Pegasus. Without trying to use military language, how would you describe Exercise Pegasus and beyond as a means of stress testing the whole command and control system, including bringing in the military and the blue-light services? Is that beyond the scope of the LRFs? How would you see that being commanded and controlled in the event of a genuine national emergency?

Zainab Agha : It is what Jon was talking about at the start and what the UK resilience action plan underlines. The system that we have in the UK is around a whole-of-society resilience approach and making sure that we are enabling and empowering all partners to participate and work collaboratively to deliver the plan for, respond to and recover from emergencies.

As I said before, one of the strengths of the local resilience tier in England is the fact that we can flex to the scale of various different emergencies, whether they are very localised, whether we need different configurations of local authorities to come together to respond, or indeed whether they are national emergencies.

We do this across the resilience cycle. We have various different forums, as mentioned before, where we will use and share situational awareness with local partners. By that, I mean local partners in the widest sense. We will have the mechanisms in place to make sure that we are engaging with each LRF to identify where there needs to be escalation to a lead government department, such as DHSC, which leads on pandemic preparedness, making sure that we are joining the local and national in any training and exercising, and indeed to identify whether there are things that need to be done at the Cabinet Office level.

Scotland has a model that formally has regional structures, but builds on the local into the regional and then national. The work we are doing, which is committed to in the resilience action plan, is to think about the role of strategic authorities and mayors in providing it. We are thinking about how we strengthen and clarify that and whether that provides an additional regional lens to our current structures. Flexibility and making sure that we can respond to the range of impacts that can happen and risks that can materialise is important. The strength of the system is its ability to respond to all of those.

Jonathan Martin : I would only add a little bit on the value that we derived from having VCSEP and the Red Cross with us at a national level during the op Pegasus, so that we can reach in and understand what their capability is. That ability to, at each level, have somebody who genuinely understands that sector and how the linkages can be made is really significant.

A lot of what we are trying to understand within the department in an event of a crisis or a pandemic is the impact that it has on a group of our sectors that are particularly vulnerable to areas where people cannot gather, given that that is an awful lot of what DCMS’s core requirements are. We are gathering data in order to understand the impact and what effect it is immediately having on things such as tourism bookings all the way through to attendance at various major events as they are going through. There is a bit about how you take action to ensure that all that information is fed in and that you can take sensible decisions at that point, with the right people in the room, which is significant.

Q185 In no way do I underestimate the importance of having structures, and I congratulate you on the work that you have outlined and what you are doing on that. In order to engage those groups, and indeed individuals and the wider public, there has to be a narrative that tells them why this matters. Why is it important? Why should these organisations be playing a role? Is this not a far-off problem? We have seen how, therefore, that leads to levels of inactivity, which we then have to work very fast to retrofit.

What consistent messages are being put out to all these organisations as to why we are doing that? It is not the what, but the why. Where in central government is that core point where they are pulling this together by getting on to opinion-formers and by putting in very straightforward narrative terms to the general public why it is important and why they also need to be engaged and involved? Where is the centre of gravity for all this in government? It seems very difficult to detect.

Zainab Agha : I would say, and I think Jon would agree, that it is Cabinet Office that leads on any plans on public narrative and public engagement. That is something that I can say that it is definitely thinking about quite actively. From a local perspective, we will make sure that we are amplifying those messages. Local partners will have their own communication channels that are trusted by the communities that they exist in.

In terms of engagement with local resilience forums, we are very clear collectively on the risks that the UK is facing and what we need to do collectively to respond to that, as well as preparing for any specific risks, where we work very closely with lead government departments, as well as LRFs, to make sure that those are understood, using the various different forums that we have. In terms of whether I have a level of confidence that we are sharing as much information as possible on the wider context in which we are operating, as well as the narrative and why certain risks need to be prioritised or focused on, I can say yes. It is Cabinet Office that leads and oversees some of that, in terms of both communications and any public-level engagement.
Offices cannot speak. Who should we invite before this committee to address us to reassure us and explain to us what they are doing?
Zainab Agha : You might get those answers from people who you have already invited who might be attending in the future.

Jonathan Martin : I would echo some of that. I might come on to this later. Some of the commemorative events that we engage in, and indeed a lot of what DCMS engages on, are around some of those less formal structures and how you engage young people in particular. It is not necessarily, “A government spokesman says…” As you say, the comms narrative needs to be quite nuanced and careful.

A lot of what we find, through incidents such as Southport and other things, is the desire for trusted voices to come with a clear narrative at that point. Both of our departments, in terms of the voluntary and community sector and the faith groups as well, need to find people who are willing and able, without us saying exactly what they should say, to speak with an authenticity that connects with people in a way that is more significant. I get slightly nervous about one single overarching, “Everybody must do this”, and think a bit more around how we find lots of different ways of reinforcing that message at a local and regional level to get it to people who actually listen, as opposed to being just talked at.

Q186 Compared with other countries, we seem to have a much higher degree of instability in local government structures, with what seems to be never-ending local government reorganisation. What impact does that have on the effectiveness of our resilience? Could you address that?

Zainab Agha : I keep going back to the strengths of local resilience forums, but one of their strengths is the ability to bring together various different partnerships at a local level in response structures. They are, by their very nature, multi-agency partnerships. That strength, in the context of the fact that each of those partners will be delivering a wider set of responsibilities, and where there will be reform targeted at them, means that it is very important that we are consistently thinking about the impact on resilience as a whole of those changes.

In terms of local government reorganisation, my teams are making sure that we have guidance in place so that we can make sure that local unitary authorities are very clear on their responsibilities on resilience under the Civil Contingencies Act. We are also following the Grenfell inquiry recommendation and working with the local government organisation Solace and the UK Resilience Academy to make sure that we have training in place for local authorities, local authority chief execs and wider local authority officials on resilience, so that we are underlining the importance of that.

As I said, on the changes that relate to police boundaries, we are already thinking about the role of strategic authorities, engaging with them and engaging with various other partners to make sure that we are clarifying and strengthening those. That is the commitment in the UK resilience action plan.

Jonathan Martin : From my experience working in Lancashire and other parts of the country, the structures may move, but a lot of those individuals know each other and interact with each other regularly, particularly in the policing world and some of the other blue-light services. That connecting point can survive quite a degree of administrative restructuring around the edges of it. That does not mean that it is not important to make sure, as Zainab set out, that there is a structure to support people in that process.
The public are not always as familiar with these constant changes. What impact does that have on them?

Jonathan Martin : I suppose it is at what point it impinges on the local consciousness. A lot of people in that set of circumstances just want the response to be in the right place at the right time. When you connect with those communities, you tend to go down the levels through to understanding the local council engagement officers or things like that, where we have them. Tower Hamlets is a really good example. It has a very good set of engagement officers who can go out and engage at whatever level with the public on that side. Whatever structures that sit above them, it is just getting the right messages through to them.

Zainab Agha : Can I supplement that? One thing that the LRF stronger trailblazer programme that I spoke about is testing with the trailblazer funding is how we strengthen accountability and make sure that that is as clearly communicated as possible.
Q187 How large is your team working on local resilience forums?
Zainab Agha : We are collectively, I think, at the moment 77.
Is that at the centre?
Zainab Agha : My teams are spread across England, including three place-based teams, which sit across and support LRFs. We are 77 overall. We are very distributed across the piece.
That is everybody who would be employed to be working on local resilience forums across the country.
Zainab Agha : They are working on the link between national lead government departments, Cabinet Office and local resilience forums.
Do you have a resilience headcount?

Jonathan Martin : I have a very small resilience-focused team of seven. We have some other areas, for example broadcast resilience and the voluntary and community sector piece, but we are very small in numbers across the department.

Q188 Thank you both very much for coming. You have slightly touched on this. We have heard from lots of witnesses about the changing media landscape and the proliferation of outlets, or platforms as they are called now. There is a lot of disinformation, misinformation and mischief-making, and it can be downright dangerous. We heard from the Cabinet Office about its local media action plans, which it said would address these concerns. I would like to know how they are being implemented. How is it going?

Jonathan Martin : The local media action plan was published in March. That is aimed at ensuring a healthy and plural local media for the benefit of communities across the UK. Core to that is getting that level of trust locally, so that people trust that local journalism side and so that it directly reports, as you said, on some of the institutions.
